quote: Use font sizes that most people can read easily.
rule: Body text must be set at a size people can read comfortably at normal viewing distance.

quote: Follow the recommended default and minimum text sizes for each platform
rule: Text sizes follow Apple's per-platform default and floor, on a Mac 13 pt default and never below 10 pt.

quote: If you use a custom font with a thin weight, aim for larger than the recommended sizes
rule: A typeface with a thin stroke is set larger than the usual minimum so it stays readable.

quote: Test legibility in different contexts.
rule: Check that every piece of text stays readable in each place and platform it appears, and fix any that tests as hard to read.

quote: In general, avoid light font weights.
rule: Interface text uses regular or heavier weights, not ultralight, thin or light ones.

quote: Adjust font weight, size, and color as needed to emphasize important information
rule: Weight, size and colour of text are varied to show which information matters most.

quote: Be sure to maintain the relative hierarchy and visual distinction of text elements when people adjust text sizes.
rule: When the person changes the text or interface size, headings must still read as more prominent than body text and secondary text as less.

quote: Minimize the number of typefaces you use, even in a highly customized interface.
rule: Keep the number of distinct typefaces in an interface small.

quote: Prioritize important content when responding to text-size changes.
rule: A larger text setting should enlarge the content people read first (document text, messages) and may leave chrome such as tab titles at their size.

quote: Consider using the built-in text styles.
rule: Pick text sizes from a fixed set of named styles (body, headline and so on) rather than ad hoc sizes.

quote: Modify the built-in text styles if necessary.
rule: Derive extra levels by adjusting a named style's weight or leading rather than inventing a new style.

quote: If you need to display three or more lines of text, avoid tight leading even in areas where height is limited.
rule: Text of three lines or more never uses reduced line spacing.

quote: don’t embed system fonts in your app or game.
rule: Reach Apple's system fonts through the Font.Design constants instead of bundling them.

quote: If necessary, adjust tracking in interface mockups.
rule: Mockups of system-font text apply the per-size tracking values to match the running app.

quote: Make sure custom fonts are legible.
rule: A custom typeface respects the recommended minimum sizes for its styles and weights.

quote: Implement accessibility features for custom fonts.
rule: Text drawn in an app's own font must still respond to the person's text-size and bold-text settings, or the app offers its own text-size control.

quote: Make sure your app’s layout adapts to all font sizes.
rule: Check every screen at the smallest and largest text or interface size and confirm the layout still fits and reads well.

quote: Increase the size of meaningful interface icons as font size increases.
rule: Icons that carry information grow along with the text when the person picks a larger size.

quote: Keep text truncation to a minimum as font size increases.
rule: At the largest text size a view should still show about as much useful text as at the largest standard size, wrapping rather than cutting it off.

quote: Avoid truncating text in scrollable regions unless people can open a separate view to read the rest of the content.
rule: Inside a scrolling area, text is cut short only when the full text can be opened elsewhere.

quote: Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes.
rule: When large text crowds a row, move secondary items such as timestamps and icons below the text instead of beside it.

quote: Reduce the number of columns when the font size increases to avoid truncation and enhance readability.
rule: Multi-column text drops to fewer columns as the text size grows.

quote: Maintain a consistent information hierarchy regardless of the current font size.
rule: Primary elements stay at the top of a view whatever the text size, so their position never changes with scaling.

quote: When necessary, use dynamic system font variants to match the text in standard controls.
rule: On a Mac, custom text that sits beside standard controls uses the matching system font variant (control content, label, menu, menu bar, message, palette, title bar, tooltip, user document, fixed-pitch, bold, system).

quote: In general, prefer 2D text.
rule: Readable text in space has little or no depth.

quote: Make sure text looks good and remains legible when people scale it.
rule: Spatial text is tested for legibility at several scales.

quote: Maximize the contrast between text and the background of its container.
rule: Spatial text keeps strong contrast against its container material.

quote: If you need to display text that’s not on a background, consider making it bold to improve legibility.
rule: Text floating without a surface is set bold rather than given a shadow.

quote: Keep text facing people as much as possible.
rule: Labels anchored to 3D objects rotate to face the wearer.

quote: The emphasized weights can be medium, semibold, bold, or heavy.
rule: An emphasized variant of a text style is one of four heavier weights given per style.

quote: iOS, iPadOS Dynamic Type sizes
rule: iPhone and iPad text styles have fixed sizes and leading for each of seven text-size settings (Body is 17 pt at the default).

section: iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes
quote: iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes
rule: iPhone and iPad text styles have five further accessibility sizes, AX1 to AX5.

quote: macOS built-in text styles
rule: Mac text styles run from Large Title 26 pt down to Caption 10 pt, with Body and Headline at 13 pt.

quote: tvOS built-in text styles
rule: Apple TV text styles run from Title 1 76 pt to Caption 2 23 pt.

quote: watchOS Dynamic Type sizes
rule: Watch text styles have sizes for each text-size setting and case size.

quote: watchOS larger accessibility type sizes
rule: Watch text styles have three further accessibility sizes.

quote: iOS, iPadOS, visionOS tracking values
rule: SF Pro, SF Pro Rounded and New York take a set letter-spacing per point size on these devices.

quote: macOS tracking values
rule: On a Mac, SF Pro takes a set letter-spacing per point size (for example -6/1000 em at 13 pt).

quote: tvOS tracking values
rule: Apple TV text takes a set letter-spacing per point size.

quote: watchOS tracking values
rule: SF Compact and SF Compact Rounded take a set letter-spacing per point size on the watch.

quote: Use alerts sparingly.
rule: Show a modal alert only when the person must know something or decide something now; every alert must carry essential content and useful actions.

quote: Avoid using an alert merely to provide information.
rule: News that needs no decision goes in the relevant place in the window (a status indicator the person can open for detail), not in an alert.

quote: Avoid displaying alerts for common, undoable actions, even when they’re destructive.
rule: Deleting an item the person can undo, such as a file or a message, happens without a confirmation alert.

quote: when people take an uncommon destructive action that they can’t undo, it’s important to display an alert
rule: A rare destructive action that cannot be undone asks for confirmation in an alert before it runs.

quote: Avoid showing an alert when your app starts.
rule: No alert appears at launch; news for the person at start-up is placed where they can find it without being interrupted.

quote: you could show cached or placeholder data and a nonintrusive label that describes the problem.
rule: A problem found at start-up, such as no network, is shown as a quiet label next to cached or placeholder content rather than an alert.

quote: alerts display a title, optional informative text, and up to three buttons.
rule: An alert has a title, optional explanatory text and no more than three buttons.

quote: In all alert copy, be direct, and use a neutral, approachable tone.
rule: Alert text states the problem plainly and calmly, neither blaming the person nor playing down how serious it is.

quote: Write a title that clearly and succinctly describes the situation.
rule: The alert title says what happened, where and why, specifically and briefly.

quote: Avoid writing a title that doesn’t convey useful information — like “Error” or “Error 329347 occurred”
rule: An alert title is never a bare 'Error' or an error code.

quote: avoid overly long titles that wrap to more than two lines.
rule: An alert title fits in at most two lines.

quote: If the title is a complete sentence, use sentence-style capitalization and appropriate ending punctuation.
rule: A full-sentence alert title is sentence-case with a closing full stop; a fragment title is title-case with no closing punctuation.

quote: Include informative text only if it adds value.
rule: Add explanatory text under the alert title only when it tells the person something the title does not.

quote: keep it as short as possible, using complete sentences, sentence-style capitalization, and appropriate punctuation.
rule: Explanatory alert text is brief, in full sentences, sentence-case and punctuated.

quote: Avoid explaining alert buttons.
rule: Alert text does not describe what each button does; the button titles carry that.

quote: refer to a button using its exact title without quotes.
rule: When alert text must point to a button, it says 'choose' and names the button by its exact title, unquoted.

quote: If supported, include a text field only if you need people’s input to resolve the situation.
rule: An alert holds a text field only when the person's input is needed to resolve it, such as a password.

quote: Create succinct, logical button titles.
rule: Alert buttons are titled with one or two words naming their result, verbs tied to the alert text, e.g. 'Reply' or 'Ignore'.

quote: In informational alerts only, you can use “OK” for acceptance, avoiding “Yes” and “No.”
rule: 'OK' is used only in alerts that just inform; 'Yes' and 'No' are never button titles.

quote: Always use “Cancel” to title a button that cancels the alert’s action.
rule: The button that abandons the alert's action is titled exactly 'Cancel'.

quote: As with all button titles, use sentence-style capitalization and no ending punctuation.
rule: Button titles are sentence-case and end without punctuation.

quote: Avoid using OK as the default button title unless the alert is purely informational.
rule: In an alert that confirms an action, the default button names the action ('Erase', 'Delete', 'Convert') instead of 'OK'.

quote: Place buttons where people expect.
rule: In a row of alert buttons the most likely choice sits at the trailing end; in a vertical stack it sits at the top.

quote: Always place the default button on the trailing side of a row or at the top of a stack.
rule: The default button is always the trailing button in a row, or the top one in a stack.

quote: Cancel buttons are typically on the leading side of a row or at the bottom of a stack.
rule: Cancel sits at the leading end of a row of buttons, or at the bottom of a stack.

quote: Use the destructive style to identify a button that performs a destructive action people didn’t deliberately choose.
rule: Mark a button as destructive only when its destruction is not what the person asked for; the confirm button of a deliberately chosen action like Empty Trash stays unmarked.

quote: If there’s a destructive action, include a Cancel button to give people a clear, safe way to avoid the action.
rule: Every alert that offers a destructive action also has a Cancel button.

quote: Note that you don’t want to make a Cancel button the default button.
rule: Cancel is never the default button of an alert.

quote: encourage people to read an alert and not just automatically press Return to dismiss it, avoid making any button the default button
rule: When the person should read the alert before answering, give it no default button so Return does nothing.

quote: if you must display an alert with a single button that’s also the default, use a Done button, not a Cancel button.
rule: A one-button alert whose button is the default titles it 'Done', not 'Cancel'.

quote: Provide alternative ways to cancel an alert when it makes sense.
rule: Esc cancels an open alert, and on a Mac Command-Period does too, in addition to its Cancel button.

quote: Exit to the Home Screen
rule: On iPhone and iPad going to the Home Screen cancels an alert, and on Apple TV the remote's Menu button does.

quote: Use an action sheet — not an alert — to offer choices related to an intentional action.
rule: Choices that follow a deliberate action are offered in an action sheet rather than an alert.

quote: When possible, avoid displaying an alert that scrolls.
rule: Alert text is kept short enough that the alert does not scroll at large text sizes.

quote: Configure repeating alerts to let people suppress subsequent occurrences of the same alert.
rule: An alert that can recur offers a 'do not show again' checkbox.

quote: Append a custom view if it’s necessary to provide additional information
rule: An alert may carry an extra content area only when it needs to show information the text cannot.

quote: Include a Help button that opens your help documentation
rule: An alert can include a Help button that opens the relevant help page.

quote: Use a caution symbol sparingly.
rule: Reserve the warning sign in an alert for cases that truly need extra attention, such as possible unexpected loss of data.

quote: Don’t use the symbol for tasks whose only purpose is to overwrite or remove data, such as a save or empty trash.
rule: An alert confirming an action whose whole purpose is to overwrite or remove data (Save over, Empty Trash) carries no warning sign.

quote: create a view that has a maximum height of 154 pt and a 16-pt corner radius.
rule: A visionOS alert accessory view is at most 154 pt tall with 16 pt rounded corners.

quote: Add motion purposefully, supporting the experience without overshadowing it.
rule: Animate only where the movement tells the person something; no decorative or excessive animation.

quote: Make motion optional.
rule: No information is conveyed by animation alone, and the app works fully with reduced motion turned on.

quote: supplement visual feedback by also using alternatives like haptics and audio to communicate.
rule: Back up animated feedback with another channel, such as a sound or a text change, where it carries meaning.

quote: Strive for realistic feedback motion that follows people’s gestures and expectations.
rule: Motion follows the person's action: something revealed by sliding down is dismissed by sliding back up, not sideways.

quote: Aim for brevity and precision in feedback animations.
rule: Feedback animations are short and tied exactly to the action they confirm.

quote: In apps, generally avoid adding motion to UI interactions that occur frequently.
rule: Controls the person uses many times a session do not animate on each use.

quote: Let people cancel motion.
rule: Input is never blocked until an animation ends; the person can act or skip it at once.

quote: Consider using animated symbols where it makes sense.
rule: Symbols may be animated with SF Symbols animation effects.

quote: Make sure your game’s motion looks great by default on each platform you support.
rule: A game's default graphics settings hold a steady 30 to 60 fps on each platform.

quote: Let people customize the visual experience of your game to optimize performance or battery life.
rule: A game offers settings trading visual quality for performance or battery.

quote: As much as possible, avoid displaying motion at the edges of a person’s field of view.
rule: No motion in the wearer's peripheral vision.

quote: Help people remain comfortable when showing the movement of large virtual objects.
rule: Large moving objects are made more translucent or lower in contrast.

quote: consider also keeping a window’s size fairly small.
rule: Keep movable spatial windows fairly small to avoid discomfort.

quote: Consider using fades when you need to relocate an object.
rule: Relocate objects by fading out and in rather than moving them visibly.

quote: In general, avoid letting people rotate a virtual world.
rule: Do not rotate the virtual world; change direction instantly behind a fade.

quote: Consider giving people a stationary frame of reference.
rule: Keep moving content inside a frame that stays still.

quote: Avoid showing objects that oscillate in a sustained way.
rule: No sustained oscillation, especially near 0.2 Hz.

quote: Let your app’s tasks inform the types of help people might need.
rule: Match help to the task: a short inline note for a one- or two-step task, a guided walkthrough for a long multistep one.

quote: directly relate the help you provide to the precise action or task people are doing right now
rule: Help shown in the interface concerns the action the person is doing at that moment.

quote: make it easy for people to dismiss or avoid the help if they don’t need it.
rule: Every piece of in-app help can be closed or skipped in one step.

quote: Use relevant and consistent language and images in your help content.
rule: Help text and pictures match the input device and context the person is actually using.

quote: don’t write copy that tells people to click a button on an iPhone or tap a menu item on a Mac.
rule: Help copy uses the platform's interaction verbs: on the desktop, 'click' and 'choose', never 'tap'.

quote: Make sure all help content is inclusive.
rule: Help content follows inclusive-language guidance.

quote: Avoid bloating your help content by explaining how standard components or patterns work.
rule: Help explains what a standard control does in this app, not how such controls work in general.

quote: orient people quickly, preferring animation or graphics to educate instead of a lengthy description.
rule: A control or input method unique to the app is introduced briefly with a picture or short demo rather than long text.

quote: Use the most appropriate tip type for your app’s user interface.
rule: Use a popover tip to keep the content flow, an inline tip when nearby content must stay visible, pointing at a control when the tip is about it.

quote: Use tips for simple features.
rule: A tip covers only a feature done in three actions or fewer.

quote: Make tips short, actionable, and engaging.
rule: A tip is one or two sentences of direct, action-led text saying what the feature does and how to use it.

quote: avoid including content that’s promotional or related to a different feature or user flow.
rule: Tips never advertise or sell, and never cover a feature other than the one in front of the person.

quote: Define rules to help ensure your tips reach the intended audience.
rule: Show a tip only to people who have not used the feature yet and could benefit from it.

quote: When your app has more than one tip, set the display frequency so tips display at a reasonable cadence
rule: With several tips, show at most one per interval, such as one a day.

quote: If there’s an image or symbol that people associate with the feature, consider including it in the tip, and prefer the filled variant.
rule: A tip may show the feature's symbol, in its filled form.

quote: avoid repeating the same image in both the tip and the UI.
rule: A tip attached to a pictured control does not repeat that picture.

quote: Use buttons to direct people to information or options.
rule: A tip can carry a button that opens the feature's settings or further reading.

quote: Describe only the control that people indicate interest in.
rule: A tooltip describes only the control under the pointer, not its neighbours or the wider task.

quote: Explain the action or task the control initiates.
rule: A tooltip says what the control does, ideally starting with a verb, e.g. 'Restore default settings'.

quote: In general, avoid repeating a control’s name in its tooltip.
rule: A tooltip does not restate the control's visible name.

quote: Be brief.
rule: A tooltip stays within about 60 to 75 characters, allowing for growth in translation.

quote: consider using a sentence fragment and omitting articles.
rule: Tooltip text may be a fragment without articles to stay short.

quote: If you need a lot of text to describe a control, consider simplifying your interface design.
rule: A control that needs a long tooltip is a sign the control should be redesigned.

quote: Use sentence case.
rule: Tooltips are written in sentence case.

quote: If you write complete sentences, omit ending punctuation unless it’s required to be consistent with your app’s style.
rule: Tooltips end without a full stop, even when they are whole sentences, unless the app's style says otherwise.

quote: Consider offering context-sensitive tooltips.
rule: A control's tooltip can change with its state, e.g. different text when on and off.

quote: Prefer the system-provided edit menu.
rule: Editing commands appear in the standard edit menu with its usual contents, never in a separate custom menu repeating them.

quote: Let people reveal an edit menu using the system-defined interactions they already know.
rule: The edit (context) menu opens with the platform's usual gesture, a secondary click on the desktop, never a custom interaction.

quote: Offer commands that are relevant in the current context, removing or dimming commands that don’t apply.
rule: Edit commands that cannot act are hidden or disabled: no Cut or Copy without a selection, no Paste with an empty clipboard.

quote: List custom commands near relevant system-provided ones.
rule: App-specific edit commands sit next to the standard commands they relate to, e.g. custom formatting after the standard formatting group.

quote: Avoid overwhelming people with too many custom commands.
rule: Keep the number of app-specific commands in the edit menu small.

quote: When it makes sense, let people select and copy noneditable text.
rule: Read-only content text, such as captions and statuses, can be selected and copied.

quote: In general, let people copy content text, but not control labels.
rule: Labels on controls are not selectable; content text is.

quote: Support undo and redo when possible.
rule: Edit menu actions run without confirmation and every one of them can be undone and redone.

quote: In general, avoid implementing other controls that perform the same functions as edit menu items.
rule: Do not add on-screen buttons for Cut, Copy, Paste and the like; the edit menu and standard shortcuts cover them.

quote: Differentiate different types of deletion commands when necessary.
rule: Keep Delete (removes, same as the Delete key) and Cut (copies to the clipboard, then removes) as distinct commands.

quote: Create short labels for custom commands.
rule: Custom edit commands are labelled with a verb or short verb phrase.

quote: Ensure your edit menu works well in both styles.
rule: The edit menu works in both the horizontal touch style and the vertical pointer style.

quote: Adjust an edit menu’s placement, if necessary.
rule: Move the touch edit menu so it does not cover important content.

quote: To learn about the order of items in a macOS app’s Edit menu, see Edit menu.
rule: On a Mac, the menu-bar Edit menu lists its items in Apple's standard Edit menu order.

quote: Use a text field to request a small amount of information, such as a name or an email address.
rule: Use a single-line field for short entries like a name or address; longer text goes in a multi-line text view.

quote: Show a hint in a text field to help communicate its purpose.
rule: An empty field may show placeholder text naming what to enter, e.g. 'Email'.

quote: it can also be useful to include a separate label describing the field to remind people of its purpose.
rule: Because placeholder text vanishes on typing, give the field a separate visible label too.

quote: Use secure text fields to hide private data.
rule: Passwords and other secrets are entered in a field that masks the characters.

quote: To the extent possible, match the size of a text field to the quantity of anticipated text.
rule: A field's width reflects how much text it expects, e.g. a postcode field is narrower than a street field.

quote: Evenly space multiple text fields.
rule: Space several fields evenly so each label clearly belongs to its field.

quote: Stack multiple text fields vertically when possible, and use consistent widths to create a more organized layout.
rule: Stack fields in a column and give related fields the same width.

quote: Ensure that tabbing between multiple fields flows as people expect.
rule: Tab moves focus between fields in reading order.

quote: Validate fields when it makes sense.
rule: A field that accepts only certain input (for example digits) tells the person when they enter something else.

quote: when entering an email address, it’s best to validate when people switch to another field
rule: Validate an email address when focus leaves the field; validate a new user name or password before focus is allowed to leave.

quote: Use a number formatter to help with numeric data.
rule: Numeric fields accept only numbers and show them formatted (decimals, percent, currency).

quote: Don’t assume the actual presentation of data, however, as formatting can vary significantly based on people’s locale.
rule: Number formatting follows the person's locale, never a hard-coded separator or symbol.

quote: Adjust line breaks according to the needs of the field.
rule: Choose per field whether overflowing text clips, wraps, or is truncated with an ellipsis at start, middle or end.

quote: Consider using an expansion tooltip to show the full version of clipped or truncated text.
rule: Hovering a field whose text is cut off shows the full text in a tooltip.

quote: In iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, and visionOS apps, show the appropriate keyboard type.
rule: Show the virtual keyboard suited to the field's content.

quote: Minimize text entry in your tvOS and watchOS apps.
rule: Replace typing with buttons where possible on TV and watch.

quote: Display a Clear button in the trailing end of a text field to help people erase their input.
rule: A touch text field carries a trailing clear button.

quote: Use images and buttons to provide clarity and functionality in text fields.
rule: The leading end of a field shows its purpose and the trailing end holds extra actions.

quote: Consider using a combo box if you need to pair text input with a list of choices.
rule: When typed input should also offer a list of choices, use a combo box rather than a plain field.

quote: Present a text field only when necessary.
rule: On the watch, offer a list of options instead of text entry wherever possible.

quote: Use a pull-down button to present commands or items that are directly related to the button’s action.
rule: A menu button lists only commands that refine its own action, e.g. Add listing what to add, Sort listing the sort keys.

quote: If you need to provide a list of mutually exclusive choices that aren’t commands, use a Pop-up buttons instead.
rule: Picking one value from a set of options is a pop-up (select) button, not a pull-down command menu.

quote: Avoid putting all of a view’s actions in one pull-down button.
rule: A view's primary actions are visible buttons, not hidden inside one menu button.

quote: Balance menu length with ease of use.
rule: A pull-down menu holds at least three items.

quote: If you need to list only one or two items, consider using alternative components to present them
rule: With only one or two items, use plain buttons for actions or toggles for settings instead of a menu button.

quote: listing too many items in a pull-down button’s menu can slow people down because it takes longer to find a specific item.
rule: Keep a pull-down menu short enough to scan quickly.

quote: Display a succinct menu title only if it adds meaning.
rule: A pull-down menu has no title of its own unless the title adds information the button and items lack.

quote: Let people know when a pull-down button’s menu item is destructive, and ask them to confirm their intent.
rule: A destructive item in a pull-down menu is marked as destructive and asks for confirmation in a separate prompt before running.

quote: Menus use red text to highlight actions that you identify as potentially destructive.
rule: Destructive menu items are drawn in red.

quote: Include an interface icon with a menu item when it provides value.
rule: Give a menu item an icon, after its label, only when the icon clarifies the item.

quote: You can also let people reveal a pull-down menu by performing a specific gesture on a button.
rule: A touch-and-hold on a button can reveal a related menu.

quote: Consider using a More pull-down button to present items that don’t need prominent positions in the main interface.
rule: Secondary items can go in a More button, weighing space saved against discoverability.

quote: Write succinct labels that describe the current value and both endpoints of the range.
rule: A gauge has short labels for its current value and its minimum and maximum, which screen readers announce.

quote: Consider filling the path with a gradient to help communicate the purpose of the gauge.
rule: A gauge's track may use a colour gradient suggesting its meaning, e.g. hot to cold.

quote: Consider using the continuous style for large ranges.
rule: A level indicator over a large range uses a continuous fill rather than discrete segments.

quote: Consider changing the fill color to inform people about significant parts of the range.
rule: A level indicator's fill colour may change at thresholds such as very low or very high.

quote: Use a text view when you need to display text that’s long, editable, or in a special format.
rule: Use a multi-line text view for long, editable or formatted text; short text uses a label or, if editable, a text field.

quote: Although you can use multiple fonts, colors, and alignments in creative ways, it’s essential to maintain the readability of your content.
rule: Styled text in a text view keeps fonts, colours and alignment readable.

quote: Be sure to test your content with accessibility options turned on, such as bold text.
rule: Check text views with the person's text-size and bold-text settings turned on.

quote: Make useful text selectable.
rule: Text people may want to reuse, such as error messages, serial numbers and IP addresses, can be selected and copied.

quote: Show the appropriate keyboard type.
rule: Editing a text view shows the virtual keyboard suited to its content.

quote: you need to label Dock menu items succinctly and organize them logically.
rule: Dock menu items have short labels and are grouped in a logical order, like any menu.

quote: Make custom Dock menu items available in other places, too.
rule: Every custom Dock menu command is also reachable from the menu bar or the window.

quote: Prefer high-value custom items for your Dock menu.
rule: The Dock menu lists the app's open or recent windows so people can jump to one.

quote: listing a few of the actions that are most likely to be useful when your app isn’t frontmost or when there are no open windows.
rule: The Dock menu adds a few actions useful when the app is in the background or has no window, e.g. 'New Message'.

quote: When present in the menu bar, the following menus appear in the order listed below.
rule: Order the menu bar as: app-name menu, File, Edit, Format, View, any app-specific menus, Window, Help, leaving out only menus the app has no use for.

quote: Support the default system-defined menus and their ordering.
rule: Include the standard menus in their standard order and make standard items such as Edit > Copy work on whatever text the user has selected in any text field.

quote: Always show the same set of menu items.
rule: A menu's set of items never changes with context: an item that cannot act right now is shown disabled, not removed.

quote: Represent menu item actions with familiar icons.
rule: Give menu items for common actions such as Copy, Share and Delete the platform's own icons for those actions.

quote: Support the keyboard shortcuts defined for the standard menu items you include.
rule: Every standard menu item the app includes (Cut, Copy, Paste, Save, Print and so on) answers to the platform's standard shortcut for it.

quote: Define custom keyboard shortcuts only when necessary.
rule: Add a non-standard shortcut only when a command truly needs one, rather than giving every command a key combination.

quote: Prefer short, one-word menu titles.
rule: Name each top-level menu with a single word where possible so the bar stays compact and quick to scan.

quote: If you need to use more than one word in the menu title, use title-style capitalization.
rule: A top-level menu title of two or more words is written in title case.

quote: The app menu typically contains the following menu items listed in the following order.
rule: The app-name menu holds, in order: About App, Settings…, any app-level configuration items, Services, Hide App, Hide Others, Show All, Quit App.

quote: Prefer a short name of 16 characters or fewer. Don’t include a version number.
rule: The app name shown in the About item is at most 16 characters and carries no version number.

quote: Use the same short app name you supply for the About item.
rule: Hide App and Quit App use exactly the same short app name as the About item.

quote: Use only for app-level settings. If you also offer document-specific settings, put them in the File menu.
rule: Settings… opens only settings that apply to the whole app; settings that belong to one document are reached from the File menu instead.

quote: List custom app-configuration items after the Settings item and within the same group.
rule: Extra app-wide configuration commands sit directly after Settings…, inside the same separator group.

quote: Display the About menu item first.
rule: About App is the first item of the app menu and is followed by a separator so it forms a group of its own.

quote: If your app doesn’t handle any types of files, you can rename or eliminate this menu.
rule: An app that works with no files may drop the File menu or give it a name that fits what it does manage.

quote: The File menu typically contains the following menu items listed in the following order.
rule: The File menu holds, in order and only where relevant: New Item, Open, Open Recent, Close, Close Tab, Close File, Save, Save All, Duplicate, Rename…, Move To…, Export As…, Revert To, Page Setup…, Print….

quote: use a term that names the type of item your app creates.
rule: The New command names the kind of thing it makes, e.g. 'New Event' or 'New Calendar', not just 'New'.

quote: If people need to select an item in a separate interface, an ellipsis follows the command to indicate that more input is required.
rule: A command that opens a chooser or asks for more input before acting ends its label with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Open…'.

quote: List document and filenames that people recognize in the submenu; don’t display file paths.
rule: Open Recent lists entries by recognisable document or file name only, never by full path.

quote: List the documents in the order people last opened them, with the most recently opened document first.
rule: Open Recent is ordered by last opening time, newest at the top, and offers a Clear Menu item.

quote: In a tab-based window, consider adding a Close Window item to let people close the entire window with one click or tap.
rule: In a window with tabs, where Close becomes Close Tab, also offer Close Window to shut every tab at once.

quote: Consider supporting this menu item if your app can open multiple views of the same file.
rule: When one file can be shown in several windows, offer Close File, which closes that file together with all its windows.

quote: Automatically save changes periodically as people work so they don’t need to keep choosing File > Save.
rule: Save the user's work automatically at intervals so nothing depends on remembering to choose Save.

quote: For a new document, prompt people for a name and location.
rule: The first save of a never-saved document asks for its name and folder.

quote: prefer a pop-up menu that lets people choose a format in the Save sheet.
rule: When a document can be saved in several formats, the format is picked from a drop-down inside the save dialog rather than through separate commands.

quote: Prefer Duplicate to menu items like Save As, Export, Copy To, and Save To
rule: Offer Duplicate, which leaves both the original and the copy open, in preference to Save As, Copy To or Save To, whose effect on the original is unclear.

quote: Reserve the Export As item for when you need to let people export content in a format your app doesn’t typically handle.
rule: Use Export As… only for writing a format the app does not normally open or save.

quote: After exporting the file, the current document remains open; the exported file doesn’t open.
rule: After an export, the user stays in the original document and the exported file is not opened.

quote: Include the Page Setup item if you need to support printing parameters that apply to a specific document.
rule: Offer Page Setup… only when the app stores print settings such as paper size or orientation with each document.

quote: that people change frequently, like the number of copies to print, belong in the Print panel.
rule: Printer choice, copy count and other per-print or global options are set in the Print dialog, not in Page Setup.

quote: Determine whether Find menu items belong in the Edit menu.
rule: Put Find commands in the Edit menu when they search inside the current content; when they search for files or objects, the File menu may suit them better.

quote: The Edit menu typically contains the following top-level menu items, listed in the following order.
rule: The Edit menu holds, in order: Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Paste and Match Style, Delete, Select All, Find, Spelling and Grammar, Substitutions, Transformations, Speech, then the system's Start Dictation and Emoji & Symbols.

quote: Clarify the target of the undo.
rule: Undo and Redo labels name the action they reverse, e.g. 'Undo Typing' or 'Redo Paste and Match Style'.

quote: Provide a Delete menu item instead of an Erase or Clear menu item.
rule: The command that removes a selection without touching the clipboard is called Delete, matching the Delete key, never Erase or Clear.

quote: Removes the selected data, but doesn’t place it on the Clipboard.
rule: Delete removes the selection and leaves the clipboard as it was, unlike Cut.

quote: The Clipboard contents remain unchanged, permitting people to choose Paste multiple times.
rule: Paste inserts at the insertion point and leaves the clipboard intact so the same content can be pasted repeatedly.

quote: You can exclude this menu if your app doesn’t support formatted text editing.
rule: Leave out the Format menu when the app has no rich-text editing.

quote: The Format menu typically contains the following top-level menu items, listed in the following order.
rule: The Format menu holds Font (Show Fonts, Bold, Italic, Underline, Bigger, Smaller, Show Colors, Copy/Paste Style) and then Text (alignments, Writing Direction, Show/Copy/Paste Ruler).

quote: The View menu doesn’t include items for navigating between or managing specific windows; the Window menu provides these commands.
rule: Keep commands that switch between or manage windows out of the View menu; they go in the Window menu.

quote: Provide a View menu even if your app supports only a subset of the standard view functions.
rule: Have a View menu whenever any standard view command applies, even if it holds only Enter Full Screen.

quote: Ensure that each show/hide item title reflects the current state of the corresponding view.
rule: A toggle item for a panel reads 'Show Toolbar' while the toolbar is hidden and 'Hide Toolbar' while it is shown.

quote: The View menu typically contains the following top-level menu items, listed in the following order.
rule: The View menu holds, in order and as relevant: Show/Hide Tab Bar, Show All Tabs, Show/Hide Toolbar, Customize Toolbar, Show/Hide Sidebar, Enter/Exit Full Screen.

quote: Your app’s custom menus appear in the menu bar between the View menu and the Window menu.
rule: Place the app's own menus after View and before Window.

quote: Provide app-specific menus for custom commands.
rule: Every custom command, including rarely used and advanced ones, appears in a menu-bar menu even when it is also reachable elsewhere in the app.

quote: As much as possible, reflect your app’s hierarchy in app-specific menus.
rule: Order custom menus to mirror how the app's objects contain one another, e.g. Mailbox, then Message, then Format.

quote: Aim to list app-specific menus in order from most to least general or commonly used.
rule: Arrange custom menus from the most general or most used to the least.

quote: The Window menu doesn’t help people customize the appearance of windows or close them.
rule: The Window menu holds no appearance or close commands: appearance goes in View and closing is File > Close.

quote: Provide a Window menu even if your app has only one window.
rule: Every app has a Window menu, even with a single window, including Minimize and Zoom so they can be reached from the keyboard.

quote: Consider including menu items for showing and hiding panels.
rule: Give each auxiliary panel a Window-menu item that shows or hides it, except panels the Format menu already opens.

quote: The Window menu typically contains the following top-level menu items, listed in the following order.
rule: The Window menu holds, in order: Minimize, Zoom, Show Previous Tab, Show Next Tab, Move Tab to New Window, Merge All Windows, Enter/Exit Full Screen (only without a View menu), Bring All to Front, then the open windows.

quote: Avoid using Zoom to enter or exit full-screen mode.
rule: Zoom toggles between a content-fitted size and the user's size; it never enters or leaves full screen.

quote: Include this item in the Window menu only if your app doesn’t have a View menu.
rule: Enter/Exit Full Screen lives in the View menu; it moves to the Window menu only when there is no View menu, alongside separate Minimize and Zoom.

quote: List the currently open windows in alphabetical order for easy scanning. Avoid listing panels or other modal views.
rule: The list of open windows at the end of the Window menu is sorted alphabetically and omits panels and modal views.

quote: The Help menu — located at the trailing end of the menu bar — provides access to an app’s help documentation.
rule: The Help menu is the last menu in the bar and starts with an 'App Help' item that opens the app's documentation.

quote: Use a separator between your primary help documentation and additional items
rule: Separate the main help item from secondary entries such as release notes or registration with a divider.

quote: Keep the total the number of items you list in the Help menu small
rule: Keep the Help menu short; link to further material from inside the help content instead of adding menu items.

quote: Avoid making a dynamic menu item the only way to accomplish a task.
rule: Any command revealed only by holding a modifier while a menu is open must also be possible another way.

quote: Use dynamic menu items primarily in menu bar menus.
rule: Do not put modifier-revealed alternate items in context menus or dock/taskbar menus.

quote: Require only a single modifier key to reveal a dynamic menu item.
rule: An alternate menu item appears with one modifier key held, never a combination.

quote: ensure that people can access all of your app’s functions through its UI.
rule: On iPad, where the menu bar is often hidden, make every function reachable from the app's own interface.

quote: Avoid using the menu bar as a catch-all location for functionality that doesn’t fit in elsewhere.
rule: On iPad, do not park functions in the menu bar just because they have no other home.

quote: Reserve the YourAppName > Settings menu item for opening your app’s page in iPadOS Settings.
rule: On iPad, Settings opens the system Settings page for the app; in-app preferences get their own item below it.

quote: For apps with tab-style navigation, consider adding each tab as a menu item in the View menu.
rule: On iPad, list each tab of tab-style navigation in the View menu, ideally with a shortcut each.

quote: Consider grouping menu items into submenus to conserve vertical space.
rule: On iPad, use submenus more often than on a Mac because menu rows are taller.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Menu bar extras
quote: Consider using a symbol to represent your menu bar extra.
rule: Draw the menu bar extra as a monochrome template symbol that the system can recolour.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Menu bar extras
quote: Display a menu — not a popover — when people click your menu bar extra.
rule: Clicking the menu bar extra opens a menu, not a popover, unless the function is too complex for a menu.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Menu bar extras
quote: Let people — not your app — decide whether to put your menu bar extra in the menu bar.
rule: The menu bar extra appears only when the user has turned it on in settings (optionally offered during setup), never by the app's own decision.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Menu bar extras
quote: Avoid relying on the presence of menu bar extras.
rule: Assume the menu bar extra may be hidden by the system or the user and never depend on it being visible or at a known position.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Menu bar extras
quote: Consider exposing app-specific functionality in other ways, too.
rule: Anything the menu bar extra offers is also reachable elsewhere, for example from the Dock menu.

quote: Choose items deliberately to avoid overcrowding.
rule: Keep the toolbar to a number of items each of which can be told apart and clicked easily.

quote: To accommodate variable view widths, define which items move to the overflow menu as the toolbar becomes narrower.
rule: Decide in advance which toolbar items move into the overflow menu, and in what order, as the window narrows.

quote: Don’t add an overflow menu manually, and avoid layouts that cause toolbar items to overflow by default.
rule: The overflow menu appears only when items stop fitting, and at the default window width every item fits without it.

quote: Add a More menu to contain additional actions.
rule: Put lower-priority actions in a More menu only when they cannot all fit in the toolbar itself.

quote: consider letting people customize the toolbar to include their most common items.
rule: In apps with many toolbar actions or long working sessions, let users choose which items the toolbar shows.

quote: Reduce the use of toolbar backgrounds and tinted controls.
rule: Avoid custom toolbar backgrounds and tinted controls; let the content shape the toolbar's look.

quote: Avoid applying a similar color to toolbar item labels and content layer backgrounds.
rule: Do not colour toolbar labels like the content behind them; prefer a monochrome toolbar over colourful content.

quote: Prefer using standard components in a toolbar.
rule: Use standard toolbar components whose corner radii nest within the bar's corners.

quote: Consider temporarily hiding toolbars for a distraction-free experience.
rule: If the toolbar can be hidden for focus, hide it only in context and always provide a dependable way to bring it back.

quote: Provide a useful title for each window.
rule: Give every window a title that tells the user where they are and distinguishes it from other open windows of the same kind.

quote: Don’t title windows with your app name.
rule: A window's title names its content or area, not the application.

quote: Write a concise title.
rule: Keep a window or view title to a word or short phrase, under 15 characters, so controls keep their room.

quote: Use the standard Back and Close buttons.
rule: Use the standard Back and Close buttons, shown as their usual icons rather than the words 'Back' or 'Close', and implement any custom version identically everywhere.

quote: Provide actions that support the main tasks people perform.
rule: Fill the toolbar with the commands for the main tasks, usually the most frequent ones or those acting on the most important objects.

quote: Make sure the meaning of each control is clear.
rule: Every toolbar item's purpose is obvious without trying it.

quote: Prefer simple, recognizable symbols for items instead of text, except for actions like _edit_ that aren’t well-represented by symbols.
rule: Label toolbar items with recognisable icons, falling back to text for actions such as Edit that have no clear icon.

quote: Prefer system-provided symbols without borders.
rule: Use borderless system symbols in the toolbar; do not draw outlined or circled icons.

quote: Use the `.prominent` style for key actions such as Done or Submit.
rule: Give the key action, such as Done or Submit, a tinted prominent style that sets it apart.

quote: Only specify one primary action, and put it on the trailing side of the toolbar.
rule: A toolbar has at most one primary action and it sits at the trailing end.

quote: show or hide a sidebar appear at the far leading edge, followed by the view title.
rule: The leading end holds Back and the sidebar toggle, then the title and an optional document menu (Duplicate, Rename, Move, Export); these items are not customisable.

quote: Common, useful controls appear in the center area, and the view title can appear here if it’s not on the leading edge.
rule: The centre holds the common controls, which are the customisable ones and the first to collapse into the overflow menu when the window shrinks.

quote: Items on the trailing edge remain visible at all window sizes.
rule: The trailing end holds items that must stay available (inspector toggles, search, the More menu, the primary action) and never overflows.

quote: Group toolbar items logically by function and frequency of use.
rule: Group toolbar items into sections by what they do and how often they are used.

quote: Group navigation controls and critical actions like Done, Close, or Save in dedicated, familiar, and visually distinct sections.
rule: Navigation controls and critical actions such as Done, Close or Save each get their own clearly separated section of the toolbar.

quote: Keep consistent groupings and placement across platforms.
rule: Toolbar groups and their positions are the same on every platform the app runs on.

quote: Minimize the number of groups.
rule: Use no more than three groups of controls in a toolbar.

quote: Keep actions with text labels separate.
rule: Put fixed space between a text-labelled toolbar button and its neighbours so adjacent labels or icons never read as one button.

quote: Prioritize only the most important items for inclusion in the main toolbar area.
rule: On iPhone, put only essential actions in the toolbar and the rest in a More menu.

quote: Use a large title to help people stay oriented as they navigate and scroll.
rule: On iPhone, use a large title that shrinks on scroll and returns at the top.

quote: Consider combining a toolbar with a tab bar.
rule: On iPad, a toolbar and a tab bar can share the top row to save space.

quote: Make every toolbar item available as a command in the menu bar.
rule: Every toolbar command also exists as a menu-bar command, since the toolbar can be hidden or customised; the reverse is not required.

quote: Prefer using a system-provided toolbar.
rule: In visionOS, use the system toolbar placed by the system.

quote: Avoid creating a vertical toolbar.
rule: In visionOS, keep toolbars horizontal because tab bars are vertical there.

quote: Try to prevent windows from resizing below the width of the toolbar.
rule: In visionOS, stop windows shrinking below the toolbar's width.

quote: If your app can enter a modal state, consider offering contextually relevant toolbar controls.
rule: In visionOS, swap in task-specific toolbar controls during a modal task and restore the standard ones afterwards.

quote: Avoid using a pull-down menu in a toolbar.
rule: In visionOS, do not attach pull-down menus to toolbar items.

quote: Use a scrolling toolbar button for an important action that isn’t a primary app function.
rule: On Apple Watch, place a related secondary action in a toolbar button revealed by scrolling up.

quote: Use placeholder text to help people know what they can search for.
rule: Give each search field placeholder text that says what it searches, e.g. 'Search messages'.

quote: If possible, start search immediately when a person types.
rule: Update results with each keystroke rather than waiting for Enter, when the search is fast enough.

quote: Consider showing suggested search terms.
rule: Offer recent searches before typing starts and predicted terms while typing.

quote: Simplify search results.
rule: Rank results so the most relevant come first, and group them by category where that helps.

quote: Consider letting people filter search results.
rule: Provide a way, such as a scope bar above the results, to narrow search results quickly.

quote: Use a scope bar to filter among clearly defined search categories.
rule: Use a scope bar only for distinct, well-defined categories that move the search from broad to narrow.

quote: Default to a broader scope and let people refine it as they need.
rule: A search starts with the widest scope selected; the user narrows it.

quote: Use tokens to filter by common search terms or items.
rule: Represent common filters (a person, a content type) as tokens in the field that can be selected and edited as a single unit.

quote: Consider pairing tokens with search suggestions.
rule: Surface available tokens through search suggestions so users discover them.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search as a tab
quote: Choose the standard tab style to provide suggestions, promote discovery, and encourage exploration.
rule: On iPhone, use a standard search tab with a landing page when search should encourage browsing.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search as a tab
quote: Choose the button appearance to help people quickly find what they need.
rule: On iPhone, use a button-style search tab that opens the keyboard at once for quick lookups.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search in a toolbar
quote: Place search at the bottom if there’s room.
rule: On iPhone, put search in a bottom toolbar when space allows.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search in a toolbar
quote: Place search at the top when itʼs important to defer to content at the bottom of the screen, or thereʼs no bottom toolbar.
rule: On iPhone, put search at the top when bottom content must stay uncovered or there is no bottom toolbar.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search as an inline field
quote: Place search as an inline field when its position alongside the content it searches strengthens that relationship.
rule: On iPhone, put an inline search field next to the content when it searches only that content.

section: Platform considerations > iOS > Search as an inline field
quote: When at the top, position an inline search field above the list it searches, and consider pinning it to the top toolbar when scrolling.
rule: On iPhone, place an inline search field above its list and pin it while scrolling.

quote: try to keep the search experience as consistent as possible across both platforms.
rule: Search is placed and behaves the same way on every desktop platform the app supports.

quote: Put a search field at the trailing side of the toolbar for many common uses.
rule: A search that spans the window's content, especially in split views, sits at the trailing end of the toolbar.

quote: Include search at the top of the sidebar when filtering content or navigation there.
rule: A search that filters the sidebar sits at the top of the sidebar.

quote: Include search as an item in the sidebar or tab bar when you want an area dedicated to discovery.
rule: When search comes with rich suggestions and categories, give it its own sidebar entry leading to a search area.

quote: consider immediately focusing the field when a person navigates to the area to help them search faster and locate the field more easily.
rule: Navigating to a dedicated search area puts keyboard focus in its search field.

quote: Account for window resizing with the placement of the search field.
rule: When the window narrows, keep the search field available next to the content it searches, e.g. above the list column.

quote: Provide suggestions to make searching easier.
rule: On Apple TV, offer popular, contextual and recent search suggestions to save typing.

quote: The Cancel (or Close) button dismisses a sheet without saving any changes.
rule: In a sheet, Cancel (or Close) dismisses without keeping changes and Done dismisses after completing the task or saving.

quote: It isn’t intended to dismiss a sheet.
rule: A Back button in a multi-step sheet only returns to the previous step and never closes the sheet.

quote: For complex or prolonged user flows, consider alternatives to sheets.
rule: Use a separate window or full screen rather than a sheet for long or complex tasks such as editing a document.

quote: Display only one sheet at a time from the main interface.
rule: Never stack sheets: close the current sheet before opening another, and reopen the first afterwards if needed.

quote: Use a nonmodal view when you want to present supplementary items that affect the main task in the parent view.
rule: Supplementary tools the user needs while still working in the main window go in a non-modal panel, not a modal sheet.

quote: Provide an alternative to the Done button.
rule: A sheet with Done always also has Cancel, or Back for a later step, so finishing is never the only way out.

quote: Avoid showing all three buttons — Cancel, Done, and Back — together.
rule: A sheet never shows Cancel, Done and Back at the same time.

quote: the Cancel button belongs on the leading edge of the top toolbar.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, a single-view sheet has Cancel at the leading end and Done at the trailing end of its top bar.

quote: In an iPhone app, consider supporting the medium detent to allow progressive disclosure of the sheet’s content.
rule: On iPhone, let sheets rest at half height when the key content fits there.

quote: Include a grabber in a resizable sheet.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, resizable sheets show a grabber that can be dragged or activated.

quote: Support swiping to dismiss a sheet.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, a swipe down dismisses a sheet, with a confirmation when there are unsaved changes.

quote: Prefer using the page or form sheet presentation styles in an iPadOS app.
rule: On iPad, use the page or form sheet styles.

quote: Present a sheet in a reasonable default size.
rule: Open each sheet at a size that fits its content without resizing, and allow resizing where users may want a larger view.

quote: Let people interact with other app windows without first dismissing a sheet.
rule: A sheet blocks only its parent window: the app's other windows stay usable and can be brought forward while it is open.

quote: Use a panel instead of a sheet if people need to repeatedly provide input and observe results.
rule: Tasks that repeat input and check results, such as find and replace, use a non-modal panel rather than a sheet.

quote: Avoid displaying a sheet that emerges from the bottom edge of a window.
rule: In visionOS, centre sheets in the field of view.

quote: Present a sheet in a default size that helps people retain their context.
rule: In visionOS, keep sheets smaller than their window.

quote: Use a sheet only when your modal task requires a custom title or custom content presentation.
rule: On Apple Watch, prefer alerts or action sheets unless custom content is needed.

quote: Keep sheet interactions brief and occasional.
rule: On Apple Watch, use sheets only for short, important interruptions, never for navigation.

quote: If you change the default label, prefer using SF Symbols to represent the action.
rule: On Apple Watch, use a symbol for a custom dismiss label so it does not look like a title.

quote: Prefer displaying text in a list or table.
rule: Use lists and tables for text-centred items; use a grid or collection for items of varying size or many images.

quote: Let people edit a table when it makes sense.
rule: Let users reorder list items where order matters, even when they cannot add or remove them.

quote: Provide appropriate feedback when people select a list item.
rule: A row that navigates stays highlighted while its content is shown; a row that picks an option marks itself with a check rather than a lasting highlight.

quote: Keep item text succinct so row content is comfortable to read.
rule: Keep row text short; for long items list only titles and show the full content in a detail view.

quote: Consider ways to preserve readability of text that might otherwise get clipped or truncated.
rule: When a column can get narrow, truncate in the middle where the start and end both identify the item, e.g. long file names.

quote: Use descriptive column headings in a multicolumn table.
rule: Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no ending punctuation.

quote: If you don’t include a column heading in a single-column table view, use a label or a header to help people understand the context.
rule: A single-column list without a heading gets a label or header saying what it lists.

quote: Choose a table or list style that coordinates with your data and platform.
rule: Pick the platform list style (grouped, bordered with alternating rows, etc.) that suits the data.

quote: Choose a row style that fits the information you need to display.
rule: Lay out each row's parts to fit what it shows, e.g. a small leading image followed by a short label.

quote: Use an info button only to reveal more information about a row’s content.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, an info button in a row shows details; drilling down uses a disclosure indicator.

quote: Avoid adding an index to a table that displays controls — like disclosure indicators — in the trailing ends of its rows.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, do not combine a section index with trailing row controls.

quote: When it provides value, let people click a column heading to sort a table view based on that column
rule: Clicking a column heading sorts by that column, and clicking the heading of the sorted column reverses the order.

quote: Let people resize columns.
rule: Table columns can be resized by the user to reveal clipped data.

quote: Consider using alternating row colors in a multicolumn table.
rule: Use alternating row backgrounds in wide multicolumn tables.

quote: Use an outline view instead of a table view to present hierarchical data.
rule: Show nested data, such as folders and their contents, in an outline with expandable rows rather than a flat table.

quote: Confirm that images near a table still look good as each row highlights and slightly increases in size when it becomes focused.
rule: On Apple TV, check images next to a table against the focused-row enlargement.

quote: When possible, limit the number of rows.
rule: On Apple Watch, show the most relevant rows and a way to see more.

quote: Constrain the length of detail views if you want to support vertical page-based navigation.
rule: On Apple Watch, keep detail views short enough for vertical paging.

quote: To support navigation, persistently highlight the current selection in each pane that leads to the detail view.
rule: In every pane on the path to the detail view, the selected item stays highlighted.

quote: Consider letting people drag and drop content between panes.
rule: Let users move items between panes by drag and drop, e.g. a message onto a mailbox in the sidebar.

quote: Prefer using a split view in a regular — not a compact — environment.
rule: On iPhone, use split views only in regular width.

quote: Account for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths.
rule: On iPad, design the split view for every window width with logical pane navigation.

quote: Set reasonable defaults for minimum and maximum pane sizes.
rule: Give resizable panes minimum and maximum sizes so a divider can never be dragged until it effectively disappears.

quote: Consider letting people hide a pane when it makes sense.
rule: Let users hide secondary panes to give the main editing area more room.

quote: Provide multiple ways to reveal hidden panes.
rule: A hidden pane can be brought back by at least two routes, such as a toolbar button and a menu command with a keyboard shortcut.

quote: Prefer the thin divider style.
rule: Use the thin one-point divider unless strong row lines would hide it.

quote: Choose a split view layout that keeps the panes looking balanced.
rule: On Apple TV, use a one-third / two-thirds or even split.

quote: Display a single title above a split view, helping people understand the content as a whole.
rule: On Apple TV, title the split view as a whole, not each pane.

quote: Choose the title’s alignment based on the type of content the secondary pane contains.
rule: On Apple TV, centre the title over collections, otherwise place it over the primary pane.

quote: To display supplementary information, prefer a split view instead of a new window.
rule: In visionOS, show supplementary information in a split view rather than another window.

quote: Automatically display the most relevant detail view.
rule: On Apple Watch, open on the most pertinent detail view.

quote: If your app displays multiple detail pages, place the detail views in a vertical Tab views.
rule: On Apple Watch, put multiple detail pages in a vertical tab view for the Digital Crown.

quote: Use a segmented control to provide closely related choices that affect an object, state, or view.
rule: Use a segmented control only for a small set of closely related choices or actions on one object, state or view.

quote: Consider a segmented control when it’s important to group functions together, or to clearly show their selection state.
rule: Choose a segmented control when the options must stay visibly grouped at any size or their selected state must be seen at a glance.

quote: Keep control types consistent within a single segmented control.
rule: A segmented control either holds a selection or performs actions; never mix action segments with selectable ones.

quote: Limit the number of segments in a control.
rule: Keep a segmented control to about five to seven segments at most on a wide window.

quote: In general, keep segment size consistent.
rule: Give all segments the same width.

quote: Prefer using either text or images — not a mix of both — in a single segmented control.
rule: All segments of one control are labelled the same way: all text or all icons.

quote: As much as possible, use content with a similar size in each segment.
rule: Balance segment contents so some segments are not full while others look empty.

quote: Use nouns or noun phrases for segment labels.
rule: Segment labels are nouns or noun phrases in title case.

quote: A segmented control that displays text labels doesn’t need introductory text.
rule: A segmented control with text labels needs no separate introductory label.

quote: Consider a segmented control to switch between closely related subviews.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, a segmented control may switch closely related subviews; separate sections use a tab bar.

quote: Consider using introductory text to clarify the purpose of a segmented control.
rule: Introduce an icon-labelled segmented control with text, or label each segment below it.

quote: If your app includes tooltips, provide one for each segment in a segmented control.
rule: Every segment of a segmented control has its own tooltip naming what it does.

quote: Use a tab view in the main window area — instead of a segmented control — for view switching.
rule: Switch views in the main window area with tabs; reserve segmented view-switchers for toolbars and inspector panes.

quote: Consider supporting spring loading.
rule: Let a segment activate when dragged items are held over it and force-clicked on a Magic Trackpad.

quote: Consider using a split view instead of a segmented control on screens that perform content filtering.
rule: On Apple TV, filter content with a split view rather than segments.

quote: Avoid putting other focusable elements close to segmented controls.
rule: On Apple TV, keep other focusable items away from segmented controls.

quote: Customize a slider’s appearance if it adds value.
rule: Restyle a slider's track, thumb and end icons only when it helps convey what it adjusts.

quote: Use familiar slider directions.
rule: A horizontal slider has its minimum at the leading end and maximum at the trailing end; a vertical one has its minimum at the bottom.

quote: Consider supplementing a slider with a corresponding text field and stepper.
rule: For wide ranges, pair a slider with a numeric field showing the exact value and a stepper for whole-number steps.

quote: Don’t use a slider to adjust audio volume.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, use the system volume view for volume.

quote: Consider giving live feedback as the value of a slider changes.
rule: Apply a slider's effect continuously while it is dragged, not only on release.

quote: Choose a slider style that matches peoples’ expectations.
rule: Use a linear slider between fixed end points (e.g. opacity 0–100%) and a circular one for values that wrap or continue (e.g. rotation).

quote: Consider using a label to introduce a slider.
rule: Introduce a slider with a label in sentence case ending with a colon, e.g. 'Opacity:'.

quote: Use tick marks to increase clarity and accuracy.
rule: Add tick marks to a slider when users need to judge the scale or hit specific values.

quote: Consider adding labels to tick marks for even greater clarity.
rule: Label the minimum and maximum ticks, and periodic ticks when the scale is non-linear, without labelling every tick.

quote: It’s also a good idea to provide a tooltip that displays the value of the thumb when people hold their pointer over it.
rule: Hovering over a slider's thumb shows a tooltip with its current value.

quote: Prefer horizontal sliders.
rule: In visionOS, use horizontal sliders.

quote: If necessary, create custom glyphs to communicate what the slider does.
rule: On Apple Watch, replace the plus and minus glyphs when they do not convey the slider's purpose.

quote: Supporting all available input methods so people can choose the method that works for them
rule: Accept every input method the platform offers for a field (typing, picking, pasting, dropping) so the user can use whichever suits them.

quote: Get information from the system whenever possible.
rule: Never ask the user for data the app can read from settings or the system, with permission where needed.

quote: Be clear about the data you need.
rule: Every field states what it wants, through a label such as 'Email' or an example prompt such as 'username@company.com'.

quote: You can also prefill fields with reasonable default values, which can minimize decision making and speed data entry.
rule: Prefill fields with sensible defaults wherever one exists.

quote: Use a secure text-entry field when appropriate.
rule: Fields for passwords and other sensitive data mask each typed character.

quote: Never prepopulate a password field.
rule: A password field always opens empty; the user types it or uses the system's credential store.

quote: When possible, offer choices instead of requiring text entry.
rule: When the valid answers are known, let users pick from a list, menu or picker instead of typing.

quote: As much as possible, let people provide data by dragging and dropping it or by pasting it.
rule: Fields accept pasted and dropped data.

quote: Dynamically validate field values.
rule: Check each value as soon as it is entered and report a problem at once, not after the whole form is submitted.

quote: consider using a number formatter, which automatically configures a text field to accept only numeric values.
rule: Numeric fields accept only numbers and display them in the intended format (decimals, percent, currency).

quote: When data entry is necessary, make sure people understand that they must provide the required data before they can proceed.
rule: Keep Next or Continue disabled until every required field has a value.

quote: Consider using an expansion tooltip to show the full version of clipped or truncated text in a field.
rule: When a field's content is clipped, hovering over it shows the full text in a tooltip.

quote: Show something as soon as possible.
rule: Never show an empty window while loading; display placeholders at once and replace them as content arrives.

quote: Let people do other things in your app or game while they wait for content to load.
rule: Load in the background so the rest of the app stays usable during loading.

quote: If loading takes an unavoidably long time, give people something interesting to view while they wait.
rule: During an unavoidably long load, show useful content such as tips, sized to a realistic estimate of the remaining time.

quote: Improve installation and launch time by downloading large assets in the background.
rule: Schedule large asset downloads through the Background Assets framework after install or update.

quote: Clearly communicate that content is loading and how long it might take to complete.
rule: Whenever loading takes more than a moment or two, show a progress indicator.

quote: you use a _determinate_ progress indicator when you know how long loading will take
rule: Use a determinate progress indicator when the duration is known and an indeterminate one only when it is not.

quote: For games, consider creating a custom loading view.
rule: Games may replace standard progress indicators with a custom animated loading view.

quote: As much as possible, avoid showing a loading indicator in your watchOS experience.
rule: On Apple Watch, aim to show content immediately, using an indicator only for loads of a second or two.

quote: Leverage large displays to present more content in fewer nested levels and with less need for modality
rule: On large screens show more at once, with fewer nested levels and fewer modal steps, while keeping density comfortable.

quote: Let people resize, hide, show, and move your windows to fit their work style and device configuration
rule: Every main window can be resized, moved, hidden and shown, and supports full screen.

quote: Use the menu bar to give people easy access to all the commands they need to do things in your app.
rule: Every command of the app is reachable from the menu bar.

quote: Help people take advantage of high-precision input modes to perform pixel-perfect selections and edits.
rule: Support precise pointer selection and editing down to single pixels where the content calls for it.

quote: Handle keyboard shortcuts to help people accelerate actions and use keyboard-only work styles.
rule: Provide keyboard shortcuts and make the whole app usable from the keyboard alone.

quote: Support personalization, letting people customize toolbars, configure windows to display the views they use most
rule: Let users customise toolbars, choose which views a window shows, and pick the appearance they prefer.

quote: Make the value that a stepper affects obvious.
rule: Place a stepper directly beside the field showing the value it changes, so which value it affects is unmistakable.

quote: Consider pairing a stepper with a text field when large value changes are likely.
rule: When values can vary widely, pair the stepper with an editable field, e.g. number of copies when printing.

quote: For large value ranges, consider supporting Shift-click to change the value quickly.
rule: Shift-clicking a stepper changes the value by a larger step, such as ten times the normal increment.

quote: Use a path control in the window body, not the window frame.
rule: Place a file-path bar inside the window's content area, never in the toolbar or status bar.

quote: Avoid using the same color to mean different things.
rule: Give each colour a single meaning across the app; a colour that marks interactive elements must never also style plain, non-interactive text.

quote: Make sure all your app’s colors work well in light, dark, and increased contrast contexts.
rule: Every custom colour needs a light variant, a dark variant and a higher-contrast version of each.

quote: When possible, use system colors, which already define variants for all these contexts.
rule: Prefer the platform's predefined colours over custom ones because they already adapt to appearance settings.

quote: Test your app’s color scheme under a variety of lighting conditions.
rule: Check the palette in bright daylight and in dim rooms and tune it for the common case.

quote: Test your app on different devices.
rule: Check colours on several displays, colour profiles (P3, sRGB) and white-point settings.

quote: Consider how artwork and translucency affect nearby colors.
rule: Adjust colours next to imagery or translucent bars so the interface neither overpowers nor fades against them.

quote: If your app lets people choose colors, prefer system-provided color controls where available.
rule: When people pick a colour, offer the platform's standard colour chooser rather than a home-made one, so saved colours are shared with other apps.

quote: Avoid relying solely on color to differentiate between objects, indicate interactivity, or communicate essential information.
rule: Anything signalled by colour (state, object identity, interactivity) must also be signalled by text or a shape, so colour-blind people get the same information.

quote: Avoid using colors that make it hard to perceive content in your app.
rule: Keep text and icons in enough contrast with their background, and avoid colour pairs that colour-blind people cannot tell apart.

quote: Consider how the colors you use might be perceived in other countries and cultures.
rule: Check that a colour carrying meaning (e.g. red for danger) sends the intended message in each culture the app targets.

quote: Avoid hard-coding system color values in your app.
rule: Read platform colours through the system API at run time instead of copying their documented values into code.

quote: Avoid redefining the semantic meanings of dynamic system colors.
rule: Use each semantic colour only for the role its name states, e.g. never draw text in the separator colour or fill a background with the secondary-label colour.

quote: Apply color sparingly to the Liquid Glass material, and to symbols or text on the material.
rule: Tint glass surfaces only for status indicators or primary actions.

quote: To emphasize primary actions, apply color to the background rather than to symbols or text.
rule: A prominent action gets a coloured fill, not coloured glyphs or label text.

quote: Refrain from adding color to the background of multiple controls.
rule: Only one control in a group should carry a coloured background.
