quote: Avoid using similar colors in control labels if your app has a colorful background.
rule: Over colourful content, keep bar controls monochrome or pick an accent clearly distinct from the content.

quote: Be aware of the placement of color in the content layer.
rule: Keep content colours from overlapping similarly coloured controls, at least in the resting scroll position.

quote: Apply color profiles to your images.
rule: Embed a colour profile (normally sRGB) in every bitmap image.

quote: Use wide color to enhance the visual experience on compatible displays.
rule: Where useful, export images as 16-bit Display P3 PNGs for wide-gamut screens.

quote: Provide color space–specific image and color variations if necessary.
rule: Ship separate sRGB and P3 variants when near-identical P3 colours or gradients would clip on sRGB screens.

quote: In general, use the grouped background colors
rule: On iOS use grouped background colours for grouped tables and the system set elsewhere, primary to tertiary by depth.

quote: macOS defines the following dynamic system colors
rule: On a Mac, colour roles follow AppKit's named set: label tiers, control, selected and unemphasized selected content, focus ring, grid, separator, window and text backgrounds.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > App accent colors
quote: the system applies their chosen color to the relevant items throughout your app, replacing your accent color.
rule: When the user sets a system accent colour other than multicolour, buttons, selection and sidebar icons take that colour instead of the app's.

quote: Consider choosing a limited color palette that coordinates with your app logo.
rule: On tvOS keep a small palette tied to the logo.

quote: Avoid using only color to indicate focus.
rule: On tvOS show focus with scaling and motion, not a colour change alone.

quote: Use color sparingly, especially on glass.
rule: In visionOS windows reserve colour for important information or relationships.

quote: Prefer using color in bold text and large areas.
rule: In visionOS avoid colour on thin text or small areas.

quote: In a fully immersive experience, help people maintain visual comfort by keeping brightness levels balanced.
rule: In immersive scenes avoid bright, flashing objects on very dark backgrounds.

quote: Use background color to support existing content or supply additional information.
rule: On watchOS use a background colour only when it communicates something.

quote: Avoid using full-screen background color in views that are likely to remain onscreen for long periods of time
rule: On watchOS skip full-screen colour on long-lived views such as workouts.

quote: Recognize that people might prefer graphic complications to use tinted mode instead of full color.
rule: Watch complications must still read well when the system tints them in one colour.

quote: Make sure that your windows adapt fluidly to different sizes to support multitasking and multiwindow workflows.
rule: Every window's layout must keep working as the window is resized, so it can share the screen with other windows.

quote: Avoid opening new windows as default behavior unless it makes sense for your app.
rule: Open a separate window only where seeing two things at once helps (e.g. composing a message beside the inbox); otherwise stay in the current window.

quote: Consider providing the option to view content in a new window.
rule: Offer an 'open in new window' command for content, in its context menu or the File menu.

quote: Avoid creating custom window UI.
rule: Use the system's window frame and its close, minimise and zoom controls; do not draw imitation frames or title-bar buttons.

quote: Use the term _window_ in user-facing content.
rule: Call every window a 'window' in visible text, never 'scene', 'pane' or another implementation term.

quote: Make sure window controls don’t overlap toolbar items.
rule: On iPad move leading toolbar buttons inward when window controls appear.

quote: Consider letting people use a gesture to open content in a new window.
rule: On iPad allow a pinch to expand an item into its own window.

quote: you must support multiple windows in your app.
rule: iPad apps that preview files must still support several windows.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > macOS window states
quote: Make sure custom windows use the system-defined appearances.
rule: The key window, other main windows and inactive windows must look different, and update when their state changes, so people see which window takes input.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > macOS window states
quote: Avoid putting critical information or actions in a bottom bar
rule: Never place essential information or actions only in a window's bottom bar, since its bottom edge is often off screen.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > macOS window states
quote: use it only to display a small amount of information directly related to a window’s contents or to a selected item within it.
rule: A bottom status bar holds only brief facts about the window's content or selection (e.g. item count, selected count, free space); more detail goes in an inspector.

quote: Prefer using a window to present a familiar interface and to support familiar tasks.
rule: In visionOS use a window for familiar UI and a volume for bounded 3D content.

quote: Retain the window’s glass background.
rule: Keep the glass background of visionOS windows.

quote: Choose an initial window size that minimizes empty areas within it.
rule: Size a new visionOS window so it has little empty space.

quote: Aim for an initial shape that suits a window’s content.
rule: Give a visionOS window an opening aspect ratio that fits its content (wide for slides, tall for pages).

quote: Choose a minimum and maximum size for each window to help keep your content looking great.
rule: Set minimum and maximum sizes on visionOS windows so controls never overlap and content stays usable.

quote: Minimize the depth of 3D content you display in a window.
rule: Keep 3D content in a visionOS window shallow; use a volume for deep content.

quote: Prefer using a volume to display rich, 3D content.
rule: Use a visionOS volume for rich 3D content.

quote: Place 2D content so it looks good from multiple angles.
rule: Anchor 2D content inside a volume with attachments so it reads from every side.

quote: In general, use dynamic scaling.
rule: Let volume content scale with distance unless it represents a real-world object.

quote: Take advantage of the default baseplate appearance to help people discern the edges of a volume.
rule: Keep the baseplate glow unless content fills the volume.

quote: Consider offering high-value content in an ornament.
rule: Use at most one extra ornament on a volume, never on the toolbar's edge.

quote: Choose an alignment that supports the way people interact with your volume.
rule: Keep a volume level for passive content and tilt it toward the viewer for interactive content.

quote: avoid framing the work as merely a search for content that might give offense.
rule: Review the app for whether it welcomes everyone, not only for whether it avoids offensive content.

quote: Consider the tone of your copy from different perspectives.
rule: Keep the text's tone clear, direct and respectful, avoiding an academic register that implies a required level of education.

quote: Pay attention to how you refer to people.
rule: Address the reader as 'you'; never call them 'the user' or 'the player' in visible text.

quote: consider reserving words like _we_ and _our_ to represent your software or company
rule: Use 'we' and 'our' only to mean the software or its maker, never to suggest a shared relationship with the reader.

quote: Avoid using specialized or technical terms without defining them.
rule: Prefer plain words to jargon; where a technical term is unavoidable, define it first and make the definition easy to find.

quote: Replace colloquial expressions with plain language.
rule: Do not use idioms or slang in interface text (e.g. 'grandfathered in'); state the meaning plainly so it translates.

quote: Consider carefully before including humor.
rule: Leave jokes out of interface text unless there is a strong reason, as they translate badly and wear thin on repetition.

quote: Present a clear, straightforward interface.
rule: The app must be usable without prior special knowledge, with an interface that matches each platform's conventions.

quote: Build in ways to learn how to use your app or game.
rule: Offer a step-by-step introduction for newcomers that others can skip straight past to the content.

quote: You can help everyone feel welcome in your app or game by avoiding unnecessary references to specific genders.
rule: Write text without gendered pronouns where gender is irrelevant (e.g. 'Subscribers can post recipes' rather than 'his or her recipes').

quote: prefer giving people the tools they need to customize such items as they choose.
rule: Let people choose the look of avatars or characters themselves instead of assigning a gender.

quote: If you need to depict a generic person or people, use a nongendered human image
rule: An icon or picture standing for an unspecified person must not show a gender.

quote: consider providing inclusive options, such as _nonbinary_, _self-identify_, and _decline to state_.
rule: Ask for gender only when required, and then offer choices beyond two plus a way to decline, optionally with pronouns.

quote: As you create copy and images that represent people, portray a range of human characteristics and activities.
rule: Examples and pictures of people should vary in background, body, age and ability and avoid stereotyped roles.

quote: prefer showing places, homes, activities, and items that are familiar and relatable to most people.
rule: Use everyday, broadly familiar settings and objects in examples rather than signs of affluence.

quote: Avoiding assumptions and instead concentrating on inclusion can help you craft experiences that benefit everyone.
rule: Do not build features or prompts around experiences not everyone shares (e.g. security questions about college or a first car); use universal ones.

quote: it’s essential to support these features.
rule: Support the platform's accessibility features such as the screen reader, display accommodations, captions and switch control.

quote: It’s also essential to avoid assuming that any disability might prevent someone from wanting to enjoy the experience your software provides.
rule: Make every feature accessible rather than assuming some audience with a disability would not use it.

quote: Avoid images and language that exclude people with disabilities.
rule: Never use a disability as a metaphor for something bad, and include people with disabilities when showing people.

quote: Take a people-first approach when writing about people with disabilities.
rule: When writing about a person, lead with them and their goals before any disability, using the terms they use themselves.

quote: Prioritize simplicity and perceivability.
rule: Keep interactions familiar and consistent, and make content perceivable by sight, hearing or touch alone.

quote: first prepare your software to handle languages and regions other than your own
rule: Internationalise the app (text, dates, times, money in the user's language and region) before shipping translations.

quote: SF Symbols includes glyphs you can use in both left-to-right and right-to-left contexts
rule: Use icons that have language-specific and right-to-left variants.

quote: If you use color as a way to communicate, make sure your color choices communicate the same thing in each version of your software.
rule: Check per locale that colours carrying meaning say the same thing in each translation.

quote: The exception is when automatic selection might cause a distracting context shift, like opening a new view.
rule: Moving focus to an item may also select it, except where selecting would cause a context change such as opening a new view; then selection needs a separate action.

quote: Rely on system-provided focus effects.
rule: Draw focus with the system's focus effect and design custom effects only when unavoidable.

quote: Avoid changing focus without people’s interaction.
rule: Never move keyboard focus on the app's own initiative; focus changes only in response to the person.

quote: moving focus to one of these remaining items ensures that the focus indicator is in a location people can easily find.
rule: If the focused item disappears while the person is navigating by keyboard, move focus to a neighbouring item; otherwise hide the focus indicator.

quote: Be consistent with the platform as you help people bring focus to items in your app.
rule: Follow the platform's rule for what takes focus: on a Mac, content elements (list items, text and search fields) take focus and buttons, sliders and toggles are reached via full keyboard access.

quote: Indicate focus using visual appearances that are consistent with the platform.
rule: Draw a focused list selection in accent colour with white text and an unfocused one in grey.

quote: In general, use a focus ring for a text or search field, but use a highlight in a list or collection.
rule: Show focus on a text or search field with a ring, and in a list or collection by highlighting the whole row.

quote: Pressing the Tab key moves focus among focus groups
rule: On iPad, Tab moves between focus groups (sidebar, grid, list) and arrow keys move within one.

quote: Customize the halo focus effect when necessary.
rule: On iPad shape and position the focus halo so it matches the item and is not clipped.

quote: Ensure that focus moves through your custom views in ways that make sense.
rule: On iPad Tab visits focus groups in reading order, leading to trailing then top to bottom; group custom stacks so order is sensible.

quote: Adjust the priority of an item to reflect its importance within a focus group.
rule: On iPad mark the most likely item of a focus group primary so it is focused when the group is entered.

quote: In a full-screen experience, let people use gestures to interact with the content, not to move focus.
rule: On tvOS full-screen gestures act on content, not focus.

quote: Avoid displaying a pointer.
rule: On tvOS navigate by focus, not a pointer.

quote: Design your interface to accommodate components in various focus states.
rule: On tvOS supply art for unfocused, focused, highlighted, selected and unavailable states.

quote: Determine your app’s voice.
rule: Settle on who the app speaks to and the vocabulary that suits them before writing its text.

quote: Create a list of common terms, and reference that list to keep your language consistent.
rule: Keep a glossary of the app's terms and use the same word for the same thing everywhere.

quote: Match your tone to the context.
rule: Adjust tone to the situation: plain and direct for errors and payments, lighter for achievements.

quote: Be clear.
rule: Use easily understood words and cut every word that is not needed.

quote: Write for everyone.
rule: Write in simple language without jargon or gendered terms, with screen readers and translation in mind.

quote: Pay attention to the order of elements on a screen, and put the most important information first.
rule: Order each screen so the most important information comes first.

quote: If you’re trying to convey more than one idea, consider breaking up the text onto multiple screens
rule: Split text covering several ideas across separate steps or screens with a planned flow.

quote: When labeling buttons and links, it’s almost always best to use a verb.
rule: Label buttons and links with a plain verb (e.g. 'Send', not 'Let’s do it!').

quote: For links, avoid using “Click here” in favor of more descriptive words or phrases
rule: Link text must name its destination (e.g. 'Learn more about UX writing'), never 'Click here'.

quote: Build language patterns.
rule: Reuse the same phrasing patterns for recurring kinds of text.

quote: Adopt capitalization rules that align with your app’s style, then apply them consistently.
rule: Fix one capitalisation style per element type (e.g. title case for all alert titles) and use it throughout.

quote: Give clear guidance and use consistent language throughout processes with multiple steps.
rule: In multi-step flows start with e.g. 'Get Started', advance with one consistent label ('Continue' or 'Next'), and end with 'Done'.

quote: Use possessive pronouns sparingly.
rule: Drop 'my' and 'your' when context is clear ('Favorites', not 'Your Favorites'), and never mix perspectives.

quote: Avoid using _we_ altogether because it may be unclear who the “we” in question refers to.
rule: Never use 'we' in interface text, especially in errors ('Unable to load content', not 'We’re having trouble…').

quote: Write for how people use each device.
rule: Name interactions by the device's input: 'click' with a pointer, 'tap' on touch.

quote: Provide clear next steps on any blank screens.
rule: An empty view tells people what they can do next and offers a button or link to do it.

quote: Remember that empty states are usually temporary, so don’t show crucial information that could then disappear.
rule: Do not put information people need later only in an empty-state message.

quote: Write clear error messages.
rule: Show an error next to its cause, without blame, saying how to fix it (e.g. 'Choose a password with at least 8 characters').

quote: Interjections like “oops!” or “uh-oh” are typically unnecessary and can sound insincere.
rule: Leave exclamations such as 'Oops' out of error messages.

quote: Choose the right delivery method.
rule: Pick notification, alert or inline message by the urgency of the news and whether it needs action now.

quote: Keep settings labels clear and simple.
rule: Label each setting plainly and, if needed, add a line explaining what it does when on.

quote: If you need to direct someone to a setting, provide a direct link or button, rather than trying to describe its location.
rule: When text refers people to a setting, give a button or link that opens it instead of describing the path.

quote: Show hints in text fields.
rule: Label every input field and use placeholder text with an example or description of the expected format (e.g. 'name@example.com').

quote: Show errors right next to the field, and instruct people how to enter the information correctly
rule: Put field validation errors beside the field, phrased as how to do it right ('Use only letters for your name'), never a bare 'Invalid name'.

quote: Create value.
rule: At each stage, check that every part of the design serves what the product is for.

quote: Keep focused.
rule: Concentrate effort on the few features people use most and make those excellent.

quote: Find new ways to solve the problem.
rule: Study existing solutions and design what sets the product apart instead of copying them.

quote: Stay out of the way.
rule: Take people directly to their task or content and keep the interface unobtrusive.

quote: Give people the freedom to explore.
rule: Let people reach features freely without locking them into fixed flows or modes.

quote: When a guided flow is necessary, make it easy to skip or escape
rule: Every guided flow offers a visible way to skip or leave it.

quote: Help people recover from mistakes.
rule: Make actions reversible (undo, go back) so a mistake never costs people their work or much time.

quote: Be fully transparent about what your product does and why.
rule: State why each permission is requested and what data is collected and how it is used.

quote: Keep people’s information safe.
rule: Collect only data the product needs and guard it against misuse.

quote: Use concepts that people know.
rule: Base interactions on concepts people already know from the world and other software.

quote: Keep visuals and interactions consistent
rule: Once an element has a behaviour or look, give it the same one everywhere.

quote: Provide clear feedback.
rule: Show whether controls are available, signal when content changes, and use the standard alert and choice patterns.

quote: Design for everyone.
rule: Treat accessibility as a requirement from the start, for the full range of people who may use the app.

quote: Preserve a person’s context.
rule: Keep content and controls in the same predictable places across platforms and window sizes, easing transitions between states.

quote: Consider a variety of input methods.
rule: Make everything work with several inputs, including keyboard and pointer, not one alone.

quote: Approach every platform with intention.
rule: Give each supported platform equal care so the app feels native on each.

quote: Include just what’s necessary.
rule: Keep the important things at hand and let the rest recede, without stripping useful function.

quote: Be concise.
rule: Use exactly the words a concept or control label needs, and no more.

quote: Establish hierarchy.
rule: Use recognisable controls and a consistent structure that show where people are and what comes next.

quote: Quality sets the tone.
rule: Treat every element, including wording and sound, as a deliberate decision.

quote: Experiment and iterate.
rule: Prototype early, drop what fails, and test in real-world use for reliability and speed.

quote: Maintain your craft.
rule: Keep updating the interface to current platform capabilities and patterns after release.

quote: Identify the emotion you want to inspire.
rule: Decide the feeling the app should give and let it guide design choices.

quote: Create defining moments.
rule: Consider each interaction, down to button presses and error messages, as a chance to express the app's character.

quote: Don’t mistake delight for decoration.
rule: Never let flourishes slow people down in their task.

quote: Consider the whole.
rule: Judge the experience as a whole: freedom to act, safety to explore, familiar metaphors, smooth changes of context.

quote: Extend visually rich content beneath the sidebar.
rule: Let rich content run under a floating sidebar or mirror it there.

quote: When possible, let people customize the contents of a sidebar.
rule: Let people choose which sidebar entries appear and in what order.

quote: Group hierarchy with disclosure controls if your app has a lot of content.
rule: With many sidebar entries, group them under collapsible disclosure headings.

quote: Consider using familiar symbols to represent items in the sidebar.
rule: Give sidebar items familiar icons, preferring symbol glyphs to bitmaps.

quote: Consider letting people hide the sidebar.
rule: Let people hide and show the sidebar with the platform's usual means, such as a toggle button or Show/Hide Sidebar commands in the View menu.

quote: Avoid hiding the sidebar by default to ensure that it remains discoverable.
rule: Show the sidebar by default.

quote: In general, show no more than two levels of hierarchy in a sidebar.
rule: Limit a sidebar to two levels; deeper data gets a split view with a content list between sidebar and detail.

quote: If you need to include two levels of hierarchy in a sidebar, use succinct, descriptive labels to title each group.
rule: Title each sidebar group with a short descriptive label, dropping needless words.

quote: Make sure any sidebar icon colors you choose serve a clear purpose.
rule: Sidebar icons follow the accent colour, with fixed colours used sparingly for meaning.

quote: Consider using a tab bar first.
rule: On iOS/iPadOS prefer a tab bar to a sidebar.

quote: If necessary, apply the correct appearance to a sidebar.
rule: Use the UIKit sidebar list appearance outside SwiftUI.

quote: Consider automatically hiding and revealing a sidebar when its container window resizes.
rule: Collapse the sidebar automatically when the window gets narrow and bring it back when it widens.

quote: Avoid putting critical information or actions at the bottom of a sidebar.
rule: Do not put essential items at the bottom of a sidebar, where a moved window may hide them.

quote: If your app’s hierarchy is deep, consider using a sidebar within a tab in a tab bar.
rule: In visionOS a sidebar inside a tab must not switch tabs.

quote: Consider using a picker to offer medium-to-long lists of items.
rule: Use a scrolling picker for medium-to-long lists of values.

quote: If you need to display a fairly short list of choices, consider using a Pull-down buttons instead of a picker.
rule: Offer a short list of choices in a menu button, and a very large set in a list or table, which can have an index.

quote: Use predictable and logically ordered values.
rule: Order picker values so hidden ones are predictable (e.g. countries alphabetically).

quote: Avoid switching views to show a picker.
rule: Show a picker in context, beside or below the field it edits or in a popover, never by moving to another view.

quote: Consider providing less granularity when specifying minutes in a date picker.
rule: Where exact minutes are not needed, step the minute list by a divisor of 60 (e.g. 0, 15, 30, 45).

quote: Use a compact date picker when space is constrained.
rule: On iOS use the compact date picker in tight spaces.

quote: Choose a date picker style that suits your app.
rule: Use a typed (textual) date field for precise entry in little space, and a calendar (graphical) picker for browsing days or choosing a range.

quote: If search is important, give it a primary position in your app or view.
rule: When search matters, place the search field prominently, e.g. in the main toolbar.

quote: Aim to make your app’s content searchable through a single location.
rule: Provide one clearly marked place that searches everything, adding local filters only for clearly separate sections.

quote: Clearly display the current scope of a search.
rule: Always show what is being searched, through the placeholder, a scope control or a title (e.g. the mailbox name).

quote: Provide suggestions to make searching easier.
rule: Show recent searches before typing starts and suggestions while typing.

quote: Take privacy into consideration before displaying search history.
rule: Think about who else can see the screen before showing past searches.

quote: If you do show search history, provide a way for people to clear it if they want.
rule: Wherever search history is shown, offer a command to clear it.

quote: Make your app’s content searchable in Spotlight.
rule: Index app content with metadata for Spotlight.

quote: Define metadata for custom file types you handle.
rule: Ship a Spotlight importer describing custom file metadata.

quote: Use Spotlight to offer advanced file-search capabilities within the context of your app.
rule: Start Spotlight searches from the app's selection.

quote: Prefer using the system-provided open and save views.
rule: Use the operating system's own open and save dialogs, which bring their own search.

quote: Implement a Quick Look generator if your app produces custom file types.
rule: Provide Quick Look previews for custom document types.

quote: Help people predict the results of undo and redo as much as possible.
rule: Name the action in the Undo and Redo command labels (e.g. 'Undo Typing', 'Redo Bold').

quote: Show the results of an undo or redo.
rule: After undo or redo, bring the affected content into view and mark it (e.g. scroll to a restored paragraph).

quote: Let people undo multiple times.
rule: Keep an unlimited undo history at least back to the last open or save.

quote: Consider giving people the option to revert multiple changes at once.
rule: Let a run of related small edits undo as one step, and offer a way to revert all changes since opening or saving.

quote: Provide undo and redo buttons only when necessary.
rule: Rely on the Edit menu and the standard shortcuts for undo; add on-screen undo/redo buttons only when really needed.

quote: use the standard system-provided symbols and put the buttons in a toolbar.
rule: Dedicated undo and redo buttons go in the toolbar with the conventional undo/redo icons.

quote: Avoid redefining standard gestures for undo and redo.
rule: On iOS keep three-finger swipe and shake for undo.

quote: Briefly and precisely describe the operation to be undone or redone.
rule: On iOS add one or two words after 'Undo'/'Redo' in the alert title.

quote: Place undo and redo commands in the Edit menu and support the standard keyboard shortcuts.
rule: Undo and Redo are the first items of the Edit menu, on Command-Z and Shift-Command-Z.

quote: Use a pop-up button to present a flat list of mutually exclusive options or states.
rule: Use a pop-up (select) button for choosing one of several exclusive options, and show the chosen one on the button.

quote: Use a pull-down button instead if you need to:
rule: Use a pull-down menu button, not a pop-up button, for a list of actions, multiple selection or submenus.

quote: Provide a useful default selection.
rule: Preselect the option most people will want.

quote: Give people a way to predict a pop-up button’s options without opening it.
rule: Label a pop-up button, or put a label before it, so its options can be guessed without opening it.

quote: Consider using a pop-up button when space is limited and you don’t need to display all options all the time.
rule: Prefer a pop-up button over radio buttons when space is short and options need not all be visible.

quote: If necessary, include a Custom option in a pop-up button’s menu
rule: Put rarely used extra choices behind a 'Custom' item instead of adding controls, optionally with explanatory text.

quote: Within a popover or modal view, consider using a pop-up button instead of a disclosure indicator
rule: On iPad, in popovers, use a pop-up button rather than a detail view for small option sets.

quote: Use the standard row or grid layout whenever possible.
rule: Lay out collections as a plain row or grid, not a novel custom arrangement.

quote: Consider using a table instead of a collection for text.
rule: Present mainly textual items in a scrolling list or table, not a grid.

quote: Make it easy to choose an item.
rule: Every item in a collection must be easy to reach and select.

quote: Use adequate padding around images to keep focus or hover effects easy to see
rule: Pad collection images so focus and hover effects stay visible and items never overlap.

quote: Add custom interactions when necessary.
rule: Beyond select, edit and scroll, add further item actions only when the app needs them.

quote: Consider using animations to provide feedback when people insert, delete, or reorder items.
rule: Visibly mark items being inserted, removed or reordered, so the change can be followed.

quote: Use caution when making dynamic layout changes.
rule: On iOS avoid changing collection layout while people use it unless they asked.

quote: Populate the field with a meaningful default value from the list.
rule: Start a combo box with a sensible value from its list (not necessarily the first) rather than empty.

quote: Use an introductory label to let people know what types of items to expect.
rule: Put a label before every combo box describing what it holds.

quote: Generally, use title-style capitalization for labels and end them with a colon.
rule: Write field labels in title case followed by a colon (e.g. 'Font Size:').

quote: Provide relevant choices.
rule: Fill the list with the most likely values while still accepting typed custom values.

quote: Make sure list items aren’t wider than the text field.
rule: Size the combo box so no list item is truncated in its field.

quote: Choose a mark type based on the information you want to communicate about the data.
rule: Pick the chart form from the question it answers: bars to compare categories, parts of a whole or per-period totals, lines for change and trend over time, points for relations between two properties and for spotting outliers.

quote: Consider combining mark types when it adds clarity to your chart.
rule: Overlay a second mark kind when it helps, for example dots on a trend line so single readings stand out while the overall trend stays visible.

quote: Use a fixed or dynamic axis range depending on the meaning of your chart.
rule: Give an axis fixed bounds when its minimum and maximum mean something for every possible value (a battery level runs 0-100%), and let the bounds follow the data when values vary widely so the marks fill the plot.

quote: Define the value of the lower bound based on mark type and chart usage.
rule: Start a bar chart's value axis at zero so bar heights compare honestly, but let charts whose interesting differences lie far from zero (such as heart rate) start nearer the data.

quote: Prefer familiar sequences of values in the tick and grid-line labels for an axis.
rule: Label ticks with round, familiar steps such as 0, 5, 10 rather than offset steps like 1, 6, 11.

quote: Tailor the appearance of grid lines and labels to a chart’s use cases.
rule: Choose how many grid lines and axis labels to show from the chart's tasks: enough to estimate a value, few enough not to bury the data, and fewer still when people can inspect points directly.

quote: Write descriptions that help people understand what a chart does before they view it.
rule: Give every chart a title and labels that say what it shows and what it is for, so screen-reader users and everyone else know its purpose before exploring it.

quote: Summarize the main message of your chart to help make it approachable and useful for everyone.
rule: State the chart's key takeaway in text next to it (a title or subtitle such as the expected rain in the next hour) so nobody has to read the marks to get it.

quote: Establish a consistent visual hierarchy that helps communicate the relative importance of various chart elements.
rule: Make the data the most prominent part of a chart, with axes and descriptions present as supporting context that does not compete with it.

quote: In a compact environment, maximize the width of the plot area
rule: When space is tight, give the plot as much width as possible: keep vertical-axis labels short, move units into the title, and place long category names inside the plot where they hide nothing.

quote: Make every chart in your app accessible.
rule: Every chart must be usable with a screen reader, with names for its parts and values, not just a picture.

quote: Let people interact with the data when it makes sense, but don’t require interaction to reveal critical information.
rule: Interaction such as scrubbing to read a value may add detail, but the chart's essential information must be visible without any interaction.

quote: Make it easy for everyone to interact with a chart.
rule: When individual marks are too small to hit, make the whole plot area the target and let people sweep across it to read values.

quote: Make an interactive chart easy to navigate when using keyboard commands (including full keyboard access) or Switch Control.
rule: Give keyboard and switch users a logical, predictable route through a chart's values, for example moving along the X axis in order rather than jumping around.

quote: let people move focus among subsets of values instead of navigating through all individual data points
rule: For a large dataset, let keyboard focus step between groups of values first, instead of forcing people through every single point.

quote: Help people notice important changes in a chart.
rule: When marks or axes change, signal it by more than animation, including a screen-reader announcement, so people with reduced motion or no sight also notice.

quote: Align a chart with surrounding interface elements.
rule: Line a chart's leading edge up with the leading edge of the other content on the screen.

quote: You might also consider shifting the Y axis to the trailing side of the chart
rule: To keep that leading edge clean, put value-axis labels on the trailing side or on the trailing side of grid lines, and tie any floating label to its grid line with a tick.

quote: Avoid relying solely on color to differentiate between different pieces of data or communicate essential information in a chart.
rule: Distinguish chart series and essential values by shape, pattern or label as well as colour, e.g. two different point shapes for the two blood-pressure readings.

quote: Aid comprehension by adding visual separation between contiguous areas of color.
rule: Put a separator between adjacent coloured segments, such as the parts of a stacked bar, so each segment can be told apart.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Consider using Audio Graphs to give VoiceOver users more information about your chart.
rule: Adopt Apple's Audio Graphs sonification with a title and summary for VoiceOver.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: If you don’t use Audio Graphs, you need to provide an overview of the chart’s structure and purpose.
rule: Give screen-reader users an overview of each chart: its kind (bar, line ...), what each axis measures and the axis bounds.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: a chart often needs to offer an accessibility label for each important or interactive element.
rule: Decide per chart whether screen readers get one name per mark, per group of marks, or a single summary (fine for a small chart inside a button that opens a larger one), and give every interactive element its own name.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Write accessibility labels that support the purpose of your chart.
rule: Shape screen-reader names to the chart's job: summarise stretches when the overall shape matters (a route's climbs), name each bar when exact per-period values matter (daily steps).

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Prioritize clarity and comprehensiveness.
rule: In a mark's accessible name, give the context first (the date or place the value belongs to) and then the value, without repeating what the chart overview already says, such as the axis name.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Avoid using subjective terms.
rule: Describe data with actual numbers, not interpretive words like 'rapidly', 'gradually' or 'almost'.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Maximize clarity in data descriptions by avoiding potentially ambiguous formats and abbreviations.
rule: Spell out dates and units in descriptions: 'June 6' rather than '6/6', '60 minutes' or '60 meters' rather than '60m'.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Describe what the chart’s details represent, not what they look like.
rule: Name a series by what it stands for, not by its colour or shape, in accessible descriptions.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Be consistent throughout your app when referring to a specific axis.
rule: Mention axes in the same order in every description across the app, e.g. always X before Y.

section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
quote: Hide visible text labels for axes and ticks from assistive technologies.
rule: Leave visible axis and tick labels out of the screen-reader tree, since mark names and the overview already carry those values.

quote: In general, avoid requiring complex chart interactions in your watchOS app.
rule: On the watch, keep charts glanceable with only simple interaction.

quote: As you design your app, audit the accessibility of your interface.
rule: Audit every screen with an accessibility inspection tool to find problems and see how the app presents itself to assistive technology.

quote: You can also communicate how accessible your app is on the App Store using Accessibility Nutrition Labels.
rule: Declare accessibility support through App Store Accessibility Nutrition Labels.

quote: Support larger text sizes.
rule: Let people enlarge text and icons, ideally to at least twice the default size, and keep the interface working at that size.

quote: Use recommended defaults for custom type sizes.
rule: Follow the platform's default and minimum type sizes (macOS 13 pt default, 10 pt minimum).

quote: Bear in mind that font weight can also impact how easy text is to read.
rule: Set thin-weight fonts larger than the recommended sizes.

quote: Strive to meet color contrast minimum standards.
rule: Text and icons must reach WCAG AA contrast against their background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large (18 pt) or bold text.

quote: ensure it at least provides a higher contrast color scheme when the system setting Increase Contrast is turned on.
rule: When the desktop asks for higher contrast, switch to a scheme that meets the minimum contrast even if the default does not.

quote: If your app supports Dark Mode, make sure to check the minimum contrast in both light and dark appearances.
rule: Check contrast minimums in every appearance the app offers, light and dark alike.

quote: Prefer system-defined colors.
rule: Use the system's colours, which adapt to contrast and appearance settings.

quote: Convey information with more than color alone.
rule: Pair colour with a shape, icon or text whenever it signals a difference in function or a change of state.

quote: Consider allowing people to customize color schemes such as chart colors
rule: Consider letting people choose their own colours for things like chart series so they can pick ones they can tell apart.

quote: Describe your app’s interface and content for VoiceOver.
rule: Give every element and piece of content a description a screen reader can speak.

quote: Support text-based ways to enjoy audio and video.
rule: Never carry dialogue or vital information by sound alone: offer captions, subtitles, audio descriptions or transcripts as fits the media, and let people adjust how that text looks.

quote: Use haptics in addition to audio cues.
rule: Pair audio cues with matching haptic feedback on devices that have it.

quote: Augment audio cues with visual cues.
rule: Whenever a sound signals something (success, error, where to act), show a visible signal for it too.

quote: Offer sufficiently sized controls.
rule: Meet each platform's control size (macOS 28x28 pt default, 20x20 pt minimum).

quote: Consider spacing between controls as important as size.
rule: Leave about 12 pt around bezelled controls and 24 pt around borderless ones.

quote: Support simple gestures for common interactions.
rule: Use the simplest touch gesture for frequent actions and avoid multi-finger gestures.

quote: Offer alternatives to gestures.
rule: Every action reachable by a gesture (swipe, pinch, trackpad gesture) must also be reachable by an on-screen control or command.

quote: Let people use Voice Control to give guidance and enter information verbally.
rule: Name interface elements so voice-control software can address them by what people see and say.

quote: Integrate with Siri and Shortcuts to let people perform tasks using voice alone.
rule: Expose tasks to Siri and Shortcuts.

quote: Support mobility-related assistive technologies.
rule: Test the app with keyboard-only access, pointer and switch alternatives and screen readers, and label every element so they work.

quote: Let people use the keyboard alone to navigate and interact with your app.
rule: Every part of the app must be reachable and operable with the keyboard alone.

quote: Avoid overriding system-defined keyboard shortcuts
rule: Don't take over shortcuts the operating system or its accessibility features already define.

quote: Support Switch Control.
rule: Make every control reachable and operable by step-by-step element navigation so switch-access tools can drive the app.

quote: Keep actions simple and intuitive.
rule: Use the platform's familiar, consistent interactions rather than custom ones people must learn and remember.

quote: Minimize use of time-boxed interface elements.
rule: Avoid views or messages that close themselves on a timer; let people dismiss them with an explicit action.

quote: Consider offering difficulty accommodations in games.
rule: Offer adjustable difficulty in games.

quote: Let people control audio and video playback.
rule: Never autoplay audio or video without visible start and stop controls, and consider a setting that turns autoplay off everywhere.

quote: Allow people to opt out of flashing lights in video playback.
rule: Honour Apple's Dim Flashing Lights setting in video playback.

quote: Be cautious with fast-moving and blinking animations.
rule: Avoid fast or blinking motion, and when the desktop asks for reduced motion, cut automatic and repeating animation, zooming, scaling and peripheral movement.

quote: Replacing transitions in x-, y-, and z-axes with fades to avoid motion
rule: Under reduced motion, tighten springs, track gestures directly, use fades instead of sliding transitions and avoid blur and depth animation.

quote: Optimize your app’s UI for Assistive Access.
rule: Provide a streamlined layout for iOS Assistive Access.

quote: Identify the core functionality of your app and consider removing noncritical workflows and UI elements.
rule: In Assistive Access mode, drop non-essential workflows and elements.

quote: Break up multistep workflows so people can focus on a single interaction per screen.
rule: In Assistive Access mode, show one interaction per screen.

quote: Always ask for confirmation twice whenever people perform an action that’s difficult to recover from
rule: In Assistive Access mode, confirm hard-to-undo actions such as deleting a file twice.

quote: Prioritize comfort.
rule: Design spatial interfaces to avoid motion sickness and strain.

quote: Keep interface elements within a person’s field of view.
rule: Keep spatial UI in the field of view and prefer horizontal layouts.

quote: Reduce the speed and intensity of animated objects, particularly in someone’s peripheral vision.
rule: Slow down and soften animation in peripheral vision.

quote: Be gentle with camera and video motion
rule: Avoid camera motion that makes the surroundings seem to move uncontrolled.

quote: Avoid anchoring content to the wearer’s head
rule: Don't head-lock content.

quote: Minimize the need for large and repetitive gestures
rule: Avoid large repeated gestures in spatial apps.

quote: As much as possible, support drag and drop throughout your app.
rule: Support dragging and dropping content wherever people might try it, since they expect it to work everywhere.

quote: Offer alternative ways to accomplish drag-and-drop actions.
rule: Everything people can do by drag and drop must also be possible through menu commands or other non-drag means (e.g. Copy, then Paste or Move To).

quote: Determine when dragging and dropping content within your app results in a move or a copy.
rule: Dropping within the same container moves; dropping into a different container or another app copies; deviate only toward whichever outcome is least likely to lose data.

quote: Support multi-item drag and drop when it makes sense.
rule: Let people select several items and drag them together as one group.

quote: Prefer letting people undo a drag-and-drop operation.
rule: Make every drop undoable with Undo, returning everything to the state before the drag.

quote: asking for confirmation before completing a drag-and-drop operation that can’t be undone.
rule: When a drop can't be undone (e.g. into a write-only folder), ask for confirmation before completing it.

quote: it might make sense to provide a way to reverse the results of drag and drop when people can’t undo it.
rule: Where Undo is impossible, offer another way to reverse the drop's effect, such as cancelling the share it started.

quote: Consider offering multiple versions of dragged content, ordered from highest to lowest fidelity.
rule: Offer dragged content in several formats from richest to plainest (native object, then vector, then lossless image, then lossy image) so the destination takes the best it accepts.

quote: Consider supporting spring loading.
rule: Let buttons and segmented controls activate when people hold dragged content over them, so they can drop into the view the control opens.

quote: Display a drag image as soon as people drag a selection about three points.
rule: Start a drag, and show an image of what is being dragged, once the pointer has moved a few points with the button held, and keep it under the pointer until the drop.

quote: It works well to create a translucent representation of the content people are dragging.
rule: Make the drag image translucent so destinations show through it.

quote: If it adds clarity, modify the drag image to help people predict the result of a drag-and-drop operation.
rule: Let the drag image preview the result (for instance the size a photo will take in the document, or a grouped stack with a count for several items), without changing it constantly or radically.

quote: Show people whether a destination can accept dragged content.
rule: Show an insertion point or highlight only over destinations that accept the dragged content, and nothing or an explicit 'not allowed' sign over those that don't.

quote: Display highlighting or other visual cues only while the content is positioned above the destination
rule: Remove a destination's highlight as soon as the drag leaves it, and when several destinations are possible, highlight only the one under the pointer.

quote: When people drop an item on an invalid destination, or when dropping fails, provide visual feedback.
rule: When a drop is refused or fails, show it, for instance by sending the item back to where it came from.

quote: Scroll the contents of a destination when necessary.
rule: Auto-scroll a scrolling destination while content is dragged near its edge, and stop once the drag leaves the container.

quote: When there’s a choice, pick the richest version of dropped content your app can accept.
rule: On a drop, take the richest offered format the app understands (the native chart object rather than its picture).

quote: Extract only the relevant portion of dropped content if necessary.
rule: Take only the part of dropped content the destination needs, e.g. name and address from a contact dropped on a recipient field.

quote: When a physical keyboard is attached, check for the Option key at drop time.
rule: Read the modifier at the moment of the drop: Option held then turns a same-container move into a copy, and releasing it before the drop keeps it a move.

quote: Provide feedback when dropped content needs time to transfer.
rule: When dropped content takes time to arrive, show progress and a placeholder where it will appear.

quote: Provide feedback when dropped content initiates a task or action.
rule: When a drop starts a task such as printing, show that it began and report its progress.

quote: Apply appropriate styling to dropped text.
rule: Keep dropped text's formatting when the destination supports the same styles; otherwise give it the destination's style.

quote: After a drop, maintain the content’s selection state in the destination, updating it in the source as needed.
rule: After a drop, leave the dropped content selected at the destination and clear the selection in the source (copy within a container or any drop to another container).

quote: Let people perform multiple simultaneous drag activities.
rule: On iPad, let people add items to a drag in progress with more fingers.

quote: Consider letting people drag content from your app into the Finder.
rule: Let people drag content out to the file manager, saved in a format the app can open again (an event as an .ics file, text as a clipping).

quote: Let people drag selected content from an inactive window without first making the window active.
rule: Allow dragging a selection out of an inactive window without bringing that window to the front.

quote: When possible, let people drag individual items from an inactive window without affecting an existing background selection.
rule: Dragging an unselected item from an inactive window must leave that window's existing selection unchanged.

quote: Consider displaying a badge during multi-item drag operations.
rule: Show a count of the dragged items during a multi-item drag, and lower it when a destination accepts only some of them.

quote: Consider changing the pointer appearance to indicate what will happen when people drop content.
rule: Change the pointer during a drag to show the outcome: copy, link, item will disappear, or not allowed.

quote: As much as possible, let people select and drag content with a single motion.
rule: Let one press-and-drag both select an item and start dragging it, without a pause in between.

quote: When possible, launch your app to handle content that people drop into empty space.
rule: Open a window to handle content dropped into empty space.

quote: Create a recognizable, highly simplified design.
rule: Draw interface icons simply with familiar metaphors.

quote: Maintain visual consistency across all interface icons in your app.
rule: Keep size, detail, stroke and perspective uniform across icons.

quote: In general, match the weights of interface icons and adjacent text.
rule: Match icon stroke weight to adjacent text weight.

quote: If necessary, add padding to a custom interface icon to achieve optical alignment.
rule: Pad asymmetric icons so they look optically centred.

quote: Provide a selected-state version of an interface icon only if necessary.
rule: Draw a separate selected icon only when the component does not restyle it.

quote: Use inclusive images.
rule: Choose icons whose meaning reads across cultures and languages, with gender-neutral figures where people are shown.

quote: Include text in your design only when it’s essential for conveying meaning.
rule: Put letters in an icon only when they are the clearest way to show the idea (text formatting), localise those letters, and supply a mirrored version of icons that suggest lines of text for right-to-left languages.

quote: If you create a custom interface icon, use a vector format like PDF or SVG.
rule: Ship custom icons as vectors.

quote: Provide alternative text labels for custom interface icons.
rule: Give every meaningful icon an accessible name that screen readers speak.

quote: Avoid using replicas of Apple hardware products.
rule: Don't draw Apple hardware in icons.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use the conventional picture for each editing action wherever it appears: scissors for Cut, stacked pages for Copy, a page on a clipboard for Paste, a check for Done, an x for Cancel, a bin for Delete, back/forward U-turn arrows for Undo/Redo, square with pencil for Compose, two overlapping squares with plus for Duplicate, pencil for Rename, folder for Move to, paperclip for Attach, plus for Add, ellipsis for More.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use a check in a circle for Select, an x for Deselect and a bin for Delete in selection modes.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use the standard formatting pictures: raised/lowered small letters for Superscript/Subscript, B, I and U letterforms for Bold, Italic, Underline, and line-alignment pictures for Align Left, Center, Justified, Align Right.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use a magnifying glass for Search, a page with a magnifier for Find, and a funnel of shortening lines for Filter.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use a box with an upward arrow for Share/Export and a printer for Print.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use a person in a circle for Account, User and Profile.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use thumbs up for Like and thumbs down for Dislike.

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use stacked layers with the top or bottom layer filled for Bring to Front/Send to Back (three layers) and Bring Forward/Send Backward (two layers).

quote: For icons to represent common actions in Menus, Toolbars, Buttons, and other places in interfaces across Apple platforms, you can use these SF Symbols.
rule: Use an alarm clock for Alarm, an archive box for Archive and a calendar page for Calendar.

quote: If your macOS app can use a custom document type, you can create a document icon to represent it.
rule: Draw document icons (folded-corner page) for custom file types.

quote: Design simple images that clearly communicate the document type.
rule: Keep document icon art simple with few distinct colours, legible down to 16 px.

quote: Designing a single, expressive image for the background fill can be a great way to help people understand and recognize a document type.
rule: Consider a single expressive background fill for a document icon.

quote: Consider reducing complexity in the small versions of your document icon.
rule: Simplify small document icon sizes.

quote: Avoid placing important content in the top-right corner of your background fill.
rule: Keep the folded corner clear and supply the listed background sizes.

quote: If a familiar object can convey a document’s type or its connection with your app, consider creating a center image that depicts it.
rule: Add a half-size centre image of a familiar object to a document icon.

quote: Define a margin that measures about 10% of the image canvas and keep most of the image within it.
rule: Keep a centre image within a 10% margin.

quote: Specify a succinct term if it helps people understand your document type.
rule: When a file type's extension is unfamiliar, label its document icon with a short descriptive word instead (e.g. 'scene' rather than 'scn').

quote: Use a toggle to help people choose between two opposing values that affect the state of content or a view.
rule: Use a toggle only to switch something between two opposite states; for picking from a list or other actions use another control, such as a pop-up button.

quote: Clearly identify the setting, view, or content the toggle affects.
rule: Make it clear what each toggle turns on or off, from its context or from a label stating the setting.

quote: If you use a button that behaves like a toggle, you generally use an interface icon that communicates its purpose
rule: A button that acts as a toggle shows an icon for what it does and changes its appearance, such as its background, to show whether it is on.

quote: Make sure the visual differences in a toggle’s state are obvious.
rule: Make on and off clearly different by fill, shape or a mark such as a check or dot, never by colour alone.

quote: Use the switch toggle style only in a list row.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, use switches only in list rows.

quote: Change the default color of a switch only if necessary.
rule: Keep the default green switch colour unless needed.

quote: Outside of a list, use a button that behaves like a toggle, not a switch.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, outside lists use toggle buttons instead of switches.

quote: Avoid supplying a label that explains the button’s purpose.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, give toggle buttons no visible explanatory label.

quote: Use switches, checkboxes, and radio buttons in the window body, not the window frame.
rule: Place switches, checkboxes and radio buttons in the window's content, never in a toolbar or status bar.

quote: Prefer a switch for settings that you want to emphasize.
rule: Use a switch for a setting with large scope, such as one that turns a whole group of settings on or off; use checkboxes for individual settings.

quote: Within a grouped form, consider using a mini switch to control the setting in a single row.
rule: Use mini switches in grouped-form rows and regular ones for parent settings.

quote: In general, don’t replace a checkbox with a switch.
rule: Where the interface already uses a checkbox for a setting, keep the checkbox rather than swapping in a switch.

quote: Use a checkbox instead of a switch if you need to present a hierarchy of settings.
rule: Show dependent settings as checkboxes aligned on their leading edge, with subordinate ones indented under the checkbox that governs them.

quote: Consider using radio buttons if you need to present a set of more than two mutually exclusive options.
rule: When a choice has more than two mutually exclusive options, use radio buttons, each with its own label, rather than a checkbox.

quote: Consider using a label to introduce a group of checkboxes if their relationship isn’t clear.
rule: Introduce a group of checkboxes with a label describing the set when their relation isn't obvious, its baseline aligned with the first checkbox.

quote: Accurately reflect a checkbox’s state in its appearance.
rule: A checkbox that controls subordinate checkboxes shows a mixed state when they differ, and on/off when they all agree.

quote: If you need to show that a setting or item has a mixed state, consider using a checkbox instead.
rule: Don't use a radio button's mixed state; show mixed state with a checkbox, or express states as more radio buttons.

quote: Prefer a set of radio buttons to present mutually exclusive options.
rule: Use radio buttons for exactly-one-of choices and checkboxes when several may be chosen.

quote: Avoid listing too many radio buttons in a set.
rule: Keep a radio group to about five options; beyond that, use a pop-up button.

quote: To present a single setting that can be on or off, prefer a checkbox.
rule: Use one checkbox for a single on/off setting; use a pair of labelled radio buttons only when a checkbox would not make the two states clear.

quote: Use consistent spacing when you display radio buttons horizontally.
rule: In a horizontal radio group, give every option the width of the longest label so spacing is even.

quote: Not every collection of data needs to be displayed in a chart.
rule: When people only need the data itself rather than insight into it, show it as a scrollable, searchable, sortable list or table instead of a chart.

quote: Use a chart when you want to highlight important information about a dataset.
rule: Use a chart only when it makes a point about the data, and make clear what people can learn from it.

quote: Keep a chart simple, letting people choose when they want additional details.
rule: Keep charts sparse and reveal more data or functions on request, e.g. by letting people pick a level of detail or a subset.

quote: Make every chart in your app accessible.
rule: Give every chart screen-reader names for its values and parts and accessible elements for its interactions.

quote: In general, prefer using common chart types.
rule: Prefer familiar chart types such as bar and line charts that people already know how to read.

quote: If you need to create a chart that presents data in a novel way, help people learn how to interpret the chart.
rule: When a chart presents data in an unfamiliar form, show people how to read it, for example by introducing its parts one at a time.

quote: Examine the data from multiple levels or perspectives to find details you can display to enhance the chart.
rule: Look at the data at overall, subset and single-point levels to find totals, averages, useful subsets or notable values worth showing.

quote: Aid comprehension by adding descriptive text to the chart.
rule: Add titles, subtitles, annotations or a one-line summary headline that state the chart's main takeaway.

quote: Although a descriptive headline or summary can make a chart more accessible, it doesn’t take the place of accessibility labels.
rule: A visible summary does not replace accessible names for the chart's elements; provide both.

quote: Match the size of a chart to its functionality, topic, and level of detail.
rule: Size a chart to what it must show and support: large enough for its labels and interaction, small only for glanceable previews that open a fuller version.

quote: Prefer consistency across multiple charts, deviating only when you need to highlight differences.
rule: Give charts with similar purposes the same type and style across the app, changing them only to signal a real difference.

quote: Maintain continuity among multiple charts that use the same data.
rule: Charts of the same dataset (a summary and its expanded view) keep the same chart type, colours, annotations, layout and wording.

quote: Aim to provide default settings that give the best experience to the largest number of people.
rule: Choose defaults that suit most people so the app works well without any adjustment, detecting what can be detected (e.g. performance) instead of asking.

quote: Minimize the number of settings you offer.
rule: Offer as few settings as possible.

quote: Make settings available in ways people expect.
rule: Open settings by the platform's usual route, such as Command-Comma on a Mac (or Esc in a game).

quote: Avoid using settings to ask for setup information you can get in other ways.
rule: Don't ask in settings for anything the app can detect itself, such as whether the desktop is in dark mode.

quote: Respect people’s systemwide settings and avoid including redundant versions of them in your custom settings area.
rule: Follow system-wide preferences (accessibility, scrolling, authentication) and don't duplicate them as app settings.

quote: Put general, infrequently changed settings in your custom settings area.
rule: Reserve the settings window for general options people rarely change, such as window configuration, key mappings or account options.

quote: When possible, prefer letting people modify task-specific options without going to your settings area.
rule: Put options that affect only the current view (show/hide parts, sort order, filters) in that view, not in the settings window.

quote: Add only the most rarely changed options to the system-provided Settings app.
rule: Add app options to the system Settings app only for the rarest ones, with a button that opens it.

quote: Include a settings item in the App menu.
rule: Put a Settings… item in the app menu that opens the settings window.

quote: Avoid adding settings buttons to a window’s toolbar
rule: Don't put a settings button in a window's toolbar; keep that space for frequent commands.

quote: If you provide document-level options, add this item to your app’s File menu.
rule: Put a command for document-level options in the File menu.

quote: Dim a settings window’s minimize and maximize buttons.
rule: Disable minimise and maximise on the settings window; it sizes itself to the current pane.

quote: In your settings window, use a noncustomizable toolbar that remains visible and always indicates the active toolbar button.
rule: Switch settings panes with a fixed, always-visible toolbar that marks the active pane.

quote: Update the window’s title to reflect the currently visible pane.
rule: Title the settings window with the current pane's name, or '<App name> Settings' when there is only one pane.

quote: Restore the most recently viewed pane.
rule: Reopen the settings window on the pane people last used.

quote: consider making a small number of essential options available at the bottom of the main view
rule: On the watch, put a few options at the bottom of the main view or in a More menu.

quote: When your app runs in other platforms, consider using a modal view to present supplementary content
rule: On non-Mac Apple platforms use a modal view instead of a panel.

quote: Use a panel to give people quick access to important controls or information related to the content they’re working with.
rule: Use a floating auxiliary window for controls or details that act on the current document or selection.

quote: Consider using a panel to present inspector functionality.
rule: Show an inspector, whose contents follow the current selection, in a panel or split-view pane; show an Info window, whose contents stay fixed, as a regular window.

quote: Prefer simple adjustment controls in a panel.
rule: Fill panels with direct adjustment controls such as sliders and steppers, avoiding text entry and select-then-act controls.

quote: Write a brief title that describes the panel’s purpose.
rule: Give each panel a title bar with a short noun or noun phrase in title case, e.g. 'Fonts', 'Inspector'.

quote: Show and hide panels appropriately.
rule: Bring all of an app's open panels to the front when the app becomes active and hide them all when it becomes inactive.

quote: Avoid including panels in the Window menu’s documents list.
rule: List panels in the Window menu only as show/hide commands, never among the document windows.

quote: In general, avoid making a panel’s minimize button available.
rule: Give panels no active minimise button.

quote: Refer to panels by title in your interface and in help documentation.
rule: Name menu commands for panels by the panel's title without the word 'panel', e.g. 'Show Fonts', 'Show Inspector'.

quote: it’s generally best to refer to a panel by its title or — when it adds clarity — by appending window to the title.
rule: In help text, call a panel by its title, adding 'window' when the title alone is unclear ('Fonts window'), never introducing 'panel' as a kind of window.

quote: Prefer standard panels.
rule: Use dark translucent HUD panels only in media apps, where a standard panel would hide content, and with no controls.

quote: Maintain one panel style when your app switches modes.
rule: Keep the same panel style when leaving or entering full screen.

quote: Use color sparingly in HUDs.
rule: Use little colour in HUDs.

quote: Keep HUDs small.
rule: Keep floating overlay panels small, never covering the content they adjust or competing with it for attention.

quote: Launch instantly.
rule: Show a usable first screen within a couple of seconds of starting.

quote: If the platform requires it, provide a launch screen.
rule: Provide a launch screen on iOS, iPadOS and tvOS.

quote: If you need a splash screen, consider displaying it at the beginning of your onboarding flow.
rule: If the app has a splash screen, show it at the start of onboarding or right after launch completes, not as a delay before launch.

quote: Restore the previous state when your app restarts so people can continue where they left off.
rule: On restart, bring back windows with their size, position and state, and views at their last scroll position and location.

quote: Downplay the launch experience.
rule: Keep launch screens plain.

quote: Design a launch screen that’s nearly identical to the first screen of your app or game.
rule: Make the launch screen match the first screen.

quote: Avoid including text on your launch screen, even if your first screen displays text.
rule: Put no text on the launch screen.

quote: Don’t advertise.
rule: Put no branding on the launch screen.

quote: Launch in the appropriate orientation.
rule: Launch in the device's current orientation.

quote: In a live-viewing app, consider automatically starting playback soon after people start the app.
rule: Autostart live TV playback.

quote: Consider launching in the Shared Space even if your app is fully immersive.
rule: Start in the Shared Space before going immersive.

quote: The most effective feedback tends to match the significance of the information to the way it’s delivered.
rule: Match how intrusive feedback is to how much it matters: show status passively where people can look, and interrupt only for things like possible data loss.

quote: Make sure all feedback is accessible.
rule: Deliver feedback through more than one channel (text, colour, sound) so people get it with sound off, eyes away or a screen reader.

quote: Consider integrating status feedback into your interface.
rule: Show status (last update, unread count) next to the things it describes so people see it without acting or leaving their context.

quote: Use alerts to deliver critical — and ideally actionable — information.
rule: Use alerts only for critical, preferably actionable information, not for routine or minor news.

quote: Warn people when they initiate a task that can cause data loss that’s unexpected and irreversible.
rule: Warn before an action that will lose data irreversibly in a way people might not expect.

quote: don’t warn people when data loss is the expected result of their action.
rule: Don't warn when losing the data is the obvious, intended result of the action, such as moving a file to the bin.

quote: When it makes sense, confirm that a significant action or task has completed.
rule: Confirm completion only for significant tasks (such as a payment); for ordinary actions report only failures.

quote: Show people when a command can’t be carried out and help them understand why.
rule: When a command can't run, say so and explain why.

quote: Avoid displaying an indeterminate progress indicator — such as a loading indicator — in a watchOS app.
rule: On the watch, notify on completion instead of showing a spinner.

quote: Make printing discoverable.
rule: Put a Print… command in the File menu (in iOS, a toolbar button that opens the share sheet).

quote: consider making it an optional button that people can add when they customize the toolbar.
rule: If the window has a toolbar, offer a Print button as an optional item people can add when customising the toolbar rather than a default one.

quote: Present a printing option only when it’s possible.
rule: Disable the Print command (and any custom print button) when there is nothing to print or no printer is available.

quote: Present relevant printing options.
rule: Offer page range, copies and two-sided printing through the system's print dialog, and only when the printer supports them.

quote: consider creating a custom category for the print panel.
rule: Add app-specific print options as an extra section in the print dialog, named after the app.

quote: If your app supports document-specific page settings, consider presenting a page setup dialog.
rule: Offer a Page Setup dialog for per-document paper size, orientation and scaling when the app has document-specific page settings.

quote: avoid implementing features the system already provides.
rule: Don't duplicate options the system print dialog already has, such as orientation or reverse order.

quote: Make sure interdependencies between options are clear.
rule: Show when one print option rules out another, e.g. disable 'transparencies' when two-sided is chosen.

quote: Separate advanced features from frequently used features.
rule: Hide rarely used print options behind a disclosure control labelled 'Advanced Options'.

quote: Consider letting people preview the effect of a setting.
rule: Show a preview thumbnail that updates as print settings change.

quote: Consider storing modified settings with the document.
rule: Remember changed print settings with the document, or at least until it is closed.

quote: Prefer keeping a box relatively small in comparison with its containing view.
rule: Keep a grouping box clearly smaller than its window; a box that nearly fills it no longer reads as a group.

quote: Consider using padding and alignment to communicate additional grouping within a box.
rule: Show sub-groups inside a box with spacing and alignment rather than nested boxes.

quote: Provide a succinct introductory title if it helps clarify the box’s contents.
rule: Title a box when the relation between its contents needs explaining; the title also tells screen-reader users what follows.

quote: If you need a title, write a brief phrase that describes the contents.
rule: Write box titles as short phrases in sentence case without ending punctuation, except a colon in a settings pane.

quote: Make it easy to change rankings.
rule: Let people change an item's rating directly in the list, without opening a separate edit screen.

quote: If you replace the star with a custom symbol, make sure that its purpose is clear.
rule: Use stars for ratings; use another symbol only if it clearly reads as a rating scale.

quote: Be consistent when responding to mouse and trackpad gestures.
rule: A mouse or trackpad gesture such as swiping between pages must do the same thing in every view of the app that it does elsewhere on the system.

quote: Avoid redefining systemwide trackpad gestures.
rule: Never capture or reassign gestures the desktop keeps for itself (showing the Dock, Mission Control, switching desktops); the app leaves them to the system, which users may have remapped.

quote: Provide a consistent experience in your app, whether people are using gestures, eyes, a pointing device, or a keyboard.
rule: Every task can be done with the mouse or with the keyboard alone, reaching the same result, so users can switch input mid-task without learning a second interaction model.

quote: Let people use the pointer to reveal and hide controls that automatically minimize or fade out.
rule: Controls that hide themselves (for example playback controls over full-screen video) reappear when the pointer moves over their area or over the content, and hide again once it leaves.

quote: Provide a consistent experience when people press and hold a modifier key while interacting with objects in your app.
rule: A modifier held during an interaction (e.g. the copy modifier while dragging) alters the outcome in exactly the same way whichever input device performs the drag.

quote: Allow multiple selection in custom views when necessary.
rule: Custom item views on iPad support rubber-band selection by dragging the pointer across items.

quote: Distinguish between pointer and finger input only if it provides value.
rule: On iPad, treat pointer and finger input differently only when the pointer adds real precision, such as clicking an exact seek point.

quote: Use clear, simple images to create custom accessories.
rule: iPad pointer accessory images stay minimal so their meaning reads at small size.

quote: Consider using the accessory transition to signal a change in an element’s state or behavior.
rule: On iPad, morph the pointer accessory (e.g. plus to prohibited sign) when an action becomes unavailable.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
quote: When possible, support the system-provided content effects.
rule: iPad elements adopt the system pointer content effects instead of inventing their own.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
quote: Use highlight for a small element that has a transparent background.
rule: On iPad, pick highlight for small transparent elements, lift for small opaque ones and hover for large ones.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
quote: Prefer the system-provided pointer appearances for standard buttons and text-entry areas.
rule: iPad buttons and text areas keep the stock pointer shapes.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
