quote: Add padding around interactive elements to create comfortable hit regions.
rule: iPad hit regions extend about 12 pt beyond bezelled elements and about 24 pt beyond unbezelled ones.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
quote: Create contiguous hit regions for custom bar buttons.
rule: Adjacent iPad bar buttons have touching hit regions so the pointer never flickers back to its default shape between them.

section: Platform considerations > iPadOS > Standard pointers and effects
quote: Specify the corner radius of a nonstandard element that receives the lift effect.
rule: Non-rectangular iPad elements using lift declare their radius so the pointer morphs to their outline.

quote: Prefer system-provided pointer effects for custom elements that behave like standard elements.
rule: An iPad custom control that acts like a stock one gets the stock pointer effect so it does not look broken.

quote: Use pointer effects in consistent ways throughout your app.
rule: On iPad, similar areas (e.g. every drawing canvas) get the same pointer treatment.

quote: Avoid creating gratuitous pointer and content effects.
rule: iPad pointer effects exist only when they tell the user something useful, never as decoration.

quote: Keep custom pointer shapes simple.
rule: A custom iPad pointer shape must be understood at a glance as the action available.

quote: Consider enhancing the pointer experience by displaying custom annotations that provide useful information.
rule: On iPad, the pointer may carry live readouts such as X/Y values over a graph or dimensions while resizing.

quote: Avoid displaying instructional text with a pointer.
rule: iPad pointers never carry how-to text; the interface itself should make the action obvious.

quote: Consider the interplay of shadow, scale, and element spacing when defining custom hover effects.
rule: On iPad, scale an element on hover only when it has room to grow, and never add shadow without scale.

quote: macOS supports a wide range of standard mouse and trackpad interactions that people can customize.
rule: Give clicks and gestures their standard meanings: primary click selects or activates, secondary click opens the context menu, wheel or two-finger scroll moves content in any direction, pinch or smart zoom changes zoom, a rotate gesture rotates content, and swiping navigates back and forward between pages.

quote: Mission Control (double-tap the mouse with two fingers or swipe up on the trackpad with three or four fingers)
rule: On a Mac, leave the system gestures (Mission Control, App Exposé, Notification Center, Launchpad, Show Desktop, switching full-screen spaces, lookup and force-click Quick Look, tap to click) to macOS and never bind app actions to them.

quote: your app can use to communicate the interactive state of an interface element or the result of a drag operation.
rule: Set the pointer shape to the one that matches what will happen: arrow by default, I-beam over editable or selectable text, open hand over pannable content and closed hand while panning, crosshair for precise rectangle selection, pointing hand over links, directional resize arrows over resizable edges, and the not-allowed shape when a dragged item cannot be dropped there.

quote: Appears when pressing the Option key during a drag operation.
rule: On a Mac, a drag shows the copy pointer while Option is held, the alias/link pointer while Option-Command is held, the disappearing-item pointer when the drop will remove the item, and the context-menu pointer while Control is held over content that has one.

quote: Make buttons easy for people to use.
rule: Leave clear space between a button and neighbouring controls or content so it reads as a separate target and is easy to hit with any input.

quote: As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt
rule: Button hit regions are at least 44x44 pt (60x60 pt in visionOS).

quote: Always include a press state for a custom button.
rule: Every button, including custom-drawn ones, shows a distinct pressed state while the mouse button or key is held so the press visibly registers.

quote: In general, use a button that has a prominent visual style for the most likely action in a view.
rule: Mark the action users are most likely to take in a view with the prominent button style and leave the others in the plain style.

quote: Keep the number of prominent buttons to one or two per view.
rule: A view never shows more than two prominent-style buttons at once.

quote: Use style — not size — to visually distinguish the preferred choice among multiple options.
rule: Buttons offered together as alternatives are the same size; the preferred one is set apart only by a more prominent style.

quote: Avoid applying a similar color to button labels and content layer backgrounds.
rule: Button label colour must not echo the colour of the content behind it; use monochrome labels over colourful content.

quote: Ensure that each button clearly communicates its purpose.
rule: Each button's icon, text or both must tell the user what it will do before they press it.

quote: In macOS and visionOS, the system displays a tooltip after people hover over a button for a moment.
rule: Buttons, especially icon-only ones, show a short tooltip describing their action after the pointer rests on them briefly.

quote: Try to associate familiar actions with familiar icons.
rule: Common actions such as share, delete or add use the icon people already associate with them, the same one everywhere in the app.

quote: If it makes sense to use an icon in your button, consider using an existing or customized SF Symbols.
rule: Button icons come from SF Symbols, stock or customised.

quote: Consider using text when a short label communicates more clearly than an icon.
rule: Choose a text label over an icon whenever a couple of words explain the action better than a picture.

quote: Using title-style capitalization, consider starting the label with a verb to help convey the button’s action
rule: Button text is a few words in title case, normally beginning with the verb for the action, e.g. 'Add to Cart'.

quote: Assign the primary role to the button people are most likely to choose.
rule: In a dialog, sheet or alert, make the likeliest choice the default button so Return activates it and closes the dialog.

quote: Don’t assign the primary role to a button that performs a destructive action, even if that action is the most likely choice.
rule: A button that deletes or discards data is never the default (Return) button, even when it is the expected choice.

quote: Configure a button to display an activity indicator when you need to provide feedback about an action that doesn’t instantly complete.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, a button whose action takes time shows a spinner and may switch to a progressive label such as 'Checking out…'.

quote: Use a flexible-height push button only when you need to display tall or variable height content.
rule: Use the taller push-button variant only for two-line text or tall icons; otherwise the standard height.

quote: Append a trailing ellipsis to the title when a push button opens another window, view, or app.
rule: A button whose action needs more input in another window, dialog or app ends its title with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Edit…'; one that acts immediately has none.

quote: Consider supporting spring loading.
rule: With a Force Touch trackpad, let a force click while dragging items over a button activate it without dropping them.

quote: The buttons appear in close proximity to their associated view — usually within or beneath it — so people know which view the buttons affect.
rule: Buttons that act on one view, such as adding or removing table rows, sit directly inside or under that view so their target is unambiguous.

quote: Use square buttons in a view, not in the window frame.
rule: View-attached add/remove buttons never go in the toolbar or status bar; toolbar commands use toolbar items.

quote: Prefer using a symbol in a square button.
rule: View-attached add/remove buttons carry an icon (plus, minus, etc.) rather than a text title.

quote: Avoid using labels to introduce square buttons.
rule: Do not put a caption beside view-attached add/remove buttons; their position next to the view explains them.

quote: Use the system-provided help button to display your help documentation.
rule: Open help from the standard round question-mark help button rather than a custom-looking control.

quote: When possible, open the help topic that’s related to the current context.
rule: A help button opens the help topic about the dialog or pane it sits in, and falls back to the help's top page only when no specific topic exists.

quote: Include no more than one help button per window.
rule: A window contains at most one help button.

quote: Position help buttons where people expect to find them.
rule: Place the help button in a dialog with OK/Cancel at the bottom corner opposite those buttons and aligned with them; in a dialog without dismiss buttons or in a settings window or pane, at the lower-left or lower-right corner.

quote: Use a help button within a view, not in the window frame.
rule: The help button lives inside the content area, never in the toolbar or status bar.

quote: Avoid displaying text that introduces a help button.
rule: Do not caption the help button; the question mark is self-explanatory.

quote: Use an image button in a view, not in the window frame.
rule: Picture-only buttons belong in the content area; a toolbar uses toolbar items instead.

quote: Include about 10 pixels of padding between the edges of the image and the button edges.
rule: Image buttons keep roughly 10 px between the picture and the clickable edge.

quote: In general, avoid including a system-provided border in an image button
rule: Image buttons are drawn without the system border.

quote: If you need to include a label, position it below the image button.
rule: When an image button needs a caption, the caption goes underneath the image.

quote: In general, buttons that contain text don’t need to display a tooltip because the button’s descriptive label communicates what it does.
rule: In visionOS, only buttons without text need a look-triggered tooltip.

quote: Prefer buttons that have a discernible background shape and fill.
rule: visionOS buttons sit on a filled shape (thin material over glass, glass when floating) except inside toolbars, menus, alerts and ornaments.

quote: Avoid creating a custom button that uses a white background fill and black text or icons.
rule: In visionOS, white-fill black-label styling is reserved for the toggled-on state.

quote: In general, prefer circular or capsule-shape buttons.
rule: visionOS buttons are round or capsule-shaped, and a lone button is a capsule.

quote: Provide enough space around a button to make it easy for people to look at it.
rule: visionOS button centres are at least 60 pt apart, and small or mini buttons are not stacked in rows.

quote: Choose the right shape if you need to display text-labeled buttons in a stack or row.
rule: In visionOS, stacked text buttons are rounded rectangles and buttons in a row are capsules.

quote: Use standard controls to take advantage of the audible feedback sounds people already know.
rule: visionOS relies on the stock button sounds for feedback because it has no haptics.

quote: Use a toolbar to place buttons in the corners.
rule: On Apple Watch, corner buttons go in the toolbar.

quote: Prefer buttons that span the width of the screen for primary actions in your app.
rule: On Apple Watch, primary actions use full-width buttons; two side-by-side buttons share one height.

quote: Use toolbar buttons to provide either navigation to related areas or contextual actions for the view’s content.
rule: On Apple Watch, toolbar buttons hold navigation or secondary actions for the view.

quote: Use the same height for vertical stacks of one- and two-line text buttons.
rule: On Apple Watch, a vertical stack of text buttons uses one shared height.

quote: Provide concise, informative notifications.
rule: A desktop notification carries one useful piece of information that can be taken in at a glance.

quote: Avoid sending multiple notifications for the same thing, even if someone hasn’t responded.
rule: Post at most one notification per event; never repeat it because the user has not reacted.

quote: Avoid sending a notification that tells people to perform specific tasks within your app.
rule: Notifications report something; they do not give the user instructions to carry out later in the app.

quote: Use an alert — not a notification — to display an error message.
rule: Errors are reported in an alert dialog (or in the window), never through a desktop notification.

quote: Handle notifications gracefully when your app is in the foreground.
rule: While the app's window is frontmost, do not post a desktop notification; fold the news into the open view quietly, e.g. add the new item to the list or bump a count.

quote: Avoid including sensitive, personal, or confidential information in a notification.
rule: Notification text contains no passwords, private message bodies, financial or health details, since bystanders may see it.

quote: Create a short title if it provides context for the notification content.
rule: Give a notification a brief, specific title (headline, event name, subject); when only a generic title such as 'New Document' is possible, omit it and let the app name show.

quote: Use title-style capitalization and no ending punctuation.
rule: Notification titles are in title case with no full stop at the end.

quote: Write succinct, easy-to-read notification content.
rule: Notification body text is short, written as complete sentences in sentence case with normal punctuation.

quote: don’t truncate your message — the system does this automatically when necessary.
rule: Pass the full notification text and let the system shorten it; never cut it off or add an ellipsis yourself.

quote: Provide generically descriptive text to display when notification previews aren’t available.
rule: Supply a short, non-revealing summary in sentence case (e.g. 'New comment', 'Reminder') for when the system hides notification content.

quote: Avoid including your app name or icon.
rule: Do not repeat the app's name or icon in a notification's text; the system already shows which app sent it.

quote: Consider providing a sound to supplement your notifications.
rule: A notification may play a sound, either a system alert sound or a short, distinctive custom one.

quote: don’t rely on it to communicate important information, because people may not hear it.
rule: Anything important in a notification must also be shown as text; sound only adds to it.

quote: Provide beneficial actions that make sense in the context of your notification.
rule: Notification buttons offer quick, common tasks that save opening the app, such as Snooze for a reminder.

quote: For each button, use a short, title-case term or phrase that clearly describes the result of the action.
rule: Each notification button label is a brief title-case phrase naming what happens, without the app name, short enough to survive translation without truncation.

quote: Avoid providing an action that merely opens your app.
rule: Do not add an 'Open' button to a notification; clicking the notification itself opens the related content.

quote: Prefer nondestructive actions.
rule: Notification buttons avoid destructive actions; if one is unavoidable, the notification gives enough context to know exactly what will be lost and the action is marked destructive.

quote: Provide a simple, recognizable interface icon for each notification action.
rule: Each notification action gets a simple SF Symbol beside its title.

quote: Use a badge only to show people how many unread notifications they have.
rule: The app icon's badge (Dock or taskbar) only ever shows the count of unread items, never weather, dates, prices or scores.

quote: Make sure badging isn’t the only method you use to communicate essential information.
rule: Essential news shown by a badge must also be easy to find inside the app as soon as it opens, since badges can be turned off.

quote: Keep badges up to date.
rule: Lower or clear the badge count as soon as the user views the corresponding items.

quote: Avoid creating a custom image or component that mimics the appearance or behavior of a badge.
rule: Do not draw your own badge-like counter on the icon or elsewhere to imitate the system badge.

quote: Avoid using a short look as the only way to communicate important information.
rule: On Apple Watch, critical information is delivered beyond the brief short-look view.

quote: Keep privacy in mind.
rule: Apple Watch short-look titles hold only basic, non-sensitive information.

quote: Consider using a rich, custom long-look notification to let people get the information they need without launching your app.
rule: Apple Watch long looks can show rich custom content so the app need not open.

quote: At the minimum, provide a static interface; prefer providing a dynamic interface too.
rule: Apple Watch notifications ship a bundled static long look and ideally a dynamic one.

quote: Choose a background appearance for the sash.
rule: Pick a coloured or blurred sash for the Apple Watch long look.

quote: Choose a background color for the content area.
rule: Pick the Apple Watch long-look background colour (white at 18% to match system ones).

quote: Provide up to four custom actions below the content area.
rule: Apple Watch long looks offer at most four custom actions above the system Dismiss button.

quote: Keep double tap in mind when choosing the order of custom actions you present as responses to a notification.
rule: On Apple Watch, list the most-used nondestructive action first because double tap runs it.

quote: Support default scrolling gestures and keyboard shortcuts.
rule: Every scrollable view responds to the mouse wheel, trackpad scrolling and the standard keys (arrows, Page Up/Down, Home/End, Space) exactly as system views do.

quote: If you build custom scrolling for a view, make sure your scroll indicators use the elastic behavior that people expect.
rule: On a Mac, custom-scrolled content rubber-bands at its ends like system scroll views.

quote: Make it apparent when content is scrollable.
rule: When content continues past the view's edge, signal it, e.g. by letting a partly visible row or item show at the edge.

quote: Avoid putting a scroll view inside another scroll view with the same orientation.
rule: Never nest a vertically scrolling region inside another vertical one (or horizontal in horizontal); crossing orientations is fine.

quote: Consider supporting page-by-page scrolling if it makes sense for your content.
rule: Offer scrolling by one view-height page at a time where it suits the content, keeping a small overlap (e.g. one line of text) so the reader keeps their place.

quote: when your app locates text that people are searching for, scroll the content to bring the new selection into view.
rule: When an operation such as Find selects content or moves the insertion point out of sight, scroll so it becomes visible.

quote: scroll back to the insertion point as soon as they begin to enter text.
rule: If the user has scrolled away from the caret and starts typing, scroll back to the caret immediately.

quote: The pointer moves past the edge of the view while people are making a selection.
rule: While a drag-selection extends past a view's edge, autoscroll in the pointer's direction.

quote: People select something and scroll to a new location before acting on the selection.
rule: When a command acts on a selection the user has scrolled away from, scroll the selection back into view before applying it.

quote: In all cases, automatically scroll the content only as much as necessary to help people retain context.
rule: Automatic scrolling moves the minimum distance needed; if part of the target is already visible, it may not need to move at all.

quote: If you support zoom, set appropriate maximum and minimum scale values.
rule: Zoomable views clamp zoom to sensible limits, e.g. text cannot be zoomed until one character fills the view.

quote: Prefer the automatic scroll edge effect style.
rule: Use the automatic scroll edge effect style; test legibility if using the soft one.

quote: Only use a scroll edge effect when a scroll view is behind floating interface elements.
rule: Add a scroll edge effect only where content scrolls under floating controls, never as decoration.

quote: Apply one scroll edge effect per view.
rule: One scroll edge effect per view, with matching heights across split-view panes.

quote: Consider showing a page control when a scroll view is in page-by-page mode.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, paged scrolling may show a page control, and then no scroll indicator on that axis.

quote: If necessary, use small or mini scroll bars in a panel.
rule: Tight Mac panels may use small or mini scroll bars, with every control in the panel at that same size.

quote: If necessary, account for the size of the scroll indicator.
rule: In visionOS, widen tight margins so the thicker scroll indicator does not cover content.

section: Platform considerations > visionOS > Look to Scroll
quote: Support Look to Scroll for reading or browsing views.
rule: visionOS reading and browsing views opt into eye-driven scrolling.

section: Platform considerations > visionOS > Look to Scroll
quote: Avoid using Look to Scroll for secondary content.
rule: visionOS views with controls or dense data use gestures only, not eye scrolling.

section: Platform considerations > visionOS > Look to Scroll
quote: Maintain consistency across content.
rule: In visionOS, if one view of a kind supports eye scrolling, all similar views do.

section: Platform considerations > visionOS > Look to Scroll
quote: Define clear scroll areas within your app.
rule: visionOS eye-scrolled views span the window or have clear edges.

section: Platform considerations > visionOS > Look to Scroll
quote: If your app uses custom scroll effects or animations, remove them before supporting Look to Scroll.
rule: Drop scroll-position effects such as parallax from visionOS views that support eye scrolling.

quote: Prefer vertically scrolling content.
rule: Apple Watch content scrolls vertically with the Digital Crown.

quote: Use tab views to provide page-by-page scrolling.
rule: Apple Watch paging uses vertically stacked tab views.

quote: When displaying paged content, consider limiting the content of an individual page to a single screen height.
rule: Apple Watch pages fit one screen where possible, with taller pages placed after fixed-height ones.

quote: Prioritize relevancy when choosing items to include in a context menu.
rule: A context menu lists only the commands most likely wanted for the clicked item (e.g. Reply and Move for a message), not advanced or rarely used ones.

quote: Aim for a small number of menu items.
rule: Keep context menus short enough to scan at a glance without scrolling.

quote: Support context menus consistently throughout your app.
rule: If one kind of object has a context menu, every comparable object in the app has one too.

quote: Always make context menu items available in the main interface, too.
rule: Every context-menu command is also reachable from the main interface (menu bar, toolbar or buttons); on a Mac the menu bar lists all of them.

quote: If you need to use submenus to manage a menu’s complexity, keep them to one level.
rule: A context menu has at most one level of submenu, never a submenu inside a submenu.

quote: If you need to include a submenu, give it an intuitive title that helps people predict its contents without opening it.
rule: Name each submenu so its contents can be guessed before it opens.

quote: Hide unavailable menu items, don’t dim them.
rule: Leave commands that do not apply out of a context menu entirely instead of showing them disabled; on a Mac, Cut, Copy and Paste may still appear disabled.

quote: Aim to place the most frequently used menu items where people are likely to encounter them first.
rule: Put the most used commands nearest the point where the menu opened, reversing the order when the menu opens upward.

quote: Show keyboard shortcuts in your app’s main menus, not in context menus.
rule: Context menu items do not display keyboard shortcuts; the shortcuts appear in the main menus.

quote: In general, you don’t want more than about three groups in a context menu.
rule: Group context-menu items with separators, using no more than about three groups.

quote: In iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS, warn people about context menu items that can destroy data.
rule: On iPhone, iPad and visionOS, destructive context-menu items such as Delete go last and are marked destructive.

quote: Include a title in a context menu only if doing so clarifies the menu’s effect.
rule: Context menus normally have no title; add one only when it clarifies scope, e.g. stating how many selected items the command will affect.

quote: Represent menu item actions with familiar icons.
rule: When menu items carry icons, common actions such as Copy, Share and Delete use the same icon in every menu and toolbar of the app.

quote: Provide either a context menu or an edit menu for an item, but not both.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, an item gets a context menu or an edit menu, never both.

quote: In iPadOS, consider using a context menu to let people create a new object in your app.
rule: On iPad, a long press in empty space may open a context menu for creating objects.

quote: Prefer a graphical preview that clarifies the target of a context menu’s commands.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, the context menu shows a preview of the targeted item.

quote: Ensure that your preview looks good as it animates.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, the preview's clipping path matches its shape during the reveal animation.

quote: Consider using a context menu instead of a panel or inspector window to present frequently used functionality.
rule: In visionOS, prefer a context menu to opening an extra panel for frequent functions.

quote: In general, avoid letting a context menu’s height exceed the height of the window.
rule: In visionOS, context menus stay shorter than their window.

quote: your app or game always needs to be prepared to save and restore their context.
rule: The app can be interrupted or put aside at any moment, so it keeps the user's work and position saved and restores them when the user returns.

quote: Pause activities that require people’s attention or active participation when they switch away.
rule: Activities that need the user's attention or participation (a game, a timed exercise) pause when the user switches away and continue from the same point on return.

quote: Respond smoothly to audio interruptions.
rule: When other audio interrupts, pause the app's own primary audio (music, podcasts) until the user resumes it, and for short interruptions lower the volume or pause briefly and restore it afterwards.

quote: Finish user-initiated tasks in the background.
rule: A task the user started that needs no further input (download, export, processing) keeps running to completion when the window is minimised or loses focus.

quote: Use notifications sparingly.
rule: Post a completion notification only for an important or time-sensitive task the user started and then left; routine background tasks finish silently.

quote: To help your app respond correctly when people open it while windowed, make sure it adapts gracefully to different screen sizes.
rule: iPad apps adapt their layout to whatever window size multitasking gives them.

quote: Avoid interfering with the system-provided multitasking behavior.
rule: In visionOS, leave window edges alone so the system's inactive-window treatment shows.

quote: Don’t pause a window’s video playback when people look away from it.
rule: In visionOS, a window's video keeps playing when the user looks at another window.

quote: people expect the playback they start in one window to continue while they view or perform a task in another window.
rule: On a Mac, media playing in one window keeps playing when the user activates or works in another window; losing focus is not a reason to pause.

quote: Be prepared for situations where your audio can duck.
rule: In visionOS, expect the app's audio to be ducked when the user looks at another app.

quote: You need to specify a system-defined interruption level for each noncommunication notification you send.
rule: Give every notification an explicit urgency level (passive for browse-later, active as default, time-sensitive, critical), mapped to the platform's equivalent priority or urgency.

quote: To support communication notifications, you adopt SiriKit intents
rule: Message and call notifications use SiriKit intents so Focus can filter them by sender.

quote: Because a Critical notification can override the Ring/Silent switch and break through scheduled delivery and Focus, you must get an entitlement to send one.
rule: Sending Critical notifications needs an Apple-granted entitlement.

quote: Build trust by accurately representing the urgency of each notification.
rule: Never raise a notification's urgency above what its content deserves; low-priority news uses the default or passive level.

quote: Use the Time Sensitive interruption level only for notifications that are relevant in the moment.
rule: Use the high-urgency level only for events happening now or within about an hour.

quote: Don’t use notifications to send marketing or promotional content unless people explicitly agree to receive such information.
rule: Promotional or marketing content is never sent as a notification unless the user has explicitly opted in to it.

quote: Never use the Time Sensitive interruption level to send a marketing notification.
rule: Marketing notifications always use a low urgency level and never break through do-not-disturb.

quote: Get people’s permission if you want to send them promotional or marketing notifications.
rule: Ask for marketing-notification consent in a dialog or view that says what kind of messages will come and offers an equally clear yes and no.

quote: Make sure people can manage their notification settings within your app.
rule: The app's settings window lets the user change every notification choice they made, including marketing opt-in.

quote: Support full-screen mode when it makes sense for your experience.
rule: Offer full screen for windows where people view media, present, or do focused in-depth work.

quote: If necessary, adjust your layout in full-screen mode
rule: In full screen, use the extra room by adjusting proportions while keeping the same set of elements, with changes small enough that switching modes is not jarring.

quote: don’t programmatically resize your window.
rule: The app never resizes its own window to fake or accompany full screen; the window size is the user's and the system's.

quote: Continue to provide access to essential features and controls so people can complete their task without exiting full-screen mode.
rule: Everything needed to finish the task (e.g. playback controls) stays visible or one pointer move away in full screen.

quote: Except in games, let people reveal the Dock while your iPadOS or macOS app is in full-screen mode.
rule: In full screen on a Mac, the Dock (and menu bar) can still be revealed in the usual way.

quote: After people switch away from your full-screen experience, help them resume where they left off when they return.
rule: When the user leaves a full-screen experience, pause anything time-based (slideshow, game) and resume from that point on return.

quote: Let people choose when to exit full-screen mode.
rule: Full screen ends only when the user asks; finishing a video or switching to another app does not leave it automatically.

quote: Prioritize content by temporarily hiding toolbars and navigation controls.
rule: When content is the focus in full screen (photos, reading), toolbars and navigation may hide temporarily.

quote: let people restore the hidden elements with a familiar gesture or action like tapping, swiping down, or moving the cursor
rule: Hidden toolbars come back through a familiar action such as moving the pointer to the top edge of the screen.

quote: Be sure to keep controls visible when they’re essential for navigation or performing tasks.
rule: Controls needed to navigate or complete the current task are never auto-hidden.

quote: Consider deferring system gestures to prevent accidental exits in a full-screen app or game.
rule: On iPhone and iPad, require two swipes to leave a full-screen game only if one swipe causes accidental exits.

quote: Use the system-provided full-screen experience.
rule: On a Mac, full screen uses the system's own mode (its own space, camera-housing area respected), not a hand-made borderless window.

quote: In a game, don’t change the display mode when players go full screen.
rule: Going full screen never changes the display's resolution or mode.

quote: Always let people choose when to enter full-screen mode.
rule: Full screen starts only at the user's request, through the window's full-screen button, View > Enter Full Screen or Control-Command-F.

quote: Avoid offering a custom menu of window modes.
rule: Do not add an app-specific menu for choosing window modes; rely on the standard full-screen commands.

quote: Use a popover to expose a small amount of information or functionality.
rule: A popover holds a few closely related settings or facts (e.g. an event's date, time and calendar), not a whole workflow.

quote: Consider using popovers when you want more room for content.
rule: Content needed only now and then goes in a popover rather than a permanent sidebar or panel.

quote: Position popovers appropriately.
rule: A popover points at the control that opened it and does not cover that control or content needed while using it.

quote: Use a Close button for confirmation and guidance only.
rule: Add Cancel/Done to a popover only when it clarifies whether changes are kept; otherwise it closes on a click outside it.

quote: If multiple selections are possible, make sure the popover remains open until people explicitly dismiss it or they click or tap outside its bounds.
rule: A single-choice popover closes when an item is picked; a popover allowing several choices stays open until dismissed or clicked outside.

quote: Always save work when automatically closing a nonmodal popover.
rule: Clicking outside a nonmodal popover keeps what was entered; only an explicit Cancel button discards it.

quote: Show one popover at a time.
rule: Only one popover is open at a time and none opens from inside another; opening a new one closes the current one first.

quote: Don’t show another view over a popover.
rule: Nothing appears on top of a popover except an alert.

quote: When possible, let people close one popover and open another with a single click or tap.
rule: With a popover open, one click on another popover-opening control both closes the first and opens the second.

quote: Avoid making a popover too big.
rule: Size a popover to its contents and no larger.

quote: Provide a smooth transition when changing the size of a popover.
rule: When a popover switches between condensed and expanded content, it resizes in place so it does not look like a new popover replaced it.

quote: Avoid using the word popover in help documentation.
rule: Help text refers to the task or control ('Select the Show button'), never to 'the popover'.

quote: Avoid using a popover to show a warning.
rule: Warnings are shown in an alert, never in a popover that can be missed or dismissed by accident.

quote: Avoid displaying popovers in compact views.
rule: On narrow iPhone/iPad layouts, use a sheet instead of a popover.

quote: Consider letting people detach a popover.
rule: Let users drag a popover off into a free-standing panel that stays open while they work elsewhere.

quote: Make minimal appearance changes to a detached popover.
rule: A popover dragged out into a panel keeps the same content and arrangement so the user stays oriented.

quote: Use a table instead of an outline view to present data that’s not hierarchical.
rule: Flat data goes in a plain table; an expandable tree is only for data with real parent-child structure.

quote: Expose data hierarchy in the first column only.
rule: In a multi-column tree, only the first column indents and has disclosure triangles; other columns show attributes of each row.

quote: Use descriptive column headings to provide context.
rule: Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no punctuation, in particular no trailing colon.

quote: Always provide column headings in a multi-column outline view.
rule: A tree with more than one column always shows headings; a single-column tree without one gets a label or other context.

quote: Consider letting people click column headings to sort an outline view.
rule: Clicking a column heading sorts by it, clicking again reverses the order, and sorting by the first column sorts each level of the hierarchy separately.

quote: Let people resize columns.
rule: Tree and table columns can be resized by dragging their heading dividers.

quote: Make it easy for people to expand or collapse nested containers.
rule: Clicking a disclosure triangle expands or collapses that node only; modifier-clicking it (Option on a Mac) expands or collapses it with all descendants.

quote: Retain people’s expansion choices.
rule: Remember which nodes are expanded and restore that state the next time the view is shown.

quote: Consider using alternating row colors in multi-column outline views.
rule: Wide multi-column trees use alternating row backgrounds.

quote: Let people edit data if it makes sense in your app.
rule: In an editable tree, a single click on a selected cell starts editing it while a double click opens the item (e.g. click a file name to rename, double-click to open).

quote: You can also let people reorder, add, and remove rows if it would be useful.
rule: Where useful, rows can be reordered by dragging, added and removed.

quote: Consider using a centered ellipsis to truncate cell text instead of clipping it.
rule: Cell text too long for its column is shortened with an ellipsis in the middle, keeping start and end, rather than cut off.

quote: Consider offering a search field to help people find values quickly in a lengthy outline view.
rule: A window built around a long tree offers a search field, usually in its toolbar.

quote: Use a disclosure control to hide details until they’re relevant.
rule: Show the most used options at all times and put advanced options behind a collapsed disclosure control.

quote: Provide a descriptive label when using a disclosure triangle.
rule: A disclosure triangle has a label naming what it shows or hides, e.g. 'Advanced Options'.

quote: Place a disclosure button near the content that it shows and hides.
rule: A disclosure button sits next to the control or area whose extra options it expands.

quote: Use no more than one disclosure button in a single view.
rule: A view contains at most one disclosure button.

quote: Add value with a context menu.
rule: Each token offers a context menu with details or editing commands for it.

quote: Consider providing additional ways to convert text into tokens.
rule: Typed text becomes a token on a comma and also on other natural keys such as Return.

quote: Consider customizing the delay the system uses before showing suggested tokens.
rule: Token suggestions appear after a short pause in typing, not on every keystroke, so they do not distract.

quote: Consider the system-provided color picker for a familiar experience.
rule: Every colour choice in the app opens the same colour picker so it behaves identically everywhere.

quote: people can drag colors from one color well to another, and from the color picker to a color well
rule: A colour swatch control shows it is active while its picker is open, updates to the chosen colour, and accepts colours dragged from other swatches or the picker.

quote: Support Full Keyboard Access when possible.
rule: Every window, menu, control and feature must be reachable and operable with the keyboard alone, and this is checked by using the app with no pointing device.

quote: avoid supporting keyboard navigation for controls, such as buttons, segmented controls, and switches
rule: On iPadOS, buttons, segmented controls and switches are left to the system's keyboard access rather than given their own key navigation.

quote: Respect standard keyboard shortcuts.
rule: A frequent app-specific action gets a newly chosen shortcut instead of borrowing one that already stands for a different action across the system.

quote: In general, don’t repurpose standard keyboard shortcuts for custom actions.
rule: A standard shortcut is reassigned only when its usual action cannot exist in the app, e.g. an app without text styling may use Command-I for Get Info instead of Italic.

quote: People expect each of the following standard keyboard shortcuts to perform the action listed in the table below.
rule: On a Mac the app honours Apple's standard map: Cmd-N new, O open, S save, Shift-Cmd-S save as/duplicate, W close window, Shift-Cmd-W close file, Opt-Cmd-W close all, P print, Shift-Cmd-P page setup, Q quit, H hide app, Opt-Cmd-H hide others, M minimize, Opt-Cmd-M minimize all, Z undo, Shift-Cmd-Z redo, X/C/V cut/copy/paste, Shift-Cmd-V paste as, A select all, Shift-Cmd-A deselect, F find, G and Shift-Cmd-G find next/previous, E use selection for find, Opt-Cmd-F go to search field, J scroll to selection, Cmd-comma settings, Cmd-? help, Cmd-` and Shift-Cmd-` next/previous window, B/I/U bold/italic/underline, T fonts, Shift-Cmd-C colours, Opt-Cmd-I inspector, Opt-Cmd-T toggle toolbar, Ctrl-Cmd-F full screen, Esc and Cmd-period cancel, Tab/Shift-Tab and Ctrl-Tab/Ctrl-Shift-Tab move focus between controls and control groups, Ctrl-arrows move between cells, Shift/Opt-Shift/Shift-Cmd-arrows extend the selection by character/word or paragraph/line or document; system-reserved keys (Cmd-Space, Cmd-Tab, Ctrl-F1 to F7, Shift-Cmd-3/4 screenshots, Opt-Cmd-Esc, Opt-Cmd-D) are never taken.

quote: The system also defines several keyboard shortcuts for use with localized versions of the system, localized keyboards, keyboard layouts, and input methods.
rule: On a Mac, Ctrl-Space, Ctrl-Opt-Space, any modifier plus Cmd-Space, and Cmd-Left/Right arrow stay free because the system uses them to switch input sources and keyboard layouts.

quote: Define custom keyboard shortcuts for only the most frequently used app-specific commands.
rule: Only the few app-specific commands people use most get new shortcuts; rarer commands are reached through menus.

quote: Use modifier keys in ways that people expect.
rule: Modifiers keep their conventional effects during direct manipulation: the primary modifier while dragging moves items as a group, Shift while resizing keeps the aspect ratio, and a held arrow key nudges the selection by the smallest unit until released.

quote: Prefer the Command key as the main modifier key in a custom keyboard shortcut.
rule: Mac custom shortcuts are built on Command, add Shift for a related variant, use Option only for rare or expert commands, and avoid Control because the system claims it.

quote: avoid using an additional modifier with characters that aren’t available on all keyboards
rule: A shortcut that needs a modifier beyond the primary one pairs it only with letters A to Z, never with punctuation that some layouts type only with a modifier (French Option-5 gives '{').

quote: List modifier keys in the correct order.
rule: When a Mac shortcut is shown with several modifiers, they appear as Control, Option, Shift, Command in that sequence.

quote: Avoid adding Shift to a shortcut that uses the upper character of a two-character key.
rule: A shortcut on a shifted symbol is written with the symbol itself, e.g. Command-? and not Shift-Command-/.

quote: Let the system localize and mirror your keyboard shortcuts as needed.
rule: Shortcuts are matched and displayed for the keyboard layout actually connected, and direction-bound shortcuts swap sides when the interface runs right to left.

quote: Avoid creating a new shortcut by adding a modifier to an existing shortcut for an unrelated command.
rule: Adding a modifier to an existing shortcut yields only a related command; e.g. Shift-Cmd-Z must stay tied to undo/redo, never an unrelated action.

quote: Write descriptive shortcut titles.
rule: In the visionOS shortcut overlay each shortcut's title must make sense without its submenu's name.

quote: Recognize that people see an overlay when they use a physical keyboard with your visionOS app or game.
rule: visionOS layouts allow for the virtual keyboard overlay shown when a hardware keyboard is attached.

quote: Order content by relative importance.
rule: The most important items sit toward the top and the leading edge (left in left-to-right, right in right-to-left), since people scan in reading order.

quote: To support right-to-left languages, prefer standard system components that can automatically adapt UI elements to better reflect each language’s natural reading order.
rule: Screens are built from library components that mirror themselves for right-to-left languages rather than from hand-placed parts that would need separate mirroring.

quote: Align elements to make them easier to scan, and use indentation to convey hierarchy.
rule: Related items share a common alignment edge, and only items that are subordinate to the one above them are indented.

quote: Group related items to clearly express related information or functions.
rule: Related controls and information are kept together and set apart from unrelated ones by space, a container or a separator.

quote: Use progressive disclosure to make layouts cleaner and easier to interact with.
rule: Secondary content and choices start hidden behind disclosure triangles, menus, nested views or scrolling sections so the first view stays short.

quote: Differentiate controls from content.
rule: Controls must be recognisable as controls and never be mistaken for the content they act on.

quote: Instead of applying a solid or semi-opaque background color beneath controls, use a scroll edge effect to visually elevate controls above content.
rule: Controls over content get Liquid Glass and a scroll-edge effect rather than a backing colour.

quote: For full-screen background content, be sure to extend it underneath sidebars, toolbars, and tab bars to fit the entire screen or window.
rule: Edge-to-edge background content runs beneath sidebars, toolbars and tab bars.

quote: you can use a background extension effect to flip and blur the image, mirroring it beneath adjacent components
rule: A background image covered by side panels can be mirrored and blurred under them with the background extension effect.

quote: Design a layout that adapts gracefully and consistently.
rule: Resizing a window or moving it to another display rearranges the layout within standard margins while keeping it recognisably the same.

quote: Be prepared for text-size changes.
rule: At larger text or interface sizes the layout reflows: side-by-side parts stack, rows grow taller, single-line rows wrap, and no text is clipped or overlaps.

quote: To support Dynamic Type in your Unity-based game, use Apple’s accessibility plug-in
rule: Unity games get Dynamic Type through Apple's accessibility plug-in.

quote: Preview your app on multiple devices, using different size classes, localizations, and text sizes.
rule: Every screen is checked for clipping at its smallest and largest window size, at the smallest and largest interface size, and in the longest localization.

quote: When necessary, scale background artwork in response to display changes.
rule: Background artwork is scaled to fill the window at any aspect ratio, never stretched.

quote: Determine layout based on size classes, not device type or orientation.
rule: Layout decisions are made from the space the window actually has, never from the operating system, device or screen it runs on.

quote: Consider all possible combinations of size classes.
rule: Layouts are designed and tested for wide-and-short and narrow-and-tall windows, not only the default shape.

quote: Keep functionality the same as size classes change, and keep layout changes recognizable and familiar to the platform.
rule: Narrowing a window may move commands into an overflow menu or collapse a sidebar, but every function stays reachable at every size.

quote: Respecting the safe area is essential to make sure system UI and hardware features like the Dynamic Island don’t obstruct content and controls.
rule: Content stays inside the device safe area so hardware cut-outs and system bars do not cover it.

quote: Avoid placing controls or critical information at the bottom of a window.
rule: Nothing essential, control or critical information, lives only along a window's bottom edge, because windows are often dragged partly below the screen.

quote: Avoid displaying content behind the camera housing at the top edge of the window.
rule: On a Mac with a notch, a full-screen window keeps content out of the camera housing area at the top.

quote: Adhere to the screen’s safe area.
rule: tvOS content is inset 60 pt top and bottom and 80 pt at the sides.

quote: Include appropriate padding between focusable elements.
rule: tvOS focusable items are spaced so their focus enlargement does not overlap other content.

quote: Be sure to use appropriate spacing between unfocused rows and columns to prevent overlap when an item comes into focus.
rule: tvOS grid rows and columns leave room for a focused item to grow.

quote: Include additional vertical spacing for titled rows.
rule: tvOS grid rows with titles get extra vertical space above and below the title.

quote: Use consistent spacing.
rule: tvOS grid items are evenly spaced so the grid reads as a grid.

quote: Make partially hidden content look symmetrical.
rule: tvOS rows that run off screen show equal partial items on both sides.

quote: In general, support resizing.
rule: visionOS windows and volumes are resizable and keep content centred at large sizes.

quote: don’t use minimum and maximum sizes as a way to prevent resizing
rule: visionOS minimum and maximum sizes prevent overlap and sprawl but never stand in for disabling resizing.

quote: Use 3D content sparingly in windows.
rule: visionOS windows show inline 3D models only for meaningful moments, inset from the edges.

quote: Display supplemental content in an adjacent window, not in an ornament.
rule: visionOS supplemental views open in a neighbouring window rather than an ornament.

quote: Include enough space around controls for them to be easy to interact with.
rule: visionOS button centres are at least 60 pt apart.

quote: Avoid placing more than two or three controls side by side in your interface.
rule: watchOS rows hold at most three glyph buttons or two text buttons.

quote: Support autorotation in views people might want to show others.
rule: watchOS views meant to be shown to others rotate when the wrist turns away.

quote: For each menu item, write a label that clearly and succinctly describes it.
rule: A menu item that performs an action is named with a short verb or verb phrase such as View, Close or Select.

quote: let your app’s or game’s communication style guide the tone of the menu-item labels you create
rule: Menu item wording follows the same voice and tone as the rest of the app's text.

quote: To be consistent with platform experiences, use title-style capitalization.
rule: Menu items are written in title case: every word capitalised except articles, coordinating conjunctions and short prepositions, with the last word always capitalised.

quote: In English, articles always lengthen labels, but rarely enhance understanding.
rule: Menu item labels drop a, an and the, e.g. 'View Settings', not 'View the Settings'.

quote: Show people when a menu item is unavailable.
rule: A command that cannot run now stays in its menu, drawn dimmed, and ignores activation instead of disappearing.

quote: If all of a menu’s items are unavailable, the menu itself needs to remain available so people can open it
rule: A menu whose items are all unavailable can still be opened so people can see what it holds.

quote: Append an ellipsis to a menu item’s label when the action requires more information before it can complete.
rule: A menu item that opens a dialog or asks for more input before acting ends with the ellipsis character (…), e.g. 'Save As…'.

quote: Represent common actions consistently.
rule: A common action such as Share, Print or Search uses the same icon wherever it appears in the app.

quote: Use menu item icons sparingly and with purpose.
rule: Menu items get icons only for key actions, places, devices, visual operations or user content, and an item without a clearly fitting icon gets none.

quote: Apply a uniform visual treatment across menu items in the same group.
rule: Within one menu group, either every item has an icon or none does.

quote: Prefer listing important or frequently used menu items first.
rule: The most used or most important items are placed at the top of a menu.

quote: Consider grouping logically related items.
rule: Related commands, e.g. Cut, Copy and Paste, form a group separated from other groups by a separator.

quote: Prefer keeping all logically related commands in the same group, even if the commands don’t all have the same importance.
rule: A rarely used command stays in the group of its related commands, e.g. Paste and Match Style next to Paste, rather than being moved elsewhere.

quote: Be mindful of menu length.
rule: An overlong menu is split into several menus or shortened with a submenu.

quote: People expect such a menu to accommodate all the items they add to it, so a long menu is fine, and scrolling is acceptable.
rule: A menu filled with user-made or generated entries, such as history or bookmarks, lists all of them and may scroll.

quote: Use submenus sparingly.
rule: Submenus are used only where they clearly help, since each one hides its items.

quote: You might consider creating a submenu when a term appears in more than two menu items in the same group.
rule: When three or more items in a group share a leading term, they become one item named by that term with a submenu, e.g. 'Sort By' > Date, Score, Time.

quote: Limit the depth and length of submenus.
rule: Submenus go one level deep, and a submenu of more than about five items becomes its own menu.

quote: Make sure a submenu remains available even when its nested menu items are unavailable.
rule: A submenu item stays openable even when every command inside it is unavailable.

quote: Prefer using a submenu to indenting menu items.
rule: Subordinate menu items are put in a submenu, never indented under another item.

quote: Consider using a changeable label that describes an item’s current state.
rule: One menu item can switch its label with state, e.g. 'Show Map' becomes 'Hide Map' while the map is shown.

quote: Include a verb if a changeable label isn’t clear enough.
rule: A state-switching label that could read as a status gets a verb, e.g. 'Turn HDR On' rather than 'HDR On'.

quote: If necessary, display both menu items instead of one toggled item.
rule: Where seeing both choices helps, both items are listed and the one that does not apply is unavailable.

quote: Consider using a checkmark to show that an attribute is currently in effect.
rule: Attributes that are on are marked with a checkmark beside their menu item.

quote: Consider offering a menu item that makes it easy to remove multiple toggled attributes.
rule: Where several attributes can be combined, one item (such as Plain) clears them all at once.

quote: Let players navigate in-game menus using the platform’s default interaction method.
rule: A custom-drawn menu responds to the same pointer and keyboard interactions as the platform's own menus.

quote: Make sure your menus remain easy to open and read on all platforms you support.
rule: In-game menus keep readable text and large enough targets after scaling to small screens.

quote: Choose a small or medium menu layout when it can help streamline people’s choices.
rule: iOS and iPadOS menus use the small or medium layout for three or four key actions.

quote: Prefer displaying a menu near the content it controls.
rule: visionOS menus appear close to the content they act on.

quote: Prefer the subtle breakthrough effect in most cases.
rule: visionOS menus over 3D content use the subtle breakthrough effect.

quote: Use app menus and keyboard shortcuts to give people convenient ways to create and open documents.
rule: A document app offers New and Open in its File menu with the standard New and Open shortcuts.

quote: Regardless of the availability of keyboard shortcuts, include an Add (+) button to help people create a new document.
rule: Besides the menu command and shortcut, a visible add (+) button creates a new document.

quote: If your app requires a custom file browser, support people’s understanding of the platform’s file system.
rule: A custom file browser may open on the most relevant folder but still lets people move anywhere in the file system.

quote: Help people be confident that their work is always preserved unless they cancel or delete it.
rule: Work is saved automatically at intervals while editing and when a document is closed or the app loses focus, without needing an explicit save.

quote: Hide file extensions by default, but let people view them if they choose.
rule: File names are shown without extensions unless the person opts to see them, and every open and save view follows that choice.

quote: Use a Quick Look viewer to let people preview a file even when your app can’t open it.
rule: Unsupported attached files are previewed in place through Quick Look.

quote: Consider implementing a Quick Look generator if your app produces custom file types.
rule: Custom file types ship a Quick Look generator so Finder and Spotlight can preview them.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Document launcher
quote: Assign the title card’s buttons to your app’s most important functions.
rule: The document launcher's primary button creates a document and the secondary offers more options.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Document launcher
quote: Provide a background that’s clearly distinct from the accessories and title card.
rule: The launcher background is plain enough not to compete with the title card.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Document launcher
quote: Be mindful of accessory placement.
rule: Launcher accessories never hide the app name or buttons.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Document launcher
quote: Use animation sparingly.
rule: Launcher accessory animation is gentle and repeating.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > File provider app extension
quote: When someone uses your file provider extension to open or import documents, display only documents that are appropriate in the current context.
rule: A file provider extension lists only files the requesting app can use.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > File provider app extension
quote: Let people select a destination when exporting and moving documents.
rule: A file provider extension lets people pick the destination folder when exporting or moving.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > File provider app extension
quote: Avoid including a custom top toolbar.
rule: A file provider extension adds no toolbar of its own on top of the system's.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: Use the default file browser unless you have an important reason to create a custom one.
rule: Opening and saving files uses the system's own file dialogs unless there is a strong reason for a custom one.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: Make your custom file-opening interface convenient.
rule: A custom open view offers recently opened files, filtering by criteria and opening several files at once.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: In a macOS open panel, you can customize the title of the Open button to reflect the task
rule: The confirm button of an open dialog names the actual task when it differs from opening, e.g. 'Insert'.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: Provide a save interface to let people change a file’s name, format, or location.
rule: Saving offers a view where the name, location and, when several are supported, the file format can be chosen.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: By default, a new document’s title is “Untitled” until people choose a custom name.
rule: A new document is called 'Untitled' until the person names it.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: a save view can also provide a browsing experience that defaults to a logical location
rule: The save view starts in a sensible folder for the document rather than an arbitrary one.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Custom file management
quote: Consider extending the functionality of the Save dialog.
rule: Options that matter when saving, such as including attachments, can be added to the save dialog itself.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Finder Sync extensions
quote: If your app syncs local and remote files, you can create a Finder Sync app extension
rule: Sync apps show status badges, context items and toolbar buttons in Finder through a Finder Sync extension.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Finder Sync extensions
quote: Help people avoid losing work if they turn off autosaving.
rule: When autosave is off, closing a document, quitting, logging out or restarting with unsaved changes brings up a save prompt.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Finder Sync extensions
quote: When autosaving is off, make sure people know when a document has unsaved changes.
rule: With autosave off, an unsaved document shows a dot in its window's close button and beside its name in the Window menu.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Finder Sync extensions
quote: When autosaving is on, showing a dot in these locations is confusing
rule: With autosave on, no unsaved-changes dot is shown, since nothing needs the person's action.

section: Platform considerations > macOS > Finder Sync extensions
quote: you can append “Edited” to the document’s title in the title bar, but be sure to remove this suffix as soon as autosave occurs
rule: An 'Edited' suffix in the title bar is allowed but must vanish the moment the document is saved, automatically or by hand.

quote: Adjust text alignment to match the interface direction, if the system doesn’t do so automatically.
rule: Text left-aligned in a left-to-right layout is right-aligned when the layout is mirrored.

quote: Align a paragraph based on its language, not on the current context.
rule: Text of three or more lines is aligned by its own script's direction, while one- and two-line text follows the interface direction.

quote: Use a consistent alignment for all text items in a list.
rule: All items of a list share one alignment, following the interface direction even for items in another script.

quote: identify the appropriate way to display such information in each locale you support
rule: Number-heavy apps decide per locale whether Western or Eastern Arabic numerals and which symbols to show; others use the platform's number formatting.

quote: Don’t reverse the order of numerals in a specific number.
rule: The digits of a single number, phone number or card number keep their order in right-to-left layouts.

quote: Reverse the order of numerals that show progress or a counting direction; never flip the numerals themselves.
rule: Scale numbers on mirrored sliders, progress bars and ratings, and ordered number sequences, run in reversed order, while each numeral's glyph stays unmirrored.

quote: Flip controls that show progress from one value to another.
rule: Sliders and progress indicators run from right to left in right-to-left layouts, with their start and end icons swapped too.

quote: Flip controls that help people navigate or access items in a fixed order.
rule: Back, next and previous controls point the other way in right-to-left layouts, e.g. Back points right.

quote: Preserve the direction of a control that refers to an actual direction or points to an onscreen area.
rule: A control meaning a physical direction, such as 'to the right', keeps pointing that way in every layout direction.

quote: Visually balance adjacent Latin and RTL scripts when necessary.
rule: Arabic or Hebrew text beside all-caps Latin text is set about 2 pt larger.

quote: Avoid flipping images like photographs, illustrations, and general artwork.
rule: Photos and illustrations are never mirrored for right-to-left; a direction-bound image gets a separate version instead.

quote: Reverse the positions of images when their order is meaningful.
rule: Images arranged in a meaningful order (by date, alphabet, rank) are laid out in reverse order in right-to-left layouts.

quote: Flip interface icons that represent text or reading direction.
rule: Icons that depict text lines or reading direction are mirrored in right-to-left layouts.

quote: Consider creating a localized version of an interface icon that displays text.
rule: Icons containing letters get localized variants for other scripts.

quote: consider designing an alternative image that doesn’t use text
rule: An icon that uses letters for a concept unrelated to writing is redrawn without text.

quote: Flip an interface icon that shows forward or backward motion.
rule: Icons that show something moving forward or backward are mirrored in right-to-left layouts so the motion keeps its meaning.

quote: Don’t flip logos or universal signs and marks.
rule: Logos and universal marks such as the checkmark are never mirrored.

quote: In general, avoid flipping interface icons that depict real-world objects.
rule: Icons of real objects (clocks, right-handed tools) stay unmirrored unless they show a direction.

quote: Before merely flipping a complex custom interface icon, consider its individual components and the overall visual balance.
rule: Parts of a composite icon such as badges or slashes are judged one by one before mirroring.

quote: if a badge represents the actual UI that people see in your app, it needs to flip if your UI flips
rule: A badge drawn to stand for real UI moves with the mirrored UI; a meaning-changing badge is placed for balance.

quote: consider preserving the orientation of the tool while flipping the base image if necessary
rule: In a mirrored icon a handed tool keeps its orientation.

quote: Avoid offering an app-specific appearance setting.
rule: The app follows the system's light or dark choice by default so people need not set appearance twice.

quote: Ensure that your app looks good in both appearance modes.
rule: The app is complete in both light and dark and switches between them live when the system changes appearance while it runs.

quote: Test your content to make sure that it remains comfortably legible in both appearance modes.
rule: Every screen is checked for legibility in dark appearance with increased contrast and reduced transparency, separately and combined.

quote: In rare cases, consider using only a dark appearance in the interface.
rule: A media-immersion app may stay dark permanently.

quote: Embrace colors that adapt to the current appearance.
rule: Colours come from semantic, appearance-aware colours, never hard-coded values.

quote: Aim for sufficient color contrast in all appearances.
rule: Text and its background have at least 4.5:1 contrast in every appearance, with 7:1 the goal for small text in custom colours.

quote: Soften the color of white backgrounds.
rule: Images with white backgrounds are slightly darkened in dark appearance.

quote: Use SF Symbols wherever possible.
rule: Icons are SF Symbols tinted with dynamic colours.

quote: Design separate interface icons for the light and dark appearances if necessary.
rule: Icons that lose their edge on one background get a separate light or dark version.

quote: Make sure full-color images and icons look good in both appearances.
rule: Full-colour images get light and dark variants when one asset does not suit both.

quote: Use the system-provided label colors for labels.
rule: Label text uses the four system label colours.

quote: Use system views to draw text fields and text views.
rule: Text fields and text views are the system's own so they adapt to vibrancy.

quote: Prefer the system background colors.
rule: iOS and iPadOS use base and elevated system backgrounds.

quote: Include some transparency in custom component backgrounds when appropriate.
rule: Neutral custom component backgrounds are slightly transparent for desktop tinting.

quote: When possible, use a determinate progress indicator.
rule: Any task whose length can be estimated shows a determinate indicator rather than an indeterminate one.

quote: Be as accurate as possible when reporting advancement in a determinate progress indicator.
rule: A determinate indicator advances at a pace that matches the real remaining work, never racing to 90 percent and then stalling.

quote: Keep progress indicators moving so people know something is continuing to happen.
rule: A progress indicator never sits still while work continues.

quote: If a process stalls for some reason, provide feedback that helps people understand the problem and what they can do about it.
rule: When an operation stalls, the app says what went wrong and what the person can do, instead of leaving the indicator frozen.

quote: When possible, switch a progress bar from indeterminate to determinate.
rule: An indeterminate bar becomes determinate as soon as the remaining work becomes known.

quote: Don’t switch from the circular style to the bar style.
rule: An operation keeps the same indicator shape from start to finish; a spinner is never swapped for a bar.

quote: If it’s helpful, display a description that provides additional context for the task.
rule: A progress description says specifically what is happening, never vague words like 'Loading…' or 'Authenticating…'.

quote: Display a progress indicator in a consistent location.
rule: Progress for a given kind of operation always appears in the same place.

quote: When it’s feasible, let people halt processing.
rule: A long operation offers Cancel when stopping is harmless, and Pause alongside Cancel when cancelling would discard work done so far.

quote: Let people know when halting a process has a negative consequence.
rule: Cancelling an operation that loses progress first asks for confirmation, with a choice to resume.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Refresh content controls
quote: Perform automatic content updates.
rule: iOS content refreshes on its own periodically besides pull-to-refresh.

section: Platform considerations > iOS, iPadOS > Refresh content controls
quote: Supply a short title only if it adds value.
rule: A pull-to-refresh title gives useful information such as last update time, never instructions.

quote: Prefer an activity indicator (spinner) to communicate the status of a background operation or when space is constrained.
rule: Background tasks and progress in tight spots (inside a field, next to a button) use a small spinner.

quote: Avoid labeling a spinning progress indicator.
rule: A spinner carries no text label, since the person just started the operation.

quote: Present content modally only when there’s a clear benefit.
rule: A modal view is used only when it helps people focus on or decide something about their content or device.

quote: Aim to keep modal tasks simple, short, and streamlined.
rule: A modal task is short and simple enough that people do not lose track of what they left.

quote: Take care to avoid creating a modal experience that feels like an app within your app.
rule: A modal task does not contain its own navigation hierarchy; if it needs subviews they form one linear path.

quote: avoid including buttons that people might mistake for the button that dismisses the modal view
rule: Inside a modal view no button may look like or be confused with the one that closes it.

quote: Consider using a full-screen modal style for in-depth content or a complex task.
rule: Media viewing and multistep editing can take over the whole window to cut distraction.

quote: Always give people an obvious way to dismiss a modal view.
rule: Every modal view has an obvious way out; on the desktop that is a button within the dialog's own content area.

quote: When necessary, help people avoid data loss by getting confirmation before closing a modal view.
rule: Closing a modal view by any means that would discard user content first explains this and offers a way to keep it, such as Save.

quote: Make it easy to identify a modal view’s task.
rule: Every modal view carries a title naming its task, plus guiding text where useful.

quote: Let people dismiss a modal view before presenting another one.
rule: A modal view is closed before another opens; modal views are not stacked, except that an alert may appear over one.

quote: you never want to display more than one alert at the same time
rule: At most one alert is on screen at any moment.

quote: Teach through interactivity.
rule: Onboarding lets people safely try the action being taught rather than only reading about it.

quote: Consider providing a collection of context-specific tips instead of a single onboarding flow.
rule: Features are taught by small tips shown when the related task comes up rather than one up-front walkthrough.

quote: When you have instructional content that refers to a specific area of the interface, display these instructions near that area.
rule: A tip about a part of the window is shown next to that part.

quote: If you need to present a prerequisite onboarding flow, design a brief, enjoyable experience that doesn’t require people to memorize a lot of information.
rule: A required introduction is short and asks people to remember very little.

quote: If it makes sense to offer a separate tutorial, consider making it optional.
rule: A tutorial can be skipped.

quote: don’t present it again on subsequent launches, but make sure it’s easy for people to find if they want to view it later
rule: A skipped tutorial is not shown again at later launches but stays reachable from Help or Settings.

quote: Keep onboarding content focused on the experience you provide.
rule: Onboarding explains the app, not how to use the operating system or device.

quote: Briefly display a splash screen if necessary.
rule: A splash screen, if any, stays only long enough to be taken in at a glance.

quote: Don’t let large downloads hinder onboarding.
rule: The app ships enough content to be usable at first launch without waiting for downloads.

quote: Avoid displaying licensing details within your onboarding flow.
rule: Licence texts and disclaimers are kept out of the first-run introduction, or if unavoidable placed so they do not interrupt it.

quote: Postpone nonessential setup flows or customization steps.
rule: The app starts with sensible defaults, and optional setup is deferred so people can work right away.

quote: If your app or game needs access to private data or resources before it can function, consider integrating the permission request into your onboarding flow.
rule: Access to private data is requested during onboarding with a reason only if the app cannot work without it; otherwise at the first use of the feature that needs it.

quote: Prefer letting people experience your app or game before prompting them for ratings or purchases.
rule: Requests for ratings or purchases wait until people have used the app for a while.

quote: Use a label to display a small amount of text that people don’t need to edit.
rule: Short read-only text is a label, short editable text a text field, and long text a text view.

quote: Prefer system fonts.
rule: Labels use the system font, and any custom styling stays legible.

quote: Use system-provided label colors to communicate relative importance.
rule: Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary label colours mark primary text, subheadings, unavailable items and watermarks.

quote: Make useful label text selectable.
rule: Read-only text people may want to reuse, such as an error message, address or IP address, can be selected and copied.

quote: Consider using date and timer components in complications.
rule: watchOS complications use the system date and timer text components.

quote: Use a tab view to present closely related areas of content.
rule: Tabs hold panes whose content is related; unrelated content does not share a tab view.

quote: Make sure the controls within a pane affect content only in the same pane.
rule: A control inside a tab pane changes only that pane's content.

quote: Provide a label for each tab that describes the contents of its pane.
rule: Each tab is labelled with a noun or short noun phrase (occasionally a verb phrase) that predicts what its pane holds.

quote: Use title-style capitalization for tab labels.
rule: Tab labels are in title case.

quote: Avoid using a pop-up button to switch between tabs.
rule: Pane switching uses a visible tab control, not a pop-up button, unless there are too many panes for tabs.

quote: Avoid providing more than six tabs in a tab view.
rule: A tab view has at most six tabs; more panes call for another design, such as a pop-up menu of views.

quote: You can choose to hide the control, which is appropriate for an app that switches between panes programmatically.
rule: The tab control is hidden only when the app itself, not the person, switches panes.

quote: In general, inset a tab view by leaving a margin of window-body area on all sides of a tab view.
rule: A tab view sits inside the window with a margin on every side rather than touching the window edges.

quote: For similar functionality, consider using a segmented control instead.
rule: On iOS and iPadOS a segmented control replaces the tab view.

quote: Consider using a column view when you have a deep data hierarchy in which people tend to navigate back and forth frequently between levels
rule: A column browser suits a deep hierarchy that people move up and down often and that needs no sorting; sortable data goes in a list or table.

quote: Show the root level of your data hierarchy in the first column.
rule: The first column always shows the top level of the hierarchy.

quote: Consider showing information about the selected item when there are no nested items to display.
rule: Selecting a leaf item fills the next column with its details or preview, e.g. dates, type and size.

quote: Let people resize columns.
rule: Browser columns can be resized by the person so long names fit.

quote: Revert to a default image when necessary.
rule: An image well that needs an image shows its default image again after being cleared.

quote: If your image well supports copy and paste, make sure the standard copy and paste menu items are available.
