rule: An image well that supports copy and paste works through the Edit menu's Copy and Paste items and their standard shortcuts.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to provide users with information, ask users a question, or allow users to select options to perform a command or task?
rule: Use a dialog only to inform, to ask a question or to gather options for a command; anything else gets a different surface.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to view and change properties for an object, collection of objects, or a program? If so, use a property window
rule: Viewing and editing an object's properties belongs in a property window, inspector or toolbar, not a one-off dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to present a collection of commands or tools? If so, use a toolbar or palette window.
rule: A set of commands or tools is offered in a toolbar or tool palette, not in a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is there a clear reason not to proceed and a reasonable chance that sometimes users won't? If so, use a confirmation.
rule: Ask for confirmation only when there is a real reason to stop and people sometimes do stop.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to give an error or warning message? If so, use an error message or warning message.
rule: Errors and warnings follow the error and warning message patterns rather than a general-purpose dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: If so, use the appropriate common dialog instead. Many of these common dialogs are extensible.
rule: Opening, saving, folder picking, find and replace, printing, page setup, font and colour choice, browsing and credential prompts use the system's standard dialogs.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to perform a multi-step task that requires more than a single window? If so, use a task flow or wizard instead.
rule: A task that needs several steps runs as one guided flow in one window, not as a chain of separate dialogs.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: use a notification instead.
rule: An event unrelated to what the person is doing, needing no immediate action and safe to ignore, is a notification, not a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to show program status? If so, use a status bar instead.
rule: Program status is shown in a status area of the window, never in a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Would it be preferable to use in-place UI? Dialog boxes can break the user's flow by demanding attention.
rule: Prefer showing the options in place (a pane, or revealed on demand) over a dialog that breaks the flow, unless the action really lies outside the current context.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the purpose to display a non-critical user input problem or special condition? If so, use a balloon instead.
rule: A minor input problem or special state of a field is shown at the field (a balloon on Windows), not in a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Generally you want a task to flow from page to page within a single window.
rule: Keep a task moving within its window; use dialogs only to confirm or collect input for in-place commands and for separate stand-alone tasks.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Using the default options without asking, but allowing users to make changes later.
rule: When people rarely change a command's options, run it with sensible defaults and let them change the options afterwards instead of asking first.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Generally, toolbar commands should be immediate and avoid displaying dialog boxes.
rule: A toolbar button acts at once without a dialog; offer the options variant separately in the menu, such as Print… in the menu and Print on the toolbar.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Using a split button to select variations of a command.
rule: Offer variations of a command through a split button, and simple choices (checks, radio items, short lists) through a submenu, instead of a dialog.

quote: Make sure that your dialog box design (determined by its purpose, type, and user interaction) matches its usage
rule: Choose a dialog's kind (modal or modeless, required or optional answer) to fit how often it appears, who starts it and how likely people are to act on it.

quote: Question dialogs (using buttons) ask users a single question or to confirm a command, and use simple responses in horizontally arranged command buttons.
rule: A question dialog asks exactly one question with short answers on buttons; a dialog that asks several questions is a choice dialog with options and a confirm button.

quote: Don't use scrollable dialog boxes.
rule: A dialog never needs scrolling in normal use; redesign it with progressive disclosure or tabs instead.

quote: Don't have a menu bar or status bar.
rule: A dialog has no menu bar or status bar; its commands and status sit on the dialog or in context menus, unless the dialog is the app's main window.

quote: flash its taskbar button three times to draw attention, and leave it highlighted.
rule: When a dialog needs attention while the app is in the background, flash its taskbar button three times and leave it highlighted, without activating the window or making a sound.

quote: Use for critical or infrequent, one-off tasks that require completion before continuing.
rule: Make a dialog modal only for critical or rare one-off tasks that must be finished before going on.

quote: Use a delayed commit model so that changes don't take effect until explicitly committed.
rule: Changes in a modal dialog take effect only when the confirming button is pressed.

quote: Implement using a task dialog whenever appropriate to achieve a consistent look.
rule: Build modal dialogs with the Windows task dialog API for a consistent look.

quote: Use for frequent, repetitive, on-going tasks.
rule: Make a dialog modeless when it serves frequent, repeated or ongoing work alongside the main window.

quote: Use an immediate commit model so that changes take effect immediately.
rule: Changes made in a modeless dialog apply at once, without a confirming button.

quote: For modeless dialogs, use an explicit Close command button in the dialog to close the window.
rule: A modeless dialog closes with a Close button in its body as well as the title bar's close control.

quote: Consider making modeless dialog boxes dockable.
rule: Consider letting a modeless tool dialog dock into the main window for flexible placement.

quote: Don't display more than one owned choice dialog at a time from an owner choice dialog.
rule: From a choice dialog open at most one further choice dialog at a time; question dialogs may still appear over it.

quote: For a sequence of related dialogs, consider using a multi-page dialog if possible.
rule: Present a sequence of related dialogs as one multi-page dialog; unrelated ones stay separate.

quote: Use a multi-page dialog box instead of individual dialog boxes when you have the following sequence of related pages:
rule: When a task is an optional input page, a progress page and a single results page, show them as pages of one dialog rather than three dialogs.

quote: Don't use a multi-page dialog if the input page is a standard dialog.
rule: If the input step is a standard system dialog, keep it standard rather than folding it into a multi-page dialog.

quote: Don't use Next or Back buttons and don't have more than three pages.
rule: A multi-page dialog has no Next or Back buttons and at most three pages; anything longer is a guided flow.

quote: On the input page, use specific command buttons or command links to initiate the task.
rule: The input page starts the task with a button or link named for the task, not a generic one.

quote: Use a Cancel button on the input and progress pages, and a Close button on the results page.
rule: Offer Cancel on the input and progress pages and Close on the results page.

quote: Initially display dialogs "centered" on top of the owner window.
rule: Open a dialog centred over its owner window the first time; later it may reopen where it was last, relative to the owner.

quote: If a dialog is contextual, display it near the object from which it was launched.
rule: A dialog about a particular object opens near that object, offset down and to the right so it does not cover it.

quote: For modeless dialogs, display initially on top of the owner window to make it easy to find.
rule: A modeless dialog first opens on top of its owner window so it is easy to find.

quote: If necessary, adjust the initial location so that the entire dialog is visible within the target monitor.
rule: Move a dialog so it is wholly on its monitor, and shrink a resizable one that is larger than the monitor.

quote: When a dialog is redisplayed, consider displaying it in the same state as last accessed.
rule: Reopen a dialog on the same monitor with its last size, position and maximised state, remembered per user across runs.

quote: For resizable windows, set a minimum window size if there is a size below which the content is no longer usable.
rule: Give a resizable window a minimum size below which its content would stop working, and adapt the layout for small sizes.

quote: Don't use the Always on Top attribute.
rule: Never keep a dialog always on top, except one that is essentially modal but must let people briefly reach the owner, such as a spelling checker.

quote: Dialog boxes don't have title bar icons.
rule: Dialogs show no title-bar icon, unless the dialog is the app's main window on the taskbar.

quote: Dialog boxes always have a Close button.
rule: Every dialog has a title-bar Close button; modeless dialogs may add Minimize and resizable ones Maximize.

quote: Don't disable the Close button.
rule: Never disable the title-bar Close button, except in a progress dialog whose task must finish to avoid losing data.

quote: The Close button on the title bar should have the same effect as the Cancel or Close button
rule: The title-bar Close button does what the dialog's Cancel or Close button does, never what OK does.

quote: However, you still have to set a suitable title internally for use by Windows.
rule: A window whose title caption is hidden still sets a proper title for the system and assistive technology.

quote: When displayed, user initiated dialog boxes should always take input focus.
rule: A dialog the person opened takes keyboard focus; one the program opened on its own does not, so typing meant for another window is not misdirected.

quote: Assign initial input focus to the control that users are most likely to interact with first
rule: Put initial focus on the control people are most likely to use first, usually the first one, never a Help link.

quote: For keyboard navigation, tab order should flow in a logical order, generally from left to right, top to bottom.
rule: Tab order follows reading order, with frequently used controls allowed earlier and Help links placed after the commit buttons.

quote: Pressing the Esc key always closes an active dialog box.
rule: Escape always closes the active dialog, including when Cancel has become Close.

quote: Whenever possible, assign unique access keys to all interactive controls or their labels.
rule: Give every interactive control, including read-only text boxes, a unique access key on its label.

quote: OK, Cancel, and Close buttons. Enter and Esc are used for their access keys.
rule: OK, Cancel and Close get no access key since Enter and Escape serve them, but a button meaning OK or Cancel under another label does get one.

quote: Normally, the individual controls within a group are assigned access keys, so the group label doesn't need one.
rule: Group labels get no access key (the controls in the group do), unless access keys run short.

quote: Generic Help buttons, which are accessed with F1.
rule: A generic Help button gets no access key because F1 reaches it.

quote: Access links with the Tab key instead.
rule: Links get no access key; people reach them with Tab.

quote: Tabs are cycled using Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab.
rule: Tab names get no access key; Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab move between tabs.

quote: Browse buttons labeled "...". These Browse buttons can't be assigned access keys uniquely.
rule: A browse button labelled with an ellipsis alone gets no access key.

quote: Unlabeled controls, such as spin controls, graphic command buttons, and unlabeled progressive disclosure controls.
rule: Controls without a text label (spin arrows, symbol buttons, bare disclosure buttons) get no access key.

quote: Non-label static text or labels for controls that aren't interactive,
rule: Static text and labels of non-interactive controls such as progress bars get no access key.

quote: Whenever possible, assign access keys for commonly used commands according to the Standard Access Key Assignments
rule: Use the standard access key assignments for common commands, especially in frequently used dialogs.

quote: Assign commit button access keys first to ensure that they have the standard key assignments.
rule: Assign commit button access keys first, using the standard letter or else the first letter of the first word; Yes is always Y and No is N.

quote: To make access keys easy to find, assign the access keys to a character that appears early in the label,
rule: Choose an access key letter early in the label, ideally the first letter, even when a later word is the keyword.

quote: Prefer characters with wide widths, such as w, m, and capital letters.
rule: Prefer wide letters such as w, m and capitals as access keys so the underline is easy to see.

quote: Prefer a distinctive consonant or a vowel, such as "x" in Exit.
rule: Prefer a distinctive consonant or a vowel as the access key, as x in Exit.

quote: Avoid using characters that make the underline difficult to see,
rule: Avoid access keys whose underline is hard to see: narrow letters like i and l, letters with descenders, and letters next to a descender.

quote: assume that users will do something else while the task is completing
rule: Design long-running work to run unattended, expecting people to turn to something else meanwhile.

quote: Present users with progress feedback dialog box if an operation takes longer than five seconds to complete
rule: An operation longer than five seconds shows progress with a way to cancel or stop it; in a guided flow use a progress page or in-place progress unless people can do nothing while waiting.

quote: long-running task (over 30 seconds) and can be performed in the background, use a modeless progress dialog
rule: Work longer than about 30 seconds that can run in the background shows modeless progress so the app stays usable.

quote: Have a Minimize button on the title bar.
rule: A modeless progress window can be minimised and appears on the taskbar.

quote: Implement modeless progress dialogs so that they continue to run even if the owner window is closed.
rule: Background work keeps running after the window that started it is closed.

quote: Provide a command button to halt the operation if it takes more than a few seconds to complete, or has the potential never to complete.
rule: Offer a halt button for work longer than a few seconds: Cancel when stopping leaves no trace, Stop when partial results remain, switching from Cancel to Stop once undoing is no longer possible.

quote: Provide a command button to pause the operation if it takes more than several minutes to complete,
rule: Offer Pause for work lasting several minutes that gets in the way of other work.

quote: Gather as much information as you can before starting the task.
rule: Ask for everything a long task needs before it starts, so it can then run unattended.

quote: If recoverable problems are detected, have users deal with all problems found at the end of the task.
rule: Collect recoverable problems found during long work and present them together at the end, or as they happen if that is impractical.

quote: Don't abandon tasks as the result of recoverable errors.
rule: A recoverable error never ends the whole task; let people continue, as when a file copy skips one file.

quote: Indicate problems by turning the progress bar red.
rule: A problem during long work shows on the progress indicator itself (red on Windows).

quote: If the results are clearly apparent to users, close the progress dialog automatically on successful completion.
rule: Close the progress dialog by itself on success when the result is plain to see; otherwise report only problems, simply in the dialog (Cancel becomes Close) or in a follow-up dialog when detailed.

quote: Don't use a notification for completion feedback. Use either a progress dialog or an action success notification, but not both.
rule: Report a completion once, in the progress dialog or in a success notification, never both.

quote: Use the following time formats.
rule: Write time remaining from the largest non-zero unit down, two units at most ("2 hours, 5 minutes remaining", compact "2 hrs, 5 mins remaining", title "02:05 remaining"), stepping down as the larger unit reaches zero.

quote: Make estimates accurate, but don't give false precision.
rule: Do not overstate precision: with hours give minutes but not seconds.

quote: Keep the estimate up-to-date. Update time remaining estimates at least every 5 seconds.
rule: Refresh a time-remaining estimate at least every five seconds.

quote: Focus on the time remaining because that is the information users care about most.
rule: Show time remaining rather than elapsed time (elapsed only where it helps, as for repeated tasks), and no percentage text beside a progress bar.

quote: Be grammatically correct. Use singular units when the number is one.
rule: Use the singular unit for one (1 minute, 1 second), never "1 minutes".

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write progress and time-remaining text in sentence case.

quote: Don't use large graphics that serve no purpose beyond filling space with eye candy.
rule: No large decorative pictures in dialogs.

quote: Choose the body icon based on the design pattern:
rule: A question dialog shows a warning symbol only when the answer can lose data or system access; choice, progress and informational dialogs show no message symbol.

quote: This technique is most effective when the icons are easily recognizable and used in several locations within your program.
rule: A symbol that stands for a feature is recognisable and used for that feature everywhere in the app.

quote: Use icons to help users recognize the object in question.
rule: Show the object's own symbol (such as its file type) where a dialog is about that object.

quote: Consider using icons to help make features self-explanatory.
rule: Use pictures that show a setting's effect where that makes the setting self-explanatory.

quote: Use an icon in About Box dialogs for application branding.
rule: The About box shows the app's icon for branding.

quote: If you have a footnote, consider using a footnote icon to summarize the footnote's subject.
rule: A dialog footnote may carry a small icon for its subject.

quote: Don't use a footnote icon that repeats the body icon.
rule: The footnote icon never repeats the main message icon.

quote: Don't use the error or information standard icons.
rule: Footnotes never use the error or information icons; the warning icon or security shield may mark risk.

quote: Choose the commit buttons based on the design pattern:
rule: Commit buttons by dialog kind: question dialogs use Yes/No, Yes/No/Cancel, [Do it]/Cancel, [Do it]/[Don't do it] (/Cancel); link questions Cancel; modal choice OK/Cancel or [Do it]/Cancel; modeless Close; progress Cancel or Stop; informational Close.

quote: All commit buttons except Apply result in closing the dialog box window.
rule: Every commit button closes the dialog; only Apply leaves it open.

quote: Don't confirm commit buttons.
rule: Do not ask again after a commit button, unless the action is potentially catastrophic, out of line with other actions, or could lose much data, time or effort.

quote: Don't disable commit buttons.
rule: Do not disable commit buttons, except under the rules for disabling controls (the reason must be easy to see).

quote: Right-align commit buttons in a single row across the bottom of the dialog box,
rule: Commit buttons form one right-aligned row at the bottom of the dialog, even a single OK; never centred.

quote: Present the commit buttons in the following order:
rule: Order commit buttons left to right: OK or [Do it] or Yes, then [Don't do it] or No, then Cancel, then Apply, then Help.

quote: If you have many related commit buttons, consolidate them using split buttons.
rule: Fold several related commit buttons into one split button.

quote: Have a clear separation from commit buttons (which close the window) and all other command buttons (such as Advanced).
rule: Keep commit buttons visibly apart from other buttons such as Advanced that do not close the dialog.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Use positive commit buttons that are specific responses to the main instruction, instead of generic labels such as OK or Yes/No.
rule: Label the confirming button with the specific response to the dialog's question or task, so the button text alone says what happens.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Use Close for dialogs that don't have settings, such as informational dialogs. Never use Close for dialogs that have settings.
rule: A dialog without settings (informational) has Close; a dialog with settings never uses Close.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Use OK when the "specific" responses are still generic, such as Save, Select, or Choose.
rule: Use OK when the specific verb would still be generic (Save, Select, Choose) and for dialogs that change settings.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: For legacy dialog boxes without a main instruction, you can use generic labels such as OK.
rule: Legacy dialogs without a main instruction may keep OK.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: In such cases, you can purposely use generic commit button labels to force users to read the main instructions and prevent hasty decisions.
rule: For confirmations that need thought, generic Yes/No buttons may be used on purpose so people must read the question.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: you can add the word "anyway" to the positive commit button label to indicate that the dialog box presents a reason not to proceed
rule: When the dialog gives a reason not to go ahead, the confirming button adds "anyway" (Install anyway).

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Use Cancel or Close for negative commit buttons instead of specific responses to the main instruction.
rule: The button that backs out is Cancel or Close, not a reworded response, so it is easy to find.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Don't use Yes/Cancel. Always use Yes/No as a pair.
rule: Yes always pairs with No, never with Cancel.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Use a specific response when Cancel is ambiguous.
rule: Replace Cancel with a specific response when it is unclear what would be cancelled.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Responding to main instructions
quote: Don't map generic labels to their specific meaning with text in the content area.
rule: Never explain in the body what OK or Cancel will mean ("Click OK to continue"); name the buttons for what they do or use command links.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Yes and No buttons
quote: Prefer specific responses to Yes and No buttons.
rule: Prefer specific responses to Yes and No; confirmations usually keep Yes and No to make people think.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Yes and No buttons
quote: Use Yes and No buttons only to respond to yes or no questions.
rule: Yes and No answer only a question phrased as yes or no, and a yes-or-no question is never answered with OK and Cancel.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Yes and No buttons
quote: Consider phrasing the main instruction as a yes or no question if commit buttons with specific phrasing turn out to be long or awkward.
rule: When specific button labels would be long or awkward, ask a yes-or-no question instead, or use command links for answers of five words or more.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Yes and No buttons
quote: Don't use Yes and No buttons if the meaning of the No response is unclear.
rule: If it is unclear what No would do, use specific responses rather than Yes and No.

quote: In modal dialogs, clicking OK means apply the values, perform the task, and close the window.
rule: In a modal dialog OK applies the values, performs the task and closes the window.

quote: Don't use OK buttons to respond to questions.
rule: OK never answers a question.

quote: Label OK buttons correctly. The OK button should be labeled OK, not Ok or Okay.
rule: Where OK is used it is spelled OK, never Ok or Okay.

quote: Don't use OK buttons for errors or warnings. Problems are never OK. Use Close instead.
rule: An error or warning is dismissed with Close, never OK.

quote: Don't use OK buttons in modeless dialog boxes.
rule: A modeless dialog has no OK; it uses task buttons such as Find, or only Close.

quote: Clicking Cancel means abandon all changes, cancel the task, close the window, and return the environment to its previous state, leaving no side effect.
rule: Cancel discards every change, including those made in nested dialogs, closes the window and leaves no side effect.

quote: Provide a Cancel button to let users explicitly abandon changes.
rule: A dialog with settings has a Cancel button in its body rather than relying on the title-bar close; one without settings has none.

quote: Don't use Cancel buttons to respond to questions.
rule: Cancel never answers a question.

quote: Don't use Cancel buttons in modeless dialog boxes. Rather, use Close instead.
rule: A modeless dialog closes with Close, never Cancel.

quote: Don't disable the Cancel button. Users should always be able to cancel dialog boxes.
rule: Cancel is never disabled, except in a progress dialog during a stretch that truly cannot be cancelled.

quote: Use Close buttons for modeless dialog boxes, as well as modal dialogs that cannot be cancelled.
rule: Use Close for modeless dialogs and for modal ones that can no longer be cancelled.

quote: Clicking Close means close the dialog box window, leaving any existing side effects. Don't use Done, because it isn't an imperative construction.
rule: Close shuts the dialog and keeps whatever was already done; the label is Close, never Done.

quote: Don't use Apply buttons in dialog boxes that aren't property sheets or control panels.
rule: Only property windows have an Apply button (apply but stay open); other dialogs do not.

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Commit buttons for indirect dialog boxes
quote: If users need to both cancel the dialog box and the task, give commit buttons to do both.
rule: When a dialog interrupts a larger task, give one button that answers no to the dialog (Don't save) and Cancel for abandoning the whole task (the New or Exit).

section: Guidelines > Commit buttons > Commit buttons for indirect dialog boxes
quote: If users just need to cancel the dialog but not the task, use a button with a specific, negative response to the main instruction,
rule: When only the dialog can be declined, use a specific negative answer (Don't run) and no Cancel.

quote: Present a set of lengthy commands using command links, instead of command buttons or a combination of radio buttons and an OK button.
rule: For a single question with long answers, offer each answer as a command link that acts in one click instead of radio buttons plus OK.

quote: Present the most commonly used command links first.
rule: Order command links by likelihood of use in a logical flow, with a do-everything choice first.

quote: If a command link requires further explanation, provide a supplemental explanation.
rule: Add a supplemental line under a command link only when it needs one, saying why to choose it or what follows.

quote: Don't use supplemental explanations that are wordy restatements of the command link.
rule: A command link's explanation never just restates the link, and one explanation does not oblige the others to have one.

quote: Use phrases that start with a verb, without ending punctuation.
rule: Command link text starts with a verb, in sentence case, without ending punctuation.

quote: If a command is strongly recommended, consider adding "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Add "(recommended)" to the label itself of a strongly recommended choice.

quote: If a command is intended only for advanced users, consider adding "(advanced)" to the label.
rule: Add "(advanced)" to the label itself of a choice meant only for advanced users.

quote: Always provide an explicit Cancel button. Don't use a command link for this purpose.
rule: A command-link dialog always has an explicit Cancel button; cancelling is never a command link.

quote: Consider using a Don't show this <item> again option to allow users to suppress a recurring dialog box, only if there isn't a better alternative.
rule: Offer a don't-show-again option on a recurring dialog only when neither always showing nor removing it is better.

quote: Use this specific phrasing replace <item> with the specific item.
rule: Word the option "Don't show this <item> again" with the item named (Don't show this reminder again), or "Don't show this message again" for a dialog in general.

quote: Clearly indicate when user input will be used for future default values
rule: When the choices made will become future defaults, say so under the option: "Your selections will be used by default in the future."

quote: Don't select the option by default. If the dialog box really should be displayed only once, do so without asking.
rule: The don't-show-again option starts cleared; a dialog meant to appear once simply appears once without asking.

quote: Make the setting persist on a per-user basis.
rule: Remember a don't-show-again choice per user.

quote: If users select the option and click Cancel, this option does take effect.
rule: A ticked don't-show-again option takes effect even when the dialog is cancelled.

quote: If users may need to restore these dialog boxes, provide a Restore messages command in the program's Options dialog box.
rule: Offer a command in the app's settings that brings back suppressed messages.

quote: Provide this option to dismiss a dialog box only when:
rule: Offer "Ask me later" only on an indirect dialog that needs an answer but not now, deserves thought, and will really come back by itself; otherwise expect an answer now, with Cancel or Close.

quote: Use More/Fewer progressive disclosure buttons to show or hide advanced or rarely used options, commands, or details
rule: Hide only advanced or rarely used options behind a More/Fewer disclosure; never hide common ones.

quote: Don't use More/Fewer controls unless there really is more detail to show.
rule: Use a More disclosure only when there is genuinely more to show, not the same information in another form.

quote: Don't use More/Fewer controls to show Help. Use Help links or footnotes instead.
rule: A disclosure never reveals help text; help goes in a help link or footnote.

quote: With task dialogs, avoid combining More/Fewer controls with Don't show this <item> again.
rule: Avoid a More/Fewer control and a don't-show-again box together in a task dialog because it looks awkward.

quote: Use footnotes for information that's not essential to a dialog box's purpose, but that users may find helpful in making decisions.
rule: Put helpful but non-essential information in a footnote that most people can skip and still decide well.

section: Guidelines > Disabling or removing controls vs. giving error messages
quote: Remove the control when there is no way for users to enable it, or users don't expect it to apply
rule: Remove a control that people cannot enable, or do not expect to apply and whose state rarely changes.

section: Guidelines > Disabling or removing controls vs. giving error messages
quote: Disable the control when users expect it to apply or its state changes frequently, and users can easily deduce why the control is disabled.
rule: Disable a control when people expect it or its state changes often, and the reason is easy to see, such as a commit button with its one required field empty.

section: Guidelines > Disabling or removing controls vs. giving error messages
quote: Otherwise, leave the control enabled, but give an error message when it is used incorrectly.
rule: Otherwise leave the control enabled and explain the problem in an error message when it is used.

section: Guidelines > Disabling or removing controls vs. giving error messages
quote: If you aren't sure whether you should disable a control or give an error message, start by composing the error message that you might give.
rule: When unsure, draft the error message: if it tells people something they would not quickly guess, keep the control enabled and show it; otherwise disable.

section: Guidelines > Disabling or removing controls vs. giving error messages
quote: If you disable a control, also disable all associated controls
rule: Disabling a control also disables its label, explanation and related buttons, but not its group box, group label or group explanation.

quote: To indicate that users must provide information in a control, consider the following options:
rule: Mark required input one way: not at all (catch it with errors), an asterisk before the label explained as Required input, "All input required" at the top, or "(optional)" after optional labels.

quote: For consistency, try to use the same method to indicate required input throughout your program.
rule: Use the same required-input method across the app, marking either required or optional fields but never both.

quote: Prevent errors by using controls that are constrained to valid user input.
rule: Prevent errors with controls that accept only valid values and with sensible defaults.

quote: Validate user input as soon as possible, and show errors as closely to the point of input as possible.
rule: Check input as early as possible and show the error right beside the input.

quote: Use balloons for non-critical, single-point user input problems detected while in a text box or immediately after a text box loses focus.
rule: Report a minor problem in one field, found while typing or on leaving it, in a single balloon at the field, without an error symbol; it goes when clicked, fixed or after a timeout.

quote: Use in-place errors for delayed error detection, usually errors found by clicking a commit button.
rule: Errors found on pressing a commit button appear in place next to each problem, several at once if needed, and stay until fixed; not for settings that apply at once.

quote: Use modal error handling (task dialogs or message boxes) for all other problems,
rule: Problems spanning several controls, or not tied to input, are reported in a modal message.

quote: When an input problem is found and reported, set input focus to the first control with the incorrect data.
rule: After reporting input problems, move focus to the first control in error and scroll it into view.

quote: Give interactive controls self-explanatory labels.
rule: Help people first with self-explanatory control labels, then with explanatory text in place, and only then with a link to a specific help topic.

quote: Locate Help links at the bottom of the content area of the dialog box.
rule: Put a dialog's help link at the bottom of its content (in the footnote if related, or under each group with its own topic).

quote: Don't use general or vague Help topic links or generic Help buttons.
rule: Never offer a vague help link or generic Help button; link to the specific relevant topic.

quote: Include a default commit button on every dialog box.
rule: Every dialog has a default commit button.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access), most secure response to be the default.
rule: In a question dialog the default answer is the safest one, else the most likely; never a destructive one unless easily undone.

quote: For the initial default values, select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure values for each control.
rule: A choice dialog's controls start on the safest values, or the most likely where safety is not at stake.

quote: For the subsequent default values, reselect the previously selected options if those values are likely to be repeated
rule: Reopen a choice dialog with the previous choices where they are likely to be repeated and safe, but not values that usually change, such as the number of copies.

quote: Support the minimum Windows Vista screen resolution of 800 x 600 pixels.
rule: Windows must work on an 800 x 600 screen, with resizable layouts optimised for 1024 x 768.

quote: Use resizable windows whenever practical to avoid scroll bars and truncated data.
rule: Make windows resizable where practical, especially those with lists or changing content, to avoid scrolling and cut-off text.

quote: Fixed-sized windows must be entirely visible and sized to fit within the work area.
rule: A fixed-size window fits entirely within the screen's work area.

quote: Resizable windows may be optimized for higher resolutions, but sized down as needed at display time to the actual screen resolution.
rule: A resizable window designed for larger screens shrinks to fit the actual screen when shown.

quote: Choose a default window size appropriate for its contents.
rule: Open a window at a size that fits its typical content, larger if the space is used well.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Say each thing once across title, main instruction, supplemental text, content, links and buttons, keeping the full text in instructions and controls.

quote: Use positive phrasing. Positive phrasing is easier for users to understand.
rule: Phrase questions and options positively (enable rather than disable), except to match a command that is itself negative.

quote: If necessary, use the word "window" to refer to the dialog box itself.
rule: Text that refers to the dialog itself calls it a window.

quote: Use the second person ("you/your") to tell users what to do
rule: Instructions address the reader as you, often implied (Choose an account).

quote: Use the first person ("I/me/my") to let users tell the program what to do
rule: Options that answer the main instruction may speak as the reader in the first person (Print the photos on my camera).

quote: Use the title to identify the command, feature, or program where a dialog box came from.
rule: A dialog's title names the command or feature that opened it (the program's name when many commands share it, when it would repeat the instruction, or when the program opened it), and never says what to do.

quote: Use the exact command name for command-based names, but don't include the ellipsis if there is one.
rule: A dialog named after a command repeats the command's exact name without its ellipsis, adding the menu name if needed (Insert Object).

quote: If a modeless dialog box appears on the taskbar, optimize the title for display on the taskbar
rule: A window shown on the taskbar puts its distinguishing information first in the title (66% Complete, 3 Reminders).

quote: Don't include the words "dialog" or "progress" in the title.
rule: A title never contains the words dialog or progress.

quote: Use title-style capitalization, without ending punctuation.
rule: Dialog titles are in title case without ending punctuation.

quote: Use the main instruction to explain concisely what to do in the dialog.
rule: A dialog's main instruction says in a specific statement, command or question what the person is trying to do there.

quote: Omit the main instruction when the only thing you can say is obvious.
rule: Leave out the main instruction when the dialog's purpose is obvious, as in Open and Save.

quote: Omit control labels that restate the main instruction. In this case, the main instruction takes the access key.
rule: Drop a control label that only repeats the main instruction; the instruction then labels the control and carries its access key.

quote: Be concise use only a single, complete sentence.
rule: Keep the main instruction to one complete sentence; more goes in the supplemental instruction.

quote: Use specific verbs whenever possible.
rule: Use specific verbs (connect, save, install) rather than generic ones (configure, manage, set).

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Main instructions are in sentence case.

quote: Don't include final periods if the instruction is a statement. If the instruction is a question, include a final question mark.
rule: A main instruction that is a statement has no full stop; a question ends with a question mark.

quote: For progress dialogs, use a gerund phrase briefly explaining the operation in progress, ending with an ellipsis.
rule: A progress dialog's instruction is an -ing phrase naming the operation, ending in an ellipsis (Printing your pictures…).

quote: You can evaluate a main instruction by imagining what you would say to a friend.
rule: Test a main instruction by saying it aloud to a friend; rework it if it sounds unnatural or unhelpful.

quote: When necessary, use an optional supplemental instruction to present additional information helpful to understanding or using the page.
rule: Add a supplemental instruction only for information that helps understand or use the dialog, such as defining a term.

quote: use the supplemental instruction to explain why the dialog has appeared.
rule: A dialog the program opened by itself explains in its supplemental text why it appeared.

quote: Don't repeat the main instruction with slightly different wording.
rule: Never reword the main instruction as supplemental text; omit it if there is nothing to add.

quote: Use complete sentences, sentence-style capitalization, and ending punctuation.
rule: Supplemental instructions are complete sentences in sentence case with full stops.

quote: Choose concise link text that clearly communicates and differentiates what the command link does.
rule: Each command link says concisely what it does, answers the main instruction and is clearly distinct from the others.

quote: Start commit button labels with a verb. Exceptions are OK, Yes, and No.
rule: Commit button labels start with a verb; only OK, Yes and No are exempt.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Commit buttons are in sentence case (Don't save).

quote: Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: Commit button labels have no ending punctuation.

quote: Everywhere else, refer to dialog boxes by their title. If the title bar is hidden, refer to the dialog using the main instruction.
rule: Help text names a dialog by its title (or its main instruction when there is no title); "dialog box" is for technical documentation only.

quote: If you must refer to a dialog box in general, use window in user documentation.
rule: Help text calls dialogs in general windows, and a simple question or confirmation a message.

quote: Use the exact title or main instruction text, including its capitalization.
rule: Quote a dialog's title or instruction exactly, with its capitalisation.

quote: When possible, format the title using bold text.
rule: Show UI names in bold in help text, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion (In Windows Security, click More Options).

quote: Display tips only as the result of user interaction never display them on their own.
rule: A tip appears only when the pointer rests on its object, never by itself.

quote: Does a control have a text label? If not, use a tooltip to provide the label.
rule: A control without a text label, such as a symbol toolbar button, gets a tooltip as its label; labelled controls normally need none.

quote: If it is essential, put it directly in the UI so that users don't have to discover or hunt for it.
rule: Use a longer hover tip only for supplemental description; anything essential goes in the window itself.

quote: Is the supplemental information an error, warning, or status? If so, use another UI element,
rule: Errors, warnings and status never go in a tip (a tray icon's tip is the exception for status).

quote: Do users need to interact with the tip? If so, use another control, such as a balloon.
rule: Content people must click or select is never in a tip, since moving the pointer hides it.

quote: Do users need to print the supplemental information? If so, use another control,
rule: Information people may print is shown on the page, not only in a tip.

quote: If you do use tips in such contexts, allow users to turn them off.
rule: Where tips could annoy or distract, consider none; if used there, let people turn them off.

quote: Never use tips as a substitute for good design.
rule: If people must keep checking a tip to understand something, redesign it rather than relying on the tip.

quote: Users don't expect tips to change from one instance to the next,
rule: Tip text is static; changing content such as status does not belong in tips, except on tray icons.

quote: Provide more than one way to access a control if that control requires a tip that doesn't have keyboard access.
rule: A control whose meaning depends on a hover tip it cannot show to the keyboard also has another route, such as a menu command with a shortcut.

quote: In fact, the alt text tip pattern is the preferred way to make graphics accessible.
rule: Give each meaningful graphic a text description that screen readers announce.

quote: Because these tips serve as labels, their text follows the label guidelines for the underlying control.
rule: A tooltip that labels an unlabeled control follows that control's label rules, often just the command name.

quote: Full name infotips display the full name of an item when the name is truncated or not fully visible.
rule: Hovering a cut-off name shows the full name, drawn directly over the item in lists and trees.

quote: notification area icons are an exception because these icons communicate status,
rule: A tray icon's tip may show changing status, since the icon has no other room for it.

quote: Use the default initial and reshow timeouts.
rule: Tips appear after the system's standard delays (half a second, a tenth when moving between targets); only a non-redundant thumbnail beside its object may appear at once.

quote: For tooltips, use the default five-second tip removal timeout.
rule: A short tooltip disappears after the standard five seconds.

quote: For infotips, turn off the tip removal timeout.
rule: A longer descriptive tip stays until the pointer leaves.

quote: make them multiples of the SPI_GETMOUSEHOVERTIME and SPI_GETMESSAGEDURATION system parameters instead of using fixed times.
rule: Derive any custom tip delay from the system's hover-time and message-duration settings so it follows the person's speed.

quote: Avoid covering the object the user is about to view or interact with.
rule: Place a tip beside its object, even away from the pointer, so it never covers what the person is looking at; full-name tips in lists are the exception.

quote: For collections of items, avoid covering the next object that the user is likely to view or interact with.
rule: In a row of items a tip does not go to the right, and in a column not below, so the next item stays visible.

quote: For potentially distracting (often large) tips, make sure that the information is helpful for most users.
rule: Large, distracting tips must help most people; otherwise make them optional or drop them.

quote: Controls with prompts are considered labeled, such as text boxes and combo boxes.
rule: Tooltips label unlabeled toolbar, symbol and disclosure buttons; a text box or combo box with a prompt counts as labelled; every other control has a visible label.

quote: Use sentence fragments without ending punctuation.
rule: Tooltips are sentence fragments without ending punctuation.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Tooltips are in sentence case.

quote: Add an ellipsis if the label is for a command that needs additional information.
rule: A tooltip naming a command that asks for more input ends with an ellipsis.

quote: keep tooltips brief typically five words or less but prefer specific labels over vague ones.
rule: Keep tooltips to about five words, preferring specific over vague.

quote: Tooltips may also provide more detail for labeled toolbar buttons if doing so is helpful.
rule: A labelled toolbar button's tooltip may explain more, but never just repeats or pads out the label.

quote: You don't have to give labeled controls tooltips simply for the sake of consistency.
rule: Labelled controls need no tooltip just for consistency with unlabeled ones.

quote: make tooltips more helpful by providing keyboard shortcuts and default values.
rule: Add the keyboard shortcut and default value to a tooltip in parentheses, not counted against its brevity.

quote: For infotips in nonstandard places, favor consistency over helpfulness to improve discoverability.
rule: Give descriptive tips to all similar objects or to none; if only a few would help, use clear labels or in-place text instead.

quote: Use full sentences with ending punctuation.
rule: Descriptive tips are full sentences with ending punctuation, except tray icon tips.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Descriptive tips are in sentence case.

quote: Use present tense, not future.
rule: Descriptive tips use the present tense, not the future.

quote: Use parallel grammatical constructions.
rule: Phrase descriptive tips in parallel form; a full-name tip copies the item's text exactly.

quote: Avoid large infotips.
rule: Keep descriptive tips small enough to read and to place without covering their object.

quote: Format infotips to make their content easier to read and scan.
rule: Break a longer tip into scannable parts rather than one block of text.

quote: On first use within an infotip, spell out the names of acronyms, followed by the acronym in parentheses.
rule: Spell out an acronym at its first use, followed by the acronym in parentheses.

quote: describe the item concisely and list the primary tasks that users can perform with the item.
rule: An app's Start menu description says briefly what it is and lists the main tasks it does.

quote: Be helpful. Focus on what users can do. Don't just repeat the item name or even use it in the description at all.
rule: The Start menu description says what people can do and does not repeat the app's name.

quote: Be specific. Avoid generic verbs and catch-all phrases like and other tasks.
rule: The description lists specific tasks without catch-alls like "and other tasks".

quote: Be concise. Use 25 words or less. Longer infotips discourage reading.
rule: Keep the Start menu description to 25 words or fewer.

quote: Start with a present-tense, imperative verb such as create, edit, show, and send.
rule: Start the description with a specific imperative verb (create, edit, send), not manage or open.

quote: Don't use language that sounds like marketing.
rule: The description avoids marketing language.

quote: describe your program's important tasks using terms for which users are most likely to search.
rule: Use the words and synonyms people search for, since the description is indexed by Start menu search.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: The Start menu description is in sentence case.

quote: Use a tooltip with the format: Launch (full program name)
rule: A Quick Launch tooltip reads Launch followed by the full program name.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: Quick Launch tooltips have no ending punctuation.

quote: Don't use additional text to describe the program or what it does.
rule: A Quick Launch tooltip does not describe the program.

quote: concisely describe the Control Panel tasks and the hardware and software configured.
rule: Control Panel tips describe the tasks and what hardware or software the item configures.

quote: Control Panel names and icons must have infotips.
rule: Every Control Panel name and icon has a tip; its individual tasks do not.

quote: Be helpful. Focus on what users can do. Don't just repeat the Control Panel item name
rule: A Control Panel tip says what people can do without repeating the item name.

quote: Be specific. Avoid generic verbs and catch-all phrases like and other hardware.
rule: A Control Panel tip lists specific hardware rather than catch-alls.

quote: Be concise. Use 25 words or less.
rule: A Control Panel tip has 25 words or fewer.

quote: Start with a present-tense, imperative verb.
rule: A Control Panel tip starts with an imperative verb.

quote: Get right to the point. Don't use language that applies to any Control Panel,
rule: A Control Panel tip skips boilerplate that would fit any item.

quote: Don't use language that sounds like marketing.
rule: A Control Panel tip avoids marketing language.

quote: describe items using terms for which users are most likely to search.
rule: A Control Panel tip uses the terms people search for.

quote: If a Control Panel item is likely to be confused with others, explain how it is different in the infotip.
rule: A Control Panel tip explains how its item differs from a similar one.

quote: For tooltips, don't use icons.
rule: Tooltips carry no icon.

quote: For infotips, use icons only if they aid in recognition or comprehension, or provide context.
rule: Descriptive tips carry an icon only when it aids recognition.

quote: The icon must use the Aero-style and have an unobtrusive appearance.
rule: Tip icons use the Aero style and stay unobtrusive.

quote: Everywhere else, simply call it a tip.
rule: Help text calls any tooltip or infotip a tip; the specific names are for technical documentation.

quote: The following variations are incorrect: tool tip, Tooltip, and ToolTip.
rule: Spell the term tooltip, never tool tip, Tooltip or ToolTip.

quote: To describe user interaction, use hover.
rule: Help text says hover for resting the pointer on something to see its tip.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the user being alerted of a condition that might cause a problem in the future? If not, the message isn't a warning.
rule: A warning is only for a condition that might cause a problem later; routine questions are not phrased as warnings.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the UI presenting an error or problem that has already occurred? If so, use an error message instead.
rule: A problem that has already happened is an error message, not a warning.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: If not, the condition doesn't justify interrupting the user so it's better to suppress the warning.
rule: Drop a warning that would not lead people to act or change what they do.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the condition the direct result of an action initiated by the user? If not, consider using a non-critical event notifications.
rule: A condition not caused by the person's own action is better reported as a notification.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the condition a special condition in a control? If so, use a balloon instead.
rule: A special state of a control that affects input (such as Caps Lock on in a password field) is shown at the control.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: a warning is appropriate if the action has significant consequences or cannot be easily undone.
rule: Warn before a risky action only when its consequences are significant or hard to undo.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Don't display warnings if users can continue to work productively without immediate problems.
rule: Postpone a warning until the condition is near and relevant, as long as people can keep working meanwhile.

quote: The mere potential for data loss or a future problem alone is insufficient to call for a warning.
rule: Warn only about results that are unexpected, unintended and not easily corrected, not merely possible data loss.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of good warnings
quote: Involve risk. Good warnings alert users of something significant.
rule: A warning concerns something significant; do not, for example, confirm quitting the app as if it were usually an accident.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of good warnings
quote: Don't display a warning to state the obvious consequence of an action.
rule: Never warn about an obvious consequence, such as an unfinished task not being done after Cancel.

section: Design concepts > Determine the appropriate message type
quote: To determine the appropriate message type, focus on the most important aspect of the issue that users need to know or act upon.
rule: Choose error if the issue blocks progress and warning if people can go on, then make the text and the symbol match that type.

quote: Warnings are more compelling when the following information is specific and clear:
rule: A warning names its source, the condition and possible problem, what to do and what happens if nothing is done.

quote: However, in such cases, use wording that indicates that there are other possibilities.
rule: When the cause or remedy is uncertain, give the most likely one and say other causes are possible.

quote: Error prevention warnings are best presented using an in-place warning icon and explanatory text.
rule: A warning that helps avoid a mistake while choosing appears in place, beside the choice, with a warning symbol and text.

quote: Choose the presentation UI based on the type of information:
rule: Present warnings by kind: modal for critical ones needing an answer now, in place while choosing, a banner tied to finishing a task, a notification for ignorable events, a balloon for a control state affecting input.

quote: Use task dialogs whenever appropriate to achieve a consistent look and layout.
rule: Build modal warnings with the Windows task dialog API.

quote: Display only one warning message per condition.
rule: Explain a condition in one complete warning, not a series of dialogs one detail at a time.

quote: Don't display a warning more than once per condition.
rule: Warn once per condition; if repeated warning is needed, escalate gradually.

quote: Don't accompany warnings with a sound effect or beep.
rule: Warnings make no sound, unless the person must respond at once.

quote: Don't place a warning icon in the title bar of a dialog box.
rule: No warning icon in a dialog's title bar.

quote: Use a warning icon.
rule: A warning carries the warning symbol, or the feature's own symbol with a warning mark.

quote: For modal dialog boxes with a warning footnote, put the warning icon in the footnote instead of the content area.
rule: When the warning is in a footnote, its icon sits there.

section: Guidelines > Don't show this message again
quote: If a warning dialog box needs this option, reconsider the warning and its frequency.
rule: A warning that people would want to suppress is not a good warning; rethink it instead of adding don't-show-again.

quote: If you must include advanced information in a warning message, reveal it by using progressive disclosure buttons
rule: Hide advanced detail in a warning behind Show details, but never information people need.

quote: Don't use "Show details" unless there really is more detail.
rule: Offer Show details only when there is more to show, not a restatement.

quote: Select the safest, least destructive, or most secure response to be the default.
rule: A warning's default answer is the safest, least destructive one.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Say each thing once across a warning's title, instructions, content and buttons.

quote: Don't use the terms "warning" or "caution" in the text.
rule: Warning text never says warning or caution; the symbol already does.

quote: Use the title to identify the command or feature where the warning came from.
rule: A warning's title names the command or feature it came from (or the program), not "Security Warning", and never says what to do.

quote: Use title-style capitalization, without ending punctuation.
rule: Warning titles are in title case without ending punctuation.

quote: The main instruction for a warning is based on its design pattern:
rule: A warning's main instruction describes the condition (awareness), says what to do now (imminent problem) or asks whether to proceed (risky action).

quote: Be concise use only a single, complete sentence.
rule: Keep the warning's main instruction to one complete sentence.

quote: Use words like "now" and "immediately" if the user must act immediately.
rule: Say now or immediately only when action really is urgent.

quote: Be specific if there are objects involved, give their full names.
rule: Name the objects involved in full.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Warning main instructions are in sentence case.

quote: The supplemental instruction for a warning is based on its design pattern:
rule: The supplemental text explains the implication (awareness), the condition (imminent problem) or non-obvious reasons not to proceed (risky action).

quote: Don't repeat the main instruction with slightly different wording.
rule: Never reword the main instruction as supplemental text.

quote: Use complete sentences, sentence-style capitalization, and ending punctuation.
rule: Supplemental text is complete sentences in sentence case with full stops.

quote: Close. Don't use OK because it suggests that potential problems are OK.
rule: An awareness warning closes with Close, an imminent problem has a button per option (or OK when the action happens elsewhere), and a risky-action confirmation has Yes and No.

quote: If the warning asks a question, refer to a warning by its question; otherwise, use the main instruction.
rule: Help text refers to a warning by its question or main instruction, summarised if long.

quote: If necessary, you may refer to a warning dialog box as a message.
rule: Help text may call a warning dialog a message.

quote: When possible, format the text using bold.
rule: Show the warning's text in bold in help, using quotation marks only when needed.

quote: check boxes should be used only to toggle an option on or off or to select or deselect an item.
rule: Use a check box only to turn one option on or off or to select an item; its label names the on state and off is its plain opposite.

quote: Are the selected and cleared states clear and unambiguous opposites? If not, use radio buttons or a drop-down list
rule: If on and off are not clear opposites, use radio buttons or a select so each state has its own label.

quote: When used in a group, does the group comprise independent choices, from which users may choose zero or more?
rule: A group of check boxes holds independent choices of which any number, including none, may be chosen; dependent choices use radio buttons or a check box tree.

quote: If so, use a group of check boxes and handle the error when none of the options are selected.
rule: When at least one of several options must be chosen, use check boxes and report an error if none is ticked.

quote: Since the screen space used is proportional to the number of options, keep the number of check boxes to 10 or fewer.
rule: Keep a group to ten check boxes at most; beyond that use a checkable list.

quote: Use radio buttons if the meaning of the cleared check box isn't completely obvious.
rule: Choose radio buttons over a check box when the meaning of off is not obvious, such as Landscape versus Portrait.

quote: Use radio buttons on wizard pages to make the alternatives clear, even if a check box is otherwise acceptable.
rule: On guided-flow pages use radio buttons to make the alternatives explicit, even where a check box would do.

quote: Use radio buttons if you have enough screen space and the options are important enough to be a good use of that screen space.
rule: Use radio buttons when space allows and the options matter; for a peripheral option use a check box or select.

quote: Use a check box if there other check boxes on the window.
rule: Prefer a check box when the window already uses check boxes.

quote: Does the option present a program option, rather than data?
rule: Check boxes are for program options whose values do not depend on data; choosing among data items uses a checkable or multi-select list.

quote: Group related check boxes.
rule: Group related check boxes and separate unrelated ones, at most ten per group.

quote: Reconsider using group boxes to organize groups of check boxes
rule: Avoid framing check box groups in group boxes, which clutters the window.

quote: List check boxes in a logical order,
rule: Order check boxes logically (related together, common first), not alphabetically, which breaks in translation.

quote: Align check boxes vertically, not horizontally.
rule: Stack check boxes in a column, not in a row.

quote: Don't use the mixed state to represent a third state.
rule: The mixed state only reflects children that differ; people cannot set it directly and it never stands for a third value.

quote: Clicking a mixed state check box should cycle through all selected, all cleared, and the original mixed states.
rule: Clicking a mixed check box cycles through all on, all off and back to the original mix.

quote: Don't use check boxes as a progress indicator.
rule: Never show progress as a list of check boxes; use a progress indicator.

quote: Show disabled check boxes using the correct selection state.
rule: A disabled check box shows the state that actually applies, such as cleared when the option cannot take effect.

quote: Don't use the selection of a check box to:
rule: Ticking a check box never runs a command, opens a window or makes other controls appear.

quote: Consider using a Don't show this <item> again option to allow users to suppress a recurring dialog box only if there isn't a better alternative.
rule: Offer don't-show-again only when it is unclear whether people need the dialog; otherwise always show it or remove it.

quote: Place subordinate controls to the right of or below (indented, flush with the check box label) the check box and its label.
rule: Put a check box's dependent controls to its right or indented below it, and end the check box label with a colon.

quote: Leave dependent editable text boxes and drop-down lists enabled if they share the check box's label.
rule: A dependent field that shares the check box's label stays enabled, and typing or pasting into it ticks the box.

quote: disable these subordinate controls until the high-level option is selected.
rule: Nested check boxes or radio buttons stay disabled until their parent option is on.

quote: Make subordinate controls to a check box contiguous with the check box in the tab order.
rule: Dependent controls follow their check box directly in tab order.

quote: If selecting an option implies selecting subordinate check boxes, explicitly select those check boxes to make the relationship clear.
rule: When turning on an option implies its sub-options, tick those sub-options visibly.

quote: Use dependent check boxes if the alternatives add unnecessary complexity.
rule: In rare cases let check boxes be mutually dependent (such as superscript and subscript) when radio buttons would add complexity without clarity.

quote: set the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access), most secure and private state by default.
rule: A check box starts in its safest, most secure and private state, or the most likely one where that is not at stake.

quote: Label every check box.
rule: Every check box has a label.

quote: Assign a unique access key to each label.
rule: Each check box label has a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Check box labels are in sentence case.

quote: Write the label as a phrase or an imperative sentence, and use no ending punctuation.
rule: A check box label is a phrase or command without ending punctuation, or with a colon when it also labels a following control.

quote: Write the label so that it describes the selected state of the check box.
rule: The label describes what being ticked means.

quote: For a group of check boxes, use parallel phrasing and try to keep the length about the same for all labels.
rule: Labels in a group are parallel in phrasing and similar in length.

quote: If all the options have the same introductory text, move that text to the group label.
rule: Labels in a group state their differences; shared opening words move to the group label.

quote: Use positive phrasing. Don't phrase a label so that selecting a check box means not to perform an action.
rule: Phrase labels so ticking turns something on, never off; Don't show again is the exception.

quote: Describe just the option with the label. Keep labels brief so it's easy to refer to them in messages and documentation.
rule: Keep the label to the option itself; put any explanation in separate text as full sentences.

quote: Adding an explanation to one check box in a group doesn't mean that you have to provide explanations for all check boxes in the group.
rule: Explain only the check boxes that need it, without restating labels for consistency.

quote: If an option is strongly recommended, consider adding "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Add "(recommended)" to the label of a strongly recommended option.

quote: If you must use multi-line labels, align the top of the label with the check box.
rule: Align the top of a multi-line label with its box.

quote: Don't use a subordinate control, the values it contains, or its units label to create a sentence or phrase.
rule: Never build a sentence around an embedded control (Remind me [5] minutes before), which cannot be translated.

quote: Use the group label to explain the purpose of the group, not how to make the selection.
rule: A group label says what the group is for, not how to tick boxes.

quote: End each label with a colon.
rule: Group labels end with a colon.

quote: Don't assign an access key to the label.
rule: A check box group label has no access key.

quote: For a selection of one or more dependent choices, explain the requirement on the label.
rule: When at least one option is required, the group label says so.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or colon. Include the word check box.
rule: Help text quotes the exact label without the colon and adds the words check box (Select the Underline check box).

quote: Refer to a check box as a check box, not option, checkbox, or just box,
rule: Call it a check box, never option, checkbox or box.

quote: To describe user interaction, use select and clear.
rule: Help text says select and clear for ticking and unticking.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Show check box labels in bold in help text, quoted only when needed.

quote: Is the control used for numeric input? If not, use another control, such as a drop-down list or slider,
rule: Use a stepper only for numbers; fixed sets of values use a select or slider.

quote: Use spin boxes only for exact, known numeric values.
rule: A value people think of as relative (volume low or high) gets a slider; a stepper is for exact numbers.

quote: Is the control paired with a text box? If not, don't use.
rule: A stepper is always paired with a number field, never alone or with another control.

quote: Are contiguous value ranges valid? If not, use a drop-down list of valid values instead.
rule: When not every value in the range is valid, offer a select of the valid ones instead of a stepper.

quote: Entering a small number, typically under 100.
rule: A stepper suits small numbers (under about 100) and small changes to an existing value.

quote: Is the control used in a context where users are likely to be using their mouse? If not, consider a spin control optional.
rule: Where people are mostly typing, the stepper is optional.

quote: Are the sibling controls drop-down lists? If there are other drop-down lists, consider using a drop-down list for consistency.
rule: Next to other selects, use a select for consistency.

quote: Are touch or pen users a primary target? If so, consider using a drop-down list instead.
rule: For touch or pen use, prefer a select to tiny spin arrows.

quote: If a slider or a spin box is possible, use a spin box if:
rule: Between a slider and a stepper, choose the stepper when space is tight or the keyboard is likely, and the slider when instant feedback helps.

quote: To be consistent with other text boxes on the same user interface (UI), use spin controls even if they aren't always practical.
rule: Use steppers where practical, and also on fields beside other stepper fields for consistency.

quote: Always make a spin control the "buddy" of the text box. Doing so places the spin control inside the text box.
rule: The spin arrows sit inside their number box.

quote: Disable a spin control when its associated text box is disabled.
rule: The stepper is disabled with its field, and is never the only way to enter the value.

quote: Define the top button to increase the value by one unit and the bottom button to decrease by one unit.
rule: Up adds and down subtracts one step, the step being the smallest common change (such as 0.1).

quote: Use the spin control to limit input to valid values.
rule: Stepping never produces an invalid value.

quote: At the end of a range of valid values, restart the range.
rule: Stepping past the end wraps to the other end, unless the wrapped value would certainly be wrong.

quote: Use text instead of special numeric values.
rule: Special values appear as words people can step to (Never), not codes to type.

quote: If the value has delimiters, the associated text box should have multiple input focus points.
rule: A value with parts (hours:minutes) lets each part take focus and be stepped separately.

quote: If the value has units, use the spin control to change those units as well.
rule: When the value has units, stepping can change the unit too.

quote: Apply the text box labeling guidelines to label the associated text box. Spin controls are never labeled directly.
rule: Label the number field; the stepper shares that label and has none of its own.

quote: Don't refer to spin controls in user documentation. Instead, refer to the label of the associated text box.
rule: Help text names the field by its label (In the Date box…), never the spin control.

quote: Whenever possible, put crucial text on interactive controls instead of static text.
rule: Words the reader must not miss belong on the controls themselves (button and option labels), not in surrounding static text.

quote: Avoid putting crucial information in the lower-left corner or at the bottom of a long scrollable control or page.
rule: Never leave essential information where scanning ends: the bottom leading corner of a window or the end of a long scrolling area.

quote: Don't present big blocks of text. Eliminate unnecessary text. Use the inverted pyramid presentation style.
rule: Keep text in a window short, cut whatever is not needed, and put the conclusion before the detail.

quote: If you do something to attract users' attention, make sure that attention is warranted.
rule: Give extra emphasis only to an element that really deserves to be looked at first; an emphasised element that is not the starting point misleads.

quote: Don't require any interaction, such as pointing or hovering, to see the element you are emphasizing.
rule: A primary element is visible as such without hovering or pointing; only secondary controls may reveal themselves on hover.

quote: Use prominent text, including large text and bold text.
rule: Emphasise primary elements with large or bold text, dark-on-light contrast and generous space, and de-emphasise secondary ones with grey text, light-on-dark and tight space.

quote: Put secondary UI elements outside the scan path.
rule: Keep elements people seldom need out of the main reading path, toward the bottom of the window or behind progressive disclosure.

section: Design concepts > Using screen space effectively
quote: Effective layout has respect for open space and doesn't attempt to cram everything into the smallest space possible.
rule: Do not shrink a window to the smallest size that holds its content; when choosing, err toward a little too much room rather than too little.

quote: To avoid visual clutter, the lightest weight grouping that does the job well is the best choice.
rule: Show grouping with the lightest means that works: spacing first, then a separator, and a boxed group only when those are not enough.

quote: Controls that are peers to each other should be left-aligned, and dependent controls are indented
rule: Align peer controls on one leading edge and indent a control that depends on another beneath it (the indent amount is Kvit's own).

quote: The window or pages has at most 7 groups.
rule: A window or page presents its content in no more than seven groups, each with an obvious purpose.

quote: This style is the easiest to localize because the layout doesn't depend upon the length of the labels
rule: Put labels above their controls for short forms (about ten controls or fewer) that will be translated, and on the leading side of the controls for long forms people scan by label.

quote: Prefer a style that you can use consistently across your program.
rule: Use one label placement style throughout the app, preferring labels above or leading-aligned beside their controls.

quote: Using larger margins on the left side than the right.
rule: Balance a left-heavy layout with a wider leading margin than trailing margin.

quote: Windows or pages with similar content or function have similar layout.
rule: Windows and pages that do similar things share one layout, with repeated elements in the same places.

quote: Uses lightweight controls, such as links instead of command buttons for secondary commands, and drop-down lists instead of lists for choices.
rule: Prefer light controls where they suffice: a link for a secondary command and a drop-down rather than a full list for a choice.

quote: Uses a single font with a small number of sizes and text colors.
rule: A window uses one typeface with few sizes and few text colours.

quote: if a layout element can be eliminated without harming the effectiveness of the UI, it probably should be.
rule: Remove any layout element whose absence would not hurt the task.

quote: Support the minimum Windows effective resolution of 800x600 pixels.
rule: Every window must fit and work on an 800x600 effective screen less the taskbar's height (640x480 for anything needed in safe mode).

quote: Optimize resizable window layouts for an effective resolution of 1024x768 pixels.
