rule: Design a resizable window's default layout for a 1024x768 effective screen and shrink it automatically, still usable, on smaller screens.

quote: Be sure to test your windows in 96 dots per inch (dpi) (at 800x600 pixels), 120 dpi (at 1024x768 pixels), and 144 dpi
rule: Test every window at 100, 125 and 150 percent display scaling for clipped controls, clipped text and stretched images.

quote: For programs with touch and mobile use scenarios, optimize for 120 dpi.
rule: Programs used with touch should be optimised for 120 dpi screens.

quote: Choose a default window size appropriate for its contents.
rule: A window opens at a size that shows its typical content without resizing or scrolling, larger rather than cramped when the space is used well.

quote: Use a balanced height to width aspect ratio.
rule: Keep window proportions between 3:5 and 5:3 (message boxes may be 1:3).

quote: Use resizable windows whenever practical to avoid scroll bars and truncated data.
rule: Make a window resizable whenever its content (documents, images, lists, trees) can use more room, instead of scrolling or truncating.

quote: For text documents, consider a maximum line length of 80 characters
rule: Limit lines of running text to about 80 characters.

quote: Fixed-sized windows must be entirely visible and sized to fit within the work area.
rule: A window of fixed size opens wholly on screen, inside the area the taskbar leaves free.

quote: Resizable windows may be optimized for higher resolutions, but sized down as needed at display time to the actual screen resolution.
rule: A resizable window's saved or default size is reduced when it opens on a smaller screen so that it fits.

quote: Progressively larger window sizes must show progressively more information.
rule: Enlarging a window shows more content, so at least one part of it grows with the window.

quote: Keep the upper-left origin of the content fixed as the window is resized.
rule: Resizing a window keeps its content anchored at the top leading corner; never re-centre content to balance it.

quote: Set a maximum content size if the content can be too stretched too wide.
rule: Stop widening content that becomes unwieldy past a maximum width, keeping it anchored rather than centred in a wide window.

quote: Set a minimum window size if there is a size below which the content is no longer usable.
rule: Give a window, pane or column a minimum size at the point where it stops working, and drop optional parts entirely rather than squeezing them.

quote: Consider altering the presentation to make the content usable at smaller sizes.
rule: When a window gets too small for its normal layout, switch to a compact presentation that still works.

quote: Make all interactive controls at least relative 16x16 pixels.
rule: Interactive controls are at least 16x16 relative pixels.

quote: Size controls to avoid truncated data.
rule: Make controls and list columns wide enough that data needed for the task is never cut short.

quote: Size controls to eliminate unnecessary scrolling.
rule: Enlarge a control slightly when that removes a scroll bar, so that few vertical and no needless horizontal scroll bars remain.

quote: Reduce the number of control sizes on a surface.
rule: Use few control widths in one window (one list width, at most three button and drop-down widths), except that a text field's width suggests its expected input.

quote: For controls that are sized based on their text, include an additional 30 percent (up to 200 percent for shorter text)
rule: Leave room for translation in any control sized by its text: about 30 percent more, up to double or triple for short words.

quote: Extend static text controls, check boxes, and radio buttons to the maximum width that will fit in the layout.
rule: Let static text, checkbox and radio button labels take all the width the layout allows, so longer or translated text is not cut off.

quote: If controls aren't touching, have at least 3 DLUs (5 relative pixels) of space between them.
rule: Controls either touch or have at least 3 DLUs between them.

quote: Arrange the UI elements within a surface to flow naturally in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order
rule: Arrange a window's elements in reading order so that their sequence mirrors the steps of the task.

quote: Place UI elements that initiate a task in the upper-left corner or upper-center.
rule: What starts a task goes at the top leading corner or top centre and gets the most emphasis.

quote: Place UI elements that complete a task in the lower-right corner.
rule: The controls that finish a task, such as commit buttons, go at the bottom trailing corner.

quote: Place related UI elements together, and separate unrelated elements.
rule: Keep related elements together and unrelated ones apart.

quote: Place required steps in the main flow.
rule: Every required step sits on the main path through the window.

quote: Place optional steps outside the main flow,
rule: Optional steps sit off the main path, quieter or behind progressive disclosure.

quote: Place frequently used elements before infrequently used elements
rule: Elements used often come before elements used rarely in the reading path.

quote: Choose a single UI element that users need to look at first to be the focal point.
rule: Each window has exactly one obvious place to look first, and it is something the reader must find and understand quickly.

quote: Give the focal point the greatest visual emphasis, such as prominent text, default selection, or initial input focus.
rule: The element people use first gets the initial keyboard focus or default selection along with the strongest emphasis.

quote: Normally, use left alignment.
rule: Align content to the leading edge unless there is a reason not to.

quote: Use right alignment for numeric data, especially columns of numeric data.
rule: Numbers, especially columns of numbers, align to the trailing edge.

quote: Use right alignment for commit buttons, as well as controls aligned with right window edge.
rule: Commit buttons, and controls placed against the window's trailing edge, align to that edge.

quote: Use center alignment when either left or right alignment is inappropriate or appears unbalanced.
rule: Centre an element only when leading or trailing alignment would look wrong; never centre content just to fill a window.

quote: When vertically aligning controls with text, align the text baselines
rule: A control and the text beside it line up on their text baselines.

quote: Don't use layout as the only means to convey important information about a UI.
rule: Relationships between controls are stated in their labels, not shown only by their position.

quote: Don't embed subordinate controls within control labels to create a sentence or phrase.
rule: Never place a field or menu inside a label so that together they read as a sentence; put the control after the label.

quote: Make grouping accessible.
rule: A group shown only by placement or a background is also declared as a group to screen readers.

quote: The following table lists the recommended sizes
rule: Use the recommended control sizes for 9 pt Segoe UI at 96 dpi (for example command buttons 75x23 relative pixels).

quote: The following table lists the recommended spacing between common UI elements
rule: Use the recommended spacing values (dialog margins 7 DLUs, related controls 4 DLUs, unrelated 7 DLUs and so on).

quote: Will the operation complete in about five seconds or less? If so, use an activity indicator instead
rule: Work that finishes within about five seconds shows an activity indicator, not a progress bar; work that usually does but sometimes runs longer starts with a busy pointer and switches to a bar after five seconds.

quote: Progress bars are for computer progress, not user progress.
rule: Never use a progress bar to show the reader's own progress or to wait for them to finish something.

quote: Is the operation a very lengthy (longer than two minutes) background task
rule: Background work that runs longer than about two minutes and whose end matters more than its progress (backup, printing, bulk conversion) reports by notification instead of a progress bar.

quote: When the operation is complete, will users be able to replay the results? If so, use a slider instead.
rule: When the result can be replayed (audio or video recording and playback), show the position with a slider, not a progress bar.

quote: This pattern is usually unnecessary and should be avoided.
rule: Do not show one bar for the current step and another for the whole; give each step a share of a single bar that fills once.

quote: Provide progress feedback when performing a lengthy operation.
rule: Any operation of two seconds or more shows progress, so people never have to guess whether work is happening.

quote: Clearly indicate real progress.
rule: The bar moves whenever work advances, using a non-linear scale for widely varying durations, so it never looks hung while working.

quote: Clearly indicate lack of progress.
rule: The bar stops when no work is being done, so people do not wait for something that will never finish.

quote: Provide useful progress details.
rule: Show extra progress details (such as a transfer rate) only when people can act on them, and long enough to be read.

quote: Don't provide unnecessary details.
rule: Leave out operation details people have no expectations about, such as the files a setup copies; a well-labelled bar is usually enough, and debug details never ship.

quote: Provide useful animations.
rule: Use an animation when it shows something text cannot, such as whether deleted items can be recovered.

quote: Don't use unnecessary animations.
rule: Do not add animation to entertain; it can suggest progress while the work is stuck.

quote: Position animations centered over the progress bar.
rule: Centre a progress animation above the bar and its label.

quote: Play a sound effect at the completion of an operation only if it is very lengthy (longer than two minutes), infrequent, and important.
rule: Play a completion sound only for rare, important work lasting more than about two minutes that people may walk away from.

quote: Don't steal input focus to show a progress update or completion.
rule: Progress updates and completion never take the keyboard focus or bring the window forward.

quote: Don't worry about technical support.
rule: Information only support staff need goes in a log file, not in the progress display.

quote: Don't put the percentage complete or any other text on a progress bar.
rule: Never draw text on top of a progress bar; screen readers cannot reach it.

quote: Don't combine a progress bar with a busy pointer.
rule: Show either a progress bar or a busy pointer, never both at once.

quote: Don't use vertical progress bars.
rule: Progress bars run horizontally.

quote: Use determinate progress bars for operations that require a bounded amount of time,
rule: Use a determinate bar whenever the work is bounded, even if its length cannot be predicted well; uncertainty alone is no reason for an indeterminate one.

quote: Clearly indicate the progress phase.
rule: The bar shows whether work is at its start, middle or end; never jump to 99 percent and sit there, and start at no more than a third while early.

quote: Don't let a progress bar go to 100 percent unless the operation has completed.
rule: The bar reaches full only when the work is done.

quote: Provide a time remaining estimate if you can do so accurately.
rule: Show time remaining only once it can be estimated accurately; hide it while early estimates would jump about.

quote: Don't restart progress.
rule: One bar covers the whole operation and fills once; it never starts over when a step ends.

quote: Don't back up progress.
rule: Progress only ever increases, although a time remaining estimate may rise as well as fall.

quote: Use indeterminate progress bars only for operations whose overall progress cannot be determined.
rule: Use an indeterminate bar only for unbounded work or an unknown number of items, and bound timed operations with timeouts.

quote: Convert to a determinate progress bar once the overall progress can be determined.
rule: Switch from an indeterminate to a determinate bar as soon as the total is known, for example after counting the items.

quote: Don't combine indeterminate progress bars with percent complete or time remaining estimates.
rule: An indeterminate bar never comes with a percentage or a time estimate; if those are known, the bar is determinate.

quote: Don't combine indeterminate progress bars with animations.
rule: Show either an indeterminate bar or an animation, never both.

quote: If users can do something productive while the operation is in progress, provide modeless feedback.
rule: When people can keep working during an operation, show its progress without blocking them, disabling only what needs the result.

quote: If the window has an address bar, display the modeless progress in the address bar.
rule: Show modeless progress in the window's address bar if it has one, otherwise in its status bar with the text to the bar's leading side.

quote: Place modal progress bars on progress pages or progress dialog boxes.
rule: A blocking progress bar appears on a progress page of a flow or in a progress dialog.

quote: Label the button Cancel if canceling returns the environment to its previous state
rule: Work that may take more than a few seconds has a halt button: Cancel when halting leaves no trace, Stop when it keeps the partial result, relabelled from Cancel to Stop once going back is no longer possible.

quote: Use the following time formats.
rule: Write time remaining from the largest non-zero unit down ("m minutes, s seconds remaining", or "Time remaining: ..." in a colon layout, abbreviated where space is short) and as "mm:ss remaining" in a title bar.

quote: Make estimates accurate, but don't give false precision.
rule: Give no more precision than the estimate has: with hours, show minutes but not seconds.

quote: Keep the estimate up-to-date.
rule: Refresh a time remaining estimate at least every five seconds.

quote: Focus on the time remaining
rule: Lead with time remaining, show elapsed time only where it helps, and add no percentage text beside a bar that already shows it.

quote: Be grammatically correct. Use singular units when the number is one.
rule: Use the singular unit for one (1 minute, not 1 minutes).

quote: Use red or yellow progress bars only to indicate the progress status, not the final results of a task.
rule: Red and yellow bars mark a status during the work, never the final result; an unrecoverable failure leaves the bar green with an error message.

quote: Turn the progress bar red when there is a user recoverable condition that prevents making further progress.
rule: When work is blocked by something the reader can fix, mark the bar as stopped and show a message naming the problem and the fix.

quote: If the user has paused, change the Pause button label to Resume.
rule: A paused or impeded operation shows that state on its bar, the Pause button becomes Resume, and an impediment gets a message with a suggested fix.

quote: Use progress bars only for progress.
rule: A level that is not progress, such as disk space used, is a meter, not a progress bar.

quote: Always use the recommended progress bar height.
rule: Use the standard bar height and a width between the recommended minimum and maximum, centred when the window is much wider.

quote: Start the label with a verb (for example, Copying) and end with an ellipsis.
rule: Label a progress bar with a short phrase saying what is happening, starting with a verb and ending with an ellipsis (Copying…), updated per step or item.

quote: Don't assign a unique access key because the control isn't interactive.
rule: A progress label gets no access key, since nothing there can be operated.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Progress labels, details and time remaining text use sentence case.

quote: Start this extra label with the phrase, Please wait while.
rule: When the reader did not start the operation, add a fixed label beginning "Please wait while" that says why they are waiting.

quote: Position the label above the progress bar and align the label with the left edge of the progress bar.
rule: Put the progress label above the bar, aligned with its leading edge.

quote: Provide details in static text, preceding the data with a label ending with a colon.
rule: Each progress detail has a label ending in a colon and states its unit after the value (Speed: 2 MB/s).

quote: Position the details below the progress bar and align the label with the left edge of the progress bar.
rule: Put progress details below the bar, aligned with its leading edge.

quote: Don't give the percentage completed or remaining because that information is conveyed by the progress bar itself.
rule: Progress details never repeat the percentage the bar shows.

quote: Don't use what should be the progress bar label for the dialog box title.
rule: A modal progress dialog is titled with the program or operation name, never with the progress label's text.

quote: optimize the title for display on the taskbar by concisely placing the distinguishing information first.
rule: A modeless progress window's title puts the distinguishing fact first so the taskbar shows it (66% Complete).

quote: Does the list present data, rather than program options? If not, consider using a list box instead.
rule: A table or multi-column list is for data; a choice among program options is a simple list.

quote: Do users need to change views, group, sort by columns, or change column widths and order? If not, use a list box instead.
rule: Use the full table control only when people need to switch views, group, sort or rearrange columns; otherwise a simple list.

quote: Does the control need to be a drag source or a drop target? If so, use a list view.
rule: A list whose items are dragged, dropped, copied or pasted is the full list control with that support.

section: Is this the right control? > Check box list views
quote: Is the control used to choose zero or more items from a list of data? To choose one item, use single selection instead.
rule: Use a checkbox list to choose zero or more items and single selection to choose one.

section: Is this the right control? > Check box list views
quote: Is multiple selection essential to the task or commonly used? If so, use a check box list view to make multiple selection obvious
rule: When picking several items is essential or common, show checkboxes so multiple selection is evident; otherwise plain multiple selection.

section: Is this the right control? > Check box list views
quote: Is the stability of the multiple selection important? If so, use a check box list, list builder, or add/remove list
rule: When losing a multiple selection by a stray click would hurt, use checkboxes or an add/remove list, where a click changes one item only.

quote: the selection can be extended by dragging or with Shift+click or Ctrl+click
rule: A multiple-selection list extends the selection by dragging, Shift-click for a range and Ctrl-click for single items.

quote: Sort list items in a logical order.
rule: Sort by default in the order the data suggests: names alphabetically, numbers numerically, dates chronologically.

quote: If appropriate, allow users to change the sort order.
rule: Let people change the sort order when the list is long or other orders help them find things.

quote: Use the Always Show Selection attribute
rule: The selected item stays visibly selected when the list does not have focus.

quote: Avoid presenting empty list views.
rule: A list the reader builds starts with instructions or example items rather than empty.

quote: make those settings persist so they take effect the next time the list view is displayed.
rule: A list's view, grouping, sort and column choices are remembered per list and per user.

quote: Use single-click to select the list item the user is pointing to.
rule: A single click selects the item under the pointer (except in a command-link list, where it also acts).

quote: Double clicking should have the same effect as selecting an item and performing its default command.
rule: Double-clicking an item selects it and runs its default command.

quote: Make double-click behavior redundant.
rule: Whatever double-click does is also available as a button or context menu command.

quote: Use complete sentences and ending punctuation.
rule: An item that needs more explanation gets it in a hover tip written in complete sentences with a full stop.

quote: Provide context menus of relevant commands.
rule: Items have a context menu with the commands that apply: Cut, Copy, Paste, Remove or Delete, Rename, Properties.

quote: If users can change the sort order and grouping, provide Sort By and Group By context menus.
rule: When sorting and grouping can be changed, the list's context menu offers Sort By and Group By submenus.

quote: Make the list view column header accessible using the keyboard.
rule: Column headings can be reached and used with the keyboard.

quote: When disabling a list view, also disable any associated labels and command buttons.
rule: Disabling a list also disables its label and the buttons that act on it.

quote: Avoid horizontal scrolling.
rule: Prefer layouts that scroll vertically; scroll horizontally only for many sorted items with plenty of width.

quote: Consider displaying the number of selected items below the list
rule: Show below a multiple-selection list how many items are selected, or a more meaningful total such as the space they need.

quote: add Select all and Clear all command buttons.
rule: A long checkbox list where choosing or clearing everything is likely has Select all and Clear all buttons.

quote: Use mixed-state check boxes to indicate partial selection of the items in a container.
rule: A container's checkbox shows the mixed state when only some of its items are checked; an individual item never has a third state.

quote: Choose the most convenient view by default.
rule: Open a list in the most useful view and remember the view the reader picks.

quote: Change the view using a split button, menu button, or drop-down list.
rule: Switch views with a split button, menu button or drop-down, preferably a toolbar split button labelled with the current view.

quote: Provide a View context menu.
rule: The list's context menu has a View submenu.

quote: Consider using tiles view to improve readability.
rule: When a details table would truncate much of its data, consider a tile presentation that shows it whole.

quote: Choose default column widths appropriate for the longest data.
rule: Default column widths fit their data so few values are truncated; size the list to its columns, and make it and its window resizable if normal data would still be cut.

quote: Choose an appropriate default column order.
rule: Order columns: the item's name first, then distinguishing data, then useful short data, then less useful data, with long variable-length data last.

quote: When appropriate, allow users to add and remove columns, as well as change the order.
rule: Show the most useful columns by default and let people add, remove and reorder columns, from the heading's context menu and a column chooser.

quote: Right-align numbers, currencies, and times.
rule: Right-align numbers, money and times; left-align text, identifiers (even numeric ones) and dates.

quote: the first click on a heading sorts the list in ascending order for the column, the second click sorts in descending order.
rule: The first click on a heading sorts ascending, the second descending, and the previous sort column becomes the secondary key.

quote: Use the Full Row Select attribute
rule: Selecting an item highlights its whole row across every column.

quote: Don't use a sortable column header unless the data can be sorted.
rule: A heading responds to clicks only if its column can be sorted.

quote: Don't use a column header if there is only one column and there is no need to reverse sort.
rule: A single-column list that never needs reverse sorting has a label, not a column heading.

quote: Choose a list view height that displays an integral number of items.
rule: A list's height shows a whole number of rows.

quote: List views should display between 3 and 20 items.
rule: A list shows between 3 and 20 items, at least five when it may hold many.

quote: If users benefit from making the list view larger, make the list view and its parent window resizable.
rule: When a bigger list helps, the list grows with a resizable window, never shrinking below three rows.

quote: Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, ending with a colon using static text.
rule: Every list has a label: a word or phrase, not a sentence, ending in a colon.

quote: Assign a unique access key for each label.
rule: Each list label has its own access key, unique in the window.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: List labels use sentence case.

quote: Position the label above the control and align the label with the left edge of the control.
rule: A list's label sits above it, aligned with its leading edge.

quote: For multiple-selection list views, write the label that clearly indicates multiple selection is possible.
rule: The label of a multiple-selection list says that several items may be chosen, unless checkboxes already show it.

quote: You may specify units (seconds, connections, and so on) in parentheses after the label.
rule: Units may follow the label in parentheses.

quote: Use a single noun or noun phrase with no ending punctuation.
rule: Column headings are a noun or noun phrase of three words or fewer, without ending punctuation.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Column headings use sentence case.

quote: Align the heading the same way as the data.
rule: A heading is aligned like the data in its column.

quote: Use the following group labels for high-level collections:
rule: Group by standard ranges (initial letters for names, size bands, and Today, Yesterday, Last week, Earlier this year, A long time ago for dates); otherwise use the grouped data's exact text.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Text the app writes into list data uses sentence case.

quote: If you need to add instructional text about a list view, add it above the label.
rule: Instructions about a list go above its label, in complete sentences with ending punctuation and sentence case.

quote: Additional information that is helpful but not necessary should be kept short.
rule: A short optional note goes in parentheses between the label and its colon, or below the control.

quote: Use the exact label text including its capitalization but don't include the access key underscore or colon, and include the word list.
rule: Help text names a list by its exact label without colon, followed by the word list (the Programs and services list), uses the exact item text, and never says list box or list view.

quote: To describe user interaction, use select for the data, and click for the headings.
rule: Help says select for list items and checkboxes (clear to uncheck) and click for headings.

quote: When possible, format the label and list options using bold text.
rule: Help text shows control labels and option names in bold, using quotation marks only where bold is unavailable and confusion is likely.

quote: Understand your target users' goals and craft a feature set that enables them to achieve those goals productively.
rule: Choose features from what the target users are trying to achieve, judging power by their productivity rather than by the number of features.

section: What makes a user experience simple?
quote: Start your design process with the simplest designs that do the job well.
rule: Begin with the simplest design that works, and when a design disappoints, first strip out everything unessential.

quote: To obtain simplicity, focus on what is likely; reduce, hide, or remove what is unlikely; and eliminate what is impossible.
rule: Design for what people will probably do: make likely actions easy, push unlikely ones back or out, and drop impossible ones.

quote: Remove elements that aren't likely to be used or have preferable alternatives.
rule: Take out elements that will rarely be used or that something better already covers.

quote: Remove unnecessary redundancy.
rule: When there are several ways to do a task, pick the best one for the users instead of offering them all and a setting to choose.

quote: Make it "just work" automatically.
rule: Where an acceptable default behaviour exists, make it work without setup and hide or minimise the setting.

quote: Combine what should be combined.
rule: Put everything a task needs in one place with one continuous flow, splitting a complex task into clear steps.

quote: Separate what should be separated.
rule: Keep core tasks central and obvious, optional features peripheral, and separate tasks apart but linked to each other.

quote: Eliminate what can be eliminated.
rule: Remove every element and word that does not help perform the important tasks, if removing it harms nothing.

quote: Review your design for misguided efforts in consistency (such as having redundant text), generalization
rule: Cut complexity added for its own sake: redundant text for consistency, needless generality, and options people will not change.

quote: Put the elements in the right place.
rule: Place each element by its use: essentials in context and in order, more options behind a disclosure, more information in a hover tip, and less important things in a separate window or page.

quote: Use meaningful high-level combinations.
rule: Offer meaningful bundles (folders, themes, styles, groups) that people can pick or act on as a whole instead of many individual settings.

quote: Select the right controls.
rule: Choose controls that show the result and recent choices in place, such as a font list with previews or errors marked inline, rather than a separate dialog.

quote: Make tasks discoverable and visible.
rule: Every task, above all the frequent ones, can be found in the interface and its steps can be seen, not remembered.

quote: Present tasks in the user's domain.
rule: Present features in terms of the problem people have (remove red eye) rather than the technology underneath.

quote: Put domain knowledge into the program.
rule: The app carries the knowledge the task needs, down to making clear what input is valid, so people need no outside reference.

quote: Use text that users understand.
rule: Use words and concepts the users know and explain what is asked in plain language.

quote: Use safe, secure, probable defaults.
rule: Default each setting to the value that suits most people when that value is also safe and secure; ask only when needed.

quote: Use constraints.
rule: Where only some ways of doing a task are right, allow only those, preventing mistakes that can be prevented.

quote: Removal of the essential just produces a poor design.
rule: Never simplify by removing something essential; if people become confused or cannot finish tasks, too much was removed.

quote: Can the controls comfortably fit on a single, reasonably sized page? If so, use a single page.
rule: Use one page instead of tabs when everything fits comfortably or there would be only one tab.

quote: Are the tabs related to each other in some obvious way? If not, consider splitting the information into separate windows
rule: Tabs in one set are clearly related; unrelated content goes in separate windows.

quote: If hierarchical, consider using progressive disclosure or child dialog boxes to show related information.
rule: Tabs are peers; content that is subordinate to other content uses progressive disclosure or a secondary dialog instead.

quote: Are the tabs used to display steps within a task?
rule: Do not use tabs for the steps of a task unless they look like steps and a Next button also advances; required steps go in a page flow, optional ones in dialogs.

quote: Are the tabs different views of the same data? If so, consider using a split button or drop-down list to change views.
rule: Switching between views of the same data is better done with a split button or drop-down than with tabs.

quote: The window has seven or fewer tabs.
rule: Use one row of horizontal tabs for up to seven tabs that fit even when translated, and vertical tabs for eight or more.

quote: Don't nest tabs or combine horizontal tabs with vertical tabs.
rule: Never put tabs inside tabs or mix horizontal and vertical tabs; use fewer tabs or another control.

quote: Don't scroll horizontal tabs.
rule: A horizontal tab row never scrolls (vertical tabs may).

quote: For tabs on a resizable window or pane, put a scrollbar, when needed, on the page, not the window or pane.
rule: In a resizable window the tab row stays in view and only the tab page scrolls.

quote: Make sure the tabs look like tabs and not another type of control.
rule: Tabs are recognisable as tabs, not mistaken for buttons.

quote: When controls apply only to a page, place them within the border of the tabbed page.
rule: Controls that affect one page sit inside that page.

quote: When controls apply to the entire window, place them outside the tabbed page.
rule: Controls that affect the whole window, such as its commit buttons, sit outside the tab pages.

quote: Changing the current tab should never have side effects, apply settings, or result in an error message.
rule: Switching tabs only navigates: it never applies settings, causes side effects or shows an error, and tabs can be visited in any order.

quote: Don't assign a special meaning to the last tab selected.
rule: Which tab was open last is never treated as a setting.

quote: Don't make the settings on a page dependent on settings on other pages.
rule: Settings on one tab never depend on settings on another; dependent settings share a page, or the task becomes a step flow.

quote: If users are likely to start with the last tab displayed, make the tab persist and select it by default.
rule: Reopen on the last tab shown, per window and per user, when people usually return to it; otherwise open on the first.

quote: Don't put icons on tabs.
rule: Tabs carry text only, except standard symbols or clearly recognisable icons when the window is too narrow for meaningful labels.

quote: Don't use product logos for tab graphics.
rule: Tabs carry no product logos or branding.

quote: Don't use scroll bars on tab pages.
rule: A tab page does not scroll; tabs already extend the window's area.

quote: Use concise tab labels.
rule: Tab labels are one or two words that describe the page.

quote: Use specific, meaningful tab labels.
rule: Name tabs for their specific content, never General, Advanced or Settings.

quote: If a tab doesn't apply to the current context and users don't expect it to, remove it.
rule: Remove a tab that does not apply now and that people would not look for.

quote: Don't disable the tab, because doing so isn't self-explanatory and prohibits exploration.
rule: When a tab does not apply but people might look for it, keep the tab, disable the controls on its page and say there why.

section: Guidelines > Multiple views and documents patterns
quote: Use the view or document names on tab labels.
rule: Tabs for views or documents are labelled with the view or document name.

section: Guidelines > Multiple views and documents patterns
quote: Avoid excessively long tab names.
rule: Cap the length of document tab labels, shortening longer names with an ellipsis.

section: Guidelines > Multiple views and documents patterns
quote: If a tab doesn't apply to the current context, remove the tab.
rule: Remove a view or document tab that does not apply in the current context.

quote: Don't use this pattern! Use radio buttons or a drop-down list instead.
rule: Never use tabs to make an exclusive choice in which only the selected tab applies; use radio buttons or a drop-down.

quote: Use nouns rather than verbs, without ending punctuation.
rule: Tab labels are nouns, not verbs, with no ending punctuation.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Tab labels use sentence case.

quote: Don't assign an access key. Tabs are accessible through their shortcut keys (Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+Shift+Tab, Ctrl+PgUp, Ctrl+PgDn).
rule: Tabs get no access keys; Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Page Down move to the next tab, Ctrl+Shift+Tab and Ctrl+Page Up to the previous.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, and include the word tab.
rule: Help names a tab by its exact label followed by the word tab, in bold, and says click (click the View tab).

quote: use the noun tab alone to refer only to a tab control.
rule: Keep the bare word tab for tab controls; say the Tab key, a tab stop or a tab mark for the others.

quote: Is there more than one control in the group? If not, use a plain text label instead.
rule: A boxed group holds more than one control; a single control gets a plain label.

quote: Are the controls related? Does showing the relationship add clarity? If not, present the controls separately outside of a group box.
rule: Box controls together only when they are related and showing that helps.

quote: Are all the controls inside the group? If so, indicate the relationship on the larger surface
rule: Do not box every control in a window; the window itself already groups them.

quote: Can you effectively communicate the relationships using layout alone? If so, use layout instead.
rule: Use a group box sparingly, only when spacing, headings, indenting or a separator cannot show the relationship.

quote: Don't nest group boxes.
rule: Never put a group box inside another; show sub-relationships with layout.

quote: Don't put controls in group box labels.
rule: A group's title holds no controls, except a checkbox that enables or disables everything in the group.

quote: Don't disable group boxes.
rule: To show a group does not apply, disable the controls inside it, not the group itself.

quote: Label all group boxes.
rule: Every group box has a title.

quote: Don't assign an access key to the label.
rule: Give access keys to the controls in a group, not to its title, unless the window runs short of keys.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Group titles use sentence case.

quote: Write the label using a noun or a noun phrase, not as a sentence, and use no ending punctuation, including colons.
rule: A group title is a noun or noun phrase with no ending punctuation, not even a colon.

quote: Use parallel phrasing for group box labels within the same surface.
rule: Group titles in one window are phrased in parallel.

quote: Keep group box labels concise. Don't use instructional text as the label.
rule: Group titles are short names; any instructions go inside the group, not in its title.

quote: Don't repeat the group box label in control labels within the box.
rule: Controls inside a group do not repeat its title (under Alignment: Left, Right, not Left alignment).

quote: Don't refer to group boxes in user interface text.
rule: Interface text never mentions group boxes as such.

quote: In such cases, use under with the group box name.
rule: Help names a group only to tell apart options with the same name, as "Under Effects, select Hidden".

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the user interface (UI) presenting a problem that has already occurred? If not, the message isn't an error.
rule: Call something an error only when the problem has already happened; a condition that could cause trouble later is presented as a warning.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Can the problem be corrected automatically? If so, handle the problem and suppress the error message.
rule: When the app can fix a problem itself, it fixes it and shows no message.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are users likely to perform an action or change their behavior as the result of the message? If not
rule: Show an error only when the reader will do something or act differently because of it; otherwise leave it out.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the problem relevant when users are actively using other programs? If so, consider showing the problem using a notification area icon.
rule: A problem that still matters while the reader works in other programs is shown on the app's notification-area (tray) icon rather than only in its window.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the problem not related to the current user activity, does it not require immediate user action, and can users freely ignore it?
rule: A failure unrelated to what the reader is doing, needing no immediate action and safe to ignore, is reported by an action-failure notification instead of a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the problem relate to the status of a background task within a primary window? If so, consider showing the problem using a status bars.
rule: A problem with a background task of the main window is shown in that window's status area, not in a dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are the primary target users IT professionals? If so, consider using an alternative feedback mechanism, such as log file entries or e-mail alerts.
rule: Non-critical problems meant for administrators go to a log rather than to a message on screen.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of poor error messages
quote: Developers must conditionally compile all such messages so that they are automatically removed from the release version of a product.
rule: Messages written by programmers for themselves (assertions, internal state) never reach a released build's interface.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of poor error messages
quote: Have your error messages crafted and reviewed by a writer.
rule: Every error message's text is written and reviewed deliberately, in context, not composed on the spot by whoever writes the code.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of good error messages
quote: A solution. Provides a solution so that users can fix the problem.
rule: An error message states what went wrong, why, and what the reader can do to fix it.

section: Design concepts > Characteristics of good error messages
quote: Rare. Displayed infrequently. Frequently displayed error messages are a sign of bad design.
rule: An error message that appears often is a design fault to be removed, not a message to keep showing.

section: Design concepts > Avoiding unnecessary error messages
quote: Some error messages can be eliminated because they aren't problems from the user's point of view.
rule: Show no error when the reader got the outcome they wanted, such as deleting a file that is already being deleted or cancelling a task on purpose.

section: Design concepts > Avoiding unnecessary error messages
quote: As long as the user's request is reasonable, a well designed e-commerce program should return reasonable results not errors.
rule: When a sensible request has no exact match (a search with a typo), return the closest results or a corrected query instead of an error.

section: Design concepts > Avoiding unnecessary error messages
quote: Using constrained interactions. For drag operations, allow users to drop only on valid targets.
rule: While dragging, only targets that can take the item accept the drop.

section: Design concepts > Avoiding unnecessary error messages
quote: Making things just work.
rule: When a small mistake has a clear intention, such as a minor formatting slip, correct it automatically.

section: Design concepts > Providing necessary error messages
quote: In such cases, it's much better to leave the control enabled and give a helpful error message instead.
rule: When the reason a control would be disabled is not obvious (a Next button blocked by a missing entry), leave it enabled and explain the problem when it is used.

section: Design concepts > Providing necessary error messages
quote: If you aren't sure whether you should give an error message, start by composing the error message that you might give.
rule: To decide whether a message is needed, draft it: keep it if the reader would act on it, drop it if they would just dismiss it.

section: Design concepts > Designing for good error handling
quote: Low-level problems must be handled at a sufficiently high level so that the error message can be presented from the user's point of view.
rule: Error handling keeps the specific cause and its details (names, values) and reports at the level of the reader's task, so the message can be specific.

quote: it is better to be up front about the lack of information than to present problems, causes, or solutions that might not be right.
rule: When the cause is truly unknown, say so plainly rather than guess at a cause or fix that may be wrong.

section: Design concepts > Determine the appropriate message type
quote: To determine the appropriate message type, focus on the most important aspect of the issue that users need to know or act upon.
rule: Classify a message by what the reader must act on: something that blocks them is an error, something they can proceed past is a warning, and the icon matches the text.

quote: Generally, you should prefer to use the lightest weight presentation that does the job well.
rule: Report an error in the lightest way that works (in place, status area, notification) and use a modal dialog only when it must be acknowledged before going on.

quote: it is important to reduce the text down to its essentials, and use progressive disclosure and Help links when necessary to provide additional information.
rule: Cut message text to its essentials and move further detail behind a disclosure or a help link.

quote: Many system problems can be solved by the user:
rule: For device, network or program problems, the message gives the fix the reader can do: reconnect or turn on the device, insert media, change an option or restart.

quote: Use task dialogs whenever appropriate to achieve a consistent look and layout.
rule: Present error messages with the Windows task dialog (or message box with a blank line between instructions).

quote: Whenever possible, prevent or reduce user input errors by:
rule: Prevent input errors with controls limited to valid values, by disabling commands that would fail when the reason is obvious, and with good defaults.

quote: Use modeless error handling (in-place errors or balloons) for contextual user input problems.
rule: Report a problem with one field's input beside that field without a modal dialog.

quote: Use balloons for non-critical, single-point user input problems detected while in a text box or immediately after a text box loses focus.
rule: A minor problem in a single field found while typing or on leaving the field is shown in a callout at the field, one at a time.

quote: Balloons go away when clicked, when the problem is resolved, or after a timeout.
rule: An input-problem callout disappears when clicked, when the input is corrected, or after a timeout.

quote: Use in-place errors for delayed error detection, usually errors found by clicking a commit button.
rule: Problems found when the reader commits are shown in place next to each faulty field, several at once if needed, and stay until a commit finds no errors; not for settings applied at once.

quote: Use modal error handling (task dialogs or message boxes) for all other problems,
rule: Use a modal message only for problems that involve several controls, are not tied to one place, or are not input errors.

quote: When a user input problem is reported, set input focus to the first control with the incorrect data.
rule: After reporting an input problem, focus the first faulty field, scroll it into view and select all of its text.

quote: Don't clear incorrect input.
rule: Keep the wrong input so the reader can fix it; only a wrong password or PIN is cleared, since masked text cannot be corrected.

quote: Use a different error message (typically a different supplemental instruction) for each detectable cause.
rule: Never report several detectable causes with one message; give each cause its own message, so the reader does not have to troubleshoot.

quote: Use a message with multiple causes only when the specific cause can't be determined.
rule: Only when the cause cannot be determined may a message list several causes, with their fixes ordered from most to least likely.

quote: Modal error message dialogs don't have title bar icons.
rule: Error dialogs carry no icon in their title bar.

quote: Use an error icon.
rule: An error message shows the error symbol, except an input problem shown in a dialog or callout; an in-place error always has a small error symbol so it is not overlooked.

quote: you can use the feature icon with an error overlay.
rule: A feature's own icon with an error overlay may replace the error icon, with the feature named as the subject.

quote: Don't use warning icons for errors.
rule: Never mark an error with the warning symbol to make it seem milder.

quote: Use a Show/Hide details progressive disclosure button to hide advanced or detailed information in an error message.
rule: Put advanced detail of an error behind a details disclosure, never information the reader needs.

quote: Don't use Show/Hide details unless there really is more detail.
rule: Offer a details disclosure only when it reveals something new, not the same text reworded at greater length.

quote: Don't use Show/Hide details to show Help information. Use Help links instead.
rule: Help content is reached through a help link, not through a details disclosure.

section: Guidelines > Progressive disclosure > Don't show this message again
quote: If an error message needs this option, reconsider the error and its frequency.
rule: An error message offers no option to stop showing it; if it seems to need one, the error is unnecessary or too frequent and is redesigned.

quote: Select the safest, least destructive, or most secure response to be the default.
rule: The default button of an error message is the safest, least destructive response; only when safety is not at stake is it the most likely one.

quote: Design error messages to avoid the need for Help.
rule: An error message is complete on its own; the reader needs help text only when the fix takes several steps.

quote: Make sure the Help content is relevant and helpful.
rule: A help link from a message leads to content beyond the message, such as how to avoid the problem, and is added only when such content exists.

quote: Use specific, concise, relevant Help links to access Help content. Don't use command buttons or progressive disclosure for this purpose.
rule: Reach help from a message with a short specific link, never a button or a disclosure.

quote: For error messages that you can't make specific and actionable, consider providing links to online Help content.
rule: When a message cannot be made specific and actionable, link to online help that can be updated after release.

quote: For error messages that you can't make specific and actionable or they benefit from Help, consider also providing error codes.
rule: Add an error code only to messages that cannot be made specific or that benefit from looking up more information.

quote: Always provide a text description of the problem and solution. Don't depend just on the error code for this purpose.
rule: An error code never replaces the written problem and fix.

quote: Assign a unique error code for each different cause.
rule: Each distinct cause has its own error code.

quote: Choose error codes that are easily searchable on the Internet.
rule: Write error codes in a searchable form: 32-bit codes as hexadecimal with 0x and capital letters (0xC0001234), never negative decimals.

quote: Use Show/Hide details to display error codes. Phrase as Error code: <error code>.
rule: Show an error code inside the message's details disclosure, written as Error code: followed by the code.

quote: Don't accompany error messages with a sound effect or beep.
rule: Error messages play no sound, except a problem critical to the computer that needs immediate action.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Say each thing once across a message's title, instructions and buttons, keeping the full words in the instruction and on the controls.

quote: Use user-centered explanations. Describe the problem in terms of user actions or goals, not in terms of what the software is unhappy with.
rule: Explain a problem in terms of what the reader was doing, in their words, without technical jargon.

quote: Don't use the following words:
rule: In messages avoid error and failure (say problem), failed to (unable to), illegal, invalid or bad (incorrect), abort, kill or terminate (stop), catastrophic or fatal (serious).

quote: Don't use phrasing that blames the user or implies user error. Avoid using you and your in the phrasing.
rule: Phrase a problem so it does not blame the reader: avoid you and your, and use the passive voice where the active would make the reader the culprit.

quote: Be specific. Avoid vague wording, such as syntax error and illegal operation.
rule: Name the actual objects, places and values involved instead of vague phrases such as File not found or Value out of range.

quote: Don't give possibly unlikely problems, causes, or solutions in an attempt to be specific.
rule: State a problem, cause or fix only when it is likely to be right; otherwise say an unknown error occurred.

quote: Avoid the word "please," except in situations in which the user is asked to do something inconvenient
rule: Say please only when asking the reader to put up with something (such as waiting) or when the app is at fault.

quote: Use the word "sorry" only in error messages that result in serious problems for the user
rule: Apologise only for serious harm such as lost data, never for normal behaviour such as waiting for a network.

quote: Refer to products using their short names.
rule: Refer to products by their short names, without trademark symbols, version numbers or the company name unless people know the product by it.

quote: Use double quotation marks around object names.
rule: Put names of objects such as files in double quotation marks, but not full paths, URLs or domain names.

quote: Avoid starting sentences with object names.
rule: Do not begin a sentence with an object's name, which makes it hard to read.

quote: Don't use exclamation marks or words with all capital letters.
rule: No exclamation marks and no words in capitals in messages; both read as shouting.

quote: Use the title to identify the command or feature from which the error originated.
rule: The window title of an error dialog names the command or feature it came from (or the program name when many commands show it), never the problem itself.

quote: Use title-style capitalization, without ending punctuation.
rule: Write the error dialog's window title in title case with no ending punctuation.

quote: Use the main instruction to describe the problem in clear, plain, specific language.
rule: The main instruction states the problem plainly and specifically.

quote: Be concise use only a single, complete sentence.
rule: Keep the main instruction to one complete sentence, adding the reason only if it fits briefly; anything more goes in the supplemental text.

quote: Avoid putting full file paths and URLs in the main instruction.
rule: Name a file by its short name in the main instruction and give the full path or URL in the supplemental text, unless the message has no other text.

quote: Don't give the full file path and URL at all if it's obvious from the context.
rule: Leave out the path or URL altogether when the context makes it obvious, such as when renaming a file in place.

quote: Use present tense whenever possible.
rule: Write the main instruction in the present tense where possible.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write the main instruction of an error in sentence case.

quote: Don't include final periods if the instruction is a statement. If the instruction is a question, include a final question mark.
rule: A main instruction that is a statement has no full stop; one that is a question ends with a question mark.

quote: try using the following main instruction templates whenever possible:
rule: Prefer the standard shapes for a problem statement, such as "<subject> can't <action> because <reason>", "There is not enough <resource> to <action>" or "<device> isn't turned on".

quote: Use the supplemental instruction to:
rule: Use the supplemental text for detail, the cause, the steps to fix the problem and how to prevent it next time.

quote: Whenever possible, propose a practical, helpful solution so users can fix the problem.
rule: Offer a practical fix that is likely to work, never possible but improbable ones.

quote: If the problem is an incorrect value that the user entered, use the supplemental instruction to explain the correct values.
rule: When the reader entered a wrong value, say what values are accepted.

quote: Don't provide a solution if it can be trivially deduced from the problem statement.
rule: Leave out a fix that is obvious from the problem statement.

quote: If the solution has multiple steps, present the steps in the order in which they should be completed.
rule: List the steps of a fix in the order they are done, keep to two or three, and refer to help for longer procedures.

quote: Keep supplemental instructions concise. Provide only what users need to know. Omit unnecessary details.
rule: Keep supplemental text to what the reader needs, at most about three moderate sentences.

quote: To avoid mistakes while users perform instructions, put the results before the action.
rule: In an instruction, state the goal before the action (To restart, click Restart), not the action first.

quote: Don't recommend contacting an administrator unless doing so is among the most likely solutions to the problem.
rule: Suggest contacting an administrator only when only an administrator can fix the problem.

quote: Don't recommend contacting technical support.
rule: Never tell the reader to contact technical support; write the message so they can fix the problem themselves.

quote: Use complete sentences, sentence-style capitalization, and ending punctuation.
rule: Supplemental text is in complete sentences, sentence case, with ending punctuation.

quote: If the program must terminate as a result of the error, provide an Exit program button. To avoid confusion, don't use Close for this purpose.
rule: When an error forces the program to end, the button says Exit program, not Close.

quote: Otherwise, provide a Close button. Don't use OK for error messages, because this wording implies that problems are OK.
rule: An error message with no action of its own is dismissed with a Close button, never OK.

quote: Refer to errors by their main instruction. If the main instruction is long or detailed, summarize it.
rule: Help text refers to an error by its main instruction (summarised if long) and calls it a message, not an error message.

quote: When possible, format the text using bold. Otherwise, put the text in quotation marks only if required to prevent confusion.
rule: In help text, show a message's wording in bold, using quotation marks only where bold is unavailable and confusion is likely.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the user being asked a question to proceed with an action that has two or more responses? If not, the message isn't a confirmation.
rule: A confirmation asks whether to go on with an action the reader started and offers two or more answers; a problem that already happened is an error message instead.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does proceeding with the action require the user to make a choice that doesn't have a suitable default? If so, a confirmation may be appropriate.
rule: Ask before an action when going on needs a choice that has no suitable default.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is there an alternative design that eliminates the need for the confirmation?
rule: Treat the need for a confirmation as a sign of a design flaw and look first for a design that needs none.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the user about to perform a risky action? If so, a confirmation is appropriate if the action has significant consequences
rule: Confirm a risky action whose consequences are significant or which cannot easily be undone.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the user about to abandon a task? If so, don't confirm. Assume users understand the consequences of not completing a task.
rule: Do not ask for confirmation when the reader abandons a task; assume they know what leaving it unfinished means.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the action have consequences that users might not be aware of? If so, a confirmation may be appropriate.
rule: Confirm an action whose consequences the reader may not know about.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Given the current context, are users likely to be performing an action in error? If so, a confirmation may be appropriate.
rule: Confirm an action that in its context is probably a mistake.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Do users perform the action frequently? If so, consider an alternative design.
rule: Do not confirm a frequent action; people learn to click through and the question stops protecting them.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the action have security implications? If so, a confirmation may be required even if the previous tests indicate otherwise.
rule: An action with security consequences may be confirmed even when the other tests say not to.

section: Design concepts > Consider the design alternatives
quote: Prevent errors. Design tasks so that significant mistakes are difficult to do accidentally.
rule: Make serious mistakes hard to make by accident: keep destructive commands apart from others and require more than one action.

section: Design concepts > Consider the design alternatives
quote: Provide undo. Provide the ability to revert actions.
rule: Make actions reversible (deleted items recoverable) instead of asking before them.

section: Design concepts > Consider the design alternatives
quote: Provide feedback. Make undesirable outcomes obvious.
rule: Make the result of an action, especially a drag and drop, plainly visible so a mistake is noticed and undone.

section: Design concepts > Consider the design alternatives
quote: Assume the probable outcome, but make it easy to change.
rule: When a likely, safe choice exists, take it without asking, show what happened, and offer an easy way to reverse it (as automatic spelling correction does).

section: Design concepts > Consider the design alternatives
quote: Eliminate the choice completely. If the choice isn't important, users just won't care.
rule: Remove choices that do not matter to people instead of asking about them.

section: Design concepts > Provide all the information
quote: If you are going to ask a question, you must provide sufficient information for users to answer that question intelligently.
rule: A confirmation gives the information needed to choose each answer and offers the answers people want (e.g. keep both files when copying over one); choices, not dilemmas.

section: Design concepts > How to determine if a confirmation is necessary
quote: if only one response is likely (say 98 percent of the time), the confirmation is clearly unnecessary and should be removed.
rule: Keep a confirmation only if people really choose each of its answers; one that is almost always answered the same way is removed, except for security, legal and safety questions.

quote: Routine confirmations confirm that the user wants to proceed with a routine, low risk action.
rule: Do not ask "are you sure" before routine, low-risk actions.

quote: however, this pattern requires that the consequences are truly unintended.
rule: Present a confirmation as pointing out unintended consequences only when they really are unintended; otherwise it is a routine confirmation.

quote: This pattern should be avoided because it is better to design actions without ambiguous consequences and assume the most likely desired result.
rule: Avoid asking how an ambiguous action such as a drag should behave; design it to do the likely thing.

quote: This pattern is not recommended because there is usually a better, more direct alternative.
rule: Do not dress up teaching or feature promotion as a confirmation question.

quote: Use "Save changes" confirmations only when there are significant changes.
rule: Ask to save changes only when the reader made significant changes themselves, never for an untouched document or automatic reformatting.

quote: Confirmations don't use title bar icons.
rule: Confirmation dialogs carry no title-bar icon.

quote: The content area icon for a confirmation is based on its design pattern:
rule: A confirmation shows the warning symbol only for risky, security and risky unintended-consequence questions, and no symbol for routine ones.

quote: Don't use warning icons for routine questions.
rule: Never put the warning symbol on a routine question.

quote: Use specific responses to the main instruction if the reason for the confirmation is obvious or can be made self explanatory.
rule: When the reason for asking is obvious, label the buttons with the specific answers (Save, Don't save).

quote: Otherwise, use Yes and No buttons for confirmation responses. Doing so makes users give the confirmation some thought before responding.
rule: When the reason for asking is not obvious, answer the question with Yes and No so the reader must read it; never OK and Cancel.

quote: To close a program or restart Windows, use specific responses to the main instruction.
rule: A confirmation that closes the program or restarts the computer names that action on its button, never Close or Yes.

quote: For the clarifications pattern, consider using command links to make the alternatives clear.
rule: When asking how to proceed, present the alternatives as command links that each spell out an outcome.

quote: Present the most commonly used command links first.
rule: Order the answers by how often they are chosen, keeping a logical flow.

quote: provide a supplemental explanation.
rule: Give an answer that needs it a short explanation of why one would choose it or what it does.

quote: The default response for a confirmation is based on its design pattern:
rule: The default answer depends on the kind of confirmation: proceed for routine ones, the safe answer for risky or security ones, the likeliest for a clarification.

section: Guidelines > Don't show this message again
quote: Use this option only for the routine and ulterior motive confirmation patterns.
rule: Offer "Don't show this message again" only on routine or informational confirmations; necessary ones always show.

section: Guidelines > Don't show this message again
quote: Don't provide this option to justify displaying an unnecessary confirmation.
rule: Remove an unnecessary confirmation rather than adding an option to hide it.

quote: For confirmations that apply to bulk operations, provide an option to apply the confirmation to the entire operation.
rule: A confirmation raised during an operation on many items offers to apply the answer to all of them.

quote: Eliminate or postpone confirmations in a bulk operation.
rule: Avoid stopping a bulk operation item by item: proceed without asking, or collect the questions and ask at the end.

quote: If you must include advanced information in a confirmation message, reveal it by using progressive disclosure buttons
rule: Put advanced information in a confirmation behind a details disclosure, never what the reader needs.

quote: Don't use "Show details" unless there really is more detail.
rule: Offer a details disclosure only when it reveals something new.

quote: Don't use the User Account Control (UAC) elevation UI as a substitute for a confirmation.
rule: The elevation prompt is not a confirmation; confirm separately.

quote: Display the confirmation before the elevation UI.
rule: Show the confirmation before asking for elevation.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Say each thing once across the title, instructions, command links and buttons.

quote: Don't use "warning" or "caution" in the text.
rule: Do not write Warning or Caution in a confirmation; the symbol carries that.

quote: Use the title to identify the command or feature where the confirmation came from.
rule: A confirmation's window title names the command or feature that raised it (the program name when many raise it), always the command for one arriving late from long work, and never explains what to do.

quote: If it adds clarity, start the title with the word Confirm.
rule: A confirmation's window title may begin with Confirm when that helps.

quote: For risky action confirmations, you may add the name of the object involved for extra emphasis.
rule: The title of a risky confirmation may name the object at stake, such as the drive to be formatted.

quote: Use title-style capitalization, without ending punctuation.
rule: Write a confirmation's window title in title case without ending punctuation.

quote: The main instruction for a confirmation is based on its design pattern:
rule: A confirmation's main instruction is one question asking whether to proceed, in one sentence; for an unintended consequence it states the consequence unless the question already implies it.

quote: Be specific if there are objects involved, give their full names.
rule: Name the objects involved in full.

quote: Use positive phrasing. Positive phrasing is easier for users to understand.
rule: Phrase the question positively (enable rather than disable), unless the command itself is negative, in which case use its word.

quote: these common confirmation phrases have the indicated connotation:
rule: Use Are you sure you want to... for the direct result of a request, Do you want to... for a side effect, and Would you like to... for a clarification.

quote: For risky action confirmations, use the term permanently to indicate that an action can't be undone.
rule: Say permanently when a confirmed action cannot be undone.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write a confirmation's main instruction in sentence case.

quote: Explain any non-obvious reasons why the user might not want to proceed.
rule: The supplemental text explains any reason not to proceed that is not obvious, such as loss of data, money, access or privacy, or that it cannot be reversed.

quote: Don't repeat the main instruction with slightly different wording.
rule: Leave out the supplemental text rather than restate the main instruction.

quote: For unintended consequence confirmations, consider using the term anyway to concisely indicate that there is a reason not to continue
rule: When there is a reason not to continue, put anyway on the proceeding button (Uninstall anyway) so a reader who skipped the text still notices.

quote: Use complete sentences, sentence-style capitalization, and ending punctuation.
rule: Supplemental text is in complete sentences, sentence case, with ending punctuation.

quote: Refer to a confirmation by its title if the title is specific to the confirmation
rule: Help names a confirmation by its title when specific, otherwise by its main instruction, and may call it a message.

quote: Use the exact text, including its capitalization.
rule: Help quotes the confirmation's exact text and capitalisation, in bold where possible.

quote: Is it practical to enumerate all the valid values efficiently? If so, consider a single-selection list,
rule: When the valid values can be listed, use a list, drop-down or slider; a free text field is for values constrained only by length or character type, or not at all.

quote: Does the value represent a data type that has a specialized common control?
rule: Dates, times and network addresses are entered with their dedicated controls, not plain text fields.

quote: Do users perceive the setting as a relative quantity? If so, use a slider.
rule: A number people think of as a relative amount, or whose effect they want to see at once, is set with a slider, perhaps with a number field.

quote: a control that is constrained to United States ZIP Codes isn't globalized, but an unconstrained text box that accepts any postal code format is.
rule: Do not constrain input to one country's formats (such as US ZIP codes); accept every locale's form.

quote: Textual input A multi-line, unconstrained text box used to enter or edit long strings.
rule: Use a single-line field for short strings, a multi-line one for long text, a numeric field (optionally with a stepper) for numbers and a masked field for passwords.

quote: Unlike static text, data displayed using a text box can be scrolled (useful if the data is wider than the control), selected, and copied.
rule: Show read-only values people may copy in a borderless read-only field that can be scrolled, selected and copied.

quote: When disabling a text box, also disable any associated labels, instruction labels, spin controls, and command buttons.
rule: Disabling a field also disables its label, instructions, stepper and buttons.

quote: Use auto-complete to help users enter data that is likely to be used repeatedly
rule: Offer completion for values typed again and again (names, addresses, file names), never for passwords, PINs, card numbers or medical data.

quote: Don't make users scroll unnecessarily.
rule: Make a field large enough for its expected data when the layout allows, so it need not scroll.

quote: Don't put horizontal scroll bars on multi-line text boxes. Use vertical scrolling and line wrapping instead.
rule: A multi-line field wraps lines and scrolls only vertically.

quote: Don't put any scroll bars on single-line text boxes.
rule: A single-line field shows no scroll bar.

quote: For numeric input, you may use a spin control. For textual input, use a drop-down list or editable drop-down list instead.
rule: Steppers are only for numbers; to step through text values use a drop-down or editable drop-down.

quote: Don't use the auto-exit feature except for formatted data input. The automatic shift of focus can surprise users.
rule: Do not move focus to the next field automatically when one is full, except between the fixed segments of formatted input.

quote: Limit the length of the input text when you can.
rule: Limit a field's length to what valid input needs (three digits for 0 to 999).

quote: Be flexible with data formats.
rule: Accept the common ways people write a value, with optional spaces and punctuation and any capitalisation where it does not matter.

quote: If you can't handle the likely formats, require a specific format by using formatted data input or indicate the valid formats in the label.
rule: When the likely formats cannot all be accepted, either enforce one with segmented input or state the accepted format in the label.

quote: Consider format flexibility when choosing the maximum input length.
rule: Set the maximum length for the longest accepted format, so that a value written with spaces still fits (card numbers up to 19 characters).

quote: Don't use the formatted data input pattern if users are more likely to paste in long, complex data.
rule: Do not split a value into segment fields when people are likely to paste it whole (IPv6 addresses).

quote: If users are more likely going to reenter the entire value, select all the text on input focus.
rule: On focus, select the whole value if people usually replace it; put the caret at the end if they usually add to it.

quote: Always use a multi-line text box if new-line characters are valid input.
rule: A field that accepts line breaks is multi-line.

quote: When the text box is for a file or path, always provide a Browse button.
rule: A field for a file or folder path has a button beside it that opens the system's file dialog.

quote: Choose the most convenient unit and label the units.
rule: Use the unit that spares people decimals or conversion (millilitres rather than litres, percentages) and label it.

quote: Use a spin control whenever it is helpful.
rule: Add a stepper when values are small (under about 100), changes are small, or people mostly use the pointer.

quote: Right-align numeric text whenever:
rule: Align numbers on the trailing side when there are several stacked number fields whose values people compare or add.

quote: Always right-align monetary values.
rule: Money amounts are always aligned on the trailing side.

quote: Don't assign special meanings to specific numeric values
rule: Never give a number a special meaning (-1 for unlimited); offer the special case as an explicit checkbox or radio button.

quote: Always use the password common control instead of creating your own.
rule: Enter passwords and PINs only through the platform's secure password field, never a home-made one.

quote: Consider using the white background system color for large, multi-line read-only text.
rule: Large read-only text sits on the window-background colour of text areas, not a grey surface.

quote: Don't use a border for single-line, read-only text boxes. The border is a visual clue that the text is editable.
rule: A single-line read-only field does not look editable.

quote: Don't disable single-line, read-only text boxes.
rule: A read-only field is not disabled, so its text can still be scrolled, selected and copied.

quote: Don't set a tab stop on single-line, read-only text box unless the user is likely to need to scroll or copy the text.
rule: A single-line read-only field takes Tab focus only when people are likely to scroll or copy it.

quote: If the user enters a character that isn't valid, ignore the character and display an input problem balloon that explains the valid characters.
rule: A character a field cannot accept is ignored, and a note at the field says which characters are valid.

quote: If the input data has a value or format that isn't valid, display an input problem balloon when the text box loses input focus.
rule: A wrong value or format is reported at the field when the reader leaves it.

quote: If the input data is inconsistent with other controls on the window, give an error message when the entire input is complete,
rule: A value inconsistent with other fields is reported once the whole input is committed (on OK), not while typing.

quote: Don't clear invalid input data unless users aren't able to correct errors easily.
rule: Keep invalid input for correction; clear it only when it cannot be corrected, as with a masked password or PIN.

quote: Screen space is at such a premium that using a label or instruction is undesirable, such as on a toolbar.
rule: Use a prompt inside a field in place of a label only where space is very tight, as on a toolbar, and only to name its purpose, never for information needed while typing.

quote: Don't use prompts just to direct users to type something or to click buttons.
rule: Prompt text names what the field is for; it does not tell people to type or to click a button (not Enter a filename and then click Send).

quote: Draw the prompt text in italic gray and the actual input text in normal black.
rule: Prompt text is drawn in italic grey, real input in normal black.
