quote: Keep the prompt text concise. You can use fragments instead of full sentences.
rule: Prompt text is a short fragment in sentence case with no ending punctuation or ellipsis.

quote: The prompt text should not be editable and should disappear once users click in or tab into the text box.
rule: Prompt text cannot be edited, disappears when the field takes focus (or at the first keystroke if the field starts focused), and returns if the field is left empty.

quote: Choose a width appropriate for the longest valid data.
rule: Make a field wide enough that the longest likely value does not scroll.

quote: Include an additional 30 percent (up to 200 percent for shorter text) for any text (but not numbers) that will be localized.
rule: Leave extra width (about 30 percent, more for short strings) for text that will be translated; numbers need none.

quote: If the expected input has no particular size, choose a width that is consistent with the other text boxes or controls on the window.
rule: A field with no particular expected length is as wide as the window's other fields.

quote: Size multi-line text boxes to display an integral number of lines of text.
rule: A multi-line field's height shows whole lines.

quote: All text boxes need labels. Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, ending with a colon, and using static text.
rule: Every field has a visible label that is a word or phrase, not a sentence.

quote: If a text box is subordinate to a radio button or check box, and is introduced by its label ending with a colon
rule: A field that completes a radio button or checkbox label takes no label of its own; a group of segment fields shares one label.

quote: Omit control labels that restate the main instruction.
rule: Drop a field label that only repeats the window's main instruction; the instruction then serves as the label.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: Give each field label a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write field labels in sentence case.

quote: Position the label either to the left of or above the text box, and align the label with the left edge of the text box.
rule: Place a field's label before it or above it; a label above aligns with the field's leading edge, one beside it with the text inside the field.

quote: You may specify units (for example, seconds or connections) in parentheses after the label.
rule: Units may follow the label in parentheses.

quote: If a text box accepts an arbitrarily small maximum number of characters, you can state the maximum input in the label.
rule: When a field accepts only a few characters, the label may state the maximum and the field's width suggests it.

quote: Don't make the content of the text box (or its units label) part of a sentence, because this is not localizable.
rule: Never build a sentence around a field and its value; it cannot be translated.

quote: If the text box can be used to enter several items, make it clear how to separate the items in the label.
rule: A field that takes several items says in its label how to separate them.

quote: If you need to add instructional text about a text box, add it above the label. Use complete sentences with ending punctuation.
rule: Instructions about a field go above its label in complete sentences in sentence case.

quote: Additional information that is helpful but not necessary should be kept short.
rule: Short optional notes go in parentheses after the label or below the field.

quote: Use type to refer to user interactions that require typing or pasting; otherwise use enter
rule: In help, say type for values typed or pasted, enter when they can also come from a list or Browse, and select for read-only text.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, and include the word box.
rule: Help names a field by its exact label followed by box (the Password box), without colon or access-key mark, never text box or field.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Help shows field labels in bold, using quotation marks only when bold is unavailable and needed.

quote: If the text box requires a specific format, document only the most commonly used acceptable format.
rule: When a field needs a format, help documents only the most common accepted one.

quote: Accurate. Users should feel reassured that the information is technically accurate.
rule: Every statement in the interface is technically accurate.

quote: use "you can" rather than "Windows lets you" or "this feature allows you."
rule: Say you can rather than the app lets you or allows you; allow is kept for features that permit or deny something.

quote: treat users as intelligent people who happen to need help with a particular problem.
rule: Acknowledge when a task is complicated and guide through it, while treating the reader as intelligent.

quote: Objective. Sometimes users want a richer explanation; often though they just want to know what they need to move on.
rule: Give people what they need to move on, serving their goal and not the writer's, with fuller explanation available for those who want it.

quote: User-focused. Write from the user's perspective and preferably from the perspective of what you can do for the user.
rule: Write from the reader's point of view, about what the app can do for them.

quote: You can further develop communication with your users by being:
rule: Keep the voice light, candid and trustworthy: easy to take in, without pretence, never straining to be profound.

quote: By contrast, be sure to avoid the following tones, which are much more likely to receive a negative reaction:
rule: Avoid machine, corporate, interrogating, lawyerly, sales, condescending or angry, boastful and flippant tones.

quote: Use everyday words when you can and avoid words you wouldn't say to someone else in person.
rule: Use the words you would say aloud to someone beside you (Follow these steps, not Use this procedure).

quote: Use short, plain words whenever possible.
rule: Prefer short plain words (use, not utilize or employ; also, not in addition).

quote: Don't invent words or apply new meanings to standard words.
rule: Do not coin words or give ordinary words new meanings (categorize, not bucketize); define a needed industry term where it is used.

quote: Don't use symbols as a substitute for simple words.
rule: Write and, or and number of in words, not &, +, / or #.

quote: Choose words with a clear meaning.
rule: Choose words with one clear meaning: because, not since or as.

quote: Omit needless words
rule: Never use several words where one will do (To change your password:, not Follow these steps in order to...).

quote: Avoid unnecessary adverbs.
rule: Drop intensifying adverbs such as terribly.

quote: Choose single-word verbs over multi-word verbs.
rule: Prefer a one-word verb to a phrasal one (lock, not lock down).

quote: Don't convert verbs to nouns and nouns to verbs.
rule: Do not turn nouns into verbs or verbs into nouns (protect with a password, not password-protect; connect, not establish connectivity).

quote: Consistent terminology promotes learning and a better understanding of technical concepts.
rule: Use one term for one concept throughout (not switch and toggle, or start, run and launch, for the same thing).

quote: Consistent syntax helps set users' expectations.
rule: Write the same kind of text in the same grammatical form, such as instructions always in the imperative.

quote: Use them as appropriate and in context. Don't use contractions with product names or other proper nouns.
rule: Use contractions for a conversational rhythm, but never with product names or other proper nouns.

quote: Consider using colloquialisms or slang only in special situations, such as product tours, setup screens, or content that won't be localized.
rule: Keep colloquial phrases and slang to tours, introductions and untranslated content, and use them sparingly.

quote: Use the second person (you, your) to tell users what to do.
rule: Address the reader as you, stated or implied (Choose the pictures you want to print).

quote: Use the first person (I, me, my) to let users tell the program what to do.
rule: When the reader is telling the app what to do (an option they choose), phrase it in the first person: Print the photos on my camera.

quote: Use we judiciously. The first-person plural can suggest a daunting corporate presence.
rule: Use we sparingly, for the maker only, and prefer we recommend to it is recommended.

quote: Avoid third-person references (the user) because they create a more formal, less personal tone.
rule: Never refer to the reader as the user.

quote: Use the active voice, which emphasizes the person or thing doing the action.
rule: Write in the active voice (You can arrange icons..., not Icons can be arranged...).

quote: Use the passive voice only to avoid a wordy or awkward construction;
rule: Use the passive only when the active is clumsy, the action matters more than the doer, the doer is unknown, or the reader would feel blamed for an error.

quote: Phrase statements in the positive form, and emphasize what users can accomplish, rather than what they can't.
rule: State things positively, stressing what the reader can do rather than what they cannot.

quote: Be polite, supportive, and encouraging. The user should never feel condescended to, blamed, or intimidated.
rule: Be polite and supportive; never make the reader feel talked down to, blamed or intimidated.

quote: Strike the right balance: be warm toward the user without being too intimate or too business-like.
rule: Be warm as with a neighbour you are helping, neither familiar nor businesslike.

quote: Limit please to situations that inconvenience the user in some way,
rule: Say please when the reader is asked to wait or redo something, when a flaw stops them, when they are doing the maker a favour, or when leaving it out would sound curt.

quote: Use sorry only in error messages that result in serious problems for the user
rule: Apologise only for serious problems such as data loss or being unable to go on, never for normal behaviour.

quote: Because users often scan text, make every word count.
rule: Keep sentences and paragraphs tight, but not so tight that they sound abrupt.

quote: Avoid repetition. Review each window and eliminate duplicate words and statements.
rule: Remove repeated words and statements from each window and do not explain what goes without saying.

quote: Use sentence fragments if appropriate.
rule: Short fragments, often questions, are fine (Save changes to "My Photos"?).

quote: Start sentences with conjunctions (and, but, or) if you need to.
rule: A sentence may begin with and, but or or.

quote: Substitute lists and tables for complex sentences.
rule: Turn a complex sentence into a list or table.

quote: Use parallel grammatical constructions.
rule: Items of equal function (headings, labels, list items, page titles) share one grammatical form: Listen, Watch, Share, not Music, Video, Share.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Setup experience
quote: If so, consider presenting the settings during the setup experience.
rule: Ask in the installer only for settings that apply to all users, are core, have no safe default, or need elevation.

section: Is this the right user interface? > First use experience
quote: If so, consider presenting the tasks and settings during the first use experience of the program or feature.
rule: Ask at first use only for per-person settings that are required or core, have no safe default, and are better chosen in context and unlikely to be changed later.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: Setup questions
rule: Replace installer questions with defaults, options and typical or custom setup paths.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: Select appropriate defaults, and allow users to change from program options.
rule: Instead of first-use questions, choose good defaults that can be changed in the settings.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: First use tasks
rule: Present setup tasks in context when the feature is first needed, not all at first start.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: Make the most common and important tasks discoverable and contextual.
rule: Instead of advertising features at first use, make the important ones easy to find where they are needed.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: Make program features self-explanatory.
rule: Instead of a first-use tutorial, make features explain themselves.

section: Design concepts > Use the first experience when you must
quote: Provide command in Help menu and About box.
rule: Product registration is offered as a command in the Help menu and the About box, not as a first-start step.

quote: Limit first experiences to tasks and settings required to use a program or feature, and only include these when there is no better alternative.
rule: First start contains only what is needed to use the app, plus personalisation only when it is core to the experience.

quote: Use the setup experience for tasks and settings if they apply to all users or changing settings requires elevation.
rule: Put machine-wide or elevated settings in setup.

quote: Use the first use experience for tasks and settings if they apply to individual users.
rule: Settings that belong to one person are asked, if at all, at that person's first use, not in the installer.

quote: Prefer optional tasks and settings to required tasks and settings. Avoid forcing users to configure your program.
rule: Make first-run tasks and settings optional; never force configuration before use.

quote: Take optional tasks and settings out of the main task flow whenever practical.
rule: Move optional tasks and rarely changed settings out of the main first-run flow (a custom path).

quote: Start simple. Begin with simple, personalization settings and progress towards more complex, technical tasks and settings.
rule: Order first-run steps from simple personal choices to technical ones.

quote: Use a contextual first experience for tasks and settings if they apply only to features that aren't fundamental to the main program.
rule: Set up a secondary feature when it is first used, not at app start.

quote: Don't present everything all at once.
rule: Do not show several first-run surfaces at once; consolidate them into one or spread them over time.

quote: Express questions and options in terms of users' goals and tasks, not in terms of technology.
rule: Phrase first-run questions in terms of people's goals, with clearly different options and enough information to decide.

quote: If the need for personal information isn't obvious, explain why your program needs the information and how it will be used.
rule: When asking for personal information whose need is not obvious, say why and how it will be used.

quote: Present first experiences full screen only if users can't productively perform other tasks.
rule: First-run screens are not full screen unless nothing else can be done meanwhile.

quote: For all settings, select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access), most secure and private value by default.
rule: Every setting defaults to the safest, most secure and private value; only where none of these is at stake, to the likeliest or most convenient.

quote: Require users to opt in for:
rule: Require an explicit opt-in, with no preselection, for legal agreements, automatic system changes, sharing personal or system information, desktop changes, and extra software or subscriptions.

quote: If a setting is strongly recommended, add "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Mark a strongly recommended choice by adding (recommended) to its own label, not to a note.

quote: If a setting is intended only for advanced users, add "(advanced)" to the label.
rule: Mark a choice meant only for experts by adding (advanced) to its own label.

quote: Help users pass waiting time productively.
rule: For a wait of one to two minutes show something useful; for longer, show the estimated time, suggest doing something else, and make completion unmistakable.

quote: Reconsider presenting tutorials during the first experience.
rule: Do not start with a tutorial; people want to use the app first.

quote: Don't use feature advertisement notifications in the first experience.
rule: Never advertise features with notifications; make them discoverable where they are needed.

quote: Design your program assuming users won't see any such notifications.
rule: Nothing at first start may depend on a notification being seen.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Don't use interactions that aren't single tasks
rule: A step-by-step flow carries out exactly one task; never use one to bundle unrelated tasks or to make a whole app.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: try to simplify the task so that it can be presented on a single page (such as a dialog box)
rule: Cut questions that have workable defaults until the task fits one dialog or needs no input at all.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Must the required questions be provided sequentially?
rule: When the questions need not be answered in order (as with print options), use a dialog, tabbed if needed, rather than a sequence of pages.

quote: A wizard should not be used as a band-aid to fix a more basic problem with the program.
rule: Fix a confusing feature by redesigning it, not by putting a step-by-step flow in front of it.

quote: An infrequent task may deploy a longer wizard, whereas frequent tasks should definitely favor brevity.
rule: The more often a task is done, the shorter its step-by-step flow must be; only rare tasks may take more pages.

section: Design concepts > Providing a navigation guide
quote: Navigation guides can be useful when there are many steps in the task, and users may lose their place in the sequence
rule: Give a long flow a list of its steps beside the pages, marking the current one, so people know where they are and how much remains.

section: Design concepts > Providing a navigation guide
quote: Pages that can be visited should be visibly distinguished from those that can't
rule: In a step list people can jump through, steps that can be visited look different from those that cannot, and required steps from optional ones, whose defaults must suit most cases.

section: Design concepts > Providing a navigation guide
quote: give your Back button the Web navigation meaning (clicking Back should lead to the last page or section viewed)
rule: Back returns to the page last viewed, as in a browser; moving through the steps in order is the job of the step list.

quote: don't move the Back button from the upper-left corner back down into the commit buttons area for a page or two
rule: Keep each navigation and commit control in the same place on every page of a flow.

section: Design concepts > Finding the right level of communication
quote: Get right to the point of the page with a concisely written main instruction, using language your target audience uses to describe the task
rule: Open each page with a short main instruction in the words the audience uses for the task, not the team's internal jargon.

section: Design concepts > Finding the right level of communication
quote: users do appreciate having enough information to make wise choices
rule: Trim text, but keep whatever people need to make the choice the page asks for.

quote: Consider lightweight alternatives first, such as dialog boxes, task panes, or single pages.
rule: Before building a step-by-step flow, try a dialog, a pane or a single page; use a flow only when they will not do.

quote: Use wizards for multi-step tasks. Use multi-page dialog boxes for single-step tasks with feedback.
rule: A task with one input step followed by progress and results is a multi-page dialog without Back and Next, not a step flow.

quote: Choose a window size that can display all the wizard pages without vertical or horizontal page scrolling.
rule: Size a flow's window so no page needs scrolling as a whole; only a control inside a page may scroll.

quote: Size windows large enough to perform their tasks comfortably.
rule: Make the window big enough that its pages are not cramped and need no scrolling or resizing to use.

quote: But don't make windows excessively large.
rule: Do not make the window larger than its task needs; an oversized window makes the task feel harder and the pointer travel further.

quote: Use resizable windows for a wizard that can benefit from more screen space but doesn't require it.
rule: Let the flow's window be resized, with a sensible minimum, when a page holds resizable content such as a long list.

quote: Consider using dynamically sized wizards whose page size changes as needed for its content.
rule: A flow may let its page size follow each page's content when the pages differ widely.

quote: Prefer static sizing over dynamic if users may perceive the changes as a lack of stability
rule: Keep one fixed page size through a flow unless resizing per page is really needed; a steady frame matters more than a snug fit.

quote: Make your wizard as concise and streamlined as possible.
rule: Drop needless questions and use good defaults to keep a flow's pages few; technical audiences tolerate somewhat longer flows.

quote: Make your wizard a minimum of two pages.
rule: A flow with only one page is turned into a dialog.

quote: Don't reduce the wizard's page count simply by increasing the complexity of each page.
rule: Never shrink a flow by cramming pages together; a page holding three tabs of input becomes three pages.

quote: Don't increase the wizard's page count by making each page so simple that users mindlessly click Next
rule: Drop any page that asks for no real decision, so people are never just pressing Next through it.

quote: Prefer non-branching wizard design over branching.
rule: Design a flow as one straight sequence whenever possible; branches hide how many steps remain.

quote: Ensure that the endpoint (Y) is stable.
rule: When a flow branches, show the position on each page as Step X of Y, with a total that never changes.

quote: Include the notion of sub-steps (such as Step 2a of 6).
rule: Pages added by a branch can be numbered as sub-steps (Step 2a of 6) so the main count stays put.

quote: Make steps independent of pages, where each step may involve several pages.
rule: Count named steps rather than pages when a step may span several pages, as checkout flows do.

quote: Treat optional steps as persistent in the enumeration sequence.
rule: Skipped optional steps keep their numbers: after skipping 3 and 4, show steps 5 and 6 of 6, not renumbered ones.

quote: If the wizard employs a single branch, and the branch happens early in the task, start the sequence at that point
rule: With one early branch, start counting steps after the branch so the rest reads as a straight sequence.

quote: limit the number of branches to one or two within a single wizard. Never include more than one branch within a branch
rule: Allow at most two branches in a flow and never more than one branch nested inside another.

quote: When users are committing to a task, use a commit button that is a specific response to the main instruction
rule: The button that commits the task is a verb answering the page's instruction (Print, Connect, Start), never Next or Finish; Finish only when the verb would be generic (Save, Choose) or the flow just changes settings.

quote: A single wizard can have multiple commit points, but a single point is preferred.
rule: Prefer a single point in a flow at which the task is committed.

quote: Avoid disabling a positive commit button.
rule: Leave the commit button enabled and explain any problem with a message when it is pressed; disable it only when the reason is obvious.

quote: clicking Back should undo the effect of the last Next button
rule: Next moves on without committing anything and Back, always offered on the following page, fully reverses it; if it cannot, the button is a specific commit verb instead.

quote: Don't ask users to confirm whether they really intend to cancel.
rule: Cancel a flow without asking, unless cancelling loses significant time or effort, has consequences not easily fixed, or clearly contradicts what was just done.

quote: Allow users to restart wizards in case they have cancelled by mistake.
rule: A flow cancelled by mistake can be started again.

quote: Don't disable the Cancel button.
rule: Cancel stays enabled throughout a flow except where cancelling would do harm or cannot be done.

quote: Use Close for Follow-Up and Completion pages.
rule: Pages shown after the task is done (follow-up, completion) are left with Close, not Cancel (nothing remains to abandon) and not Done.

quote: Once the task has been performed, Cancel should become Close (for self-contained wizards).
rule: Once the task has been carried out, the Cancel button is relabelled Close, since it only closes the window.

quote: Use command links only for choices, not commitments.
rule: Large command links on a page make choices; committing the task is done with a specific commit button.

quote: When using command links, hide the Next button, but leave the Cancel button.
rule: On a page whose choices are command links, there is no Next button, but Cancel remains.

section: Guidelines > Using pages (vs. dialog boxes or inline UI)
quote: In general, prefer pages to dialog boxes.
rule: Put a flow's steps on its own pages, not in dialogs over it.

section: Guidelines > Using pages (vs. dialog boxes or inline UI)
quote: Use dialog boxes to assist in completing pages,
rule: Open a dialog from a page only to help fill it in, such as a chooser for objects or files.

section: Guidelines > Using pages (vs. dialog boxes or inline UI)
quote: Use dialog boxes to give error messages that apply to the whole page, and result from clicking a commit button.
rule: A problem with the whole page found on pressing a commit button is reported in a dialog.

section: Guidelines > Using pages (vs. dialog boxes or inline UI)
quote: Use inline presentation for simple dynamic behaviors,
rule: Show simple changes such as extra options or context-dependent controls in place on the page.

section: Guidelines > Using pages (vs. dialog boxes or inline UI)
quote: Use inline presentation for error messages that apply to specific controls.
rule: A problem with one control is shown next to that control on the page.

quote: Focus on efficient decision making.
rule: Keep only pages that ask for real decisions: merge related pages and move optional ones out of the main path.

quote: Design each page to have a single purpose and visual consistency.
rule: Every page deals with one part of the task, and everything on it serves its main instruction.

quote: Don't use Welcome pages
rule: Start a flow on a page that already asks something; a getting-started page ("Before you begin:") only for prerequisites or an unclear purpose, otherwise state the purpose atop the first page.

quote: On pages in which users are asked to make choices, optimize for the most likely cases.
rule: Pages that ask for choices offer real choices, preset for the most likely case.

quote: Use Commit pages to make it clear when users are committing to the task.
rule: Make the last page of choices the commit page, with Next renamed to the task being committed.

quote: Upon successful completion, the progress page should advance to the next step automatically.
rule: Show a long operation on a progress page that moves on by itself when done, stays only if there is a problem to see, and has no side effect when revisited with Back.

quote: Use a single, determinate progress bar.
rule: A progress page has one determinate bar that runs to completion once, never restarts, and reaches the end only when the work is done.

quote: Provide a concise description of the current step above the progress bar.
rule: For work taking a minute or more, label the bar above it with a verb fragment ending in an ellipsis (Copying files...).

quote: Refrain from cluttering the progress page with unnecessary details.
rule: Keep technical detail such as identifiers off a progress page.

quote: Don't use Congratulations pages that do nothing but end the wizard.
rule: When the result is plain to see, close the flow on its final commit button instead of showing a page that only says it is done.

quote: Use Follow-Up pages when there are related tasks that users are likely to perform as follow-up.
rule: End with a follow-up page only when it offers related next tasks people are likely to want, not familiar ones like sending an email.

quote: Use Completion pages only when the results aren't visible and there's no better way to provide feedback for task completion.
rule: Show a completion page only when the result cannot be seen otherwise.

quote: For long-running tasks, close the wizard on the Commit page and use notifications to give feedback.
rule: A flow with a progress page ends on a completion or follow-up page; for very long work, close the flow at commit and report completion by notification.

quote: Use Summary pages only if input is complex and users need to review,
rule: Show a page summarising earlier choices only when the input is complex, the task is risky (money, security) or the action taken is not obvious.

quote: Use error pages if the wizard can't be completed due to a problem from which recovery isn't possible.
rule: When a flow cannot finish, end on a page explaining the problem in plain words with practical steps to solve it.

quote: Use positive, success-oriented, encouraging language, not terms like error, failure, or problem.
rule: If the flow finishes with a minor recoverable problem, present it as one more task to do, in encouraging words, without error wording or an error symbol.

quote: Use Next only when advancing to the next page without commitment.
rule: Label the forward button Next only when Back or Cancel can still undo its effect; otherwise it is a commit button with a specific verb.

quote: Use Back only to correct mistakes.
rule: Design the flow so that Back is needed only to fix a mistake, never to make progress.

quote: Preserve user selections through navigation.
rule: Going Back and then Next keeps everything the reader entered unless they chose to clear it.

quote: Don't disable the Back button unless repeating the steps is harmful.
rule: Back stays enabled unless repeating the earlier steps would cause harm.

quote: Permit users to browse or revise choices in the following navigation scenarios:
rule: After committing, people can go Back to review: committing again unchanged simply moves on, and committing with changes redoes the task with the new input.

quote: Design wizard pages to provide enough information so that referring to documentation in program Help is unnecessary.
rule: Each page explains enough that nobody needs to open the help to complete it.

quote: If you must provide an access point to Help, use a link in the lower-left portion of the content area
rule: If a page needs help, give a short link worded as the question people are likely to have, at the bottom leading corner of the content above the buttons.

quote: Don't use the first person (I, my) to refer to the computer or the wizard.
rule: Address the reader as you; the program never says I or my, though an option the reader picks may (My use only).

quote: Every wizard page must have a main instruction.
rule: Every page of a flow carries a main instruction.

quote: Put the name of the wizard in the title bar. Use title-style capitalization.
rule: The flow's window title is its name, in title case.

quote: Titles shouldn't include punctuation, except for those with question marks.
rule: Titles carry no punctuation except a question mark.

quote: Don't include the word Wizard in wizard titles.
rule: Name a flow by its task (Connect to a Network), never with the word wizard (Network Setup Wizard).

quote: Don't include text on the Back button. Use the arrow glyph instead, unlabeled.
rule: Back is an unlabelled back-arrow button (with a tooltip and an accessible name), not a captioned button.

quote: Do include text on the Next button. Don't use glyphs (such as > or >>) in addition to the word Next.
rule: Next is a text button reading Next, with no > or >> added.

quote: Start commit button labels with a verb. Exceptions are OK, Yes, and No.
rule: Commit buttons start with a verb; Windows allows OK, Yes and No as the only exceptions.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Button labels in a flow use sentence case.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: Button labels end without punctuation.

quote: it's acceptable to refer to wizards as wizards in documentation. This reference should be lowercase.
rule: Help may call a flow a wizard, in lowercase, after its name in bold (the Connect to a Network wizard).

quote: When referring to one of those wizards, it's acceptable to use the [X] Wizard
rule: For legacy flows whose title already ends in Wizard, help writes the [X] Wizard rather than doubling the word.

quote: Refer to an individual screen within a wizard as a page.
rule: Help calls each screen of a flow a page.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does setting the properties require users to perform a fixed, non-trivial sequence of steps? If so, use a wizard or task flow instead.
rule: Settings that must be made in a fixed sequence of steps belong in a guided flow, not a properties window.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the content solely an application's options? If so, use an options dialog box.
rule: The app's own options go in its options window, kept apart from properties of objects.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the content solely an application's attributes? If so, use an About box.
rule: Facts about the app itself (version and the like) go in the About window.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the content mostly an object's properties (its settings or attributes)? If not, use a standard dialog box or tabbed dialog box.
rule: Use a properties window only when its content is mostly an object's settings and attributes; anything else is an ordinary dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: likely to view or change properties frequently or over an extended period of time?
rule: Use an inspector pane when people change properties often, for long stretches or across several objects; otherwise a properties dialog.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Property sheets and property inspectors aren't exclusive.
rule: An inspector can show the most used properties while a properties dialog holds the full set.

quote: All property window patterns except property inspectors use a delayed commit
rule: Properties and options dialogs take effect on OK or Apply; an inspector applies each change at once and has no OK, Cancel or Apply.

quote: Options dialog boxes. Properties for an application are displayed in a modal dialog box.
rule: An object's properties dialog is modeless; the app's options dialog is modal.

quote: Select the Properties command for an object.
rule: Open an object's properties window from its Properties command and with Alt+Enter on the focused object.

quote: Display the common properties of all the selected objects.
rule: With several objects selected, show the properties they share, with mixed-state controls where their values differ.

quote: display the properties of the single grouped object instead of a multiple-object property sheet for the discrete objects.
rule: For a container such as a folder, show the container's own properties, not a combined view of its contents.

quote: Don't separate options from customization.
rule: Do not offer both an Options and a Customize command; reach customisation through the options.

quote: Follow these guidelines for page order:
rule: Order settings pages: the general page first, the advanced page last, the rest in groups ordered by likely use, never so many that they need alphabetical order.

quote: Make pages coherent by relating all properties on each page to a single, specific, task-based purpose.
rule: Every property on a page serves one specific task.

quote: If space allows, explain the purpose of the property window at the top of the page if it isn't obvious to your target users.
rule: When a page's purpose is not obvious, explain it at the top in complete sentences, as an instruction if the page has a single task.

quote: Make similar content consistent across pages by using consistent control names and locations.
rule: Controls that recur across pages (a Name field, say) keep the same label and position.

quote: Place the same property on the same page throughout your application.
rule: A property sits on the same page for every kind of object that has it.

quote: If users are likely to start with the last page displayed, make the page tab persist, and select it by default.
rule: Reopen a settings window on the page last shown, per window and per user, when people tend to return there; otherwise on the first page.

quote: Don't make the settings on a page dependent upon settings on other pages.
rule: Settings that depend on each other share a page; changing one page never changes another, and dependencies across windows are explained in both.

quote: Don't scroll property pages.
rule: Settings pages do not scroll; enlarge and rearrange them instead.

quote: For object properties, put the object's name on the first page.
rule: An object's properties window shows the object's name on its first page.

quote: display the appropriate icon in the upper-left corner
rule: Show the object's icon at the top left of the first properties page.

quote: Avoid General pages.
rule: Have a General page only for widely used properties that serve several tasks and fit no more specific page; keep specialised ones off it.

quote: Avoid Advanced pages.
rule: Have an Advanced page only for properties of uncommon tasks meant for experts that fit no more specific page.

quote: Don't call properties advanced based solely on technological measures.
rule: A setting meaningful to everyone (a printer's stapling option) is not advanced just because the technology behind it is.

quote: Don't display more than one owned property window from a property window.
rule: Open at most one level of settings window from a settings window; choosers and similar helpers are fine.

quote: make sure users can cancel changes made in an owned property window by clicking Cancel on the owner window.
rule: Changes made in a settings window opened from another are undone by Cancel in the owning window, and its OK only keeps them until the owner applies.

quote: indicate that changes were committed by renaming the Cancel button on the owner window to Close.
rule: When an owned window has applied changes that cannot be undone, the owner's Cancel becomes Close, returning to Cancel after Apply.

quote: If an owned window is used to perform an auxiliary task, don't rename the Cancel button.
rule: A helper task run from a settings window (such as a clean-up) leaves the owner's Cancel unchanged.

quote: don't close the owner property window when the command button is clicked.
rule: Starting a helper task from a settings window leaves that window open.

quote: Use concise tab labels.
rule: Tab labels are one or two words that describe the page, with no ending punctuation.

quote: Use specific, meaningful tab labels.
rule: Name each tab for its content, never a label that could fit any tab (General, Advanced, Settings).

quote: The property window has seven or fewer tabs (including any third-party extensions).
rule: Use a row of tabs when there are at most seven and they fit on one row even when translated.

quote: Using horizontal tabs would require more than one row.
rule: Use a vertical list of tabs when there are eight or more or a row would wrap, and use the same orientation throughout the app.

quote: For property inspectors, to conserve space, consider using a drop-down list instead of tabs
rule: In a narrow inspector, choose its page with a drop-down list instead of tabs, especially when the page rarely changes.

quote: If a tab doesn't apply to the current context and users don't expect it to, remove the tab.
rule: Remove a tab that does not apply and that nobody would expect to find.

quote: Include text explaining why the controls are disabled.
rule: If a tab does not apply but people might look for it, keep it enabled, disable its controls and say why on the page.

quote: Don't assign effects to changing tabs.
rule: Switching tabs never applies settings, has side effects or raises errors.

quote: Don't nest tabs or combine horizontal tabs with vertical tabs.
rule: Never put tabs inside tabs or mix a tab row with a vertical tab list.

quote: Don't use tabs if a property window has only a single tab and isn't extensible.
rule: A settings window with one page has no tab; it is a plain dialog.

quote: Don't put icons on tabs.
rule: Tabs carry text only, unless a standard symbol really helps understanding.

quote: Don't use product logos for tab graphics.
rule: No product logos or branding on tabs.

quote: Don't scroll horizontal tabs.
rule: A row of tabs never scrolls sideways; a vertical tab list may scroll.

quote: Right-align the buttons and use this order (from left to right): OK, Cancel, and Apply.
rule: Buttons for the whole window sit at its bottom, at the trailing side, in the order OK, Cancel, Apply.

quote: Place command buttons that apply only to individual property pages directly on the property page.
rule: Buttons that act on one page sit on that page.

quote: the OK button means apply the pending changes (made since the window was opened or the last Apply), and close the window.
rule: OK applies everything changed since opening or the last Apply and closes; Cancel discards those changes and closes.

quote: the OK button means keep the changes, close the window, and apply the changes when the owner window's changes are applied.
rule: OK in a settings window opened from another keeps the changes but applies them only when the owner window is confirmed.

quote: Don't rename the OK button.
rule: A properties window keeps its button named OK; a window whose OK would read Print is not a properties window.

quote: Don't assign an access key.
rule: OK and Cancel get no access key; Enter and Esc serve them.

quote: If all pending changes can't be abandoned, rename the Cancel button to Close.
rule: Cancel must undo every pending change; when some cannot be undone, the button is called Close.

quote: the Apply button means apply the pending changes (made since the window was opened or the last Apply), but leave the window open.
rule: Apply puts pending changes into effect and keeps the window open so people can judge them.

quote: Place all settings that users may want to apply on owner pages.
rule: No Apply button in a settings window opened from another; settings worth trying out belong in the owning window.

quote: Provide an Apply button only if the property sheet has settings (at least one) with effects that users can evaluate in a meaningful way.
rule: Offer Apply only when some setting has a visible effect to evaluate; otherwise remove it rather than disable it.

quote: Use Apply buttons only with property sheets, not with options dialog boxes.
rule: Options dialogs have no Apply button; only properties windows do.

quote: Enable the Apply button only when there are pending changes
rule: Apply is enabled only while there are unapplied changes.

quote: Assign "A" as the access key.
rule: Apply's access key is A.

quote: Don't confirm if users discard their changes.
rule: Discarding changes with Cancel needs no confirmation; only closing from the title bar after effortful changes may ask, since some think it means OK.

quote: make sure the Close button on the title bar has the same effect as Cancel or Close.
rule: The title bar's close button does what Cancel (or Close) does.

quote: Make sure the properties are necessary.
rule: Include only properties people need; do not pad pages to avoid hard decisions.

quote: Present properties in terms of user goals, not technology.
rule: Describe each property by what it does for the reader; if a technology name must appear, add a short note on the benefit.

quote: Present properties at the right level.
rule: Offer properties at the level people think in, not every low-level switch.

quote: Design property pages for specific tasks.
rule: Work out the tasks people do in the window and give each a clear path.

quote: Organize property pages efficiently
rule: Keep the number of pages small and decide what goes on each by logical grouping.

quote: If an option is strongly recommended, consider adding "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Mark a strongly recommended option by adding (recommended) to its label.

quote: Provide a Restore Defaults command button for a property page or the entire property window when:
rule: Offer Restore Defaults on a page or window whose settings are complex, can break things when wrong, or are easier to start over.

quote: Confirm the Restore Defaults command if its effect isn't obvious or the settings are complex.
rule: Restore Defaults asks first (and its label then ends in an ellipsis) when its effect is not obvious or the settings are complex.

quote: When appropriate, display a preview of the results of a setting.
rule: Show a live preview of a setting's result on the page where it helps, even for non-graphical settings such as fonts.

quote: Give interactive controls self-explanatory labels.
rule: Explain settings first through clear control labels, then through short static text, and only then with a link to a specific help topic.

quote: Locate Help links at the bottom of each page.
rule: Put help links at the bottom of the page, or at the bottom of the group they explain.

quote: Don't use general or vague Help topic links or generic Help buttons.
rule: Never offer a vague help link or a generic Help button; link to the specific topic.

quote: The settings within a property window must reflect the current state of the application, object, or collection of objects.
rule: Settings show the current state of what they control, never recommended values that are not in effect.

quote: Choose the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure initial state.
rule: Start each setting at its safest, most secure value; where safety is not at stake, at the likeliest or most convenient value.

quote: To display program options, use "Options."
rule: The command that opens the app's options is called Options, never Settings or Preferences.

quote: To display an object's property window, use "Properties."
rule: The command that opens an object's properties is called Properties.

quote: To display a summary of the commonly used program customization settings, use "Personalize."
rule: A command opening a summary of the common customisation settings is called Personalize.

quote: Don't use ellipses for these commands.
rule: Options, Properties and Personalize take no ellipsis.

quote: For a single object, use "[object name] Properties."
rule: Title an object's properties window with its name followed by Properties, or its type name when it has none (User Account Properties).

quote: For multiple objects, use "[first object name], ... Properties."
rule: For several objects, the title is the first name, an ellipsis and Properties, or the plural type name, or Selection Properties for mixed types.

quote: Use title-style capitalization.
rule: Properties, inspector and options window titles are in title case.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: Window titles end without punctuation.

quote: Don't use hyphens, such as "[object name] - Properties."
rule: Do not join the object name and Properties with a hyphen.

quote: Use "Properties."
rule: An inspector pane is titled Properties.

quote: Use "Options."
rule: The app's options window is titled Options.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Tab labels are in sentence case.

quote: Don't assign a unique access key.
rule: Tabs get no access keys; Ctrl+Tab and the arrow keys move between them.

quote: Avoid large blocks of text.
rule: Keep text on settings pages short, with no large blocks.

quote: Provide enough room for the text to expand 30 percent if it will be localized.
rule: Leave room for text to grow by about a third in translation.

quote: Don't use text phrased as a command on property windows.
rule: Text on settings pages describes; it does not order people to change settings they may only be looking at.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization and ending punctuation.
rule: Explanatory text on a settings page is in sentence case with full stops.

quote: Everywhere else, use dialog box, especially in user documentation.
rule: User help calls properties and options windows dialog boxes and their pages tabs.

quote: Use the exact title text, including its capitalization.
rule: Help names a window or tab by its exact title, capitalisation included.

quote: To describe user interaction, use open and close.
rule: Help says open and close for windows and click for tabs.

quote: When possible, format the title using bold text.
rule: Help shows window and tab names in bold, quoting them only if bold is unavailable and confusion is likely.

quote: Does the list present data, rather than program options?
rule: A list box suits data of any size; radio buttons and check boxes suit only a few program options.

quote: Do users need to change views, group, sort by columns, or change column widths and order? If so, use a list view instead.
rule: When people need views, grouping, column sorting or column resizing, use a table rather than a simple list.

quote: Does the control need to be a drag source or a drop target? If so, use a list view instead.
rule: A list that items are dragged from or dropped onto is a full list view, not a simple choice list.

quote: Do the list items need to be copied to or pasted from the clipboard? If so, use a list view instead.
rule: A list whose items are copied or pasted is a full list view.

quote: Is the control used to choose one option from a list of mutually exclusive values?
rule: A single-choice list picks one of mutually exclusive values; several choices need a multiple-choice pattern.

quote: Is there a default option that is recommended for most users in most situations?
rule: When one choice suits nearly everyone and the alternatives should not tempt, use a drop-down list instead of an open list.

quote: Does the list require constant interaction?
rule: A choice changed again and again while working is an open list, not a drop-down.

quote: Would users benefit from instant feedback
rule: A setting that is a relative amount and benefits from instant feedback is a slider.

quote: Is there a significant hierarchical relationship between the list items?
rule: Items with a real hierarchy go in a tree.

quote: Is screen space at a premium? If so, use a drop-down list instead
rule: Where space is short, a single choice is a drop-down, whose size does not grow with its items.

quote: Is multiple selection essential to the task or commonly used?
rule: When multiple selection is essential or common, show check boxes in the list so it is obvious.

quote: Is the stability of the multiple selection important?
rule: When losing a multiple selection by one stray click would hurt, use a check box list or a list builder.

quote: Is the control used to choose zero or more items from a list of values?
rule: Multiple-selection lists are for picking any number of items, including none.

quote: Are the options easier to select with images than with text alone?
rule: When pictures of each option's effect choose better than words, show a preview list.

quote: Does the order of the selected items matter?
rule: When the order of chosen items matters, let people build and reorder them.

quote: Is it important for users to see a summary of all the selected items?
rule: When people must review everything chosen, use a list builder that shows only the chosen items.

quote: Are the possible choices unconstrained? If so, use an add/remove list
rule: When values outside the current list may be added, use an add/remove list.

quote: Does adding a value to the list require a specialized dialog box for choosing objects?
rule: When adding needs a special chooser, use an add/remove list whose Add opens it.

quote: If so, use an add/remove list instead because it uses less screen space
rule: Where space is short, prefer an add/remove list to a two-list builder.

quote: the number of items in the list isn't a factor in choosing the control
rule: Choose a list by what it is for, not by how many items it holds; data lists can be empty or huge.

quote: apply the guidelines based on usage, not implementation.
rule: Judge a control by how it is used, not by how it is built.

quote: the selection can be extended by dragging or with Shift+click and Ctrl+click
rule: In a multiple-selection list, dragging and Shift-click select a range and Ctrl-click adds or removes one item.

quote: There are two command buttons between the lists:
rule: A list builder has Add and Remove buttons between the available and chosen lists (double-click does the same), plus Move Up and Move Down when order matters.

quote: they are best used to create short lists or modify lists that already exist.
rule: Use list builders for short lists or for editing existing ones, not for building long lists from nothing.

quote: Sort list items in a logical order,
rule: Order items logically (related together, most used first, names alphabetical, numbers numeric, dates chronological); lists of 12 or more are alphabetical.

quote: Place options that represent All or None at the beginning of the list
rule: All and None choices come first, whatever the sort order.

quote: Enclose meta-options in parentheses.
rule: A choice that means the option is not used, such as (none), is written in parentheses.

quote: Don't have blank list items use meta-options instead.
rule: Never use a blank item; use an explicit (none).

quote: Consider providing double-click behavior.
rule: Double-clicking an item selects it and runs its default command.

quote: Make double-click behavior redundant.
rule: Whatever double-click does is also available from a button or context-menu command.

quote: If users can't do anything with the selected items, don't allow selection.
rule: A read-only list that nothing acts on does not let items be selected.

quote: When disabling a list box, also disable any associated labels and command buttons.
rule: Disabling a list also disables its label and its buttons.

quote: Don't use the change of the selected item in a list box to:
rule: Selecting a list item never runs a command, opens a window or makes other controls appear; only text describing the item may change.

quote: Avoid horizontal scrolling.
rule: Lists scroll vertically; multi-column lists that scroll sideways only for long sorted lists with plenty of width.

quote: Consider displaying the number of selected items below the list,
rule: Below a multiple-selection list show how many items are selected, or a more meaningful total such as the disk space needed.

quote: If there are potentially many list items and selecting or clearing all of them is likely, add Select all and Clear all command buttons.
rule: Add Select all and Clear all buttons to long lists where all-or-nothing is likely.

quote: For standard multiple-selection lists, don't use multiple-selection mode because this selection mode has been deprecated.
rule: Never make a plain click toggle items in and out of a selection; use a check box list for that.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure option by default.
rule: Preselect the safest, most secure item, or the likeliest when safety is not at stake.

quote: Don't select any items if the control represents a property in a mixed state,
rule: Select nothing when the list shows a property whose value differs across the selected objects.

quote: Choose a list box width appropriate for the longest valid data.
rule: Make a list wide enough for its longest valid item, since it cannot scroll sideways.

quote: Include an additional 30 percent
rule: Leave a third more width (up to double for short text) for translated text, not for numbers.

quote: Choose a list box height that displays an integral number of items.
rule: Size a list to show whole rows, none cut off at the bottom.

quote: Choose a list box height that eliminates unnecessary vertical scrolling.
rule: Show between 3 and 20 rows, at least five when there may be many, and lengthen slightly if that removes the scroll bar.

quote: If users benefit from making the list box larger, make the list box and its parent window resizable.
rule: Let a list grow with its resizable window when a bigger list helps, never shrinking below three rows.

quote: All list boxes need labels.
rule: Every list has a label, a word or phrase rather than a sentence, ending with a colon.

quote: Omit the label if it is merely a restatement of a dialog box's main instruction.
rule: Drop a list label that only repeats the main instruction; the instruction then takes the colon and the access key.

quote: If a list box is subordinate to a radio button or check box and is introduced by that control's label ending with a colon
rule: A list introduced by the radio button or check box it belongs to has no label of its own.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: Give each list (through its label) a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: List labels are in sentence case.

quote: Position the label either to the left of or above the control, and align the label with the left edge of the control.
rule: Put the label before or above the list, aligned with its leading edge; a label beside it lines up with the first row's text.

quote: For multiple-selection list boxes, use a label that clearly indicates multiple selection is possible.
rule: The label of a multiple-selection list says several may be chosen; with check boxes it need not.

quote: You may specify units (seconds, connections, and so on) in parentheses after the label.
rule: Units may follow the label in parentheses.

quote: Assign a unique name to each option.
rule: Every item in a list has a distinct name.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization, unless an item is a proper noun.
rule: List items are in sentence case except proper nouns.

quote: Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, and use no ending punctuation.
rule: List items are words or phrases with no ending punctuation.

quote: Use parallel phrasing, and try to keep the length about the same for all options.
rule: Phrase list items in parallel and at similar length.

quote: If you need to add instructional text about a list box, add it above the label.
rule: Instructions about a list go above its label, in full sentences with ending punctuation and sentence case.

quote: Additional information that is helpful but not necessary should be kept short.
rule: Keep optional extra notes short, in parentheses between the label and colon or below the list.

quote: Include the word list. Don't refer to a list box as a list box or a field.
rule: Help names a list by its exact label without colon or access-key mark, followed by list (the Go to what list), never list box or field.

quote: For list items, use the exact item text, including its capitalization.
rule: Help quotes list items exactly as shown.

quote: To describe user interaction, use select.
rule: Help says select for choosing a list item.

quote: When possible, format the label and list items using bold text.
rule: Help shows list labels and items in bold (In the Go to what list, select Bookmark).

quote: Do users need to see the information in some but not all scenarios, or some but not all of the time?
rule: Put behind a disclosure control what is needed only in some situations or some of the time.

quote: If the information is displayed by default, are users ever likely to choose to hide it?
rule: If nobody would bother to hide shown information, show it plainly with no disclosure control.

quote: Is the additional information advanced, substantial, complex, or related to an independent subtask?
rule: Advanced, bulky or separate-task information opens in its own window from a button or link, not in place.

quote: Is the additional information a sentence or sentence fragment that describes what an item does or how it can be used?
rule: A short description of what an item does belongs in a tooltip, not a disclosure.

quote: Is the additional information related to the current task, but independent of the currently displayed information?
rule: Separate but related information goes in tabs, though collapsible sections are often more flexible.

quote: Is showing or hiding the additional information essentially a data filter?
rule: Hiding items that amounts to filtering uses a drop-down or check boxes that filter the whole list.

quote: Showing contextual detail only in context.
rule: Show commands or toolbars that apply to a selection or mode only while it is active.

quote: Reducing the weight of affordances for secondary UI.
rule: Secondary in-place controls may look quiet until hovered; primary ones always look interactive.

quote: Showing follow-up steps only after prerequisites are done.
rule: In familiar tasks, fields that depend on an earlier one (password confirmation) may appear once it is filled.

quote: Users should be able to predict a progressive disclosure control's behavior correctly by inspection alone.
rule: A disclosure control shows at a glance that it discloses, whether it is open, and how to undo it; use each pattern consistently.

quote: the associated object receives input focus and the single chevron is activated with the space bar.
rule: A chevron button takes focus and opens or closes with the Space bar.

quote: the arrow is activated with Alt+down arrow and Alt+up arrow keys, as with the drop-down list control.
rule: An arrow that opens a pop-up command menu opens with Space when it is its own control, or Alt+Down and Alt+Up when part of another; the menu stays until a choice or a click elsewhere.

section: Usage patterns > Plus and minus controls
quote: The plus is activated with the right arrow key, and the minus with the left arrow key.
rule: In a collapsible tree or list, the focused item expands with Right arrow and collapses with Left arrow and stays as left until changed.

quote: Rotating triangles show or hide additional information in place for an individual item.
rule: Use a rotating triangle to show an item's extra detail in place or open a container, pointing where it has opened.

quote: Preview arrows are best reserved for situations where a standard chevron doesn't adequately communicate the control's behavior
rule: Use a pictured disclosure symbol only when a plain chevron cannot convey a complex or multiple disclosure.

quote: Select the progressive disclosure pattern based on its usage.
rule: Pick the disclosure pattern (chevron, arrow, expand control, triangle) by what it does.

quote: Don't use links for progressive disclosure controls.
rule: Links navigate to another page, window or help topic; showing more in place uses a disclosure control.

quote: For chevrons and arrows that aren't directly labeled, use tooltips to describe what they do.
rule: An unlabelled chevron or arrow has a tooltip saying what it does.

quote: make the state persist so it takes effect the next time the window is displayed
rule: Remember each expanded or collapsed state per window and per user for next time, unless people would rather start fresh.

quote: Make sure that all expanded content can be collapsed and vice versa, and that the inverse operation is obvious.
rule: Whatever expands can collapse again with the same control, kept in the same place.

quote: Don't use Enter to activate progressive disclosure.
rule: Disclosure controls answer only to their own keys (Space, arrows), never Enter, which belongs to the default button.

quote: Don't use triangular-shaped arrowheads for a purpose other than progressive disclosure.
rule: Keep the triangular arrowhead symbol for disclosure only; use a bullet or other mark elsewhere.

quote: Remove (don't disable) progressive disclosure controls that don't apply in the current context.
rule: Remove a disclosure control when there is nothing more to show, instead of disabling it.

quote: Use single chevrons to show or hide in place. Use double chevrons to show or hide using a pop-up menu.
rule: A single chevron opens content in place, a double chevron opens a pop-up menu; a captioned button uses the double form.

quote: Provide a visual relationship between the chevron and its associated control.
rule: Keep a chevron visibly tied to what it expands, not floating at a distance.

quote: Don't use arrow graphics that could be confused with Back, Forward, Go, or Play.
rule: Disclosure arrows must not look like Back, Forward, Go or Play, and those must not look like disclosure.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: A chevron button with a label beside it has a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Disclosure labels are in sentence case.

quote: Write the label as a phrase and use no ending punctuation.
rule: Disclosure labels are phrases with no ending punctuation.

quote: Write the label so that it describes the effect of clicking the button, and change the label when the state changes.
rule: The label says what clicking will do and changes with the state.

quote: If the surface always displays some options, commands, or details, use the following label pairs:
rule: When some items always show, label the disclosure More/Fewer options, commands, details or <things>.

quote: Show/Hide options. Use for options or a mixture of options, commands, and details.
rule: When nothing shows until opened, label it Show/Hide options, commands, details or <things>.

quote: For chevrons on a command button with an internal label, follow the standard command button guidelines.
rule: A chevron inside a captioned button follows the ordinary button label rules.

quote: If the control has a fixed label, refer to the control by its label only; don't try to describe the control.
rule: Help names a labelled disclosure control by its exact label only, without describing it.

quote: If the control has no label or it isn't fixed, refer to the control by its type: chevron, arrow, triangle, or plus/minus button.
rule: Help names an unlabelled disclosure control by its kind and place (click the triangle next to the folder), first saying how to reveal it if hidden.

quote: Don't refer to the control as a button, unless to contrast with other progressive disclosure controls that aren't buttons.
rule: Help does not call a disclosure control a button.

quote: To describe user interaction, use click.
rule: Help says click, or click to expand or collapse.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Help shows disclosure labels in bold.

quote: Support the minimum Windows effective resolution of 800x600 pixels.
rule: Every window, fixed or resizable, works on an 800x600 effective screen with room left for the taskbar.

quote: Optimize resizable window layouts for an effective resolution of 1024x768 pixels.
rule: Design resizable windows for a 1024x768 screen and have them shrink to smaller screens and still work.

quote: Be sure to test your windows in 96 dpi (100 percent) at 800x600 pixels
rule: Test every window at 100, 125 and 150 percent scaling for clipped controls, text and windows.

quote: For programs with touch and mobile use scenarios, optimize for 120 dpi.
rule: Programs used by touch are tuned for 125 percent scaling.

quote: Resizable windows no longer must show the resize glyph
rule: No resize grip is needed in the corner; the borders and resize pointers show that a window resizes.

quote: All primary and secondary windows with a standard window frame should have a Close button on the title bar.
rule: Every framed window has a title-bar Close that cancels or closes it.

quote: All primary windows and long-running modeless secondary windows (such as progress dialogs) should have a Minimize button.
rule: Main windows and long-running modeless windows such as progress windows can be minimised, and so carry an icon for the taskbar.

quote: All resizable windows should have a Maximize/Restore down button.
rule: Every resizable window can be maximised and restored; a window that gains nothing from full screen maximises only to its largest useful size.

quote: Choose a default window size appropriate for its contents.
rule: Open a window at a size that suits its content; larger is fine when the space is used well.

quote: Use resizable windows whenever practical to avoid scroll bars and truncated data.
rule: Make windows resizable wherever practical, especially those with lists or changing content.

quote: For text documents, consider a maximum line length of 65 characters
rule: Limit lines of running text to about 65 characters for easy reading.

quote: Must be entirely visible and sized to fit within the work area.
rule: A fixed-size window fits entirely inside the screen's work area.

quote: May be optimized for higher resolutions, but sized down as needed at display time to the actual screen resolution.
rule: A resizable window may be designed for large screens but shrinks to the actual screen when shown.

quote: For progressively larger window sizes, must show progressively more information.
rule: Enlarging a window always shows more; at least one part of it grows with the window.

quote: Should avoid default restored sizes that are maximized or near maximized.
rule: Do not open a restored window at or near full-screen size; pick the most useful smaller size and let people maximise.

quote: Should set a minimum window size if there is a size below which the content is no longer usable.
rule: Give a window, and each resizable part such as a column, a minimum size at which it still works.

quote: Should change the presentation if doing so makes the content usable at smaller sizes.
rule: Switch to a compact arrangement when a window becomes too small for the normal one.

quote: "centering" means to bias vertical placement slightly towards the top of the monitor
rule: Centre a window slightly high: 45 percent of the free space above it and 55 percent below.

quote: If a window is contextual, always display it near the object that it was launched from.
rule: Open a window launched from an object (a context menu, a tray icon) near that object without covering it, below and to the trailing side when opened by pointer.

quote: If displayed using a pen, when possible place it so as not to be covered by the user's hand.
rule: When opened with a pen, place the window where the writing hand will not cover it.

quote: Place progress dialogs out of the way in the lower-right corner of the active monitor.
rule: Put a progress window out of the way in the bottom trailing corner of the active monitor.

quote: If a window isn't related to the current context or user action, place it away from the current pointer location.
rule: A window that appears without the reader asking opens away from the pointer so it is not clicked by accident.

quote: If a window is a top-level application or document, always cascade its origin off the upper-left corner of the monitor.
rule: Open new app and document windows cascaded from the top leading corner of the active monitor (the default monitor if the app is not active).

quote: If a window is a top-level utility, always display it "centered" in the monitor.
rule: Open a stand-alone utility window centred on the active monitor.

quote: If a window is an owned window, initially display it "centered" on top of the owner window.
rule: Show a dialog first centred over its owner window, later where it was last placed relative to the owner if that is handier.

quote: For modeless dialogs, always display initially on top of the owner window to make them easy to find.
rule: A modeless dialog first appears over its owner window so it is easy to find.

quote: If necessary, adjust the initial location so that the entire window is visible within the target monitor.
rule: Move a window, and shrink it if needed, so it is wholly visible on its monitor.

quote: Always place owned windows on top of their owner window.
rule: A dialog always sits above its owner window, never under it.

quote: Respect users' Z order selection.
rule: Bringing a window forward raises only it and its own owner or owned windows, never other windows or other instances.

quote: If an existing window needs attention, flash the taskbar button three times to draw attention and leave it highlighted, but don't do anything else.
rule: A window that needs attention flashes its taskbar button three times and stays highlighted, without activating itself or playing a sound.

quote: Restoring a primary window should also restore all its secondary windows
rule: Restoring a main window also restores its secondary windows, placed above it.

quote: Windows displayed by user-initiated actions should take input focus, but only if the window is rendered immediately
rule: A window the reader opened takes focus once, and only if it appears within about five seconds.

quote: Windows that aren't immediately displayed or displayed by a system-initiated action shouldn't take input focus.
rule: A slow window or one the reader did not open appears on top without taking focus.

quote: When a window is redisplayed, consider displaying it in the same state as last accessed.
rule: Reopen a window on the same monitor with its last size, position and maximised state, per user, unless people would rather start over.

quote: If the current monitor configuration prevents displaying a window using its last state:
rule: If the saved place no longer fits the monitors, use the last monitor, shrink and shift the window to fit, and fall back to default placement.

quote: Support the minimum Windows effective resolution of 800x600 pixels.
rule: Every window works on an 800x600 effective screen, 640x480 for anything needed in safe mode, leaving room for the taskbar.

quote: Optimize resizable window layouts for an effective resolution of 1024x768 pixels.
rule: Design resizable windows for 1024x768 and keep them working when smaller.

quote: Be sure to test your windows in 96 dots per inch (dpi) (at 800x600 pixels), 120 dpi (at 1024x768 pixels), and 144 dpi
rule: Test windows at 100, 125 and 150 percent scaling for clipping and stretched images.

quote: For programs with touch and mobile use scenarios, optimize for 120 dpi.
rule: Programs for touch use are tuned for 125 percent scaling.

quote: If a window is an owned window, initially display it "centered" on top of the owner window.
rule: A dialog first opens centred over its owner, never beneath it.

quote: If a window is contextual, always display it near the object that it was launched from.
rule: A window opened from an object appears near it, offset so the object stays visible.

quote: Size controls and panes within a window to match their typical content.
rule: Size controls and panes so their usual content shows without truncation, scrolling or resizing; keep those for unusually large content.

quote: there should never be truncated labels, or truncated text within windows that have plenty of available space.
rule: Never truncate labels or text where there is room; widen, heighten or wrap the control instead, keeping reading lines near 65 characters.

quote: Make sure list view columns have suitable default, minimum, and maximum sizing.
rule: Give table columns default, minimum and maximum widths, with defaults that avoid truncation when there is room.

quote: The layout of a window should feel roughly balanced.
rule: A window's layout looks balanced rather than left-heavy.

quote: When a window is resizable and data is truncated, make sure larger window sizes show more data.
rule: When data is truncated, enlarging the window reveals more of it.

quote: Set a minimum window size if there is a size below which the content is no longer usable.
rule: Give windows and resizable parts a minimum size at which they still work.

quote: Use ordinary, conversational terms when you can.
rule: Write in everyday words about the reader's goal, not the technology, as if explaining over their shoulder.

quote: Be polite, supportive, and encouraging.
rule: Never let text condescend, blame or intimidate.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Say a thing once: keep the full wording in the main instruction and controls, and cut repeats from titles, extra text and buttons.

quote: Use title-style capitalization for titles, and sentence-style capitalization for all other UI elements.
rule: Use title case only for titles; everything else, buttons, menus and column headings included, is in sentence case.

quote: For feature and technology names, be conservative in capitalizing.
rule: Capitalise only the names of major features, sparingly.

quote: For feature and technology names, be consistent in capitalizing.
rule: A feature name is capitalised the same way every time it appears.

quote: Don't capitalize the names of generic user interface elements,
rule: Generic interface words (toolbar, menu, scroll bar, button, icon) stay lowercase.

quote: Don't use all capital letters for keyboard keys.
rule: Write key names as printed on the keyboard (Ctrl, Enter), lowercase for unlabelled keys, never in capitals.

quote: Indicate that a command needs additional information.
rule: A command ends in an ellipsis only when it needs more information; commands that merely show a window (Options, Properties, Advanced, Help) take none.

quote: Indicate that text is truncated.
rule: An ellipsis in data shows that text has been cut short.

quote: Indicate that a task is in progress (for example, "Searching...").
rule: An ellipsis on a label shows that work is in progress (Searching...).

quote: Don't use blue text that isn't a link, because users may assume that it is a link.
rule: Keep the link colour for links; emphasise other text with bold or a muted tone.

quote: Use bold sparingly to draw attention to text users must read.
rule: Bold only text people must not miss.

quote: Use the main instruction to explain concisely what users should do in a given window or page.
rule: Each window or page has a short main instruction stating what the reader should do, in terms of their goal.

quote: Express the main instruction in the form of an imperative direction or specific question.
rule: A main instruction is an imperative or a specific question.

quote: Don't place periods at the end of control labels or main instructions.
rule: Control labels and main instructions end without a full stop.

quote: Use one space between sentences.
rule: Separate sentences with a single space.

quote: Label every control or group of controls.
rule: Every control or group has a label; text boxes and drop-downs may use a prompt instead, and subordinate controls share their parent's label.
