quote: For all controls, select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access), most secure value by default.
rule: Every control starts at its safest, most secure value, or the likeliest where safety is not at stake.

quote: Prefer constrained controls.
rule: Prefer lists, sliders and other constrained controls to free text entry.

quote: Reconsider disabled controls.
rule: Disable a control only when people expect it and can tell why; remove it when they cannot enable it or would not expect it; otherwise keep it enabled and explain on use.

quote: Prefer specific labels over generic ones.
rule: Button labels are specific enough to understand without reading anything else.

quote: rename Cancel if it is unclear what action is being canceled, such as when there are several pending actions.
rule: Keep Cancel when its meaning is clear; rename it only when several pending actions make unclear what it cancels.

quote: When asking a question, use labels that match the question.
rule: Answer buttons match the question asked, Yes and No for a yes-or-no question.

quote: Don't use Apply buttons in dialog boxes that aren't property sheets or control panel items.
rule: Apply belongs only in properties windows, where judging changes before closing matters.

quote: Label a button Cancel if canceling returns the environment to its previous state (leaving no side effect)
rule: Call the button Cancel only if it leaves no trace; otherwise Close when the work is done or Stop while it is running.

quote: Always present command links in a set of two or more.
rule: Command links come in sets of at least two.

quote: Provide an explicit Cancel button.
rule: A set of command links has a separate Cancel button rather than a cancelling link.

quote: If providing an explicit Cancel button leaves a single command link, provide both a command link to cancel and a Cancel button.
rule: If only one command link would remain, add a link for the alternative, worded by how it differs, as well as Cancel.

section: Controls > "Don't show this <item> again" check boxes
quote: Consider using a "Don't show this <item> again" option to allow users to suppress a recurring dialog box, only if there isn't a better alternative.
rule: Offer a don't-show-again option on a recurring dialog only when neither always showing it nor removing it is better.

section: Controls > "Don't show this <item> again" check boxes
quote: Replace <item> with the specific item.
rule: The option names what it suppresses (Don't show this reminder again), or says message for a dialog in general.

section: Controls > "Don't show this <item> again" check boxes
quote: Clearly indicate when user input will be used for future default values
rule: When choices will become future defaults, say so under the option: Your selections will be used by default in the future.

section: Controls > "Don't show this <item> again" check boxes
quote: Don't select the option by default.
rule: The don't-show-again box starts cleared; a dialog meant to show once simply does so without asking.

section: Controls > "Don't show this <item> again" check boxes
quote: If users select the option and click Cancel, this option does take effect.
rule: Ticking don't-show-again and then pressing Cancel still suppresses the dialog.

quote: Don't assign an access key.
rule: Links get no access key; Tab reaches them.

quote: Don't add "Click" or "Click here" to the link text.
rule: Link text never includes Click or Click here.

quote: Use tooltips to provide labels for unlabeled controls.
rule: Unlabelled controls get a tooltip as their label; labelled ones need none for consistency's sake.

quote: Tooltips may also provide more detail for labeled toolbar buttons if doing so is helpful.
rule: A labelled toolbar button's tooltip may add detail but never just repeats or pads its label.

quote: Avoid covering the object the user is about to view or interact with.
rule: Place a tooltip beside its object, never over it, except full-name tips in lists and trees.

quote: For collections of items, avoid covering the next object that the user is likely to view or interact with.
rule: In a row of items keep tips off the next item to the trailing side; in a column, off the next one below.

quote: Use More/Fewer progressive disclosure buttons to hide advanced or rarely used options, commands, and details that users typically don't need.
rule: Hide only advanced or rarely used items behind a disclosure, never common ones, and only things worth having.

quote: If the surface always displays some options, commands, or details, use the following label pairs:
rule: When some items always show, label the disclosure More/Fewer options, commands, details or <things>.

quote: Show/Hide options. Use for options or a mixture of options, commands, and details.
rule: When nothing shows until opened, label it Show/Hide options, commands, details or <things>.

quote: Use determinate progress bars for operations that require a bounded amount of time,
rule: Use a determinate bar for any bounded operation, even when its length cannot be predicted exactly.

quote: Provide a time remaining estimate if you can do so accurately.
rule: Show time remaining only when the estimate is accurate and steady; hold it back until it is.

quote: Don't restart progress.
rule: One bar runs once to completion across all steps; it never restarts.

quote: Provide useful progress details.
rule: Add progress details only when people can act on them, and leave each up long enough to read.

quote: Don't combine a progress bar with a busy pointer.
rule: Show a progress bar or a busy pointer, never both.

quote: Use a prompt when screen space is at such a premium that using a label or instruction is undesirable,
rule: Use a prompt in a field only where there is no room for a label, as on a toolbar.

quote: It must not be crucial information that the user needs to see while using the control.
rule: A prompt only identifies the field; nothing needed while typing goes in it.

quote: The prompt text must not be confused with real text.
rule: Prompt text looks unlike entered text, cannot be edited, and disappears when the field gains focus, or on the first keystroke if the field starts focused.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation or ellipsis.
rule: Prompts end without punctuation or an ellipsis.

quote: Use notifications for events that are unrelated to the current user activity, don't require immediate user action, and users can freely ignore.
rule: Notify only about events unrelated to the current activity that need no immediate action and can be ignored.

quote: Use notifications only if you need to.
rule: Notify only when the interruption is justified.

quote: For critical events or situations that require immediate user action, use an alternative UI element (such as a modal dialog box).
rule: Critical events needing immediate action use a dialog, not a notification.

quote: Don't use notifications for feature advertisements!
rule: Never use notifications to advertise features.

quote: Assign initial input focus to the control that users are most likely to interact with first,
rule: Put initial focus on the control people will most likely use first, often the first one.

quote: Assign tabs stops to all interactive controls, including read-only edit boxes.
rule: Every interactive control, read-only text fields included, is a tab stop; a group that acts as one control (radio buttons) is a single stop.

quote: Tab order should flow from left to right, top to bottom.
rule: Tab follows reading order through all stops and wraps around in both directions; frequently used controls may come earlier.

quote: Within a tab stop, the arrow key order should flow from left to right, top to bottom,
rule: Inside a group the arrow keys move in reading order and wrap around, staying within the group.

quote: Present the commit buttons in the following order:
rule: Order commit buttons: OK or the affirmative verb or Yes, then the negative or No, then Cancel, then Apply.

quote: Don't confuse access keys with shortcut keys.
rule: Access keys (Alt plus an underlined letter) and shortcuts are separate mechanisms with separate rules.

quote: Whenever possible, assign unique access keys to all interactive controls or their labels.
rule: Give every interactive control a unique access key, except OK, Cancel and Close, which use Enter and Esc.

quote: Assign shortcut keys to the most commonly used commands.
rule: Give shortcuts only to the most used commands.

quote: Don't make a shortcut key the only way to perform a task.
rule: Every shortcut's command is also reachable by pointer and by Tab, arrows and access keys.

quote: Don't assign different meanings to well-known shortcut keys.
rule: Never give a well-known shortcut a different meaning.

quote: Don't try to assign system-wide program shortcut keys.
rule: Shortcuts work only while the app has focus; never claim system-wide ones.

quote: Never require users to click an object to determine if it is clickable.
rule: Primary controls look clickable at rest; only secondary ones may reveal it on hover.

quote: Use the hand (or "link select") pointer only for text and graphic links.
rule: The hand pointer appears only over links.

quote: Modal dialog boxes require interaction, so use them for things that users must respond to before continuing with their task.
rule: Use a modal dialog only for something that must be answered before continuing, such as critical or one-off tasks.

quote: Modeless dialog boxes don't require interaction, so use them when users need to switch between a dialog box and the owner window.
rule: Use a modeless window for frequent or ongoing tasks done alongside the main window, if a toolbar or panel will not do.

quote: Make sure the properties are necessary.
rule: Include only the properties people need.

quote: Present properties in terms of user goals instead of technology.
rule: Describe properties by the reader's goals, adding the benefit when a technology must be named.

quote: Use specific, meaningful tab labels.
rule: Tab labels name their content, not General, Advanced or Settings.

quote: Avoid General pages.
rule: Use a General page only for common, widely meaningful properties that fit no specific page.

quote: Avoid Advanced pages.
rule: Use an Advanced page only for expert, uncommon properties that fit no specific page.

quote: Don't use tabs if a property window has only a single tab and isn't extensible.
rule: A one-page settings window has no tab.

quote: Consider lightweight alternatives first, such as dialog boxes, task panes, or single pages.
rule: Try a dialog, pane or single page before a step-by-step flow.

quote: Use Next only when advancing to the next page without commitment.
rule: Next only for steps that Back or Cancel can still undo.

quote: Use Back only to correct mistakes.
rule: Progress through a flow never requires Back.

quote: When users are committing to a task, use a commit button that is a specific response to the main instruction
rule: The committing button is a verb answering the instruction (Print, Connect, Start), Finish only for settings or generic verbs.

quote: Use command links only for choices, not commitments.
rule: Command links make choices; commitment uses a specific button.

quote: When using command links, hide the Next button, but leave the Cancel button.
rule: With command links there is no Next, but Cancel stays.

quote: Use Close for Follow-Up and Completion pages.
rule: Pages after the work is done end with Close, not Cancel or Done.

quote: Don't use "wizard" in wizard names.
rule: Name a flow by its task, without the word wizard; help may still call it a wizard.

quote: Preserve user selections through navigation.
rule: Back then Next keeps everything entered.

quote: Focus on efficient decision making.
rule: Keep only pages that need decisions; merge related ones and move optional ones out of the main path.

quote: Don't use Welcome pages
rule: The first page already does something; a Before you begin page only for prerequisites or an unclear purpose.

quote: On pages in which users are asked to make choices, optimize for the most likely cases.
rule: Choice pages offer real choices preset for the likeliest case, and the first one states the flow's purpose.

quote: Use Commit pages to make it clear when users are committing to the task.
rule: The last choice page is the commit page, its Next renamed to the task.

quote: Don't use Summary pages that merely summarize the user's previous selections,
rule: No summary page unless the task is risky or people may need to review choices they might not understand.

quote: Don't use Congratulations pages that do nothing but end the wizard.
rule: No page that only says the flow is done; close on the final commit when the result is visible.

quote: Use Follow-Up pages when there are related tasks that users are likely to do as follow-up.
rule: A follow-up page only offers likely related next tasks.

quote: Use Completion pages only when the results aren't visible
rule: A completion page only when the result is not visible otherwise.

quote: Wizards that have Progress pages must use a Completion page or Follow-Up page to indicate task completion.
rule: A flow with a progress page ends on a completion or follow-up page; long work closes at commit and reports by notification.

quote: Don't give error messages when users aren't likely to perform an action or change their behavior
rule: Suppress an error message that leads to no action or concerns nothing significant.

quote: Whenever possible, propose a solution so users can fix the problem.
rule: Offer a fix that is likely to work, not improbable possibilities.

quote: Avoid vague wording, such as syntax error and illegal operation.
rule: Be specific: name the objects, places and values involved.

quote: Don't use phrasing that blames the user or implies user error.
rule: Never blame the reader; avoid you and your in errors, using the passive where the reader would be the subject.

quote: Don't use OK for error messages.
rule: An error with no action is dismissed with Close, not OK.

quote: Don't use the following words:
rule: Avoid error and failure (say problem), failed to (unable to), illegal, invalid, bad (incorrect, not valid), abort, kill, terminate (stop), catastrophic, fatal (serious).

quote: Don't accompany error messages with sound effects.
rule: Error messages play no sound.

quote: Warnings aren't errors or questions, so don't phrase routine questions as warnings.
rule: A warning describes a condition that may cause trouble later; routine questions are not warnings.

quote: Don't give warning messages when users aren't likely to perform an action or change their behavior as the result of the message.
rule: Drop a warning that leads to no action or concerns nothing significant.

quote: Don't use unnecessary confirmations.
rule: Confirm only when there is a real reason not to proceed, serious or hard-to-undo or unexpected consequences, no suitable default, or a likely mistake.

quote: Phrase confirmations as a yes or no question, and provide yes or no answers.
rule: A confirmation asks a yes-or-no question and offers Yes and No.

quote: All icons should adhere to the Aero-style icon guidelines.
rule: Draw every icon in the Aero style, replacing Windows XP-style ones.

quote: Choose standard icons based their message type, not the severity of the underlying issue:
rule: Choose the message symbol by kind (error for what has happened, warning for possible future trouble, information otherwise), not by severity.

quote: Icons must always match the main instruction or other corresponding text.
rule: A message's symbol always agrees with its text.

quote: Error icons aren't needed for non-critical user input problems.
rule: Minor input problems in a dialog need no error symbol, but errors shown in place next to a field do.

quote: Don't use warning icons to "soften" non-critical errors.
rule: An error is shown as an error, never softened into a warning.

quote: For question dialogs, use warning icons only for questions with significant consequences.
rule: A question carries a warning symbol only when its consequences are significant.

quote: Link to specific, relevant Help topics.
rule: Help links go to a specific relevant topic, never a home page, contents, search results, long FAQ or empty page.

quote: Don't put Help links on every window or page for the sake of consistency.
rule: Add help links only where they help, not everywhere for consistency.

quote: Whenever possible, phrase Help links text in terms of the primary question answered by the Help content.
rule: Word a help link as the question it answers, not Learn more about or Get help with this.

quote: Use the entire Help link for the link text,
rule: The whole help link is the clickable text, not just keywords inside it.

quote: Use complete sentences.
rule: Help links are complete sentences.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation or ellipses, except for question marks.
rule: Help links end with no punctuation except a question mark.

quote: If the Help content is online, make that clear in the link text.
rule: A help link to online content says so in its text.

quote: Use toolbars in addition to or in place of menu bars.
rule: A toolbar gives one-click access to the frequent commands; it need not mirror the menu bar, which stays the complete catalogue.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Toolbars work well for primary windows, but are usually overwhelming for secondary windows.
rule: Give toolbars only to main windows; dialogs and other secondary windows use buttons, menu buttons and links.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are there a small number of frequently used commands?
rule: A toolbar suits a small set of frequently used commands; a large set belongs in menus.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are most of the commands immediate?
rule: Choose a toolbar only when most of its commands act without asking for more input; commands that need input fit menus better.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Can most of the commands be presented directly? That is, users interact with them using a single click?
rule: Most toolbar items should work with a single click; a toolbar that is mostly menu buttons is a menu bar in disguise.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are the commands well represented by icons?
rule: Use a toolbar only when its commands have clear, self-explanatory symbols; otherwise menus with text serve better.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: most of the commands are accessible indirectly through menu buttons and split buttons, this toolbar is essentially a menu bar.
rule: A toolbar made mostly of menu and split buttons with no menu bar beside it is treated as a menu bar and follows the menu rules.

quote: Removing the menu bar means that all commands not available directly from a window or its context menus must be accessible from the toolbar
rule: When there is no menu bar, every command not reachable in the window itself or its context menus must be on the toolbar, however rarely used.

quote: hiding a menu bar should be treated the same as removing it completely when making design decisions.
rule: Design as if a hidden menu bar did not exist: never expect people to reveal it to find a command.

quote: If hiding the menu bar results in an inefficient toolbar, don't hide the menu bar!
rule: Keep the menu bar visible when moving everything onto the toolbar would make the toolbar slow to use.

quote: use this style if there are few commands or the program isn't frequently used.
rule: Label toolbar buttons with text when there are few commands or the app is used only occasionally; leave labels off when there are too many or the app is used constantly.

quote: use this style for simple utilities that have easily recognizable icons and are usually run in small windows.
rule: Large icon-only toolbars and partial-width toolbars are styles for small utilities and windows with navigation or search.

quote: Choose a suitable toolbar style based on the number of commands and their usage.
rule: Choose the toolbar's form by how many commands it has and how often they are used, and never let it take too much room from the work area.

quote: Place toolbars just above the content area, below the menu bar and address bar, if present.
rule: The toolbar sits directly above the content it acts on, below the menu bar and any address bar.

quote: If space is at a premium, save space by:
rule: When room is short, drop labels from well-known symbols, use a partial toolbar, gather related commands into a menu or split button, move rare ones to overflow, or show commands only where they apply.

quote: For the unlabeled icons toolbar pattern, use a default configuration with no more than two rows of toolbars.
rule: Start with at most two rows of icon toolbars; if more would help, let people add them through customisation.

quote: Disable individual toolbar buttons that don't apply to the current context, instead of removing them.
rule: A toolbar button that does not apply right now stays in place, disabled, so the toolbar keeps a stable layout.

quote: Disable individual toolbar buttons if clicking on them would directly result in an error.
rule: Disable a toolbar button whose click could only produce an error.

quote: For the unlabeled icons toolbar pattern, remove entire toolbars if they don't apply to the current context.
rule: A whole toolbar that serves only one mode (a debugging toolbar while running) appears only in that mode.

quote: Display toolbar buttons left aligned. The Help icon, if present, is right aligned.
rule: Toolbar buttons start at the leading edge; Help, and in the Windows 7 style the standard Options and View commands, sit at the trailing end.

quote: Don't change toolbar button labels dynamically. Doing so is confusing and unexpected. However, you can change the icon to reflect the current state.
rule: A toolbar button's label never changes while the app runs; only its symbol may change to show state.

quote: For primary toolbars, provide comprehensive commands.
rule: A toolbar standing in for the menu bar offers every command not found in the window, its context menus or the standard Cut, Copy and Paste.

quote: For supplemental toolbars, provide commands that are used the most frequently.
rule: A toolbar beside a menu bar holds only the most used commands and skips the rest, which stay in the menus.

quote: Prefer direct controls. Use toolbar buttons in the following order of preference:
rule: Prefer, in order, an icon button, a labelled icon button, a split button, and only then a menu button.

quote: Prefer immediate commands.
rule: A toolbar beside a menu bar uses the immediate form of a command (Print) and leaves the form that asks first (Print…) to the menu; a toolbar without a menu bar uses the asking form.

quote: Provide labels for frequently used commands, especially if their icons aren't well-known icons.
rule: Give the most used toolbar commands a text label, especially when their symbol is not widely known.

quote: Don't put commands in toolbar menus that are also directly on the toolbar.
rule: A command shown directly on the toolbar is not repeated in one of the toolbar's menus.

quote: Organize the commands within a toolbar into related groups.
rule: Group related toolbar commands together.

quote: Place the most frequently used groups first. Within a group, put the commands in their logical order.
rule: The most used toolbar groups come first, and commands inside a group follow their natural sequence.

quote: Use group dividers only if the commands across groups are weakly coupled.
rule: Put a separator between toolbar groups only when the groups are loosely related.

quote: Avoid placing destructive commands next to frequently used commands.
rule: Keep a destructive command (Delete) away from frequent ones such as Print, by order or grouping, or leave it to the menus and context menus.

quote: Use the overflow chevron to indicate that not all commands can be displayed.
rule: Show the overflow control only when the commands truly do not fit, not because of a poor layout.

quote: Make sure that the most frequently used commands are directly accessible from the toolbar (that is, not in overflow) in small window sizes.
rule: At small window sizes the most used commands remain directly on the toolbar, not in overflow; reorder or move rarer ones to make it so.

quote: Hide the menu bar by default if your toolbar design makes having a menu bar redundant.
rule: When the toolbar already offers everything, the menu bar may start hidden.

quote: Hide the menu bar instead of removing it completely, because menu bars are more accessible for keyboard users.
rule: Never remove the menu bar outright; at most hide it, because keyboard users reach commands through it.

quote: To restore the menu bar, provide a Menu bar checkmark option in the View (for primary toolbars) or Tools (for secondary toolbars) menu category.
rule: A hidden menu bar comes back through a Menu bar check item in the View menu (or Tools, beside a menu bar).

quote: Display the menu bar when users press the Alt key, and set input focus on the first menu category.
rule: Pressing Alt shows a hidden menu bar with focus on its first menu.

quote: After the tooltip timeout, display the tooltip or infotip.
rule: Hovering over a toolbar button shows that it is clickable and, after the usual delay, its tooltip.

quote: For mode buttons, display the control to reflect the currently selected mode. If the mode affects the behavior of mouse interaction, also change the pointer.
rule: A mode button shows which mode is on, and when the mode changes what the mouse does, the pointer changes to match.

quote: For property buttons and drop-down lists, display the control to reflect the state of the currently selected objects, if any.
rule: Toolbar property buttons and lists show the state of the current selection, apply changes to it, and do nothing when nothing is selected.

quote: On left double-click, perform the same action as a left single-click.
rule: Double-clicking a toolbar button acts like a single click, except where a double click locks a reusable tool on (as Format Painter does) until the next single click.

quote: For customizable toolbars, display the context menu for customizing the toolbar. Display the menu on right-click on mouse down, not mouse up.
rule: Right-clicking a customisable toolbar opens its customisation menu on mouse down; on other toolbars right-click does nothing.

quote: Provide icons for all toolbar controls except drop-down lists.
rule: Every toolbar control except a drop-down list has a symbol; in the Windows 7 style only commands with well-known symbols get one and the rest use text.

quote: Make sure toolbar icons are clearly visible against the toolbar background color. Always evaluate toolbar icons in context and in high-contrast mode.
rule: Check that toolbar symbols stay clearly visible on the toolbar in every theme, high contrast included.

quote: Choose icon designs that clearly communicate their purpose, especially for the most frequently used commands.
rule: Choose symbols that say what the command does, above all for the most used ones, since tooltips are too slow to search by.

quote: Choose icons that are recognizable and distinguishable, especially for the most frequently used commands.
rule: Toolbar icons have distinctive shapes and colours so they can be found at a glance.

quote: Make sure toolbar icons conform to the Aero-style icon guidelines.
rule: Toolbar icons follow the Aero icon style.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: Unlike menu bars, toolbar commands don't take access keys.
rule: Toolbar commands get no access keys, unlike menu bar items.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: File NewCtrl+N Open...Ctrl+O Close <separator> SaveCtrl+S Save as...
rule: A toolbar File menu follows the standard order: New, Open…, Close; Save, Save as…; Send to; Print…, Print preview, Page setup; Exit.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: UndoCtrl+Z RedoCtrl+Y <separator> CutCtrl+X CopyCtrl+C PasteCtrl+V
rule: A toolbar Edit menu holds Undo, Redo; Cut, Copy, Paste; Select all; Delete, Rename…; Find…, Find next, Replace…, Go to…, with their standard shortcuts.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: Print(split button) Print...Ctrl+P Print preview Page setup
rule: Print-related commands on a toolbar form one Print split button: Print…, Print preview, Page setup.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: Zoom Zoom inCtrl++ Zoom outCtrl+-
rule: A toolbar View menu holds check items for the menu bar, panes and status bar, then Zoom in and out, Text size, Full screen and Refresh.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: Tools(menu button) ... Options
rule: The app's options are opened by Options, the last item of the Tools menu.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: Help(split button, use the Help icon) <program name> helpF1 About <program name>
rule: The Help menu offers '<app> help' (F1) followed by 'About <app>'.

section: Guidelines > Standard menu and split buttons
quote: To maintain consistency between menu bars and toolbars, use the standard menu category names if doing so wouldn't be misleading.
rule: Toolbar menu buttons use the standard menu names (Edit, not Organize, when they hold the Edit commands) unless that would mislead.

quote: Palette windows use shorter title bars to minimize their screen space.
rule: Palette windows have short title bars with a Close button.

quote: Set the title bar text to the command that displayed the palette window.
rule: A palette window's title is the name of the command that opened it.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization without ending punctuation.
rule: Palette window titles are in sentence case with no closing punctuation.

quote: Provide a context menu for window management commands.
rule: Right-clicking a palette's title bar opens a menu of window commands.

quote: When possible and useful, make palette windows resizable.
rule: Make palette windows resizable when that helps, with resize pointers over the frame.

quote: When a palette window is redisplayed, display it using the same state as last accessed.
rule: A palette reopens at its last size and position, kept per user even across launches.

quote: Provide customization for toolbars consisting of two or more rows.
rule: Offer toolbar customisation when the toolbar runs to two or more rows; simple toolbars need none.

quote: Provide a good default configuration.
rule: The default toolbar works for common tasks without customising; assume most people never customise.

quote: Provide a context menu with the following commands:
rule: A customisable toolbar's context menu lists the toolbars as check items, Lock/Unlock toolbars, and Customize….

quote: Lock customizable toolbars by default, to prevent accidental changes.
rule: Customisable toolbars start locked so they are not changed by accident.

quote: For the Customize command, display an options dialog box
rule: Customize… opens a dialog for choosing which toolbars show and which commands each holds.

quote: Provide a Reset command to return to the original toolbar configuration in the Customize options dialog box.
rule: The customisation dialog has a Reset command that restores the original toolbars.

quote: Provide the ability to customize the toolbars using drag-and-drop in the following ways:
rule: Toolbars can be reordered, resized and undocked by dragging, and while customising, their contents can be added and ordered by dragging.

quote: Save all toolbar customizations, on a per-user basis.
rule: Keep every toolbar customisation for that user across launches.

quote: Use an ellipsis to indicate that a command requires more information before it can take effect. Put the ellipsis at the end of the tooltip
rule: A toolbar command that asks for more information ends its label and its tooltip with an ellipsis (Print…).

quote: If a command cannot take effect immediately, however, no ellipsis is required.
rule: A command that by nature can never act at once (Sharing settings) has no ellipsis even though it collects input.

quote: Because toolbars are constantly displayed, and space is at a premium, ellipses should be used infrequently.
rule: Toolbar commands should rarely need an ellipsis, because toolbar commands should mostly act at once.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Toolbar labels and tooltips are in sentence case (title case only in older apps that already use it).

quote: For the tooltip text, use what the label would be if the button were labeled, but include the shortcut key if there is one.
rule: An icon-only toolbar button's tooltip is the label it would have, followed by its shortcut key if it has one.

quote: Use a concise label. Use a single word if possible, four words maximum.
rule: A labelled toolbar button uses one word where possible and never more than four.

quote: Place the label to the right of the icon.
rule: The text of a labelled toolbar button sits after its symbol.

quote: Use an infotip to describe the command. Because the buttons are labeled, using a tooltip instead of an infotip would be redundant.
rule: A labelled toolbar button's hover text describes what the command does instead of repeating the label.

quote: If the list always has a value, use the current value as the label.
rule: A toolbar list that always holds a value (the font name) lets that value serve as its label.

quote: If an editable drop-down list doesn't have a value, use a prompt.
rule: An empty editable toolbar list shows a prompt in place of a label.

section: Labels > Menu buttons and split buttons
quote: Prefer verb-based menu button names. However, omit the verb if it is Create, Show, View, or Manage.
rule: Name a menu button with a verb, except where the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage (Tools, Page).

section: Labels > Menu buttons and split buttons
quote: Use a single, specific word that clearly and accurately describes the menu contents.
rule: A menu button's name is one specific word that lets people predict what its menu holds.

section: Labels > Menu buttons and split buttons
quote: While not required, provide infotip descriptions if they are helpful.
rule: Give a menu or split button a descriptive hover tip when it helps.

quote: Use menu item names that start with a verb, noun, or noun phrase.
rule: Menu items start with a verb, or are a noun such as About, Advanced, Full screen, New, Options or Properties when the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage.

quote: Use specific verbs. Avoid generic, unhelpful verbs, such as Change and Manage.
rule: Choose a specific verb for a menu item rather than Change or Manage.

quote: Use singular nouns for commands that apply to a single object, otherwise use plural nouns.
rule: A command's noun is singular when it acts on one object and plural when it acts on several.

quote: For pairs of complementary commands, choose clearly complementary names. Examples: Add, Remove; Show, Hide; Insert, Delete.
rule: Paired opposite commands get clearly opposite names (Add and Remove, Show and Hide, Insert and Delete).

quote: Choose menu item names based on user goals and tasks, not on technology.
rule: Name menu items after what people want to do, not after the technology behind them.

quote: Preferences: Don't use. Use Options instead.
rule: The app's settings open from Options (Customize for interface layout, Personalize for a summary of personal settings, Properties for one object); never Preferences, and never Settings as a menu item.

quote: Menu items that display submenus never have an ellipsis on their label.
rule: A menu item that opens a submenu never ends in an ellipsis; the submenu arrow already says more is coming.

quote: If there is only one toolbar, refer to it as the toolbar.
rule: Help text calls a lone toolbar 'the toolbar', names several by name plus 'toolbar', and calls the main one the standard toolbar.

quote: Toolbar is a single, uncapitalized word. (By contrast, menu bar is two words.)
rule: Write toolbar as one lower-case word and menu bar as two.

quote: Refer to toolbar buttons by their tooltip labels. Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include any ellipsis.
rule: Help text names a toolbar button by its tooltip text exactly, without the ellipsis.

quote: Refer to toolbar menu buttons by their labels and the word menu.
rule: Help text names a toolbar menu button by its exact label followed by 'menu' (the Page menu), and toolbar controls in general as toolbar buttons.

quote: To describe user interaction, use click for toolbar buttons and read-only drop-down lists, and enter for editable drop-down lists. Don't use choose, select, or pick.
rule: Help text says click for toolbar buttons and fixed lists and enter for editable lists, never choose, select or pick.

quote: Don't use cascading, pull-down, drop-down, or pop-up to describe menu buttons, except in programming documentation.
rule: Help text does not call menu buttons cascading, pull-down, drop-down or pop-up.

quote: Refer to unavailable items as unavailable, not as dimmed, disabled, or grayed.
rule: Help text calls items that cannot be used unavailable, not dimmed, disabled or greyed.

quote: When possible, format the labels using bold text. Otherwise, put the labels in quotation marks only if required to prevent confusion.
rule: Help text shows control labels in bold, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion.

quote: Pressing space bar is the same as clicking the control with input focus, whereas pressing Enter is the same as clicking the default command button
rule: Space activates the focused control and Enter activates the default button wherever the focus is.

quote: In this case, assign access keys to control groups rather than each individual one.
rule: When a window has too many controls for unique access keys, give the keys to groups instead of single controls.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Providing user-selectable equivalents for non-text elements (for example, alt text for graphics and captions for audio).
rule: Every picture has a text alternative and every audio has captions, describing what a graphical control does.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Providing alternatives to color (for example, icon differentiation or the use of sounds).
rule: Back up every use of colour with another cue such as a distinct symbol.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Ensuring keyboard access (for example, a tab stop for every interactive control)
rule: Give every interactive control a tab stop so everything done with the mouse can be done with the keyboard.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Ensuring that your program offers good color contrast options for users.
rule: Offer good contrast for mild impairments and colour blindness, not only the system's high contrast mode.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Ensuring that users have a way to adjust the size of text in your program's UI
rule: Let people change the size of the interface text, and support high-density displays.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: when animation is displayed, the information should be displayable in at least one non-animated presentation mode at the option of the user.
rule: Whatever an animation shows can also be shown without animation when the reader asks.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Take the time to test UI screens in high contrast mode and at various resolutions
rule: Test every screen in high contrast, at several resolutions, and from the keyboard with access keys always underlined.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Using system-wide settings (for example, System Color) rather than hardwiring settings for your particular program.
rule: Follow the system-wide settings and accessibility features the reader has turned on instead of fixing values in the app.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Preferring common controls to custom controls, because common controls have already implemented the Windows accessibility APIs.
rule: Prefer standard controls, which already work with assistive technology, over custom ones.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Documenting all accessibility options and features (for example, all keyboard shortcuts).
rule: Help lists every accessibility option and every keyboard shortcut in one place.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Creating accessible documentation in accessible formats.
rule: Help follows the same accessibility rules as the app: resizable text, text alternatives for pictures, colour only as a supplement.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Enabling programmatic access to all UI elements and text
rule: Expose every element and its text to assistive technology, and give windows, frames and pages names and descriptions.

section: Design concepts > Designing for accessibility: three fundamental practices
quote: Ensuring programmatic events are triggered by all UI activities (for example, focus events for all UI activities involving focus movement).
rule: Every change in the interface, every focus move above all, raises the event assistive technology listens for.

quote: Don't disrupt or disable activated features of the operating system or other products that are identified as accessibility features.
rule: Never interfere with or switch off accessibility features the reader has turned on in the system.

quote: Don't force users to interact with your program as the top window on the screen.
rule: Never force the app's window to stay on top, so tools such as an on-screen keyboard are never hidden.

quote: Use system colors, fonts, and common controls whenever possible.
rule: Draw with the system's colours, fonts and controls.

quote: Never rely on color alone to convey meaning.
rule: Colour only reinforces a meaning already given by text, shape, position or sound.

quote: Use alternative (alt) text infotips to describe graphics.
rule: Describe each picture in a text alternative shown on hover.

quote: Don't use text in graphics.
rule: Never put words inside pictures; text is drawn as text.

quote: Ensure that dialog boxes and windows have meaningful names
rule: Every window and dialog has a meaningful title so a screen reader user knows where they are.

quote: Respect the user's settings for visual display by always obtaining font typefaces, sizes, and colors
rule: Take typefaces, sizes, colours and element sizes from the system theme settings.

quote: Keep balloon text concise so that it is easier to read and minimizes disruption to screen readers.
rule: Keep notification balloon text short; a title alone is often enough.

quote: Never rely on sound alone to convey meaning.
rule: Sound only reinforces a meaning already given on screen.

quote: Enable users to control the volume of audio output. Use the Windows Volume Mixer for this purpose.
rule: Let people set the app's volume, through the system's volume mixer.

quote: Target your program's sound to occur in a range between 500 Hz and 3000 Hz
rule: Keep the app's sounds between 500 and 3000 Hz, or let people shift them into that range.

quote: Make UI timeout values relative to GetDoubleClickTime() instead of using absolute times.
rule: Scale every interface timeout from the system's double-click speed instead of fixed times.

quote: Don't make double-clicking and dragging the only way to perform an action.
rule: Anything done by double-clicking or dragging can also be done another way.

quote: Don't remove menu bars from your program.
rule: Keep the menu bar; if it should not show by default, hide it rather than remove it.

quote: Make Help accessible from the keyboard by providing tab stops for Help buttons and links.
rule: Help buttons and help links take keyboard focus.

quote: To improve awareness of the access key assignments in your program, you can display them at all times.
rule: When the system setting to underline access keys is on, the app shows its access keys at all times.

quote: Use progressive disclosure to hide complexity.
rule: Hide complexity behind progressive disclosure.

quote: Use icons, toolbars, and other visual aids to reduce cognitive load of reading text.
rule: Use symbols, toolbars and other visual aids so people need to read less.

quote: provide auto-complete functionality in text boxes and editable drop-down lists
rule: Fields and editable lists complete names, file names and similar choices from a known set as people type.

quote: Demonstrate difficult concepts in Help by including tutorials and animations.
rule: Help shows hard ideas with tutorials and animations, using animation only where needed.

quote: Don't use flashing or blinking text, objects, or other elements having a flash or blink frequency in the range between 2-55 Hz.
rule: Nothing on screen flashes or blinks at between 2 and 55 times a second.

quote: Limit use of animations.
rule: Use animation sparingly, and to draw attention only to what deserves an interruption.

section: Guidelines > Addressing particular impairments > Speech or language
quote: Organize and write clear, concise, easily understood text.
rule: Write short, clear sentences that bring the key information at the end: 'To begin, click OK', 'Is the next digit three?'.

quote: Prefer characters with wide widths, such as w, m, and capital letters.
rule: Choose wide letters (w, m, capitals) as access keys so the underline is easy to see.

quote: Prefer a distinctive consonant or a vowel, such as "x" in "Exit."
rule: Choose a distinctive consonant or a vowel as the access key (the x in Exit).

quote: Avoid using characters that make the underline difficult to see
rule: Avoid access keys on narrow letters (i, l), on letters with descenders (g, j, p, q, y) and next to them.

quote: Assign access keys to all menu items. No exceptions.
rule: Every menu item has an access key, without exception.

quote: For dynamic menu items (such as recently used files), assign access keys numerically.
rule: Menu items that change (recent files) take numbers as access keys.

quote: Assign unique access keys within a menu level. You can reuse access keys across different menu levels.
rule: Access keys are unique within one menu level and may repeat in other levels.

quote: For the most frequently used menu items, choose characters at the beginning of the first or second word of the label, preferably the first character.
rule: Frequent menu items take the first letter of their first or second word as access key; rarer items a distinctive consonant or a vowel.

quote: Whenever possible, assign unique access keys to all interactive controls or their labels.
rule: Every interactive control in a dialog, read-only text boxes included, has a unique access key on it or its label.

quote: OK, Cancel, and Close buttons. Enter and Esc are used for their access keys.
rule: OK, Cancel and Close get no access key since Enter and Esc serve; a button meaning OK or Cancel under another label does get one.

quote: Normally, the individual controls within a group are assigned access keys, so the group label doesn't need one.
rule: Access keys go on the controls of a group, not its label, unless keys run short; then the label takes one instead.

quote: Generic Help buttons, which are accessed with F1.
rule: A generic Help button gets no access key; F1 opens help.

quote: Link labels. There are often too many links to assign unique access keys, and link underscores hide the access key underscores.
rule: Links get no access keys; people reach them with Tab.

quote: Tab names. Tabs are cycled using Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab.
rule: Tab names get no access keys; Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab move between tabs.

quote: Browse buttons labeled "...". These can't be assigned access keys uniquely.
rule: Short browse buttons labelled with three dots get no access key.

quote: Unlabeled controls, such as spin controls, graphic command buttons, and unlabeled progressive disclosure controls.
rule: Controls without a text label (steppers, symbol buttons, bare disclosure buttons) get no access key.

quote: Non-label static text or labels for controls that aren't interactive, such as progress bars.
rule: Text that labels nothing interactive, such as a progress bar's label, gets no access key.

quote: Assign commit button access keys first to ensure that they have the standard key assignments.
rule: Give the dialog's commit buttons their standard access keys first (Y for Yes, N for No), else the first letter of the first word.

quote: For negative commit buttons (other than Cancel) phrased as a "Don't", assign the access key to the "n" in "Don't".
rule: A negative button phrased as Don't… takes the n of Don't as its access key, so every no-answer shares N.

quote: To make access keys easy to find, assign the access keys to a character that appears early in the label
rule: Put the access key on an early character of the label, ideally the first, even if a keyword comes later.

quote: Use colons at the end of external control labels.
rule: A label placed outside its control ends with a colon, which some assistive technology uses to find labels.

quote: Position labels consistently relative to the elements that they are labeling.
rule: Place every label in the same position relative to its control throughout the app.

quote: Limit alt text to 150 characters maximum. Describe the action to activate the control
rule: A text alternative stays within 150 characters and says how to activate the element and then what it does ('Click to sign in to your account').

quote: Don't use text to draw lines, boxes or other graphical symbols.
rule: Never draw lines, boxes or symbols with text characters; screen readers read each character aloud.

quote: Refer to access keys, not shortcut keys (which have a different meaning and use), mnemonic keys, or accelerators.
rule: Help text calls underlined-letter keys access keys, never shortcut keys, mnemonics or accelerators.

quote: In general, refer to a person with a kind of disability, not a disabled person. Consider the person first, not the label.
rule: Put the person first (people with disabilities, has limited dexterity, without disabilities), never the disabled, handicapped, normal or able-bodied.

quote: Is the command button used to initiate an immediate action? If not, use another control.
rule: A command button starts an action at once; anything else uses another control.

quote: The action is to navigate to another page, window, or Help topic.
rule: Going to another page, window or help topic is a link, except Back and Next in a guided flow.

quote: The command is embedded in a body of text.
rule: A command inside running text is a link.

quote: The command is secondary in nature. That is, it does not relate to the primary purpose of the window.
rule: A secondary command, unrelated to the window's main purpose, is a link or a lightweight button.

quote: The command is part of a menu or group of related links.
rule: A command that belongs with a menu or a group of related links is itself a link.

quote: The label is lengthy, consisting of five or more words, thus giving a command button an awkward appearance.
rule: A command whose label needs five or more words is a link, not a button.

quote: Would a combination of radio buttons and generic command buttons be a better choice?
rule: Offer radio buttons plus OK and Cancel instead of a row of specific buttons when there are five or more actions, when people need more information or to try the choices first, or when the choices read as options.

quote: Indicate a command that needs additional information (including confirmation) by adding an ellipsis at the end of the button label
rule: A button whose action needs more input, a confirmation included, ends its label with an ellipsis.

quote: any command button whose implicit verb is to "show another window" doesn't take an ellipsis
rule: A button whose whole job is to show another window (About, Advanced, Help, Options, Properties, Settings) has no ellipsis.

quote: When determining if a command button needs an ellipsis, don't use the need to elevate privileges as a factor.
rule: The need for administrator elevation does not decide the ellipsis; the security shield shows it.

quote: Any command button becomes the default when users tab to it.
rule: Only one button is the default; when the focus is on another button, that button becomes the default, and otherwise the designated default answers Enter.

quote: Use a menu button when a menu bar is undesirable, such as in a dialog box, toolbar, or other window
rule: A small set of related commands in a dialog or toolbar without a menu bar goes in a menu button.

quote: Use a split button to consolidate a set of variations of a command, especially when one of the commands is used most of the time.
rule: Gather variants of one command into a split button whose main part runs the most used variant.

quote: they're usually labeled browse, other, or more, and always have an ellipsis to indicate that more information is required.
rule: A browse button that opens a chooser for a field's value is labelled Browse…, Other… or More…, always with an ellipsis.

quote: after the button is clicked, its label changes to indicate that the next click will have the opposite effect:
rule: A disclosure button's label changes to say that the next click does the opposite (More options / Fewer options).

quote: Display a busy pointer if the result of clicking a command button isn't instantaneous.
rule: When a button's result is not instant, show the busy pointer so the click is not repeated.

quote: try to use the same label text and access key, and locate it in approximately the same place in each window when practical.
rule: The same button in several windows has the same label, the same access key and about the same place.

quote: For command buttons with text labels, use a minimum button width and the standard command button height.
rule: Text buttons have a minimum width and the standard height.

quote: For each window make the command buttons the same width.
rule: Buttons in one window share a width, or at most two widths.

quote: denote the relationship by placing the command button in one of three places:
rule: A button that works with another control sits to its right aligned to its top, below it aligned to its leading edge, or centred between two lists it moves items between.

quote: vertically stack them to the right of and top-aligned with the other control, or horizontally place them left-aligned under the control.
rule: Several buttons that act on one control stack beside it at its top or line up under it at its leading edge.

quote: use the above placement and disable the subordinate command button until the superior control is selected.
rule: A button that acts on a selection in another control stays disabled until something there is selected.

quote: Don't use narrow, short, or tall command buttons with text labels because they tend to look unprofessional.
rule: Text buttons keep the standard width and height, neither cramped nor padded.

quote: Avoid combining text labels and graphics on command buttons.
rule: A button has text or a symbol, not both, unless the symbol is a standard one or shows the result of the command.

quote: Don't use command buttons to set state. Use radio buttons or check boxes instead.
rule: Never use a command button to hold a setting; settings are radio buttons or checkboxes.

quote: Make the most likely command the default behavior.
rule: The main part of a split button runs the likeliest command, preferring one that needs no further input.

quote: If the most likely command is the last user selection, change the button label to the last selection.
rule: When people tend to repeat their last choice, the split button takes the label of the last choice made.

quote: Display the default command using bold text in the menu.
rule: In a split button's menu, mark which item the main part runs.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure command to be the default
rule: Every dialog has a default button, the safest and most secure choice, or else the likeliest one.

quote: Don't make a destructive action the default command button unless there is an easy way to undo the command.
rule: A destructive button is the default only if its action is easy to undo.

quote: Label every command button.
rule: Every button has a label.

quote: If the button has a graphic label only, assign its Name property to an appropriate text label.
rule: A symbol-only button carries a text name for screen readers (Previous, Next, Copy).

quote: For short browse buttons (labeled "..."), the internal label should be Browse.
rule: A three-dot browse button is named Browse for screen readers.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: Each button has a unique access key, except OK and Cancel (Enter and Esc) and three-dot browse buttons.

quote: Prefer specific labels over generic ones. Ideally users shouldn't have to read anything else to understand the label.
rule: Prefer a label that names the action (Burn CD) over OK, since people read buttons more than other text.

quote: Don't rename the Cancel button if the meaning of cancel is unambiguous.
rule: Keep Cancel as Cancel (not Don't burn CD) unless several pending actions make it unclear what it cancels.

quote: Start labels with an imperative verb and clearly describe the action that the button performs. Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: A button label starts with an imperative verb and has no closing punctuation; Advanced, Back, Details, Forward, Less, More, New, Next, No, OK, Options, Previous, Properties, Settings and Yes are accepted without a verb.

quote: Use a direct object (a noun after the verb) when the object is not apparent from context.
rule: Add the object to the verb (Add items) when the verb alone is unclear in context.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Button labels are in sentence case (Save as), title case only in older apps that already use it.

quote: Don't use now in command button labels because the immediacy of the command can be taken for granted.
rule: Leave 'now' off button labels unless it separates doing a task at once from going to start it, and use it once per flow.

quote: Don't use later in command button labels if it implies an action that won't happen.
rule: Say later only if the action really happens later; otherwise use Don't install or Cancel.

quote: Use an Advanced button only for options that are relevant to advanced users or require advanced user knowledge.
rule: Call options Advanced only when they are for expert users, not because their technology is advanced; otherwise name them specifically.

quote: For command buttons that open other windows, choose a label that uses part or all of the secondary window's title bar text.
rule: A button that opens a window uses words from that window's title (Browse opens Browse for folder).

quote: When asking a question, use labels that match the question. Don't use OK/Cancel to answer Yes/No questions.
rule: Buttons answer the question asked; a yes-or-no question is never answered with OK and Cancel.

quote: Graphic labels don't take an ellipsis.
rule: A symbol on a button never carries an ellipsis.

quote: In case of ambiguity (for example, the command label lacks a verb), decide based on the most likely user action.
rule: When it is unclear, add the ellipsis only if people usually go on to give input (More colors…), not if they mostly just look (Version information).

quote: For browse buttons, use short browse buttons (labeled "...") when there are more than two browse buttons in a window.
rule: Use three-dot browse buttons when a window has more than two, and always inside a grid.

quote: For directional buttons, use a single angle bracket and have it point in the direction where the action takes place.
rule: Directional buttons show a single angle bracket pointing the way the action goes.

quote: Display the choices available to users for customizing a program.
rule: Options opens the program's customisation choices and Properties an object's attributes; Preferences and Settings are not used as labels.

quote: Save a file or object using a specified name.
rule: Save keeps the current name and Save as… saves under a name the reader gives.

quote: Don't use. Use a specific Help link instead.
rule: Never label a button Troubleshoot; link to the specific help topic instead.

quote: In progress dialog boxes, suspend the task.
rule: Pause in a progress dialog suspends the task; Back returns to the previous page of a flow.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or ellipsis. Don't include the word button.
rule: Help text gives a button's exact label without its ellipsis or access-key mark and without the word button.

quote: To describe user interaction, use click.
rule: Help text says click for buttons.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Help text shows button labels in bold, with quotation marks only to prevent confusion.

quote: Having hierarchical data doesn't mean that you must use a tree view.
rule: Hierarchical data does not by itself call for a tree; a list is often simpler and can sort, group and change views.

quote: To use a list view, you can flatten hierarchical information using the following techniques:
rule: Flatten a shallow hierarchy: drop the root, turn the top level into list groups, tabs, a select or headings, and show lower levels in a companion view.

quote: You must use a tree view if you need to display a hierarchy of more than two levels (not including the root node).
rule: Use a tree when the hierarchy has more than two levels below the root.

quote: Do the items have auxiliary data? If so, consider using a list view in the Details view mode
rule: Items with several attributes are better shown in a table with columns than in a tree.

quote: Does the lower-level data relate to independent subtasks? If so, consider displaying the information in an associated control or in a separate window
rule: Lower-level data that serves a separate task is shown in a companion view or its own window rather than inside the tree.

quote: If your application is aimed at novice users, avoid using tree views.
rule: Avoid trees in apps meant for beginners; experienced users handle them better.

quote: Do the items have a single, natural, hierarchical categorization that's familiar to most users?
rule: A tree suits items with one natural, familiar categorisation; when people need several views or sorting, use a list.

quote: Do users need to see the lower-level data in some but not all scenarios, or some but not all of the time?
rule: A tree suits data whose lower levels are needed only some of the time.

quote: large, complex trees need to be supplemented with other access methods, such as word search, an index, or filtering.
rule: A large tree also offers search, an index or filtering.

quote: use this tree pattern when multiple selection is essential or commonly used.
rule: Use a tree with checkboxes when choosing several items is essential or common.

quote: Within a container, sort the items in a logical order.
rule: Sort each container's items by kind: names alphabetically, numbers numerically, dates chronologically.

quote: Use the Always Show Selection attribute so that users can readily determine the selected item, even when the control doesn't have input focus.
rule: The tree shows its selection even when it does not have focus.

quote: If the tree is acting as a table of contents, use the Single Expand attribute to simplify the management of the tree.
rule: A tree used as a table of contents keeps only the branch in use expanded.

quote: Avoid presenting empty trees. If a user creates a tree, initialize the tree with instructions or example items that users might need.
rule: A tree the reader builds starts with instructions or example items, never empty.

quote: Don't make the container nodes collapsible if users have no reason to collapse them.
rule: Containers that nobody needs to collapse are not collapsible.

quote: If load performance is a problem, display only the first and second level containers of the tree by default.
rule: When loading is slow, show the first two levels and load deeper branches as they are expanded.

quote: If users expand or collapse a container, make that state persist so it takes effect the next time the tree view is displayed
rule: Remember which branches each user expanded or collapsed and restore them next time, unless starting fresh suits better.

quote: If high-level containers have similar contents, consider using visual clues to differentiate them.
rule: When top-level branches hold similar contents (a mailbox and an archive), mark them so people know which branch they are in.

quote: Reconsider connecting lines.
rule: Usually leave out the lines connecting tree nodes.

quote: Consider providing double-click behavior. Double-clicking should have the same effect as selecting an item and performing its default command.
rule: Double-clicking an item selects it and runs its default command.

quote: Make double-click behavior redundant. There should always be a command button or context menu command that has the same effect.
rule: Whatever a double click does is also available as a button or a context menu command.

quote: If an item requires further explanation, provide the explanation in an infotip.
rule: An item that needs explaining explains itself in a hover tip.

quote: Provide context menus of relevant commands. Such commands include Cut, Copy, Paste, Remove or Delete, Rename, and Properties.
rule: Tree items have a context menu with the relevant commands, such as Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Rename and Properties.

quote: When disabling a tree view, also disable any associated labels and command buttons.
rule: Disabling a tree also disables its label and the buttons that act on it.

quote: Use a natural hierarchical structure that's familiar to most users.
rule: Organise the tree in a hierarchy most people already know.

quote: If you can't use such a structure, try to balance discoverability with a predictable user model that minimizes confusion.
rule: Without a familiar hierarchy, choose one whose placement people can predict, weighing that against how easily items are found.

quote: To safely improve discoverability, place an item in multiple containers when:
rule: Put an item in more than one branch only when it has no similar items to mislead by association and only a few such items exist.

quote: Use the simplest hierarchical structure that works well.
rule: Keep the hierarchy simple: the most used items in the first two levels, and needless intermediate containers removed or merged.

quote: Prefer breadth over depth. Ideally, a tree should have no more than four levels
rule: Make trees broad rather than deep, at most four levels below the root.

quote: Provide a root node if users need the ability to perform commands on the entire tree
rule: Show a root node only when people need commands for the whole tree; otherwise leave it out.

quote: optimize the tree for browsing by focusing on the most useful content.
rule: When search or an index covers everything, trim the tree to the most useful content for browsing.

quote: Display the number of selected items below the list
rule: Show the number of ticked items below a checkbox tree.

quote: If there are potentially many items and selecting or clearing all of them is likely, add Select all and Clear all command buttons.
rule: Add Select all and Clear all buttons when there are many items and choosing all or none is likely.

quote: Use mixed-state check boxes to indicate partial selection of the items in a container.
rule: A container whose items are only partly ticked shows a mixed checkbox.

quote: Choose a tree view width that avoids the need for horizontal scrolling
rule: Make the tree wide enough that most items need no horizontal scrolling when fully expanded.

quote: Include an additional 30 percent to accommodate localization.
rule: Add about 30 percent width for translated text.

quote: Choose a tree view height that eliminates unnecessary vertical scrolling.
rule: Make the tree tall enough to avoid needless vertical scrolling, using spare room in the window.

quote: If users benefit from making the tree view larger, make the tree view and its parent window resizable.
rule: When a bigger tree helps, let the window and the tree in it be resized.

quote: All tree views need labels. Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, ending with a colon, and using static text.
rule: Every tree has a label: a word or phrase, not a sentence, ending in a colon.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: The tree's label carries a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Tree labels are in sentence case.

quote: Position the label above the control, and align the label with the left edge of the control.
rule: The tree's label sits above it, aligned with its leading edge.

quote: For multiple-selection tree views, write the label so that it's clear that multiple selection is possible.
rule: A tree allowing several selections says so in its label, unless its checkboxes already show it.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Tree item text is in sentence case.

quote: If you need to add instructional text about a tree view, add it above the label. Use complete sentences with ending punctuation.
rule: Instructions for a tree go above its label as complete, punctuated sentences in sentence case.

quote: Supplemental explanations that are helpful but not necessary should be kept short.
rule: Short optional explanations go in parentheses between the label and colon, or below the tree.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or colon.
rule: Help text names a tree by its exact label without colon or access-key mark, adding 'list' or 'hierarchical list' when needed.

quote: For tree items, use the exact item text, including its capitalization.
rule: Help text gives tree items with their exact text.

quote: Refer to tree views as tree views only in programming and other technical documentation.
rule: Outside technical documents, call a tree a list or hierarchical list, never a tree.

quote: To describe user interaction, use select for the data, and expand and collapse for the plus and minus buttons.
rule: Help text says select for items and expand or collapse for branches.

quote: When possible, format the label and tree items using bold text.
rule: Help text shows the tree's label and items in bold.

quote: Use the exact label text including its capitalization, and include the words check box. Don't include the access key underscore.
rule: Help text names a checkbox in a tree by its exact label plus 'check box', and says select and clear.

quote: severity is a factor in determining if a standard icon should be used at all.
rule: Show a status symbol only on critical messages (risk of losing data, money, access, privacy or much time, unexpected consequences, or no easy fix); ordinary errors and warnings have none.

quote: minor user input errors are usually displayed without an error icon.
rule: A dialog about a minor input problem carries no error symbol.

quote: The mere potential for data loss alone is insufficient to call for a warning icon.
rule: Use a warning symbol only when the outcome is unexpected and hard to fix and the reader has a real decision to make; routine questions and confirmations get none.

quote: Choose standard icons based their message type, not the severity of the underlying issue:
rule: Pick the symbol by message type: error for a problem that has happened, warning for one that may happen, information for useful facts.

quote: If an issue straddles different message types, focus on the most important aspect that users need to act on.
rule: When an issue fits several types, choose the type by what the reader must act on: an error if it blocks them, a warning if they can go on.

quote: Icons must always match the main instruction or other corresponding text.
rule: The symbol always matches the meaning and tone of the message text beside it; if not, change or remove it.

quote: Choose the standard icon size based on the context:
rule: Use 32 pixel status icons in dialog content and error pages and 16 pixels elsewhere.

quote: Use error icons only when an error or a problem has occurred:
rule: Use the error symbol only for a problem that has happened: in dialogs only for critical errors, always for errors shown in place, never in banners or tips.

quote: Use for critical errors only. (for action failures.)
rule: A notification may carry the error symbol only to report a critical failure of an action.

quote: For task dialogs, don't use error footnote icons. Error icons must be presented in the content area only.
rule: An error symbol appears in the dialog's main area, never in its footnote.

quote: Use warning icons only when a condition might cause a problem in the future:
rule: Use the warning symbol only for a condition that may cause a future problem: on every warning dialog, on in-place warnings and on warning notifications.

quote: Don't use warning icons to "soften" non-critical errors.
rule: Never show an error with a warning symbol to make it seem milder.

quote: For question dialogs, use warning icons only for questions with significant consequences.
rule: A question carries a warning symbol only when its answer has significant consequences.

quote: use a warning icon either in the content area or the footnote area, but not both.
rule: A risky consequence may be flagged with a warning symbol in the footnote, but the warning symbol appears in the footnote or the main area, not both.

quote: Use information icons only when the context isn't obviously presenting information:
rule: No information symbol in dialogs, notifications, tips or plain in-window text; only a banner, which could otherwise be missed, takes one.

quote: For task dialogs, don't use information footnote icons.
rule: A dialog's footnote carries no information symbol.

quote: Use the question mark icon only for Help entry points.
rule: The question-mark symbol means help and appears only where help opens.

quote: Don't use the question mark icon to ask questions.
rule: Never mark a question with the question-mark symbol; the question wording is enough.

quote: Content viewers often benefit from having the option to show content full screen.
rule: Apps for viewing content offer to show it full screen.

quote: Use standard window frames.
rule: Windows use the system's standard frame; only immersive full-screen apps may hide it.

quote: If a custom frame is appropriate, choose a design that is lightweight and doesn't draw too much attention to itself.
rule: A custom frame, where allowed, is light and unobtrusive.

quote: Don't add controls to a window frame. Put the controls within the window instead.
rule: Controls go inside the window, never in its frame or title bar.

quote: Have a modal full screen command in the menu bar or toolbar. When the user clicks the command, show the command in its selected state.
rule: Full screen is a toggle command in the menus or toolbar that shows as selected while full screen is on and cleared when off.

quote: Use F11 for the full screen shortcut key.
rule: F11 enters and leaves full screen.

quote: If there is a toolbar and full screen mode is commonly used, also have a graphic toolbar button with a Full screen tooltip.
rule: When full screen is used often, the toolbar has a Full screen button too.

quote: If not already assigned, Esc can also be used for this purpose.
rule: Esc also leaves full screen when it has no other use.

quote: Consider using glass strategically in small regions touching the window frame without text.
rule: Use translucent glass in small text-free regions touching the frame.

quote: Don't use glass in situations where a plain window background would be more attractive or easier to use.
rule: Avoid glass where a plain background reads better.

section: Design concepts > Elements of keyboard navigation
quote: any command button or command link with input focus is also always the default button
rule: When keyboard focus is on a command button, Enter presses that button; otherwise Enter presses the dialog's default button, which is shown as such.

section: Design concepts > Elements of keyboard navigation
quote: The spacebar activates the control with input focus, whereas the Enter key activates the default button. Pressing the Esc key cancels or closes the window.
rule: Space operates the focused control, Enter the default button, and Esc cancels or closes the window.

section: Design concepts > Elements of keyboard navigation
quote: For external labels, the access key is assigned to the label, and if invoked, navigates to the next control in tab order.
rule: A control without its own text (list, tree) takes its access key from its label, and the key moves focus to that control.

section: Design concepts > Elements of keyboard navigation
quote: If the assignment isn't unique, the associated control is given input focus.
rule: A unique access key operates its control at once; a shared one only moves focus, and pressing it again moves to the next control with that key.

section: Design concepts > Keyboard support for accessibility and advanced users
quote: all interactive user interface (UI) elements must be keyboard accessible
rule: Every interactive element can be reached and operated from the keyboard, the frequent ones directly with one key combination.

quote: They have effect throughout the entire program, but have no effect if they don't apply.
rule: A shortcut works wherever the app has focus and silently does nothing when its command does not apply at the moment.

quote: the best solution to this problem is not to steal input focus. Instead, either flash the program's taskbar button or display a notification
rule: A window that appears without the reader asking never takes keyboard focus; draw attention by flashing the taskbar button or with a notification instead.

quote: Don't use the Shift key to modify commands in menus or dialog boxes.
rule: Never let holding Shift change what a menu item or dialog button does (as XP turned Yes to All into No to All); it cannot be discovered.

quote: Don't disable a control with input focus.
rule: Before disabling the control that has keyboard focus, move focus to another control so the window keeps receiving keys.
