quote: If a window is displayed out of context, potentially surprising users, you may need to prevent significant unintended consequences
rule: A window that appears unprompted has no default button and no access keys, and its initial focus is not on a commit button, so stray typing cannot trigger it.

quote: Always show the input focus indicator.
rule: Keep the focus indicator visible, hiding it only where it distracts (a large icon view) and bringing it back on any key press.

quote: Assign initial input focus to the control that users are most likely to interact with first
rule: When a window opens, put focus on the control people most likely use first, usually the first one; if it is not, rethink the layout.

quote: Assign tabs stops to all interactive controls, including read-only edit boxes.
rule: Every interactive control, read-only text boxes included, is a Tab stop, except that a group acting as one control (radio buttons) is a single stop whose arrows cycle inside it.

quote: Tab order should follow reading order, which generally flows from left to right, top to bottom.
rule: Tab visits controls in reading order, wrapping around in both directions; a heavily used control may come earlier.

quote: Within a tab stop, the arrow key order should flow from left to right, top to bottom,
rule: Inside a group, arrow keys move in reading order and wrap around at both ends.

quote: Present the commit buttons in the following order:
rule: Order dialog buttons as OK or the specific affirmative (or Yes), then the specific negative (or No), then Cancel, then Apply if present.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure command button or command link to be the default.
rule: Make the safest, most secure response the default button; only when nothing is at risk choose the likeliest one.

quote: Keyboard navigation shouldn't change control values or result in an error message.
rule: Tabbing through a window never changes values or raises errors: start fields with valid values and validate only what was changed.

quote: Whenever possible, assign access keys for commonly used commands according to the following table.
rule: Give common commands their standard access keys (A About, C Close, x Exit, a Save as, a Select all, r Properties, Y Yes, N No and so on from the table).

quote: Prefer characters with wide widths, such as w, m, and capital letters.
rule: When choosing an access key letter, prefer wide letters such as w, m or a capital so the underline is easy to see.

quote: Prefer a distinctive consonant or a vowel, such as "x" in "Exit."
rule: When the first letter is taken, prefer a distinctive consonant or a vowel of the label, as x in Exit.

quote: Avoid using characters that make the underline difficult to see,
rule: Avoid access keys on narrow letters (i, l), letters with descenders (g, j, p, q, y) and letters beside a descender, whose underline is hard to see.

quote: When assigning access keys in wizard pages, remember to reserve "B" for Back and "N" for Next.
rule: In a step-by-step flow keep B for Back and N for Next free of other controls.

quote: When assigning access keys in property pages, remember to reserve "A" for Apply, if used.
rule: In a settings window with Apply, keep A for Apply.

quote: Assign access keys to all menu items. No exceptions.
rule: Every menu and every menu item has an access key, without exception.

quote: For dynamic menu items (such as recently used files), assign access keys numerically.
rule: Number the access keys of generated menu items such as recent files (1, 2, 3…).

quote: Assign unique access keys within a menu level.
rule: Access keys are unique within one menu level; the same letter may recur in a different menu or submenu.

quote: For the most frequently used menu items, choose characters at the beginning of the first or second word of the label, preferably the first character.
rule: Frequent menu items take the first letter of their first or second word; rarer ones a distinctive consonant or a vowel.

quote: Whenever possible, assign unique access keys to all interactive controls or their labels.
rule: Give each interactive control (read-only text boxes included) or its label a unique access key, but none to OK, Cancel and Close, which Enter and Esc reach; a button meaning OK or Cancel under another name does get one.

quote: Group labels. Normally, the individual controls within a group are assigned access keys, so the group label doesn't need one.
rule: Put access keys on the controls of a group, not its title, unless letters run short; then the title gets it instead.

quote: Generic Help buttons, which are accessed with F1.
rule: A plain Help button has no access key; F1 reaches it.

quote: Link labels. There are often too many links to assign unique access keys, and link underscores hide the access key underscores.
rule: Links have no access keys; they are reached with Tab.

quote: Tab names. Tabs are cycled using Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab.
rule: Tab names have no access keys; Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab move between tabs.

quote: Browse buttons labeled "...". These can't be assigned access keys uniquely.
rule: A browse button labelled only with an ellipsis has no access key.

quote: Unlabeled controls, such as spin controls, graphic command buttons, and unlabeled progressive disclosure controls.
rule: Controls with no text of their own (spin buttons, symbol-only buttons, bare disclosure arrows) have no access key.

quote: Non-label static text or labels for controls that aren't interactive,
rule: Static text and labels of non-interactive controls such as progress bars have no access key.

quote: Assign commit button access keys first to ensure that they have the standard key assignments.
rule: Assign the commit buttons' access keys before the others so they get the standard letters (Y for Yes, N for No), else the first letter of the first word.

quote: For negative commit buttons (other than Cancel) phrased as a "Don't", assign the access key to the "n" in "Don't".
rule: A negative button phrased Don't … takes n (the n of Don't) as its access key, so every No and Don't share it.

quote: To make access keys easy to find, assign the access keys to a character that appears early in the label,
rule: Put the access key on an early letter of the label, ideally the first, even when a later word is the keyword.

quote: Assign at most 20 access keys, so you have a few unassigned characters to facilitate localization.
rule: Use no more than about 20 access keys in one dialog, leaving letters free for translations.

quote: If there are too many interactive controls to assign unique access keys, you may assign non-unique access keys
rule: Share an access key between controls only when they would otherwise be hard to reach and it does not clash with a frequently used control.

quote: Don't use menu bars in dialog boxes.
rule: A dialog has no menu bar.

quote: Assign shortcut keys to the most commonly used commands.
rule: Give shortcuts only to the most used commands; rarely used programs and features need none.

quote: Don't make a shortcut key the only way to perform a task.
rule: Every shortcut's command can also be reached with the pointer and with Tab, arrows and access keys.

quote: Don't assign different meanings to well-known shortcut keys.
rule: Never give a well-known shortcut a new meaning (Ctrl+F for Forward instead of Find).

quote: Don't try to assign system-wide program shortcut keys.
rule: An app's shortcuts act only while it has focus; do not register system-wide hotkeys.

quote: Document all shortcut keys.
rule: Show every shortcut in its menu item and the toolbar tooltip and list all of them in one help page; context menus show none.

quote: If your program assigns many shortcut keys, provide the ability to customize the assignments.
rule: An app with many shortcuts lets people reassign them.

quote: For well-known shortcut keys, use the standard assignments.
rule: Standard commands use their standard shortcuts.

quote: For non-standard key assignments, use the following recommended shortcut keys for more frequently used commands.
rule: New shortcuts for frequent commands come from the unclaimed set: Ctrl+G, J, K, L, M, Q, R, T, Ctrl+digit, F7–F9, F12, Shift+F2–F5/F7–F9/F11/F12, Alt+function key except F4.

quote: Use the following recommended shortcut keys for less frequently used commands.
rule: Less frequent commands may use Ctrl+function key (not F4 or F6) or Ctrl+Shift+letter or digit.

quote: Make frequently used shortcut keys easy to remember:
rule: Frequent shortcuts use a letter, not a digit or function key, taken from the first or most memorable letter of the command's name.

quote: Use function keys for commands that have a small-scale effect,
rule: Bind commands acting on the selected object to function keys (F2 renames the selection).

quote: Use Ctrl key combinations for commands that have a large-scale effect,
rule: Bind commands acting on the whole document to Ctrl combinations (Ctrl+S saves).

quote: Use Shift key combinations for commands that extend or complement the actions of the standard shortcut key.
rule: Adding Shift to a shortcut gives its reverse or extended variant (Shift+F1 for context help after F1).

quote: When using arrow keys to move or resize an item, use Ctrl+arrow keys for more granular control.
rule: Where arrow keys move or resize an item, Ctrl+arrow does it in finer steps.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't distinguish between key locations.
rule: Left and right modifier keys and keypad keys do the same as their twins; never give only one side a meaning.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use the Windows logo modifier key for program shortcut keys.
rule: No app shortcut uses the Windows logo key, even in combinations the system does not use yet.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use the Application key as a shortcut key modifier.
rule: Never use the Application (menu) key as a shortcut modifier; use Ctrl, Alt and Shift.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use shortcut keys used by Windows for program shortcut keys.
rule: Do not bind any shortcut the operating system already uses.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use Alt+alphanumeric key combinations for shortcut keys.
rule: Never bind Alt+letter or Alt+digit as a shortcut; those belong to access keys.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use the following characters for shortcut keys: @ $ {} [] \ ~ | ^ ' < >.
rule: Do not build shortcuts on @ $ { } [ ] \ ~ | ^ ' < >, which need different keys on different keyboard layouts.

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Avoid complex key combinations,
rule: Frequent commands get simple shortcuts: not three keys at once (Ctrl+Alt+Space) nor keys far apart (Ctrl+F5).

section: Guidelines > Choosing shortcut keys (what not to do)
quote: Don't use Ctrl+Alt combinations,
rule: Never bind Ctrl+Alt combinations, which some keyboard layouts read as AltGr for typing characters.

quote: For links, use Shift+click to navigate using a new window and Ctrl+click to navigate using a new tab.
rule: Shift-click on a link opens it in a new window; Ctrl-click opens it in a new tab.

quote: Use on-screen keyboard to refer to a keyboard representation on the screen that the user touches to input characters.
rule: Call a touch keyboard drawn on the screen the on-screen keyboard.

quote: Present modifier keys in the following order: Windows logo, Application, Ctrl, Alt, Shift.
rule: Write key combinations modifiers first, in the order Windows logo, Application, Ctrl, Alt, Shift, with a keypad qualifier just before its key.

quote: Don't use all capital letters for keyboard keys.
rule: Write key names as on the keyboard (Tab, Enter, Page Up, spacebar), letters in capitals (Alt+W), punctuation and arrows spelled out (Ctrl+plus sign, left arrow), never in all capitals or as glyphs.

quote: Indicate key combinations with a plus sign, without spaces.
rule: Join the keys of a combination with a plus sign and no spaces (Ctrl+A, Shift+F5), not hyphens.

quote: To show a key combination that includes punctuation that requires use of the Shift key, such as the question mark, add Shift to the combination
rule: For a shifted punctuation key, write Shift and the shifted character or its name (Ctrl+Shift+?, Ctrl+Shift+comma), never the unshifted key.

quote: At first mention, use the and key with the key name if necessary for clarity
rule: Say the F1 key at first mention when needed for clarity, then just F1.

quote: Everywhere else use keyboard shortcut, especially in user documentation.
rule: In text for readers call both kinds keyboard shortcuts; never accelerator, mnemonic or hot key.

quote: Use press, not depress, strike, hit, or type, when pressing and immediately releasing a key initiates an action
rule: Tell people to press a key that acts at once, not depress, strike, hit or type it.

quote: Use type, not enter, to direct users to type text.
rule: Tell people to type text, not enter it.

quote: Use in situations when press might be confusing, such as when referring to a type of key such as the arrow keys or function keys.
rule: Say use the arrow keys, not press them, where press could suggest pressing all at once.

quote: Use hold when pressing and holding a key, such as a modifier key.
rule: Say hold for a key kept down, such as a modifier.

quote: Don't use press as a synonym for click.
rule: Never say press for a pointer click.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Notifications are for asynchronous information only.
rule: Information that directly results from what the reader just did appears in the app (inline, dialog), never as a desktop notification.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: If so, display the information in your application's status bar or other status area.
rule: Status that matters only while the app is in use goes in its status area, not in a notification.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the information rapidly changing, continuous, real-time information?
rule: Never use notifications for continuously changing information such as progress, quotes or scores.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are users likely to change their behavior or avoid inconvenience as the result of receiving the information?
rule: Notify only when the reader may act differently because of it; otherwise show nothing or write it to a status window or log.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the information critical? Is immediate action required?
rule: Critical information needing immediate action uses something that cannot be ignored, such as a modal dialog; if the app is in the background, flash its taskbar button three times and leave it highlighted.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are the primary target users IT professionals? If so, use an alternative feedback mechanism such as log file entries or e-mail messages.
rule: Non-critical information meant for administrators goes to a log or e-mail, not a notification.

section: Design concepts > User flow must be maintained
quote: Using sound when displaying a notification.
rule: Show notifications silently; a sound breaks the reader's concentration.

section: Design concepts > Notifications must be ignorable
quote: If you are using notifications correctly and they don't require immediate user action, then having users choose to ignore them is by design.
rule: Never try to make a notification impossible to ignore; if it must not be ignored, it should not be a notification.

quote: Don't use notifications for feature advertisements!
rule: Never use a notification to advertise a feature; make the feature easier to find where it is needed, or leave it to be discovered.

quote: Select the notification pattern based on its usage.
rule: Decide what kind of notification it is (action success, action failure, system event, optional task, FYI) and follow that kind's rules for when and how often.

quote: Don't use any notifications during the initial Windows experience.
rule: Assume notifications are not seen in a new system's first hours; first-run information must not depend on them.

quote: Don't notify of successful operations, except in the following circumstances:
rule: Notify a success only for security operations, after recent failures, or when it finished unexpectedly early, late or in an unusual way.

quote: In other circumstances, either give no feedback for success or give feedback "on demand."
rule: Otherwise give no success feedback, or show it on demand: a tray icon shown or changed while the work runs and removed when it ends.

quote: don't give a notification if users can continue to work normally or are unlikely to do anything different as the result of the notification.
rule: Skip an informational notification when the reader would carry on just the same after seeing it.

quote: You can notify users of information of questionable relevance if it is optional and users opt in.
rule: Marginally relevant notifications (a contact came online) only when the reader opted in to them.

quote: use complete notifications for a single event.
rule: One event gives one complete notification, not a series of partial ones.

quote: Display a notification based on its design pattern:
rule: Notify a success or failure when the background task ends, a system event when it happens while the reader is active (removing it as soon as the problem is fixed), an optional task when the reader is active.

quote: if the problem might correct itself within seconds, delay the failure notification for an appropriate amount of time.
rule: Hold back a failure notification for a problem that may fix itself within seconds, and say nothing if it does.

quote: use the real-time option so that stale notifications aren't queued
rule: A success or informational notification that cannot be shown right away is dropped, not shown late.

quote: don't create the potential for notification storms by staggering events tied to well-known events such as user logon.
rule: Do not fire notifications at logon or other moments when everything else does; delay them by some minutes.

quote: The number of times to display a notification is based on its design pattern:
rule: Show success, failure and informational notifications once; a problem the reader must solve once when it starts and then at most daily; an optional task once a day, three times at most.

quote: For optional user tasks, don't try to pester users into submission by constantly displaying notifications.
rule: Never repeat a notification to wear the reader down; a required task gets a modal dialog at once instead.

quote: Don't assume that users will see your notifications.
rule: Assume any notification may go unseen (reader absorbed, away, in a full-screen app, or notifications turned off).

quote: If users must eventually take some kind of action, use progressive escalation
rule: When something must eventually be dealt with, move from a quiet signal to a notification to a modal dialog as it becomes urgent.

quote: Make notifications clickable when:
rule: Make a notification clickable when the reader should act or may want more detail; the click opens a window for that.

quote: Always display a window when users click to perform an action. Don't have clicking perform an action directly.
rule: Clicking a notification opens a window for the action; it never performs the action itself.

quote: Clicking to show more information should always show more information.
rule: A click for more information must show more than the notification said, not rephrase it.

quote: For the action failure pattern, use the standard error icon.
rule: A failure notification carries the error symbol.

quote: For the non-critical system event patterns, use the standard warning icon.
rule: A system-event notification carries the warning symbol.

quote: For other patterns, use icons showing objects that relate to or suggest the subject
rule: Other notifications carry a symbol of their subject (a shield for security, a battery for power).

quote: Use icons based on your application or company branding if your target users will recognize them and there is no better alternative.
rule: A branded icon is acceptable when people recognise it and nothing fits better.

quote: consider using icons with a progressively more emphatic appearance as the situation becomes more urgent.
rule: Make the icon look more emphatic as an escalating situation grows urgent.

quote: Don't use the standard information icon.
rule: Never put the information symbol on a notification; being information goes without saying.

quote: Consider using large icons (32x32 pixels) when:
rule: Use a 32-pixel icon when the picture is grasped faster than the text.

quote: Remove queued notifications when they are no longer relevant.
rule: Withdraw a waiting notification once it no longer applies.

quote: display an icon temporarily during the asynchronous task or event that caused the notification.
rule: An app without a permanent tray icon shows one only during the task or event behind its notification.

quote: Use title text that briefly summarizes the most important information you need to communicate to users in clear, plain, concise, specific language.
rule: A notification title states the most important point plainly and specifically so it is grasped at a glance.

quote: Use text fragments or complete sentences without ending punctuation.
rule: Notification titles are fragments or sentences without ending punctuation.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Notification titles are in sentence case.

quote: Use no more than 48 characters (in English) to accommodate localization.
rule: Keep an English notification title within 48 characters so translations fit the 63-character limit.

quote: Use body text that gives a description (without repeating the information in the title)
rule: The body describes the event without repeating the title, may add details, and says what action is available.

quote: Use complete sentences with ending punctuation.
rule: Notification body text is complete sentences with full stops.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Notification body text is in sentence case.

quote: Use no more than 200 characters (in English) to accommodate localization.
rule: Keep an English notification body within 200 characters so translations fit the 255-character limit.

quote: Include essential information in the body text, such as specific object names.
rule: Name the specific object (user, file, address) in the body so the reader needn't open anything to learn it.

quote: Put double quotation marks around object names.
rule: Put object names in double quotation marks, except names always in title case, names after a colon, or names obvious from context.

quote: If you must truncate object names to a fixed maximum size to accommodate localization, use an ellipsis to indicate truncation.
rule: A shortened object name shows an ellipsis where it was cut.

quote: Use the following phrasing if the notification is actionable:
rule: An actionable notification ends its body with Click to <do something>. or Click for more information.

quote: Don't say that the user "must" perform an action in a notification.
rule: A notification never says the reader must do something; what must be done is not a notification.

quote: If users should perform an action, make the importance clear.
rule: When the reader should act, the notification makes plain how much it matters.

quote: describe problems in plain language.
rule: Describe problems in plain, non-technical words.

quote: Describe the event in a way that is relevant to the target users.
rule: Phrase the event in terms of the reader's goals rather than the technology.

quote: Use the exact title text, including its capitalization.
rule: Help text quotes a notification's title exactly, capitalisation included.

quote: Refer to the component as a notification, not as a balloon or an alert.
rule: Call it a notification, never a balloon or an alert.

quote: To describe user interaction, use click.
rule: Say click for interacting with a notification.

quote: When possible, format the title text using bold text.
rule: Show the notification title in bold in help text, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion.

quote: Refer to the notification area as the notification area, not the system tray.
rule: Call the area beside the clock the notification area, not the system tray.

quote: Is the link used to navigate to another page, window, or Help topic; display a definition; initiate a command; or choose an option?
rule: Use a link only to go somewhere, open a help topic, show a definition, start a light command or change an option.

quote: Would a command button be a better choice?
rule: Use a button, not a link, for an immediate action central to the window, one that opens a window to gather input, a short non-inline label among other buttons, a destructive or irreversible action, or a commitment in a flow.

quote: Display a busy pointer if the result of clicking a link isn't instantaneous.
rule: If following a link takes noticeable time, show the busy pointer so people do not click again.

quote: Use the theme or link system colors for visited and unvisited links.
rule: Draw links in the system's link colours.

quote: For navigation links, use different colors for visited and unvisited links.
rule: Navigation links show whether they were visited, remembering it only while the app runs.

quote: For other types of links, don't use the visited link color.
rule: Command and other non-navigation links never show a visited state.

quote: Don't color text that isn't a link because users may assume that it is a link.
rule: Do not colour ordinary text in the link style; use bold or a grey shade for emphasis, unless every link is underlined or in a standard link place.

quote: Use background colors that contrast with the link colors.
rule: Place links on a background with enough contrast against the link colour.

quote: For links that are necessary to perform a primary task, provide visual clues so that users can recognize links by visual inspection alone.
rule: A link needed for a main task is recognisable without hovering or clicking (underline, symbol or a standard link place).

quote: Don't underline text that isn't a link because users may assume that it is a link.
rule: Underline only links; use italics for emphasis.

quote: When printing, don't print underlines or link colors.
rule: Print links as plain text, without underline or link colour.

quote: Use the arrow icon only for command links.
rule: Reserve the arrow symbol for command links; ordinary links never use it.

quote: Place the icon to the left of the text.
rule: A link's icon leads into its text, on the left.

quote: Make the result of clicking the icon the same as clicking the text.
rule: Clicking a link's icon does exactly what clicking its text does.

quote: Don't use graphics-only links.
rule: Do not make a picture alone a link; it is hard to recognise and any text in it cannot be translated.

quote: Make sure navigation links don't require commitment.
rule: Following a navigation link commits nothing; Back or Cancel always returns to where the reader was.

quote: Link to specific content rather than general content.
rule: Link to the relevant section, not the start of a document.

quote: Use a link only if the linked material is relevant, helpful, and not redundant.
rule: Add a navigation link only where the target is relevant, helpful and not repeated.

quote: If a link navigates to an external site, put the URL in the infotip
rule: A link to an outside website shows its address in its tooltip.

quote: Link only the first occurrence of the link text.
rule: Link a term only at its first occurrence, except a link in an instruction or a repeat far from the first.

quote: Use task links for commands that aren't destructive or are easily reversible.
rule: A link may start only a harmless or easily reversed command, such as one opening a dialog; Delete file is a button.

quote: Group related navigation and task links into menus.
rule: Gather related links into a list in a standard navigation or command place rather than scattering them.

quote: For selection-dependent menus, remove menu links that don't apply.
rule: In a set of links that depend on the selection, leave out the ones that do not apply instead of disabling them.

quote: For selection-independent menus, disable menu links that don't apply.
rule: In a set of links that do not depend on the selection, disable a link that cannot act now rather than removing it.

quote: provide the explanation in either a supplemental explanation in a separate text control or an infotip, but not both.
rule: Explain a link either in text beside it or in its tooltip, never both, in complete sentences.

quote: Don't provide an infotip that is merely a restatement of the link text.
rule: A link's tooltip never just repeats the link text.

quote: Don't assign an access key. Links are accessed using the Tab key.
rule: Links have no access key; Tab reaches them.

quote: Users should be able to accurately predict the result of a link from its link text and optional infotip.
rule: Link text says specifically what clicking it does or where it goes, using as many words as that takes.

quote: Preserve the capitalization and punctuation of the text.
rule: An inline link keeps the capitalisation and punctuation of the sentence around it.

quote: Don't include ending punctuation in the link unless the text is a question.
rule: The sentence's ending punctuation is outside the link unless the linked text is a question.

quote: Link on the most relevant part of the text and choose link text that is large enough to be easy to click.
rule: Link the most meaningful words, enough of them to be an easy target (newsgroup, not Go).

quote: Avoid putting two different inline links next to each other.
rule: Never place two different inline links side by side, where they read as one.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: A standalone link is in sentence case, with no ending punctuation unless it is a question, and all of its text is the link.

quote: Use links that are clearly differentiated from the other links on the screen.
rule: Links on one screen are worded so their targets are clearly different (How to know if antivirus software is installed / Install antivirus software).

quote: Don't add Click or Click here to the link text.
rule: Never put click or click here in link text; it says nothing, least of all to a screen reader.

quote: Start the link with a noun and clearly describe where clicking the link will go.
rule: A navigation link names its destination, starting with a noun, without ending punctuation or verbs like View, Open or Go to.

quote: Present a navigation link as a URL if it navigates to a Web page and you expect the target users to recall the URL
rule: Show a web link as its address when people should remember and type it, keeping the address short.

quote: If the link includes a URL to a Web site starting with "www," omit the https:// protocol name and use lowercase text.
rule: Write a shown web address in lowercase without https:// or www (example.com).

quote: Start the link with an imperative verb and clearly describe the task that the link performs.
rule: A task link starts with an imperative verb naming the task, without ending punctuation.

quote: End the link with an ellipsis if the command needs additional information (including a confirmation) for successful completion.
rule: A task link ends in an ellipsis when it needs more input or a confirmation before it completes, but not merely because it shows a window.

quote: If necessary, end a task link with "now" to distinguish it from a navigation link.
rule: Add now to a task link that acts at once when a similar link only navigates (Download files now / Download files).

quote: Use the exact link text, including its capitalization, but don't include the ellipsis.
rule: Help text quotes a link's exact text and capitalisation, dropping any ellipsis.

quote: To describe user interaction, use click.
rule: Say click for following a link.

quote: When possible, format the link text using bold text.
rule: Show link text in bold in help text, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion.

quote: the best way to design for color is to start by designing without color, using either wireframes or monochrome, and then add color later.
rule: Design a screen in monochrome first and add colour afterwards, so nothing depends on colour alone.

quote: Overall dependency on color using the Gray scale filter.
rule: Check screens in grey scale and with protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia simulation to find meaning carried by colour.

quote: All the screen elements should be legible and appear as expected, even immediately after mode changes.
rule: Test in every theme including both high-contrast ones, and switch themes while running: everything stays legible right after the change.

quote: Never use color as a primary method of communication,
rule: Colour only reinforces meaning carried by text, shape or position; it is never the primary carrier.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: choose colors by selecting the appropriate theme color or system color.
rule: Take colours from the theme or system colours.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Choose theme and system colors based on their purpose.
rule: Pick a colour by its purpose, not by how it currently looks.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Match foreground colors with their associated background colors.
rule: Pair each foreground colour only with its matching background.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Don't mix color types.
rule: Never mix theme, system and fixed colours in one foreground-background pair.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Prefer to derive the color from a theme or system color over hardwiring its value.
rule: Derive an extra colour from a theme colour rather than hard-coding it.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Handle high-contrast mode as a special case.
rule: Any colour that does not come from the system is replaced in high-contrast mode.

section: Guidelines > Using theme and system colors
quote: Handle theme changes.
rule: Custom-drawn windows and controls redraw in the new colours when the system theme changes while the app runs.

quote: make sure any other use of color is compatible with the following use of color within Windows.
rule: Other uses of colour agree with Windows's meanings: red error or stop, yellow warning, green go or safe, blue commit and links, purple visited.

quote: To avoid communicating the previous meanings, choose colors have high mid to low saturation and high or low luminosity.
rule: Use paler or darker, less saturated shades when a colour should not carry a status meaning.

quote: assign color to data to help users differentiate it.
rule: Colour data to tell it apart only where it helps, knowing people read equal colours as equal meaning.

quote: Assign colors by default that are easy to distinguish.
rule: Default data colours are far apart in hue and contrast with the background.

quote: Allow users to customize these color assignments
rule: Let people change the colours given to data, as a scheme when many are coordinated.

quote: Allow users to label these color assignments.
rule: Let people name the colours they assign to data.

quote: Unlike UI colors, data should not change when the system colors change.
rule: Colours given to data stay the same when the system theme changes.

quote: Refer to UI elements by their names, not by their colors.
rule: Help and messages name an element, never describe it by its colour.

section: Design concepts > Serif and sans serif
quote: For UI text, the need for a clean appearance and the lower resolution of computer monitors makes sans serif typefaces the better choice.
rule: Use a sans serif face for interface text.

quote: If you want to make sure users read your text, use dark text on a light background.
rule: Use dark text on a light background for text that must be read.

quote: Read-only, non-selectable. Text with an arrow pointer.
rule: Text shows what it allows: editable text sits in a box with the I-beam pointer and a caret, read-only selectable text has the I-beam, other text the arrow.

section: Design concepts > Accessibility and the system font, sizes, and colors
quote: Respect the user's settings by always using the system font, sizes, and colors.
rule: Draw all text in the system font, sizes and colours.

section: Design concepts > Accessibility and the system font, sizes, and colors
quote: A simple way to ensure that your program respects users' settings is to test using a different font size and a high contrast color scheme.
rule: Test with a larger text size and a high-contrast scheme: all text resizes and shows correctly.

quote: The following fonts and colors are defaults for Windows Vista and Windows 7.
rule: Use Windows's default fonts and colours for each text pattern (9 pt Segoe UI text, 12 pt blue main instruction).

quote: Choose fonts and optimize window layouts based on the UI technology and the target version of Windows:
rule: Pick the font by UI technology and target Windows version.

quote: For Segoe UI, use a 9 point font size or larger.
rule: Do not set Segoe UI smaller than 9 points.

quote: Always match system text colors with their corresponding background colors.
rule: Pair each system text colour with its own background colour.

quote: Always create new fonts based on proportional-sized variations of the system font.
rule: Derive bold, italic, larger and smaller fonts proportionally from the system font.

quote: Display large blocks of read-only text (such as license terms) against a light background instead of a gray background.
rule: Long read-only text such as licence terms must not look disabled; never give it the disabled-looking grey background.

quote: Consider a maximum line length of 65 characters
rule: Limit lines of running text to about 65 characters.

quote: Bold. Use in control labels to make the text easier to parse. Use sparingly to draw attention to text users must read.
rule: Keep UI text plain; use bold sparingly, for text people must read, since overuse weakens it.

quote: Italic. Use to refer to text literally instead of quotation marks.
rule: Mark text quoted literally with italics instead of quotation marks, and use italics sparingly for emphasis.

quote: Bold italic. Don't use.
rule: Never use bold italic.

quote: Underline. Don't use except for links.
rule: Underline only links; emphasise with italics.

quote: Not all fonts support bold and italic, so they should never be crucial to understanding the text.
rule: Meaning never depends on bold or italic alone, since not every font has them.

quote: set defined, contiguous values (such as volume or brightness) or a range of discrete values (such as screen resolution settings).
rule: Use a slider for a continuous quantity people judge relatively (volume, brightness) or an ordered range of discrete values.

quote: Does the setting seem like a relative quantity? If not, use radio buttons, or a drop-down or single-selection list.
rule: A setting that is not a relative quantity uses radio buttons or a list instead of a slider.

quote: Is the setting an exact, known numeric value? If so, use a numeric text boxes.
rule: An exact, known number is typed into a number field, not set with a slider.

quote: Would a user benefit from instant feedback on the effect of setting changes? If so, use a slider.
rule: Use a slider where seeing the effect while changing it helps, as with hue or brightness.

quote: Does the setting have a range of four or more values? If not, use radio buttons.
rule: Fewer than four values are radio buttons, not a slider.

quote: Can the user change the value? Sliders are for user interaction.
rule: A value people can never change is shown as read-only text, not a slider.

quote: If a slider or a numeric text box is possible, use a numeric text box if:
rule: Between a slider and a number field, choose the field when space is tight or people prefer the keyboard, the slider when instant feedback helps.

quote: Use a natural orientation.
rule: Orient a slider as the real quantity is usually shown (vertical for temperature).

quote: Orient the slider to reflect the culture of your users.
rule: A horizontal slider runs low to high in reading direction: left to right, mirrored for right-to-left languages.

quote: Size the control so that a user can easily set the desired value.
rule: Make a slider long enough that every discrete value can be picked easily with the pointer.

quote: Consider using a non-linear scale if the range of values is large and users will likely select values at one end of the range.
rule: Give a slider over a very wide range a non-linear scale when people mostly pick from one end (1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, 1 month).

quote: Whenever practical, give immediate feedback while or after a user makes a selection.
rule: Show the effect of a slider's value while or right after it moves (the volume slider beeps).

quote: Use labels to show the range of values.
rule: Label a slider's ends, except a vertical one whose top reads Maximum, High or More.

quote: Use tick marks when users need to know the approximate value of the setting.
rule: Add tick marks when people need the approximate value.

quote: Use tick marks and a value label when users need to know the exact value of the setting they choose.
rule: Add tick marks and a value label when people need the exact value, and always a value label when units are needed to understand it.

quote: For horizontally-oriented sliders, place tick marks under the slider.
rule: Draw tick marks below a horizontal slider and on the trailing side of a vertical one.

quote: Place the value label completely under the slider control so that the relationship is clear.
rule: Put the value label wholly beneath the slider.

quote: When disabling a slider, also disable any associated labels.
rule: A disabled slider disables its labels too.

quote: Don't use both a slider and a numeric text box for the same setting.
rule: Use one control per setting, a slider or a number field, and both only when instant feedback and exact entry are both needed.

quote: Don't use a slider as a progress indicator.
rule: Never show progress with a slider.

quote: Don't change the size of the slider indicator from the default size.
rule: Keep the slider thumb at its default size.

quote: Don't label every tick mark.
rule: Do not put a label on every tick mark.

quote: Use a static text label ending with a colon, or a group box label with no ending punctuation.
rule: Label a slider with text ending in a colon, or with a group title without ending punctuation.

quote: Assign a unique access key to each label.
rule: Each slider label has a unique access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Slider labels are in sentence case.

quote: Position the slider label either to the left of the slider, or above and aligned with the left edge of the slider
rule: Put a slider's label before it on the leading side, or above it aligned with its leading edge.

quote: Use only word, if possible, for each label.
rule: Each slider end label is one word where possible.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation.
rule: Slider end labels have no ending punctuation.

quote: Make sure these labels are descriptive and parallel. Examples: Maximum/Minimum, More/Less, Low/High, Soft/Loud.
rule: The two end labels describe the range as a matching pair (Low/High, Soft/Loud).

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Slider end labels are in sentence case.

quote: Don't assign access keys.
rule: Slider end labels have no access keys.

quote: Center the text relative to the control and include the units (such as pixels).
rule: A slider's value label includes the units (800 by 600 pixels), centred under the control.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, and include the word slider.
rule: Help names a slider by its exact label plus the word slider, without colon or access-key mark.

quote: To describe user interaction, use move.
rule: Say move for changing a slider.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Show a slider's label in bold in help text, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion.

quote: use the prominent main instruction to explain concisely what to do in the window or page.
rule: Give each window's text a job: a title that identifies the window, one main instruction saying what to do, supplemental text only to add context, labels on controls and short explanations under choices that need them.

quote: Professional writers and editors should work with software developers on UI text as an integral part of the design process.
rule: Draft and review the interface wording together with the design, early, because trouble explaining a screen usually points at a design problem.

section: Design concepts > A design model for UI text
quote: don't assume that users carefully read the text in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order.
rule: Write a window's text to be scanned: people look at the controls and commit buttons first, read static text only when they think they must, and stop as soon as they know what to do.

section: Design concepts > Use the inverted pyramid
quote: Get right to the point with the essential information, let users stop reading at any time they choose, and use a Help link
rule: Order text by importance: the essential point first (in the main instruction), helpful detail next, and the rest behind a Help link, so stopping anywhere still leaves the reader informed.

quote: Remove redundant text.
rule: Check titles, main instructions, supplemental text, content, command links and commit buttons for repeated wording; keep the full words in the main instruction and the controls and cut the repeats elsewhere.

quote: Avoid large blocks of UI text.
rule: Break text into short sentences and paragraphs and move useful but non-essential detail behind a Help link instead of showing large blocks of text.

quote: Choose object names and labels that clearly communicate and differentiate what the object does.
rule: Name objects so each one's purpose and its difference from its siblings is obvious, e.g. distinguish two similar entries by product name rather than giving both the same generic name.

quote: If you want to make sure that users read specific text related to an action, place it on an interactive control.
rule: Text people must notice about an action goes on the control itself (e.g. a Format disk button rather than OK under a paragraph about formatting).

quote: Use one space between sentences. Not two.
rule: Separate sentences with a single space.

section: Guidelines > Text fonts, sizes, and colors
quote: Use blue text only for links and main instructions.
rule: Reserve blue text for links and main instructions.

section: Guidelines > Text fonts, sizes, and colors
quote: Use green text only for URLs in search results.
rule: Use green text only for web addresses in search results.

quote: Use bold sparingly to draw attention to text users must read.
rule: Use bold rarely, only for text that must be read (such as option labels among their explanations), since overuse cancels its effect.

quote: With labeled data, use bold to emphasize whichever is more important for the data as a whole.
rule: In label-and-value pairs, embolden the labels for generic data (numbers, dates) and the values for self-explanatory data, or grey out the less important part.

quote: Not all fonts support bold, so it should never be crucial to understanding the text.
rule: No meaning may depend on bold or italic being displayed; the text must make sense in plain type.

quote: Use to refer to text literally. Don't use quotation marks for this purpose.
rule: When mentioning a word as a word (the terms document and file), set it in italic rather than quotation marks.

quote: Use for prompts in text boxes and editable drop-down lists.
rule: Set prompt (placeholder) text in italic.

quote: Use sparingly to emphasize specific words to aid in comprehension.
rule: Italicise a word for emphasis only occasionally, where it helps comprehension.

quote: Bold italic
rule: Never combine bold and italic in interface text.

quote: Don't use for emphasis. Use italic instead.
rule: Underline only links; never underline text for emphasis.

quote: Don't place at the end of control labels, main instructions, or Help links.
rule: Control labels, main instructions and Help links have no closing full stop.

quote: Place at the end of supplemental instructions, supplemental explanations, or any other static text that forms a complete sentence.
rule: Supplemental instructions, explanations and any other static text written as a complete sentence end with a full stop.

quote: Place at the end of all questions.
rule: Every question ends with a question mark, whatever kind of text it is (labels and main instructions included).

quote: In business applications, avoid.
rule: Avoid exclamation marks; at most a download-complete Done! or a New! marker on web content.

quote: In a list of three or more items, always put a comma after the next-to-last item in the list.
rule: Use the serial comma in lists of three or more items (red, green, and blue).

quote: Use colons at the end of external control labels.
rule: A label placed outside its control ends with a colon, which assistive technology also uses to find labels.

quote: Use a colon to introduce a list of items.
rule: Introduce a list with a colon.

quote: Ellipses mean incompleteness.
rule: Use an ellipsis only for incompleteness: a command that needs more input before acting (not every command that opens a window), text cut short, and a label for work in progress (Searching...).

quote: Strive for layouts and default window sizes that eliminate or reduce the amount of truncated text.
rule: Truncated text in a window with space to spare means the layout or default size is wrong; size them so text is not cut short.

quote: Don't make ellipses interactive.
rule: Never make a truncation ellipsis clickable; let people widen the control or use a disclosure control to see the rest.

quote: Put window titles and control labels in quotation marks only if required to prevent confusion and you can't format using bold instead.
rule: Quote a window title or control label in text only when needed to avoid confusion and bold is not available.

quote: For quotation marks, prefer double-quotation marks (" "); avoid single-quotation marks.
rule: Quote names with double quotation marks, not single ones (delete "Sparky's cat folder"?).

quote: Use title-style capitalization for titles, sentence-style capitalization for all other UI elements.
rule: Capitalise titles in title case and every other piece of interface text (buttons, menus, labels, column headings) in sentence case; legacy apps may keep title case on buttons, menus and headings to avoid mixing.

quote: For feature and technology names, be conservative in capitalizing.
rule: Capitalise only the names of major components (Analysis Services) and leave common terms (cubes, dimensions) lowercase.

quote: For feature and technology names, be consistent in capitalizing.
rule: A feature name is capitalised the same way every time it appears, on one screen and across the app.

quote: Don't capitalize the names of generic user interface elements, such as toolbar, menu, scroll bar, button, and icon.
rule: Write generic interface element names (toolbar, menu, scroll bar, button, icon) in lowercase.

quote: Don't use all capital letters for keyboard keys.
rule: Write key names as printed on the keyboard (Tab, Enter, Page Up, Ctrl+Alt+Del) or lowercase when unlabelled (spacebar), never in capitals.

quote: Don't use all capital letters for emphasis.
rule: Never write words in capitals for emphasis; a warning gets a warning symbol and a clear explanation, not the word WARNING.

quote: Don't hard-code the format of dates and times.
rule: Format dates and times with the reader's locale and their own format choices, never a fixed pattern.

quote: Use the long date format for scenarios that benefit from having additional information.
rule: Show the long date form where the extra detail helps (task deadlines) and the short form where space is tight.

quote: choose a width appropriate for the longest valid data.
rule: Make controls with variable content (lists, trees) wide enough for the longest valid entry.

quote: Include space enough in the UI surface for an additional 30 percent
rule: Leave room for translated text to grow by about a third (up to double for short strings).

quote: Don't compose strings from substrings at run time.
rule: Never assemble sentences from fragments at run time; keep each message a complete translatable sentence.

quote: Don't use a subordinate control, the values it contains, or its units label to create a sentence or phrase.
rule: Never make a control, its values or its units part of a sentence (such as a text box inside a check box label), since word order differs between languages.

quote: Don't make only part of a sentence a link
rule: Link text is a complete sentence on its own, not a few words inside one (glossary terms excepted).

quote: Choose the title bar text based on the type of window:
rule: Title a document window "document name - program name", any other main window with the program name, a dialog with the command or feature it came from (not its purpose), and a guided flow with its name.

quote: you can hide the title bar caption and icon to avoid redundancy.
rule: A main window that shows its name prominently inside may hide the title bar caption, but still sets a proper window title for the system.

quote: For dialog boxes, don't include the words "dialog" or "progress" in the titles.
rule: Leave the words dialog and progress out of window titles.

quote: Use the main instruction to explain concisely what users should do in a given window or page.
rule: The main instruction says what to do in the window in terms of the reader's goal, not the mechanics of the controls.

quote: Express the main instruction in the form of an imperative direction or specific question.
rule: Phrase the main instruction as a command or a specific question, not a program name; errors, warnings and confirmations may differ.

quote: Use specific verbs whenever possible.
rule: Prefer specific verbs (connect, save, install) to generic ones (configure, manage, set); never drop the verb in errors and warnings.

quote: Don't feel obliged to use main instruction text if adding it would only be redundant or obvious from the context of the UI.
rule: Leave out the main instruction when the window's context already makes it obvious.

quote: Be concise use only a single, complete sentence.
rule: Keep the main instruction to one complete sentence with only the essential information; anything more goes in a supplemental instruction.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write the main instruction in sentence case.

quote: Don't include final periods if the instruction is a statement.
rule: A main instruction that is a statement has no full stop; one that is a question ends with a question mark.

quote: For progress dialogs, use a gerund phrase briefly explaining the operation in progress,
rule: A progress window's main instruction is a short -ing phrase ending in an ellipsis that says what is happening (Printing your pictures...).

quote: use a supplemental instruction to present additional information helpful to understanding or using the window or page,
rule: Add a supplemental instruction only to explain why the window appeared, help decide how to act, or define a term.

quote: Don't repeat the main instruction with slightly different wording.
rule: Omit the supplemental instruction rather than restate the main instruction in other words; say it all in the main instruction when it fits.

quote: Use complete sentences and sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write supplemental instructions as complete sentences in sentence case.

quote: Label every control or group of controls.
rule: Every control or group of controls has a label; only text boxes and drop-downs may use a prompt, disclosure controls and subordinate controls (spin boxes) borrow or need none.

quote: Omit control labels that restate the main instruction.
rule: Drop a control label that only repeats the main instruction; the main instruction then carries the access key.

quote: Drop-down lists, list boxes, list views, progress bars, sliders, text boxes, and tree views are labeled above, flush left, or to the left.
rule: Check boxes, buttons, links and tabs carry their own label; lists, sliders, progress bars, text boxes and trees are labelled above or to the left, aligned with the control.

quote: Assign a unique access key for each interactive control except for links.
rule: Give every interactive control except links its own access key.

quote: Keep labels brief.
rule: Keep labels short, though a word or two more is fine when it makes a separate explanation unnecessary.

quote: Prefer specific labels over generic ones.
rule: Use labels specific enough to be understood without reading anything else, e.g. a commit button named for its action rather than OK.

quote: For lists of labels, such as radio buttons, use parallel phrasing,
rule: Phrase the labels of a set of options in parallel and at similar length.

quote: For lists of labels, focus the label text on the differences among the options.
rule: Option labels state what differs between options; words they all share move to the group label.

quote: In general, prefer positive phrasing.
rule: Phrase labels positively (notify rather than do not notify); Don't show this message again is the accepted exception.

quote: Omit instructional verbs that apply to all controls of the given type.
rule: Leave out instructions that apply to every control of a kind (type a name, click here); label what is unique to the control.

quote: If an option is strongly recommended, add "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Mark a strongly advised option with (recommended), and consider (optional) or (advanced) for options that are optional or for experts.

quote: You may specify units (seconds, connections, and so on) in parentheses after the label.
rule: State the unit of a value in parentheses after its label, e.g. Size (MB).

quote: Use supplemental explanations when controls require more information than can be conveyed by their label.
rule: Add a short explanation under a control only when its label cannot carry what is needed.

quote: use bold in the control labels to make the text easier to scan
rule: Make option labels bold when they have explanations beneath them.

quote: Adding a supplemental explanation to one control in a group doesn't mean that you have to provide explanations for all the other controls
rule: Explain only the options that need it; never add explanations that merely restate a label for the sake of consistency.

quote: If a supplemental explanation follows a command link, write the supplemental text in second person.
rule: Write an explanation under a command link in the second person (This will create settings that you can transfer...).

quote: Use complete sentences and ending punctuation.
rule: Write supplemental explanations as complete sentences with ending punctuation.

quote: For windows used to perform one specific task, use a specific label instead that starts with a verb (example: Print).
rule: OK commits a window that is not task-specific (such as a properties window) and closes it; a single-task window uses a verb label (Print), and a window with nothing to change uses Close.

quote: Use Yes and No buttons only to respond to yes or no questions. Never use OK and Cancel for yes or no questions.
rule: Yes and No answer only a yes-or-no question, always as a pair and never replaced by OK/Cancel; prefer specific responses unless they would be long or awkward, or when No would be unclear.

quote: Use when all pending changes or actions can be discarded and any side effects can be undone.
rule: Label a button Cancel only when it discards all pending changes and leaves no side effect; use Close when changes cannot be discarded and Stop for work that can be halted, switching from Cancel once undoing is no longer possible.

quote: Use when changes or side effects can't be discarded. Use Close instead of Cancel for primary windows.
rule: Close shuts a window keeping whatever has happened; use it for main windows and windows where nothing can be changed (Alt+F4, Ctrl+F4).

quote: Use when work in progress and any side effects can't or won't be discarded, typically with progress bars or animations.
rule: Stop halts a running task and closes the window, keeping work already done; Esc triggers it.

quote: Provide an Apply button only if the property sheet has settings (at least one) with effects that users can evaluate
rule: Offer Apply only in an owner settings window whose changes can be seen and judged before closing; otherwise leave Apply out rather than disabling it.

quote: Use only in wizards and multi-step tasks to advance to the next step without commitment.
rule: Next only moves forward in a multi-step task without committing, and Back can always undo it.

quote: the use of Finish is discouraged because there is usually a better, more specific commit button:
rule: End a multi-step task with a specific verb button that answers the main instruction (Print, Connect), Close when the task already ran, and Finish only when the verb would be generic (Save, Select) or for changing settings.

quote: Don't use. Done as a command is grammatically incorrect.
rule: Never label a button Done.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does your program need to display a notification? If so, you must use a notification area icon.
rule: On Windows, desktop notifications come from the app's notification-area (tray) icon.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the status useful and relevant?
rule: Show status only when people are likely to watch it and act differently because of it; otherwise drop it or write it to a log.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the status critical? Is immediate action required?
rule: Status that is critical or needs immediate action goes in something that cannot be overlooked, such as a dialog, not a tray icon.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the feature already have "desktop presence"?
rule: An app with a window shows its status in the window (status bar, taskbar button); a tray icon is only for features with no window, and stays focused on notifications and status.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: The notification area isn't intended for quick program or command access.
rule: Do not use a tray icon to launch the app or reach its commands quickly; launching belongs to the Start menu and pinned taskbar buttons.

quote: never view desktop areas as ways to promote your program or its Brand.
rule: Use the shared desktop areas (taskbar, tray, desktop) only for their purpose and never to promote the app or its brand.

section: Design concepts > Keeping users in control
quote: Don't turn everything on by default and expect users to turn features off.
rule: Turn only the important features on by default and let people enable the rest, rather than switching everything on.

quote: Don't display an icon that doesn't provide useful, relevant, dynamic status just because a feature might need to display a notification in the future.
rule: A tray icon that exists only to send notifications appears with the notification and goes away afterwards; do not keep one around in case a notification comes.

quote: Provide only one notification area icon per component.
rule: Show at most one tray icon per app or component.

quote: Use an icon with 16x16, 20x20, and 24x24 pixel versions.
rule: Supply the tray icon at 16, 20 and 24 pixels.

quote: Remove the icon based on its notification design pattern:
rule: Remove a notification-only tray icon when its notification goes (success, FYI), when the problem is fixed (failure, system event), or when the optional task is done.

quote: For the temporary event status pattern, display the icon while the event is happening.
rule: A tray icon for a temporary event (printing, installing updates) shows only while the event lasts.

quote: display the icon when the program, feature, or process is running and the icon is relevant
rule: Otherwise show the tray icon while its program or process runs and the icon is relevant, unless the reader turned the icon off.

quote: Don't display icons meant for administrators to standard users.
rule: Do not show administrator-only status to ordinary users; record it in the system log instead.

quote: Display windows launched from notification area icons near the notification area.
rule: Open windows launched from the tray icon next to the tray.

quote: Choose the icon based on its design pattern:
rule: Use the program icon for a minimised app and a feature icon for status or notification icons.

quote: Choose an easily recognizable icon design.
rule: Draw tray icons as simple symbols with distinctive outlines in the Aero style.

quote: Use icon variations or overlays to indicate status or status changes.
rule: Show status on the icon itself: variations for amounts or strengths, otherwise one standard overlay (warning, error, disabled, offline) in a consistent corner.

quote: Avoid swaths of pure red, yellow, and green in your base icons.
rule: Keep red, yellow and green out of a tray icon's base design so those colours keep meaning status.

quote: use icons with a progressively more emphatic appearance as the situation becomes more urgent.
rule: As a situation grows more urgent, make its status icon progressively more emphatic.

quote: Don't change status too frequently.
rule: Keep tray status changes infrequent and subtle; when the underlying state changes rapidly, show only the high-level state.

quote: Don't use long-running animations to show continuous activities.
rule: Do not animate a tray icon for ongoing activity; a brief subtle animation is fine only during an important temporary transition.

quote: Don't flash the icon.
rule: Never flash a tray icon: use a dialog for what needs immediate attention and a notification for what needs attention.

quote: Don't disable notification area icons.
rule: Never show a tray icon disabled: remove it when it does not apply, or show it enabled with a disabled overlay when it can turn the feature back on.

quote: The following click events should occur on mouse up, not mouse down.
rule: Tray icon clicks act when the button is released, not when pressed.

quote: Display a tooltip or infotip that indicates what the icon represents.
rule: Hovering over the tray icon shows a tip naming what it represents.

quote: Display whatever users most likely want to see
rule: A left click on the tray icon always shows something: the most useful settings and tasks, a status flyout or the main window, so the icon never seems dead.

quote: Display a context menu only if the other choices don't apply
rule: Show the menu on left click only when nothing else fits, and then the same menu as right click, with the default command in bold.

quote: Prefer using a popup window over a dialog box
rule: Prefer a light popup to a dialog from the tray: the most common settings only, applied at once, closed by a click outside.

quote: Display small windows near the associated icon.
rule: Open small windows next to the tray icon; large ones may be centred on the main monitor.

quote: Perform the default command on the context menu.
rule: Double-clicking the tray icon runs the menu's default command (usually opening the main window), or does what a single click does when there is none.

quote: Display the context menu, with the default command in bold.
rule: Right-clicking the tray icon opens its menu with the default command in bold.

quote: Display the context menu near its associated icon, but away from the taskbar.
rule: Open the tray menu next to its icon, extending away from the taskbar.

quote: The context menu may include the following items, as appropriate, in the listed order
rule: Order the tray menu: Open (default, bold) and Run; a separator; ticked toggles for suspend, minimise-to-tray, notification opt-ins and Display icon in notification area; a separator; Options and Exit.

quote: Remove rather than disable any context menu items that don't apply.
rule: Leave out tray menu items that do not apply instead of disabling them.

quote: be specific about what is being opened, run, suspended, and resumed.
rule: Name what an Open, Run, Suspend or Resume command acts on (Open Windows Defender, Run a quick scan).

quote: Use Suspend/Resume running background tasks, Enable/Disable for everything else.
rule: Use Suspend and Resume for running background work and Enable and Disable for anything else.

quote: Use check marks to indicate state.
rule: Show the current state with a tick beside an always-enabled item; never disable items or reword labels to show state.

quote: All background tasks must have a Suspend/Resume command.
rule: Every background task offers Suspend and Resume from its tray menu; a suspended task restarts when resumed or when the system restarts.

quote: Allow users to opt into or out of different notification types
rule: Let people choose which kinds of notification they get; FYI notifications stay off until someone opts in.

quote: Clearing the "Display icon in notification area" option removes the icon from the notification area
rule: Offer a Display icon in notification area toggle that hides only the icon, not the program; it comes back only from the app's Options, never by itself after a restart.

quote: The Exit command quits the program for the current Windows session and removes the icon.
rule: Exit in the tray menu quits the program for this session and removes the icon; there is no Exit if the program cannot stop, and quitting for good is set in Options.

quote: Don't have an About command.
rule: A tray menu has no About command unless the app has no window of its own.

quote: Use rich tooltips only to make the information easier to understand.
rule: Use a rich tooltip (with pictures or layout) only when it makes the information clearer, not as decoration; otherwise a plain tooltip.

quote: Use a concise presentation.
rule: Keep rich tooltips compact, with a 32 by 32 pixel icon.

quote: Don't put controls or elements that appear interactive in a rich tooltip.
rule: Nothing in a tooltip may look clickable: no controls, no link-coloured or underlined text.

quote: When appropriate, present notification area flyouts with three sections:
rule: A tray flyout has a summary matching the icon's tip, the common tasks, and at most one each of related links (a frequent setting, the full settings, a specific help topic).

quote: Options not accessible directly from the context menu must be in the Options dialog box.
rule: Every tray-app option not on the tray menu is in its Options window.

quote: The Options dialog box may include the following items
rule: The Options window may hold Enable [feature] (clearing it quits the program for good) and Display icon in notification area (the only way to bring a hidden icon back).

quote: Disable features that are rarely used, or potentially annoying or distracting. Let users opt in to such features.
rule: Leave rarely used or potentially annoying features off until people opt in.

section: Guidelines > Minimizing programs to the notification area
quote: Minimizing program windows to the notification area is no longer recommended for Windows 7.
rule: Minimise to the tray only for a single-instance, long-running app whose icon shows status and sends notifications, and only when the reader opts in; otherwise use the taskbar.

section: Guidelines > Minimizing programs to the notification area
quote: Use the Minimize button on the application's title bar, not the Close button.
rule: Minimising to the tray happens through the Minimize button, never through Close.

quote: The icon infotip should have one of the following formats
rule: The tray icon's tip gives the feature or program name, optionally with a status summary or a list of status lines.

quote: Focus on the most useful information. Display other information on left single-click.
rule: Keep the tip to the most useful facts in short fragments; further detail goes in what the click shows.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation unless tip is phrased as a complete sentence.
rule: End a tip with punctuation only when it is a complete sentence.

quote: Omit unnecessary words. Don't include the software version or other extraneous information.
rule: Leave version numbers and other extraneous facts out of the tip.

quote: Don't explain how to interact with the icon.
rule: Never tell people in the tip how to use the icon (right-click to...).

quote: Refer to the notification area as the notification area, not the system tray.
rule: In help text call it the notification area, not the system tray.

quote: Refer to the icon using the exact name given in its infotip, including its capitalization, followed by icon.
rule: In help, name a tray icon exactly as its tip does, in bold, followed by icon, mentioning the notification area at first reference (click the Network icon in the notification area).

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Are you using Help to fix a bad UI?
rule: Improve the interface before writing help; a simple program with clear labels, errors and dialogs may need no separate help at all.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is your application intended for developers, IT professionals, or other software experts?
rule: Match help to the audience: motivated and expert users (developers, administrators) get reference and in-depth conceptual help, casual users get little beyond the interface.

quote: it should enable users to get help easily and then return to their task.
rule: Make help quick to reach and quick to leave so people get back to their task.

section: Design concepts > Designing UI so that Help is unnecessary
quote: Add essential information directly into the primary UI, rather than forcing users out of their immediate context and into the Help pane.
rule: Essential information lives in the interface; help only adds optional explanation, reached by links from the place it concerns.

section: Design concepts > Writing content for scanning
quote: Write Help topics knowing that they will be scanned for specific information, not read word-for-word.
rule: Write help for scanning: numbered steps for how-to topics, tables for reference, subheadings for concepts, bullet lists rather than long paragraphs.

section: Design concepts > Creating content that matters
quote: focus most of the content on answering the top questions in the top scenarios for your target users.
rule: Spend help on the top questions in the main scenarios rather than documenting every feature, since help for the obvious only restates the interface.

section: Design concepts > Creating content that matters
quote: Be sure to design your search and indexing functionality, then, to account for likely terminology variations and synonyms.
rule: Help search and index find topics under the synonyms and everyday words people actually use.

section: Design concepts > Creating content that matters
quote: Between the primary UI and the Help system, though, terms should be very similar if not identical.
rule: Help uses the same terms as the interface it describes.

quote: Procedural help should focus on "how" information rather than "what" or "why."
rule: Keep procedural topics to how, conceptual topics to what and why, and reference topics in easy-to-scan tables.

quote: Link to specific, relevant Help topics.
rule: Help links lead to one specific relevant topic, never the help home, contents, search results, a list of links, a long FAQ or an empty page.

quote: Don't put Help links on every window or page for the sake of consistency.
rule: Add help links only where they help, not on every window for consistency.

quote: Use Help links for dialog boxes, error messages, wizards, and property sheets.
rule: Put a help link in dialogs, messages, guided flows and settings windows: under the controls it concerns, left-aligned, or at the bottom left of the content when it concerns the whole window.

quote: Use Help links instead of generic textual references to Help whenever technically possible.
rule: Link straight to the topic (How can I repair disk errors?) rather than telling people to look in Help.

quote: Use a Help button with the Help icon for the hub pages of control panel items.
rule: Control panel hub pages carry an uncaptioned Help icon button at the top right.

quote: F1 Help is optional.
rule: F1 may open help for the current context, especially in complex interfaces or where people expect it.

quote: Programs with menu bars can have a Help menu category.
rule: An app with a menu bar may have a Help menu.

quote: For keyboard accessibility, provide tab stops for Help buttons and links.
rule: Help buttons and links can be reached with Tab.

quote: the UI that invoked the Help pane should remain open to preserve the contextual experience.
rule: A help link or button opens its topic in the help viewer while the window that called it stays open.

quote: Don't use the following obsolete Help entry point styles: "Learn more" or "Learn more about..." links, generic Help buttons, and context-sensitive Help buttons
rule: Do not use Learn more links, generic Help buttons or a title-bar help button; link to a specific topic instead.

quote: Don't create obvious content.
rule: Do not write help that repeats what the interface already says.

quote: Don't create content that the user can't act on in some way.
rule: Every help topic leads to something people can do, except background concepts that matter.

quote: Avoid vague resolutions to problems.
rule: Do not resolve a problem with contact your administrator or reinstall, unless that truly is the only fix and administrators expect it.

quote: Avoid content that addresses highly unlikely user scenarios.
rule: Write help for normal use and treat unlikely scenarios as low priority.

quote: Gather feedback from your users about how helpful your Help topics are.
rule: Let people rate each help topic and test the help's quality and findability.

quote: Provide multiple ways of accessing your content.
rule: Help can be reached through contents, an index and search.

quote: If there is more than one way to perform a task, in most cases you can just document the most common way
rule: Document the way a beginner would usually do a task, adding keyboard equivalents for accessibility.
