quote: Use the Help icon only for Explorer windows and the hub pages of control panel items. Don't use the Help icon with Help links.
rule: Show the Help icon only in Explorer windows and control panel hubs, never beside a help link.

quote: Provide specific information about the content of the Help topic, using as much relevant, concise text as necessary.
rule: Help link text says specifically what the topic covers so the result is predictable; a generic More information is acceptable only after an instruction already in the interface.

quote: Whenever possible, phrase Help link text in terms of the primary question answered by the Help content.
rule: Word a help link as the question its topic answers (How do I add exceptions?), never Learn more about or Get help with this.

quote: If the most relevant information can be summarized succinctly, put the summary directly in the UI instead of using a Help link.
rule: When the key point fits in a sentence, put it in the interface and keep the help link for the extra detail.

quote: Phrase Help links to clearly indicate assistance. Help links should never read like action links.
rule: A help link reads as help, never like a link that performs an action.

quote: Use the entire Help link for the link text, not just the keywords.
rule: Make the whole help sentence the link, not just its keywords; a link to an outside website uses just the site's name.

quote: Help links don't have to match Help topic headings exactly, but there should be a strong and obvious connection between the two.
rule: Write each help link together with its topic heading so they clearly match in subject and scope.

quote: If the Help content is online, make that clear in the link text.
rule: A link to online help says so (go to the Microsoft Web site).

quote: Use complete sentences.
rule: Write help links as complete sentences.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation, except for question marks.
rule: Help links end with no punctuation except a question mark.

quote: Don't use ellipses for Help links or commands.
rule: Help links never end with an ellipsis.

quote: Format UI elements using bold to make them easy to identify.
rule: Set interface element names in bold in help topics, especially in steps.

quote: Format captions using italic.
rule: Set captions of tables, pictures and screenshots in italic.

quote: Refer to Help simply as Help. Generally, don't use the phrase online Help unless you are in fact referring to content on your Web site.
rule: Call help just Help, saying online Help only for content on the web.

quote: Is the control used to choose one option from a list of mutually exclusive values?
rule: Use a drop-down or combo box only to pick one of mutually exclusive values; several picks need a multi-select list, check-box list or list builder.

quote: Use drop-down lists and combo boxes for objects (nouns) or attributes (adjectives), but not commands (verbs).
rule: Drop-down lists hold things or attributes, never commands; offer commands through a menu button or split button.

quote: By contrast, radio buttons are suitable only for a small number of program options.
rule: Data or a long set of values goes in a drop-down; radio buttons only for a few program options.

quote: Consider using a drop-down list if you don't want to encourage users to make changes by hiding the alternatives.
rule: Use a drop-down when one recommended default suits most people and seeing the current value matters more than the alternatives.

quote: Do you want to draw attention to the option? If so, consider radio buttons, a single-selection list, or an editable list box
rule: To draw attention to a choice use radio buttons or an open list; use a compact drop-down to play it down.

quote: use a drop-down list because the screen space used is fixed and independent of the number of choices.
rule: Where space is tight, use a drop-down, whose size does not grow with the number of choices.

quote: Are there other drop-down lists on the window? If so, consider using a drop-down list for consistency.
rule: When the window already has drop-down lists, prefer a drop-down for a similar choice.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Combo boxes are for unconstrained input, in which users may need to enter a value not currently in the list.
rule: Use an editable combo box only when people may need a value not in the list (otherwise a plain drop-down), and report invalid typed values with an error message.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Can you enumerate the most likely choices in advance? If not, use a text box instead.
rule: When the likely values cannot be listed in advance, use a text field instead of a combo box.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Unless users need to review the complete list of previous input, use a text box with the auto-complete option instead.
rule: For recalling earlier entries use a text field with autocomplete unless people need to review the whole history.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Will users need assistance in selecting valid values? If so, use a text box with a Browse button instead.
rule: When people need help finding a valid value, use a text field with a Browse button.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Is it important to encourage users to review the alternative choices or invite change? If so, consider using an editable list box instead.
rule: To invite review of the alternatives, show the list open (an editable list box) rather than a closed drop-down.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Do users need to locate an item rapidly in a large list?
rule: In a long list, typing the start of an item's name jumps to that item (Jun finds June), not just the last letter typed.

section: Is this the right control? > Editable drop-down lists
quote: Always include at least three items in editable list boxes to justify the additional screen space.
rule: An always-open editable list shows at least three items; the number of items is otherwise no reason to choose a drop-down or not.

quote: Don't use the change of a drop-down list or combo box to:
rule: Choosing a value in a drop-down never runs a command, opens another window, or shows or hides other controls (screen readers miss that).

quote: Sort list items in a logical order,
rule: Order list items logically (related together, common first, or alphabetical), names alphabetically, numbers numerically, dates chronologically, and lists of 12 or more alphabetically.

quote: Place options that represent All or None at the beginning of the list, regardless of the sort order of the remaining items.
rule: All and None options go first in a list whatever the order of the rest.

quote: Enclose meta-options in parentheses.
rule: Write options that describe the choice rather than being a value, such as (None), in parentheses.

quote: When disabling a drop-down list or combo box, also disable any associated labels and command buttons.
rule: Disabling a drop-down also disables its label and its buttons.

quote: change the view immediately on selection instead of requiring a separate command button.
rule: A drop-down that changes another control's view applies the choice at once, without a separate button, unless rendering is slow.

quote: Don't have blank list items use meta-options instead.
rule: Never put a blank item in a list; use a meta-option such as (None).

quote: Use previews in the list items when it is better to show with images than describe using text alone.
rule: Show previews in list items when a picture explains the options better than words.

quote: Don't use unnecessary, unhelpful icons in previews.
rule: Leave out preview pictures that tell nothing.

quote: Limit the length of the input text when you can.
rule: Limit typed input to the longest valid value (three characters for 0 to 999).

quote: If there are many possible options, focus the list contents on the most likely options.
rule: A combo box lists the likely values or a sample, not every possible one.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure option by default.
rule: Start on the safest, most secure value, then the likeliest; show a blank value when several selected objects differ.

quote: Screen space is at such a premium that using a label or instruction is undesirable, such as on a toolbar.
rule: Use a prompt instead of a label only where space is very tight (a toolbar) and the prompt just identifies the purpose; it must not hold information needed while typing.

quote: Don't use prompts just to direct users to select something from the list or to click buttons.
rule: A prompt never just tells people to pick or click (Select an option).

quote: Draw the prompt text in italic gray and real text in normal black.
rule: Draw prompt text in grey italic, unlike real input.

quote: Keep the prompt text concise. You can use fragments instead of full sentences.
rule: Write prompts as short sentence-case fragments without ending punctuation or ellipsis.

quote: The prompt text should not be editable, and should disappear once users click in or tab into the text box.
rule: A prompt cannot be edited, disappears when the field gets focus (or at the first keystroke if focused from the start) and returns when the field is left empty.

quote: Choose a width appropriate for the longest valid data.
rule: Make a drop-down wide enough for its longest valid value, since it cannot scroll sideways.

quote: Include an additional 30 percent (up to 200 percent for shorter text) for any text (but not numbers) that will be localized.
rule: Leave about a third more width for text that will be translated.

quote: Choose a list length that eliminates unnecessary vertical scrolling.
rule: A dropped list shows up to about 30 items before scrolling; an always-open list shows 3 to 12.

quote: Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, and end it with a colon.
rule: Label a drop-down with a word or phrase ending in a colon, except a prompted toolbar combo box or one introduced by its parent option's label.

quote: Assign a unique access key for each label.
rule: Give each drop-down label its own access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write drop-down labels in sentence case.

quote: Position the label either to the left of or above the control, and align the label with the left edge of the control.
rule: Put the label left of or above the drop-down, aligned with its edge, and on the same text baseline when beside it.

quote: You may specify units (seconds, connections, and so on) in parentheses after the label.
rule: Give the unit in parentheses after the label.

quote: Don't make the content of the drop-down list or combo box (or its units label) part of a sentence, because this is not localizable.
rule: Never place a drop-down or its unit inside a sentence.

quote: Assign a unique name to each option.
rule: Every option in a list has a distinct name.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization, unless an item is a proper noun.
rule: Write list options in sentence case, except proper nouns.

quote: Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, and use no ending punctuation.
rule: Options are words or phrases with no ending punctuation.

quote: Use parallel phrasing, and try to keep the length about the same for all options.
rule: Phrase options in parallel and at similar lengths.

quote: If you need to add instructional text about a drop-down list or combo box, add it above the label.
rule: Instructions about a drop-down go above its label, as complete sentences in sentence case.

quote: Place this information either in parentheses between the label and colon, or without parentheses below the control.
rule: Short optional notes go in parentheses before the label's colon or plainly below the control.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or colon; include either list or box, whichever is clearer.
rule: In help, name a drop-down by its exact label without colon plus list or box, its options by their exact text, both in bold, and use click (In the Font size list, click Large fonts).

quote: In programming and other technical documentation, refer to combo boxes as combo boxes. Everywhere else, use box.
rule: In help, name a combo box by its exact label plus box and use enter (In the Font box, enter the font you want).

quote: Is the control used to choose one option from a set of mutually exclusive choices?
rule: Use radio buttons only for one of several mutually exclusive choices; several picks need check boxes or a multi-select list.

quote: keep the number of options in a group between two and seven. For eight or more options, use a drop-down list or single-selection list.
rule: A radio group has two to seven options; eight or more go in a drop-down or list.

quote: Use radio buttons if the meaning of the cleared check box isn't completely obvious.
rule: For two choices use radio buttons rather than a check box when the unchecked meaning is not obvious or the choices are not opposites.

quote: Use radio buttons on wizard pages to make the alternatives clear, even if a check box is otherwise acceptable.
rule: On pages of a guided flow, use radio buttons to make the alternatives explicit even where a check box would do.

quote: Use radio buttons if you have enough screen space and the options are important enough to be a good use of that screen space.
rule: Spend the space on radio buttons only for important options when there is room; a peripheral option gets a check box or drop-down.

quote: Use a check box if there other check boxes on the page.
rule: When the page already uses check boxes, a two-way option is a check box too.

quote: Consider using a drop-down list if you don't want to draw attention to the options, or you don't want to encourage users to make changes.
rule: When a default suits most people and change should not be encouraged, use a drop-down, which shows the current value rather than all options equally.

quote: Consider a drop-down list if there are other drop-down lists on the page.
rule: When the page already uses drop-downs, prefer a drop-down for a similar choice.

quote: If the radio buttons are used only to affect how a command is performed, it is often better to present the command variations instead.
rule: When the options only change how a command runs, offer the variations as separate commands or a split button so one click does it.

quote: Do the options present program options, rather than data?
rule: Radio buttons present fixed program options; values that come from data or context go in a drop-down or list.

quote: consider using command links instead of radio buttons to make the interaction more efficient.
rule: On a guided-flow page where the choice answers the main instruction and can be changed later, use command links instead of radio buttons plus Next.

quote: Are the values non-numeric? For numeric data, use text boxes, drop-down lists, or sliders.
rule: Numeric values are entered with a field, drop-down or slider, not radio buttons.

quote: List the options in a logical order,
rule: Order options logically (most likely first, simplest first, least risky first), not alphabetically, which breaks under translation.

quote: If none of the options is a valid choice, add another option to reflect this choice,
rule: When none of the options may apply, add an explicit option such as None or Does not apply.

quote: Prefer to align radio buttons vertically instead of horizontally.
rule: Stack radio buttons vertically rather than in a row, which is harder to read and translate.

quote: Reconsider using group boxes to organize groups of radio buttons
rule: Avoid framing radio groups in group boxes, which mostly adds clutter.

quote: Don't use radio button labels as group box labels.
rule: Never put a radio button in a group box's title.

quote: Don't use the selection of a radio button to:
rule: Selecting a radio button never runs a command, opens a window, or shows or hides other controls; changing text in response is fine.

quote: Place subordinate controls to the right of or below (indented, flush with the radio button label) the radio button and its label.
rule: Put a control that belongs to an option to its right or indented below it, sharing the option's label (which ends with a colon) and access key; arrow keys reach it.

quote: Leave dependent editable text boxes and drop-down lists enabled if they share the radio button's label.
rule: Keep a field that shares an option's label enabled, and select the option automatically when someone types or pastes into it.

quote: Avoid nesting radio buttons with other radio buttons or check boxes.
rule: Keep options at one level instead of nesting radio buttons or check boxes under radio buttons.

quote: disable these subordinate controls until the high-level option is selected.
rule: If choices must be nested, disable the nested ones until their parent option is selected.

quote: always have one radio button selected by default. Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure and private option.
rule: A radio group always starts with one option selected: the safest, most secure and private one, or else the likeliest.

quote: Don't have a default selection if:
rule: Leave a radio group unselected when the choice must be explicit for safety, security or legal reasons (then require it with an error), when the setting has never been set, when collecting unbiased answers, or for a mixed state.

quote: Make the first option the default option, since users often expect that
rule: Make the default the first option, rewording the options if needed, unless that breaks a logical order.

quote: Label every radio button.
rule: Every radio button has a label.

quote: Assign a unique access key to each label.
rule: Give each radio button its own access key.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Write radio button labels in sentence case.

quote: Write the label as a phrase, not as a sentence, and use no ending punctuation.
rule: A radio label is a phrase without ending punctuation, except a colon when it also labels a following control.

quote: Use parallel phrasing, and try to keep the length about the same for all labels.
rule: Phrase a group's radio labels in parallel and at similar lengths.

quote: Focus the label text on the differences among the options.
rule: Radio labels state what differs; shared introductory words move to the group label.

quote: Use positive phrasing. For example, use do instead of do not, and print instead of do not print.
rule: Phrase radio labels positively (print, not do not print).

quote: Describe just the option with the label. Keep labels brief so it's easy to refer to them in messages and documentation.
rule: Keep each radio label a brief name for the option; put any explanation in separate static text written as full sentences.

quote: Adding an explanation to one radio button doesn't mean that you have to provide explanations for all the radio buttons.
rule: Explain only the options that need it; never restate a label just for consistency.

quote: If an option is strongly recommended, add "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Add (recommended) or (advanced) to the radio label itself, not to its explanation.

quote: If you must use multi-line labels, align the top of the label with the radio button.
rule: Align the top line of a multi-line radio label with the button.

quote: Don't use a subordinate control, the values it contains, or its units label to create a sentence or phrase.
rule: Never build a sentence out of a radio label and the control that follows it.

quote: Use the group label to explain the purpose of the group, not how to make the selection.
rule: A group label says what the choice is for, never how to choose (Select one of the following).

quote: All radio button groups need labels. Write the label as a word or phrase, not as a sentence, ending with a colon
rule: Every radio group has a label: a word or phrase ending with a colon, as static text or a group box title.

quote: Omit the label if it is merely a restatement of a dialog box's main instruction.
rule: Drop a group label that restates the main instruction; the main instruction then takes the colon (unless a question) and any access key.

quote: Don't assign an access key to the label.
rule: Put access keys on the radio buttons, not the group label, unless there are not enough unique keys.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or colon.
rule: In help, name a radio button by its exact label without colon, in bold, call them option buttons in user documentation, and use click (Click Current page, and then click OK).

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the status relevant when users are actively using other programs? If so, use a notification area icons.
rule: Status that matters while people work in other programs belongs in the tray, not the status bar.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the status item need to display notifications? If so, you must use a notification area icon.
rule: A status item that must notify goes through the tray icon.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Dialog boxes, wizards, control panels, and property sheets shouldn't have status bars.
rule: Only main windows have status bars; dialogs, guided flows and settings windows do not.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Status bars must not be used as a secondary menu bar or toolbar.
rule: A status bar holds status, never a second menu bar or toolbar.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Does the information explain how to use the selected control?
rule: Help on using a control goes next to that control as an explanation, not in the status bar.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the status useful and relevant? That is, are users likely to change their behavior as a result of this information?
rule: Show status only if it can change what people do; otherwise omit it or log it.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the status critical? Is immediate action required?
rule: Critical status needing action goes in a dialog or the window's content, never only in the status bar.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the program intended primarily for novice users?
rule: Think twice about a status bar in an app mainly for beginners, who seldom notice one.

quote: Make sure that the status bar information is useful and relevant but not crucial.
rule: Status bar content is useful but never crucial, and is not made noticeable with garish icons, animation or flashing.

quote: Consider providing a View Status Bar command if only some users will need the status bar information.
rule: When only some people need the status bar, offer a View command to show it and hide it by default.

quote: Don't use the status bar to explain menu bar items.
rule: Never explain menu items in the status bar.

quote: Disable modal status that doesn't apply. Modal status includes keyboard and document states.
rule: Show mode indicators (keyboard, document state) disabled when they do not apply.

quote: Remove non-modal status that doesn't apply.
rule: Remove other status items when they do not apply.

quote: Present status information in the following order: current window status; progress; and contextual information.
rule: Order the status bar: window status first, then progress, then contextual information.

quote: Choose easily recognizable status icon designs.
rule: Draw status icons with distinctive outlines.

quote: Use swaths of pure red, yellow, and green only to communicate status information.
rule: Use red, yellow and green in status symbols only to mean status.

quote: Use icon variations or overlays to indicate status or status changes.
rule: Show status changes by a variation of the symbol for amounts, otherwise one standard overlay (warning, error, disabled, offline).

quote: Don't change status too frequently.
rule: Keep status bar changes infrequent and subtle.

quote: For icons that provide important status information, prefer in-place labels.
rule: Give important status symbols a visible text label.

quote: Unlabeled status bar icons should have tooltips.
rule: Every unlabelled status symbol has a tooltip.

quote: Use a control that looks and behaves like a menu button or a split button.
rule: A clickable status area looks and acts like a menu or split button, with a drop-down arrow, to give direct access to related commands.

quote: Display the menu on left-click on mouse down, not mouse up.
rule: A status area menu opens when the left button is pressed, not released.

quote: Don't support right-clicking or double-clicking.
rule: Status areas answer only to a single left click, not to right-click or double-click.

quote: Display tooltips on hover.
rule: Status items show tooltips on hover.

quote: Prefer sentence fragments, without ending punctuation.
rule: Write status text as short fragments without ending punctuation, cutting every removable word; full sentences only when fragments are not much shorter.

quote: indicate what the operation is doing with a label that starts with a verb (gerund form) and ends with an ellipsis.
rule: A progress label starts with an -ing verb and ends with an ellipsis (Copying...), and may change with each step or object.

quote: Don't use color, bold, or italic to emphasize status bar text.
rule: Do not colour, bold or italicise status bar text for emphasis.

quote: Refer to status bars as status bars, not status lines or other variations.
rule: In help call it the status bar, not the status line.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Menu bars
quote: Do the majority of the menu items apply to the entire program and primary window?
rule: Give a main window with many commands in many categories, mostly applying to the whole program, a menu bar.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Toolbar menus
quote: If so, consider using a toolbar menu instead of or in addition to a menu bar.
rule: A main window that has a toolbar and only a few menu categories may put its menus on the toolbar as menu buttons, instead of or beside a menu bar.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Tab menus
quote: Is there one menu category that applies to each tab?
rule: When each tab of a main window serves its own set of tasks with a small set of commands, a drop-down menu on each tab can replace the menu bar.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Context menu
quote: Is there a small set of contextual commands and options that apply to the selected object or window region?
rule: Offer a context menu where a small set of commands applies to the selected object or region and those commands are also available elsewhere.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Context menu
quote: For browser-based programs, task pane menus are a more common solution for contextual commands.
rule: In browser-based programs, show contextual commands in a task pane rather than a context menu.

section: Is this the right user interface? > Task pane menu
quote: If so, consider using a task pane menu instead of a context menu.
rule: When a main window has a few contextual commands for the selected object or mode that every user must find, show them in a pane of the window instead of only in a context menu.

quote: All menu patterns except menu bars need a drop-down arrow to indicate the presence of a pull-down menu.
rule: Every control that opens a menu, other than a menu bar title, shows a drop-down arrow so people know a menu is there.

quote: Don't change menu item names dynamically.
rule: A menu item keeps its name whatever the state (not Portrait mode switching to Landscape mode); show modes with bullets or ticks instead, though items named after objects, such as recent files or window names, may change.

quote: Consider eliminating menu bars with three or fewer menu categories.
rule: A program whose menu bar would hold three or fewer menus does without one and uses toolbar menus, command buttons or links instead.

quote: Don't have more than 10 menu categories.
rule: A menu bar has at most ten menus.

quote: Consider hiding the menu bar if the toolbar or direct commands provide almost all of the commands needed by most users.
rule: When the toolbar and direct commands cover nearly everything most people need, hide the menu bar by default and let people show it again with a Menu bar check item.

quote: Hide the menu bar instead of removing it completely, because menu bars are more accessible for keyboard users.
rule: A menu bar made redundant by the toolbar is hidden, never removed, so keyboard users can still reach it.

quote: To restore the menu bar, provide a Menu bar checkmark option in the View (for primary toolbars) or Tools (for secondary toolbars) menu category.
rule: Let people bring back a hidden menu bar with a Menu bar check item in the View menu (or the Tools menu button of a secondary toolbar).

quote: Choose single word names for menu categories.
rule: Each menu in the menu bar has a one-word title, so two titles are never read as one.

quote: For programs that create or view documents, use the standard menu categories such as File, Edit, View, Tools, and Help.
rule: A program that creates or views documents uses the standard menus File, Edit, View, Tools and Help.

quote: For other types of programs, consider organizing your commands and options into more useful, natural categories
rule: A program that does not work on documents may group its commands into categories that follow its own purpose and its readers' tasks rather than the standard menus.

quote: Prefer task-oriented menu categories over generic categories.
rule: Name and group menus by task (as Media Player does with Play, Library, Rip) rather than by generic categories, so items are easier to find.

quote: Avoid menu categories with only one or two menu items.
rule: A menu with only one or two items is merged into another menu, perhaps as a submenu.

quote: Consider putting the same menu item in multiple categories only if:
rule: Put one command in several menus only when it really belongs in each, people demonstrably fail to find it in one, and only one or two items are treated that way.

quote: Don't put different menu items that use the same name in multiple categories.
rule: Two different commands never share a name in different menus (no separate Options items in several menus), except per-tab Options and Help in tab menus.

section: Guidelines > Menu item organization and order
quote: Organize the menu items into groups of seven or fewer strongly related items.
rule: Group a menu's items into sets of no more than seven closely related items, counting a submenu as one item.

section: Guidelines > Menu item organization and order
quote: Don't put more than 25 items within a single level of a menu
rule: One level of a menu holds at most 25 items, not counting the contents of its submenus.

section: Guidelines > Menu item organization and order
quote: Put separators between the groups within a menu.
rule: Separate the groups within a menu with separator lines.

section: Guidelines > Menu item organization and order
quote: Within a menu, put the groups in their logical order. If there is no logical order, place the most commonly used groups first.
rule: Order a menu's groups by their natural sequence, and fall back on most-used-first only when there is none.

section: Guidelines > Menu item organization and order
quote: Put numeric items (such as zoom percentages) in numeric order.
rule: Within a group, order items logically, else most used first, and list numeric items such as zoom levels in numeric order.

quote: Avoid using submenus unnecessarily.
rule: Use a submenu only when it is needed, since submenus take more effort and hide their items.

quote: Don't put frequently used menu items in a submenu.
rule: Keep frequently used commands out of submenus unless people normally reach them more directly, for example from a toolbar.

quote: There are three or more commands that begin with the same word. In this case, use that word as the submenu label.
rule: Consider a submenu when the parent menu is long (20 or more items) or a group exceeds seven, its items are used less often, it would hold three or more items, or three or more commands share a first word, which becomes its label.

quote: Use at most three levels of menus.
rule: Menus go at most three levels deep (a menu and two levels of submenus), and a second submenu level is rare.

quote: Disable menu items that don't apply to the current context,
rule: A menu-bar item that does not apply now is shown disabled rather than removed, so the menu stays stable.

quote: For contextual menu categories, remove rather than disable context menu items that don't apply to the current context.
rule: In a menu that appears only for a particular mode or selection, items that do not apply are removed rather than disabled.

quote: leave the menu item active and if necessary have its selection result in an error message.
rule: If working out whether a menu item applies would make the app noticeably slow, leave the item enabled and report a problem when it is chosen.

quote: Each tab menu may have context specific Options and Help menu items.
rule: Each tab's menu may carry its own Options and Help items, since each tab serves a separate set of tasks.

quote: Use context menus only for contextual commands and options.
rule: A context menu holds only commands for the clicked object or region, never program-wide commands.

quote: Don't make commands only available through context menus.
rule: Every command in a context menu is also available another way, such as the menu bar or a shortcut.

quote: Provide context menus for all objects and window regions that benefit from a small set of contextual commands and options.
rule: Give a context menu to every object and window region that has a small set of commands, because many people right-click everywhere.

quote: Consider using a menu drop-down arrow button for context menus targeted at all users.
rule: When a context menu is the right place for commands every user needs, also expose it through a visible drop-down button.

section: Guidelines > Context menus > Menu item organization and order
quote: Avoid using submenus to keep context menus simple, direct, and efficient.
rule: Context menus avoid submenus.

section: Guidelines > Context menus > Menu item organization and order
quote: Don't put more than 15 items within a context menu.
rule: A context menu holds at most 15 items.

section: Guidelines > Context menus > Menu item organization and order
quote: Present menu items using the following order:
rule: Order a context menu as: primary commands (Open, Run, Play, Print), other commands for the object, Cut/Copy/Paste, object settings, Delete and Rename, then Properties last, with separators between.

quote: Display the default command using bold. When practical, also make it the first menu item.
rule: Mark the default command (the one double-click or Enter performs) as such in the context menu, and put it first where practical.

quote: Remove rather than disable context menu items that don't apply to the current context.
rule: Leave inapplicable items out of a context menu, except the standard ones (Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Rename) and the partners of a set (Forward beside Back), which stay disabled.

quote: Menu items that are options may use bullets and checkmarks. Commands may not.
rule: Only menu items that are options carry bullets or ticks; commands never do.

quote: Use a bullet to choose one option from a small set of mutually exclusive choices.
rule: Mark the chosen one of a small set of mutually exclusive menu options with a bullet, with at least two bullet items in the group.

quote: Use a checkmark to toggle an independent setting on or off.
rule: Use a tick for an independent on/off setting, and switch to a bullet group when on and off are not clear opposites.

quote: For a mixed checkmark state, display a menu item without a checkmark.
rule: When a menu option is on for only part of a multiple selection, show the item with no tick.

quote: Put separators between the related sets of checkmarks or bullets.
rule: Set each related group of ticked or bulleted options apart with separators.

quote: If you use icons, don't feel obligated to provide them for all menu items.
rule: Give menu items symbols only where they help (most used items, standard symbols, symbols that show the action), not on every item.

quote: Make sure menu icons conform to the Aero-style icon guidelines.
rule: Draw menu icons in the Aero icon style.

quote: Assign access keys to all menu items. No exceptions.
rule: Every menu item has an access key, without exception.

quote: Whenever possible, assign access keys for commonly used commands according to the Standard Access Key Assignments.
rule: Common commands use the standard access key assignments wherever possible.

quote: For dynamic menu items (such as recently used files), assign access keys numerically.
rule: Items generated at run time, such as recent files, get numbered access keys (1, 2, 3).

quote: Assign unique access keys within a menu level.
rule: Access keys are unique within one menu level and may repeat across levels.

quote: For the most frequently used menu items, choose characters at the beginning of the first or second word of the label, preferably the first character.
rule: Pick an easy-to-find access key: the first letter of the first or second word for frequent items, a distinctive consonant or vowel (x in Exit) for rarer ones.

quote: Avoid using characters that make the underline difficult to see,
rule: Prefer wide letters for access keys and avoid narrow ones (i, l), letters with descenders and their neighbours, so the underline stays visible.

quote: Assign shortcut keys to the most frequently used menu items.
rule: Give shortcuts only to the most frequently used menu items; rarely used ones rely on access keys.

quote: Don't make a shortcut key the only way to perform a task.
rule: Every command with a shortcut can also be reached with the pointer or by Tab, arrow and access keys.

quote: For well-known shortcut keys, use the standard assignments.
rule: Commands that have well-known shortcuts use the standard ones (Ctrl+N, O, S, P, Z, Y, X, C, V, A, F, H, G, F1, F3, F5, F11, Alt+F4).

quote: Don't assign different meanings to well-known shortcut keys.
rule: Never give a well-known shortcut a different meaning; new shortcuts use keys with no standard assignment.

quote: Don't try to assign system-wide program shortcut keys.
rule: App shortcuts act only while the app has focus; never register system-wide ones.

quote: Document all shortcut keys.
rule: Show every shortcut where people can learn it, but not in context menus.

quote: Use non-standard key assignments consistently throughout your program.
rule: A shortcut the app defines means the same thing in every window of the app.

quote: If possible, choose mnemonic key assignments,
rule: Choose shortcut letters that recall the command's name, especially for frequent commands.

quote: Use function keys for commands that have a small-scale effect,
rule: Give function keys to commands that act on the selection (F2 renames the selected item).

quote: Use Ctrl key combinations for commands that have a large-scale effect,
rule: Give Ctrl combinations to commands that act on the whole document (Ctrl+S saves it).

quote: Use Shift key combinations for commands that extend or complement the actions of the standard shortcut key.
rule: Adding Shift to a shortcut gives a related or reverse variant (Alt+Shift+Tab reverses Alt+Tab, Shift+F1 gives context help).

quote: Don't use the following characters for shortcut keys: @ $ {} [] \ ~ | ^ ' < >.
rule: Never build shortcuts on characters that sit on different keys in different keyboard layouts (@ $ { } [ ] \ ~ | ^ ' < >).

quote: Don't use Ctrl+Alt combinations,
rule: No shortcut uses Ctrl+Alt, which some keyboard layouts treat as AltGr for typing characters.

quote: If your program assigns many shortcut keys, provide the ability to customize the assignments.
rule: An app with many shortcuts lets people reassign them.

quote: Use the standard menu organization for programs that create or view documents.
rule: The File menu of a document program reads New, Open..., Close, Save, Save as..., Send to, Print..., Print preview, Page setup, then the numbered recent files.

quote: Exit Alt+F4 (shortcut usually not given)
rule: The File menu ends with Exit, whose shortcut Alt+F4 is usually not shown.

quote: Undo Ctrl+Z Redo Ctrl+Y <separator> Cut Ctrl+X Copy Ctrl+C Paste Ctrl+V <separator> Select all Ctrl+A
rule: The Edit menu reads Undo, Redo, then Cut, Copy, Paste, then Select all, then Delete, then Find..., Find next, Replace..., Go to....

quote: Toolbars Status bar <separator> Zoom Zoom in Ctrl++ Zoom out Ctrl+- <separator> Full screen F11 Refresh F5
rule: The View menu reads Toolbars, Status bar, then Zoom, Zoom in, Zoom out, then Full screen and Refresh.

quote: <separator> Options
rule: The Tools menu ends with Options, which opens the program's settings.

quote: Help <program name> help F1 <separator> About <program name>
rule: The Help menu starts with <program> help (F1) and ends, after a separator, with About <program>.

quote: The standard toolbar menu buttons are as follows.
rule: Without a menu bar, use the standard toolbar menu buttons: Organize (New folder, Cut/Copy/Paste, Select all, Delete, Rename, Options), Page (New window, Zoom, Text size) and Tools (Full screen, Toolbars, Print..., Find..., Options).

quote: Indicate a command that needs additional information (including a confirmation) by adding an ellipsis at the end of the label.
rule: End a command's label with an ellipsis when it needs more information, including a confirmation, before it acts (Print...).

quote: This doesn't mean you should use an ellipsis whenever an action displays another window
rule: Commands that merely show a window (About, Advanced, Help, Options, Properties, Settings) take no ellipsis.

quote: In case of ambiguity (for example, the command label lacks a verb), decide based on the most likely user action.
rule: When it is unclear, decide the ellipsis by what people most often do in the window: More colors... (they pick one) but Version information (they just read).

quote: When determining if a menu command needs an ellipsis, don't use the need to elevate privileges as a factor.
rule: Needing elevation does not make a command take an ellipsis; the security shield shows it.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Menu titles and menu items are in sentence case (Save as, Select all).

quote: Prefer verb-based menu names. However, omit the verb if it is Create, Show, View, or Manage.
rule: Menu titles are single words, preferably verbs, dropping Create, Show, View or Manage to leave nouns such as Table, Tools and Window.

quote: use a single, specific word that clearly and accurately describes the menu contents.
rule: A non-standard menu's title is one specific word that predicts what the menu holds.

quote: Use menu item names that start with a verb, noun, or noun phrase.
rule: Menu items start with a verb, or with a noun when the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage (About, Advanced, Full screen, New, Options, Properties).

quote: The verb is the same as the menu category name to avoid repetition.
rule: Leave out a verb that repeats the menu's title: in an Insert menu, Text, Table and Picture rather than Insert text.

quote: Use specific verbs. Avoid generic, unhelpful verbs, such as Change and Manage.
rule: Menu items use specific verbs, not generic ones such as Change or Manage.

quote: Use singular nouns for commands that apply to a single object, otherwise use plural nouns.
rule: A command acting on one object names it in the singular; one acting on several uses the plural.

quote: Use modifiers as necessary to distinguish between similar commands. Examples: Insert row above, Insert row below.
rule: Similar commands are told apart by a modifier in the label (Insert row above, Insert row below).

quote: For pairs of complementary commands, choose clearly complementary names. Examples: Add, Remove; Show, Hide; Insert, Delete.
rule: Commands that undo each other carry plainly paired names (Add/Remove, Show/Hide, Insert/Delete).

quote: Choose menu item names based on user goals and tasks, not on technology.
rule: Name menu items after what people want to do, not the technology behind it.

quote: Preferences Don't use. Use Options instead.
rule: Use Options for program settings, Customize for interface configuration, Personalize for common personal settings, Properties for an object's properties, and never Preferences or Settings as a menu label.

quote: Menu items that display submenus never have an ellipsis on their label.
rule: An item that opens a submenu never ends with an ellipsis; the arrow already says more choice follows (New, not New...).

quote: In commands that show or hide menus, refer to menu bars. Don't refer to them as classic menus.
rule: Help text calls the bar of menus the menu bar, never classic menus.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore or ellipsis.
rule: Help text cites a menu or item by its exact label and capitalisation, without the access key mark or ellipsis.

quote: To refer to menu categories, use "On the <category name> menu."
rule: Help text locates an item with "On the <name> menu", omitting the menu when the context makes it clear.

quote: To describe user interaction of menu items, use click, without the word menu or command. Don't use choose, select, or pick.
rule: Help text tells people to click a menu item, not choose, select or pick it, and does not add the words menu item or command.

quote: To describe removing a check mark from a menu option, use click to remove the check mark. Don't use clear.
rule: Help text says click to remove the check mark for a ticked menu option, not clear.

quote: Refer to context menus as context menus, not shortcut menus.
rule: Help text says context menu, never shortcut menu.

quote: Don't use cascading, pull-down, drop-down, or pop-up to describe menus, except in programming documentation.
rule: Help text does not describe menus as cascading, pull-down, drop-down or pop-up.

quote: Refer to unavailable menu items as unavailable, not as dimmed, disabled, or grayed.
rule: Help text calls an item that cannot be used unavailable, not dimmed, disabled or greyed.

quote: When possible, format the labels using bold text.
rule: Help text shows menu and item labels in bold, using quotation marks only where needed to avoid confusion (On the File menu, click Print).

section: Design concepts > Some aspects of mouse use are not intuitive
quote: right-click, double-click, and keyboard modifiers shouldn't be required to perform basic tasks,
rule: Basic tasks never require a right-click, a double-click or a modifier-click; those are shortcuts for experienced users and behave consistently.

quote: You make direct manipulations forgiving by providing undo, giving good visual feedback, and allowing users to correct mistakes easily.
rule: Make direct manipulation forgiving: it can be undone, shows clear feedback, and risky actions are constrained or confirmed.

quote: Used for text and graphics links because of their weak affordance.
rule: Use the standard pointers: the arrow for most objects, the hand for links, the I-beam between characters, the crosshair for precise two-dimensional work.

quote: Used to indicate a surface isn't a valid drop target.
rule: Show the move pointer for a move mode, resize arrows over borders and grid dividers, the splitter pointer over splitters, and the unavailable pointer over a surface that refuses a drop.

quote: Thus, large targets are good. Be sure to make the entire target area clickable.
rule: Make the whole visible target clickable, not just its text or symbol, and place clickable items close to where they are used.

quote: Never require users to click an object to determine if it is clickable.
rule: People can tell what is clickable by looking: primary controls look clickable at rest, secondary ones may reveal it on hover, links look like links and show the hand on hover.

quote: Use the hand (or "link select") pointer only for text and graphic links.
rule: The hand pointer appears over links and nothing else; buttons keep the arrow.

quote: Target displays its tooltip, infotip, or equivalent.
rule: Resting the pointer on an object shows its tooltip or equivalent.

quote: Activates or selects the object. For text, sets the insertion point.
rule: A single primary click activates or selects the object, and in text places the insertion point.

quote: Selects the object and displays its context menu.
rule: A right-click selects the object and opens its context menu; a double right-click acts as a single one.

quote: Activates or selects the object, and performs the default command.
rule: A double primary click selects the object and runs its default command; in text it selects a word, and a third click the sentence or paragraph.

quote: For selectable objects, contiguously extends the selection.
rule: Shift-click extends the selection to a contiguous range, and on non-selectable objects modifies the action (Shift constrains an oval to a circle); Shift with the right button selects the same way.

quote: extends the selection by toggling the selection state of the clicked item without affecting the selection of other objects
rule: Ctrl-click toggles the clicked item in or out of the selection without touching the others; Ctrl with the right button selects the same way.

quote: Same as Shift single left-click, and performs the default command on the entire selection.
rule: A Shift- or Ctrl-double-click adjusts the selection as the single click would and then runs the default command on the whole selection.

quote: Make click targets at least 16x16 pixels so that they can be easily clicked by any input device.
rule: Click targets measure at least 16 by 16 pixels (23 by 23 for touch).

quote: Make splitters at least five pixels wide so that they can be easily clicked by any input device.
rule: Splitters are at least five pixels wide.

quote: Provide users a margin of error spatially.
rule: Tolerate a slight pointer movement as the button is released, judging the click by where the pointer was just before release.

quote: Provide users a margin of error temporally. Use the system double-click speed to distinguish between single and double clicks.
rule: Tell double-clicks from two single clicks with the system's double-click speed.

quote: Have clicks take effect on mouse button up.
rule: A click acts when the button is released, so moving off the target before release abandons it; only auto-repeat controls act on press.

quote: Capture the mouse for selecting, moving, resizing, splitting, and dragging.
rule: Keep the pointer captured for the whole of a selection, move, resize, split or drag, even when it leaves the object.

quote: Use the Esc key to let users abandon compound mouse interactions such as moving, resizing, splitting, and dragging.
rule: Pressing Esc abandons a move, resize, split or drag in progress.

quote: If an object doesn't support double clicks but users are likely to assume it does, interpret a "double click" as one single click.
rule: Where people may double-click something that takes only single clicks (a taskbar button), treat the double-click as one click.

quote: Ignore redundant mouse clicks while your program is inactive.
rule: Repeated clicks made while the app is busy count as one click.

quote: Don't use double drags or chords.
rule: No interaction starts a drag with a double-click or needs several mouse buttons at once.

quote: Don't use Alt as a modifier for mouse interactions.
rule: Alt is never a modifier for clicks or drags; it belongs to access keys.

quote: Don't use Shift+Ctrl as a modifier for mouse interactions.
rule: No click or drag needs Shift and Ctrl held together.

quote: Make hover redundant.
rule: Hover may add information or shortcuts, but every action reachable by hover can also be done by clicking.

quote: Make the mouse wheel affect the control, pane, or window that the pointer is currently over.
rule: The wheel scrolls the control, pane or window under the pointer.

quote: Make the mouse wheel take effect without clicking or having input focus.
rule: The wheel works on what the pointer is over without a click or keyboard focus.

quote: Make the mouse wheel affect the object with the most specific scope.
rule: With nested scrolling areas, the wheel scrolls the innermost one under the pointer (a list inside a pane inside a window scrolls the list).

quote: Don't change the input focus when using the mouse wheel.
rule: Using the wheel never moves keyboard focus.

quote: Rotating the mouse wheel scrolls the object vertically, where rotating up scrolls up.
rule: Rotating the wheel scrolls vertically in the direction rotated and never horizontally; tilting scrolls horizontally; Shift with Alt makes the wheel do nothing.

quote: If the Ctrl key is pressed, rotating the mouse wheel zooms the object,
rule: Ctrl with the wheel zooms the view, up to zoom in and down to zoom out.

quote: Rotating the mouse wheel zooms the object, where rotating up zooms in and rotating down zooms out.
rule: In a zoomable view that has no scroll bars, the wheel zooms (up zooms in) and tilting does nothing.

quote: Rotating the mouse wheel can change the current tab, regardless of the orientation of the tabs.
rule: Over a tab row, rotating the wheel may switch tabs, whatever the row's orientation.

quote: Use the Windows system settings for the vertical scroll size (for rotating) and horizontal scroll size (for tilting).
rule: The distance scrolled per wheel step follows the system's mouse settings.

quote: Make rotating the mouse wheel more rapidly result in scrolling more rapidly.
rule: Faster wheel rotation scrolls faster.

quote: For scrollable windows, consider having clicking the mouse wheel button put the window in "reader mode."
rule: Consider letting a click of the wheel button start autoscrolling from that point, at a speed set by the pointer's distance.

quote: Don't hide the pointer.
rule: Never hide the pointer, except in full-screen presentation, where it reappears as soon as the mouse moves and may hide again after two idle seconds.

quote: Display the busy pointer when users have to wait more than one second for an action to complete.
rule: Show the busy pointer when people must wait more than a second and cannot do anything meanwhile.

quote: Display the working in background pointer when users have to wait more than one second for an action to complete, but the program is responsive
rule: Show the working-in-background pointer when an action takes over a second, the app still responds, and nothing else shows the action is unfinished.

quote: Don't combine activity pointers with progress bars or progress animations.
rule: Never show a busy pointer together with a progress bar or animation.

quote: Don't display the caret until the text input window or control has input focus.
rule: Show a text caret only in the field that has keyboard focus, and never take focus away so a window that appeared unasked can show one.

quote: Place the caret where users are most likely to type first.
rule: Put the caret where people will most likely type: where they last typed, or at the end of the text.

quote: Users should be able to do everything with the keyboard that they can with the mouse, except actions for which fine motor skills are essential,
rule: Everything that can be done with the mouse can be done with the keyboard, except work that needs fine motor control such as drawing.

quote: Users should be able to do everything with the mouse that they can with the keyboard, except efficient text entry.
rule: Everything that can be done with the keyboard can be done with the mouse, except typing text.

quote: Don't make double-clicking and dragging the only way to perform an action.
rule: No action can be done only by double-clicking or dragging.

quote: Avoid using the plural mice; if you need to refer to more than one mouse, use mouse devices.
rule: Help text says mouse devices, not mice.

quote: Use mouse button to indicate the left mouse button. Don't use primary mouse button.
rule: Help text says mouse button for the main button and right mouse button for the other, not primary and secondary.

quote: Use wheel for the rotating part of the mouse wheel, and wheel button to refer to the clickable part.
rule: Help text says wheel for the part that rotates and wheel button for the part that clicks.

quote: Use verbs such as click, point, and drag to refer to mouse actions.
rule: Help text uses click, point and drag for mouse actions, and rotate, tilt and click for the wheel.

quote: Use drag, not drag and drop, for the action of moving a document or folder.
rule: Help text says drag for the action, keeping drag-and-drop for the adjective.

quote: Always hyphenate double-click and right-click as verbs.
rule: Help text writes double-click and right-click with hyphens.

quote: Use click, not click on.
rule: Help text says click, not click on (click in a window is fine).

quote: Refer to the mouse pointer as the pointer. Use cursor only in technical documentation.
rule: Help text says pointer, not cursor.

quote: use busy pointer for the pointer consisting of only an activity indicator, and working in background pointer
rule: Help text names the activity pointers busy pointer and working in background pointer, and shows other pointers with a picture rather than a descriptive name.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: The program type is a good indicator of the appropriate level of printing support.
rule: Match the depth of printing support to the kind of program: creation, viewing and browsing of documents and images need excellent printing, others less.

section: Is this the right user interface?
quote: Is the program used in scenarios that benefit from direct paper output?
rule: Support printing when people will want paper output of the program's data, rather than making them copy it elsewhere to print.

section: Design concepts > Design your program to eliminate unnecessary printing
quote: make sure that the need to print is optional and not the result of missing features.
rule: Review the tasks that end in printing and make sure people print by choice, not because the app lacks a feature (such as commenting on screen).

section: Design concepts > WYSIWYG and the evolving requirements of screen display
quote: While WYSIWYG is still the best approach for document creation programs,
rule: A document editor prints what it shows on screen; other programs may lay out print output differently from the display.

section: Design concepts > Design print preview for performance and usability
quote: When necessary, warn about printing situations that are unlikely to be what the user intended.
rule: Print sensibly by default (switch a too-wide sheet to landscape) and warn about results people probably did not intend, rather than relying on them to spot it in the preview.

quote: Advanced document formatting features, with options to print large objects.
rule: An advanced document editor prints exactly what it shows, with full print options including headers and footers saved in the document and a fast, accurate preview.

quote: Some document formatting features, with ability to print large objects without truncation.
rule: An intermediate document editor prints what it shows, prints large objects without cutting them off, and offers some custom options with headers, footers and an easy preview.

quote: Standard print options; custom print options are optional.
rule: A simple document editor offers the standard print options and good results without adjustment; a preview is optional.

quote: Program automatically handles page breaks, eliminates blank pages, handles large objects, and removes backgrounds and other design elements.
rule: A document viewer handles page breaks, blank pages, large objects and backgrounds by itself, since people cannot change the document.

quote: Printing support is optional depending upon supported scenarios.
rule: A utility prints only when its tasks call for it, with standard options, an optional preview, and efficient output of the selected data.

quote: Don't print blank pages or pages with just headers and footers.
rule: Never print a blank page or one with only a header and footer, unless its page number is referred to elsewhere.

quote: Completely spool out any pending print jobs before shutting down a program.
rule: Finish handing pending print jobs to the system before the program exits.

quote: Reformat text layout to fit within the target page size. Never truncate text.
rule: Reflow text to fit the printed page; never cut text off.

quote: Automatically handle large objects by scaling, rotating, or splitting across pages.
rule: When people do not control the format, fit large objects to the page automatically by scaling, rotating or splitting them.

quote: Optimize the page breaks to eliminate blank and nearly blank pages.
rule: Place page breaks so no blank or nearly blank pages are printed.

quote: Convert light text on a dark background to dark text on a white background.
rule: Print light-on-dark content as dark text on white.

quote: Remove backgrounds and other design elements, especially if they are unsuitable for a black and white printer.
rule: Leave backgrounds and decorative elements out of printed output.

quote: If your program presents separate partial documents, provide a printer-friendly format option to consolidate them into a single document for printing.
rule: When content is split over several partial documents or pages, offer to print them together as one document.

quote: Remove interactive elements:
rule: Printed output drops navigation and buttons, shows all data without scroll bars, writes links' addresses in parentheses after their text, and puts hover-only information inline.

quote: Scale the object to fit on the page.
rule: Scale an object to the page when it is only slightly too large, must stay on one page and stays legible when smaller.

quote: Rotate the page.
rule: Rotate pages that print better in the other orientation.

quote: Print the object on several pages.
rule: Split an object that cannot be scaled across pages at its internal boundaries (rows, columns), repeating headers and legends, and number the pages in reading order.

quote: Truncate the object
rule: Cut off an oversized object only as a last resort, and never cut off text.

quote: Provide headers and footers for advanced and intermediate document creation programs.
rule: Document editors print headers and footers; other programs consider them for multipage output.

quote: Make headers and footers customizable. Allow users to define the left, center, and right portions.
rule: Let people set the left, centre and right parts of headers and footers, defaulting to the document name in the header and the source and page number in the footer.

quote: Use friendly file path and URLs. Display spaces as spaces, not "%20."
rule: Show printed paths and web addresses in readable form, with spaces rather than %20.

quote: For menu bars and shortcut menus, use the Print command that displays the Print options common dialog.
rule: Print... in a menu opens the system's print dialog and carries an ellipsis.

quote: For toolbars used with a menu bar, use an immediate Print command.
rule: A toolbar Print button beside a menu bar prints one copy at once to the default printer, named in its tooltip.

quote: For toolbars used without a menu bar, use a Print split button.
rule: Without a menu bar, Print is a split button: the button prints one copy at once, the arrow offers Print, Print preview and Page setup.

quote: For the ribbon command user interface, put the Print command in the application menu.
rule: With a ribbon, Print goes in the application menu.

quote: Don't create a custom Print options dialog box.
rule: Extra print options extend the system's print dialog; never build a separate or custom print dialog.

quote: When extending the Print options common dialog, don't duplicate any features already provided.
rule: Options added to the print dialog never repeat what it already offers.

quote: If users are likely to maintain settings from one print job to the next, make those settings the defaults.
rule: Within a session keep the last printer and paper size for the next job, but not the number of copies or page range.

quote: Optimize the settings by removing options that currently don't apply.
rule: Hide print options the chosen printer or document cannot use, with a way to show all of them if wanted.

quote: For advanced document creation programs, save the document-related print options within the document itself.
rule: Advanced document editors store print options in the document; other programs store them per user.

quote: Consider selecting a non-default printer for specialized printing.
rule: A specialised program (photo printing) may remember and preselect the printer it last used rather than the system default.

quote: Don't lock up your program while detecting printer capabilities.
rule: Never freeze while querying a printer: do it in the background, give up after about ten seconds, or offer a dialog to cancel.

quote: Provide a print preview feature whenever appropriate.
rule: Document editors offer a print preview, advanced ones possibly within the main window; simple editors need not.

quote: Browse through all the pages.
rule: Print preview shows margins, page breaks, orientation, headers and footers, pages through the whole document, and prints directly; let people adjust margins in it where practical.

quote: Have print preview pages render within one second.
rule: Each preview page appears within about a second, preferring a quick, adequate rendering to a slow exact one.

quote: consider extending the standard Print dialog box by incorporating preview functionality directly within it,
rule: Advanced document editors may build the preview into the print dialog instead of a separate dialog.

quote: Provide an obvious button for closing preview mode.
rule: A preview mode has an obvious button to close it.

quote: Before spooling a print job, check for any potential printing problems the user can fix.
rule: Before sending a job, check for problems people can fix, ask briefly before continuing, and offer to fix them automatically.

quote: For the option to print on both sides of the paper, label the option Print double-sided. Don't use the phrase Manual Duplex.
rule: Label two-sided printing Print double-sided, never Manual Duplex.

quote: Use print, not print out, as a verb.
rule: Help text uses print as the verb, not print out, and may call the result a printout.

quote: Use print queue, not printer queue.
rule: Help text says print queue, not printer queue.

quote: Command links aren't appropriate for secondary or optional choices, or pure navigation.
rule: Use command links only for answers to the window's main instruction that people must give, not for secondary choices or plain navigation.

quote: Is the control used to choose one response from a set of mutually exclusive responses?
rule: Command links offer one answer out of mutually exclusive answers; separate commands are buttons or links.

quote: For dialog boxes, does clicking the control close the window?
rule: In a dialog, a command link closes the window when clicked, so it never appears in a settings or tabbed window.

quote: Don't use command links to commit to a task; use commit buttons instead.
rule: In a guided flow, command links only move to the next page without committing; committing uses a commit button.

quote: If so, and all other factors being equal, prefer command links for consistency across pages.
rule: When other pages of a flow use command links, prefer them on similar pages too.

quote: There should never be a single command link.
rule: Offer between two and five command links; six or more answers become radio buttons, links or a single-selection list.

quote: Would a combination of radio buttons and a commit button be a better choice?
rule: Use radio buttons with a commit button instead when there is a strong default, people need to inspect the choices first, or there are secondary options on the page.

quote: For dialog boxes, would a group of commit buttons be a better choice?
rule: In a dialog, prefer plain commit buttons for a few simple answers, and command links when answers need longer wording, rather than text explaining the buttons.

quote: with this pattern, the command links replace the next button, but there is still a cancel button.
rule: On a page of a guided flow, command links replace Next, while Cancel stays.

quote: with this pattern, the command links replace the commit buttons (such as ok), but there is still a cancel button.
rule: In a dialog, command links replace the commit buttons, commit when clicked, and Cancel stays.

quote: on occasion, users may need more detailed information to choose their response.
rule: When people need details to choose (thumbnails, file sizes and dates), show them within each answer.

quote: Display a busy pointer if the result of clicking a command link isn't instantaneous.
rule: Show the busy pointer when clicking a command link does not take effect at once, so people don't click again.

quote: Always present command links in a set of two or more.
rule: Command links always come in sets of two or more; a lone one means the window should be an informational message.

quote: Present the most commonly used command links first.
rule: Order command links by likelihood of use in a logical flow, with a do-everything answer first.

quote: Provide an explicit Cancel button. Don't use a command link for this purpose.
rule: Cancelling is a Cancel button, never one of the command links.

quote: If providing an explicit Cancel button leaves a single command link, provide both a command link to cancel and a Cancel button.
rule: When Cancel would leave one command link, add a second link that cancels, worded by how it differs from the first, besides the Cancel button.

quote: Use Close instead of Cancel if you can't return the environment to its previous state, leaving no side effect.
rule: Label the way out Close rather than Cancel when the window cannot undo what has already happened.

quote: Don't display disabled command links.
rule: Remove a command link that does not apply rather than disable it; if that leaves one, drop the window or turn it into a confirmation.

quote: All command links need an icon.
rule: Every command link carries an icon.

quote: Use the arrow icon only for command links.
rule: The command-link arrow icon is used on command links only.

quote: Use the security shield icon to indicate that a response requires immediate elevation.
rule: Mark an answer needing elevation with the security shield.

quote: Use custom icons only if they help users visually identify and differentiate the options.
rule: Use custom command-link icons only when they are recognisable and tell the options apart.

quote: For custom icons, use 16x16 or 32x32 pixel icons.
rule: Custom command-link icons are 16 or 32 pixels square (32 or 48 with a shield).

quote: Avoid mixing custom icons with the standard arrow icon on a window or a page.
rule: Don't mix custom icons with the standard arrow on one page.

quote: Select the safest (to prevent loss of data or system access) and most secure response to be the default.
rule: Make the safest, most secure answer the default; when safety is not at stake, the likeliest or most convenient.

quote: When practical, make the first response the default option
rule: Where it fits the logical order, the first answer is the default.

quote: For dialog boxes, don't make a destructive action the default command link unless there is an easy way to undo the action.
rule: A destructive answer is not the default unless it is easy to undo.

quote: Choose a concise label that clearly communicates and differentiates what the command link does.
rule: Each answer's label is short, self-explanatory, fits the main instruction and makes clear how it differs from the others.

quote: Focus command link labels on helping users make the right decision.
rule: Labels give what is needed to choose and leave out details that don't affect the choice.

quote: Start command links with a verb. Don't use click, however,
rule: Each command link starts with a verb other than click, unless every link would begin with the same words, which are then dropped.

quote: In general, use positive phrasing
rule: Phrase answers as things to do; a negative answer only where it reads more clearly.

quote: Use parallel phrasing and single line labels.
rule: Answer labels are parallel in form and fit on one line.

quote: Use sentence-style capitalization.
rule: Command link labels are in sentence case.

quote: Don't use ending punctuation unless the label is a question.
rule: Command link labels end without punctuation, unless they are questions.

quote: Assign a unique access key.
rule: Each command link has its own access key.

quote: Don't use ellipses.
rule: Command links never end with an ellipsis, since they act at once.

quote: If a response is strongly recommended, add "(recommended)" to the label.
rule: Mark a strongly recommended answer by adding (recommended) to its label, not to its explanation.

quote: If a response is intended only for advanced users, consider adding "(advanced)" to the label.
rule: Mark an answer meant only for experts by adding (advanced) to its label.

quote: Supplemental explanations describe why users might want to choose a response or what happens if a response is chosen.
rule: Add a short explanation under an answer only when the label cannot be made self-explanatory, saying why to choose it or what follows, focused on the decision.

quote: Don't use a supplemental explanation that is wordy restatement of the command link.
rule: An explanation never restates the label, and explaining one answer does not oblige explaining all.

quote: Use parallel phrasing and at most three lines of text.
rule: Explanations are parallel in form and no longer than three lines.

quote: Use complete sentences and ending punctuation.
rule: Explanations are complete sentences with full stops.

quote: Don't use group labels. Main instructions act as the group label for command links.
rule: A set of command links has no group label; the main instruction above serves as one.

quote: Use the exact label text, including its capitalization, but don't include the access key underscore.
rule: Help text cites a command link by its exact label, without the access key mark.

quote: If the label includes an object name, either omit the object name or use placeholder text.
rule: When the label contains an object's name, help text omits the name or uses a placeholder.

quote: To describe the user interaction, use click.
rule: Help text says click for command links.

quote: When possible, format the label using bold text.
rule: Help text shows command link labels in bold.

quote: Don't use balloons to display supplemental information for a control;
rule: A message pointing at a field reports a problem or special condition only, never supplementary information, which belongs in text, a tip or a disclosure.

quote: Can the problem or special condition be detected immediately either on input or when the owner control loses input focus?
rule: Point a message at a field only for problems found as people type or leave the field; problems found later are reported in a dialog.

quote: For problems, is the problem critical? If so, use an error message displayed in a task dialog or message box.
rule: A critical problem goes in a dialog that must be answered, not in a message beside a field.

quote: For special conditions, is the condition valid yet likely to be unintended?
rule: Point out a valid but probably unintended state (Caps Lock on, input at its maximum length); prevent invalid states instead, and say nothing about likely intended ones.

quote: Can the problem or special condition be expressed concisely?
rule: Use a field message only when the problem can be said briefly; anything needing detail goes elsewhere.

quote: Does the information describe the control currently being hovered over? If so, use a tip instead,
rule: Information about the control under the pointer belongs in a tip, unless people need to act on it.

quote: Is the information related to the user's current activity? If not, consider using a notification or dialog box instead.
rule: A message beside a field concerns what people are doing now; anything else goes in a notification or dialog.

quote: Does the information come from a single, specific source?
rule: Point a message at a field only when that field alone is the cause; a problem with the user name or password together is reported for both, in place or in a dialog.

quote: using balloons for error messages doesn't steal input focus, yet is still very noticeable if the owner control has input focus.
rule: Report a non-critical input problem with a message at the field that is noticeable but does not take focus.

quote: these balloons are especially important for password and pin boxes, where users are otherwise working with minimal feedback.
rule: Alert people to a special condition affecting input as soon as it happens, without taking focus, especially in password and PIN fields.

quote: For problems involving individual characters or the maximum input size, display the balloon immediately on input.
rule: Show a problem with a typed character or the length limit the moment it occurs, again each time it recurs.

quote: For problems involving the input value (including requiring a non-blank value), display the balloon when the owner control loses input focus.
rule: Report a problem with the value as a whole, including a required field left empty, only when the field loses focus, not while people are still typing.

quote: Display only one balloon at a time.
rule: Show one field message at a time; for several problems from one event, present them together or only the most important.

quote: The problem is resolved or special condition is removed.
rule: Remove the message when the problem is fixed, the condition ends, valid data is entered, or it times out (ten seconds by default).

quote: Remove the timeout if users can't continue until the problem is resolved.
rule: A message about a problem that blocks progress stays until the problem is resolved.

quote: Display balloons below their owner control.
rule: Place a message about a field below the field, so the field and its label stay visible.

section: Guidelines > Password and PIN text boxes
quote: Use a balloon to indicate that Caps Lock is on,
rule: In a password or PIN field, say when Caps Lock is on.

section: Guidelines > Password and PIN text boxes
